| 5 | 1336.64 | 1436.64 | 153.36 | 23519.2896

| 6 | 1147.20 | 1247.20 | 52.80 | 2787.8400

\(S(100,0.32)=191.5456+0.7056+16517.3904+709.6896+23519.2896+2787.84=43726.4608\).

Line B has the smallest \(S\) of the three lines: \(42389.2968\). But Line B is not necessarily the best line of all lines. Section 03.5 shows the line with the smallest \(S\) of all lines.

[figure]
Figure 3-2 (Added) · All 236 brainhead points, the green line \(y=335.4323+0.2608207x\), and the vertical distance from each point to the line (short orange segments). \(S\) for this line is the sum of the squared lengths of the 236 orange segments.

**Why · The partial derivatives are 0 at the minimum** Added

This part explains the arrow \(\Longrightarrow\) on Slides p.21.

\(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\) is a smooth function of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). When we expand the squares, \(S\) is a polynomial of degree 2.

At the minimum, a small change in \(\beta_0\) alone cannot make \(S\) smaller. Thus the slope of \(S\) in the \(\beta_0\) direction is 0: \(\partial S/\partial\beta_0=0\).

For the same reason, a small change in \(\beta_1\) alone gives \(\partial S/\partial\beta_1=0\).

The minimum must thus satisfy two equations. There are two equations and two unknowns. The next two sections solve them for \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\).

### 03.3 The derivative for \(\beta_0\): solve for \(\hat\beta_0\) Slides p.22–23

This section uses the first equation, \(\partial S/\partial\beta_0=0\). It gives \(\hat\beta_0\) as a function of \(\hat\beta_1\).

**What** Slides p.22–23

Least Squares Estimation · Lecture 2 · p.23 \[\frac{\partial S(\beta_0,\beta_1)}{\partial\beta_0}=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)(-1),\quad\text{set to 0 and solve:}\] \[0=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)\] \[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i-n\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\] \[\hat\beta_0=\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\right)-\hat\beta_1\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right)=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\]

The result is \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\). When you know the slope \(\hat\beta_1\), the two sample means give the intercept. The same equation is \(\bar y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\bar x\). Thus, the point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is always on the least squares line.

Slides p.22 shows only the first line, "\(\partial S/\partial\beta_0=\)". Slides p.23 shows the full slide.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat\beta_0\) when you know \(\hat\beta_1\)

- Calculate \(\bar x=\frac1n\sum x_i\).
- Calculate \(\bar y=\frac1n\sum y_i\).
- Calculate the product \(\hat\beta_1\bar x\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).

**Self-check:** Put \(x=\bar x\) into the line \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x\). The result must be \(\bar y\).

**Example · 6 observations from Slides p.10** Added

This example uses the slope \(\hat\beta_1=0.2739824\). Section 03.4 calculates this value. This example uses it first.

Step 1: \(\bar x=24050/6=4008.333\).

Step 2: \(\bar y=8334/6=1389\).

Step 3: \(\hat\beta_1\bar x=0.2739824\times4008.333=1098.213\).

Step 4: \(\hat\beta_0=1389-1098.213=290.787\).

Self-check: \(290.787+1098.213=1389.000=\bar y\). The point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is on the line.

Thus the least squares intercept for the 6 observations is \(\hat\beta_0=290.787\) g.

The same check works for all 236 observations. Slides p.38 · Lecture 1 p.23

Slides p.38 prints the estimates for all 236 observations: \(\hat\beta_0=335.4323150\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\).

Lecture 1 p.23 prints the sample means, rounded to integers: \(\bar x\approx3638\) and \(\bar y\approx1284\).

\(\hat\beta_1\bar x\approx0.2608207\times3638=948.866\).

\(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\bar x\approx335.432+948.866=1284.298\). This value agrees with \(\bar y\approx1284\). The small difference comes from the rounded means.

**Why · Derivation** Slides p.22–23

The chain below starts from \(S\) and gives \(\hat\beta_0\). It includes the lines that the slide does not show.

1

\[S(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\]

2

\[\frac{\partial S(\beta_0,\beta_1)}{\partial\beta_0}=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_0}(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\]

The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives.

3

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_0}(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)\]

Chain rule: the derivative of \(u^2\) is \(2u\) times the derivative of \(u\).

4

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)(-1)\]

The derivative of \(-\beta_0\) is \(-1\). Slides p.23, line 1.

5

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)(-1)\]

Set the derivative to 0. The solution values get a hat.

6

\[0=-2\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)\]

7

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)\]

Slides p.23, line 2.

8

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i-\sum_{i=1}^n\hat\beta_0-\sum_{i=1}^n\hat\beta_1x_i\]

9

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i-n\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\]

The sum of \(n\) copies of \(\hat\beta_0\) is \(n\hat\beta_0\). Slides p.23, line 3.

10

\[n\hat\beta_0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\]

11

\[\hat\beta_0=\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\right)-\hat\beta_1\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right)\]

12

\[\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\]

Definition of the sample mean. Slides p.23, last line. ∎

The first equation gives \(\hat\beta_0\), but \(\hat\beta_0\) contains the unknown \(\hat\beta_1\). The next section uses the second equation to get \(\hat\beta_1\).

### 03.4 The derivative for \(\beta_1\): solve for \(\hat\beta_1\) Slides p.24–25

This section uses the second equation, \(\partial S/\partial\beta_1=0\). It puts \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\) into this equation and solves for \(\hat\beta_1\).

**What** Slides p.24–25

Least Squares Estimation · Lecture 2 · p.25 \[\frac{\partial S(\beta_0,\beta_1)}{\partial\beta_1}=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)(-x_i),\quad\text{set to 0 and solve:}\] \[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-\hat\beta_0n\bar x-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\] \[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-(\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x)n\bar x-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\] \[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x+\hat\beta_1n\bar x^2-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\] \[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x+\hat\beta_1\left(n\bar x^2-\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right)\] \[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-n\bar x^2}\]

This formula uses five quantities from the data: \(n\), \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(\sum y_ix_i\), and \(\sum x_i^2\). Slides p.24 shows only the first line. Slides p.25 shows the full slide.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat\beta_1\) with the formula on Slides p.25

- Calculate \(n\), \(\bar x\), and \(\bar y\).
- Multiply each \(x_i\) by its \(y_i\). Add the products to get \(\sum y_ix_i\).
- Square each \(x_i\). Add the squares to get \(\sum x_i^2\).
- Calculate the numerator \(\sum y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x\).
- Calculate the denominator \(\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2\).
- Divide the numerator by the denominator.

**Self-check:** The denominator is more than 0 when the \(x_i\) are not all equal. Section 03.5 shows that it equals \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\). The unit of \(\hat\beta_1\) is the unit of \(y\) divided by the unit of \(x\).

**Example · 6 observations from Slides p.10** Added

Step 1: \(n=6\), \(\bar x=24050/6=4008.333\), \(\bar y=8334/6=1389\).

Step 2: The products \(y_ix_i\) are \(4512\times1530=6903360\), \(3738\times1297=4848186\), \(4261\times1335=5688435\), \(3777\times1282=4842114\), \(4177\times1590=6641430\), and \(3585\times1300=4660500\).

Their sum is \(\sum y_ix_i=33584025\).

Step 3: The squares \(x_i^2\) are \(20358144\), \(13972644\), \(18156121\), \(14265729\), \(17447329\), and \(12852225\).

Their sum is \(\sum x_i^2=97052192\).

Step 4: \(n\bar y\bar x=\bar y\,(n\bar x)=1389\times24050=33405450\). The numerator is \(33584025-33405450=178575\).

Step 5: \(n\bar x^2=(n\bar x)^2/n=24050^2/6=578402500/6=96400416.667\). The denominator is \(97052192-96400416.667=651775.333\).

Step 6: \(\hat\beta_1=178575/651775.333=0.2739824\).

Thus the least squares slope for the 6 observations is \(\hat\beta_1=0.2739824\) g/cm³. Section 03.3 uses this value.

**Why · Derivation** Slides p.24–25

The chain below starts from \(S\) and gives \(\hat\beta_1\). It includes the lines that the slide does not show.

1

\[S(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\]

2

\[\frac{\partial S(\beta_0,\beta_1)}{\partial\beta_1}=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_1}(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)\]

Sum rule and chain rule.

3

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)(-x_i)\]

The derivative of \(-\beta_1x_i\) is \(-x_i\). Slides p.25, line 1.

4

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)(-x_i)\]

Set the derivative to 0.

5

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)x_i\]

6

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_ix_i-\hat\beta_0x_i-\hat\beta_1x_i^2)\]

7

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-\hat\beta_0\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\]

8

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-\hat\beta_0n\bar x-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\]

Substitute \(\sum x_i=n\bar x\). Slides p.25, line 2.

9

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-(\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x)n\bar x-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\]

Substitute \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\) from Section 03.3. Slides p.25, line 3.

10

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x+\hat\beta_1n\bar x^2-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\]

Slides p.25, line 4.

11

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x+\hat\beta_1\left(n\bar x^2-\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right)\]

Slides p.25, line 5.

12

\[\hat\beta_1\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-n\bar x^2\right)=\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x\]

13

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-n\bar x^2}\]

Slides p.25, last line. ∎

Now we have the solution of both equations. Slides p.25 gives \(\hat\beta_1\), and then Slides p.23 gives \(\hat\beta_0\). The next section writes \(\hat\beta_1\) in the shorter form \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).

### 03.5 The short form: \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) Slides p.26

This section writes the formula from Slides p.25 with deviations from the mean. The result \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) is the form that the course uses from now on.

**What** Slides p.26

Continued · Lecture 2 · p.26 \[\hat\beta_1^{LS}=\frac{\sum y_ix_i-\frac1n\sum y_i\sum x_i}{\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2}=\frac{\sum y_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)}=\frac{\sum(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}\] because \(\sum\bar y(x_i-\bar x)=\bar y\sum(x_i-\bar x)=\bar y(\sum x_i-n\bar x)=0\).
So the least squares estimators are: \[\hat\beta_1^{LS}=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad \hat\beta_0^{LS}=\bar y-\hat\beta_1^{LS}\bar x.\]

The list below defines the new symbols.

Superscript \(LS\): the estimator comes from least squares. \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}\) is the same quantity as \(\hat\beta_1\) in Section 03.4.

Deviation \(x_i-\bar x\): the distance of \(x_i\) from the mean \(\bar x\). The deviation \(y_i-\bar y\) is the same for \(y\).

\(S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)\) (Section 01.5): the sum of the products of the deviations. It is positive when \(x\) and \(y\) usually increase together.

\(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\) (Section 01.5): the sum of the squared deviations of \(x\). It measures the spread of \(x\). It is never negative.

**How** Added

Calculate the least squares estimates \(\hat\beta_0^{LS},\hat\beta_1^{LS}\)

- Calculate \(n\), \(\bar x\), and \(\bar y\).
- Calculate each deviation \(x_i-\bar x\) and \(y_i-\bar y\).
- Calculate \(S_{xy}=\sum(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)\).
- Calculate \(S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=\bar y-\hat\beta_1^{LS}\bar x\).

**Self-check:** (1) The deviations of \(x\) add to 0, and the deviations of \(y\) add to 0. (2) \(S_{xx}>0\). (3) \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}\) has the same sign as \(S_{xy}\). (4) The point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is on the line.

**Example · 6 observations from Slides p.10** Added

This example calculates the same estimates with the short form. The results must agree with Sections 03.3 and 03.4.

Step 1: \(n=6\), \(\bar x=4008.333\), \(\bar y=1389\).

Step 2: The deviations \(x_i-\bar x\) are \(503.667,\ -270.333,\ 252.667,\ -231.333,\ 168.667,\ -423.333\). Their sum is 0.

The deviations \(y_i-\bar y\) are \(141,\ -92,\ -54,\ -107,\ 201,\ -89\). Their sum is 0.

Step 3: The products \((y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)\) are \(71017,\ 24870.667,\ -13644,\ 24752.667,\ 33902,\ 37676.667\).

\(S_{xy}=71017+24870.667-13644+24752.667+33902+37676.667=178575\). This value is the numerator from Section 03.4.

Step 4: The squares \((x_i-\bar x)^2\) are \(253680.111,\ 73080.111,\ 63840.444,\ 53515.111,\ 28448.444,\ 179211.111\).

\(S_{xx}=651775.333\). This value is the denominator from Section 03.4. Each square above is rounded, so their sum shows 651775.332.

Step 5: \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=178575/651775.333=0.2739824\).

Step 6: \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=1389-0.2739824\times4008.333=1389-1098.213=290.787\).

The short form gives the same estimates as Sections 03.3 and 03.4: \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=290.787\) and \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=0.2739824\).

Now compare this line with the three candidate lines in Section 03.2. The least squares line is \(y=290.787+0.2739824x\).

Heights \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\): \(1526.996,\ 1314.933,\ 1458.226,\ 1325.619,\ 1435.212,\ 1273.014\).

Distances: \(3.004,\ -17.933,\ -123.226,\ -43.619,\ 154.788,\ 26.986\).

Squares: \(9.03,\ 321.61,\ 15184.70,\ 1902.59,\ 23959.42,\ 728.24\).

\(S(290.787,\,0.2739824)=42105.59\). This value is smaller than 91032 (Line A), 42389.2968 (Line B), and 43726.4608 (Line C).

For all 236 observations, Slides p.38 prints \(\hat\beta_0=335.4323150\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\). Figure 3-3 shows this line. Slides p.38

[figure]
Figure 3-3 (Added) · The brainhead scatterplot (236 points) and the least squares line \(\hat y=335.432+0.2608x\) (green). The orange point is \((\bar x,\bar y)\), approximately \((3638,\ 1284)\). The gray dashed lines show its position. This point is on the line.

Unit 02 gives the meaning of \(\beta_1\). \(\beta_1\) is the change in the expectation of \(y\) when \(x\) increases by 1 unit. With the estimate from Slides p.38, 1 cm³ more head size gives approximately 0.261 g more expected brain weight.

**Why · Derivation** Slides p.26

The chains below start from the result on Slides p.25 and give \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\). The first chain is for the numerator. The second chain is for the denominator.

Numerator:

1

\[\sum y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x\]

The numerator on Slides p.25.

2

\[=\sum y_ix_i-n\left(\frac1n\sum y_i\right)\left(\frac1n\sum x_i\right)\]

Definition of the sample mean.

3

\[=\sum y_ix_i-\frac1n\sum y_i\sum x_i\]

The first numerator on Slides p.26.

4

\[=\sum y_ix_i-\bar x\sum y_i\]

\(\frac1n\sum x_i=\bar x\).

5

\[=\sum (y_ix_i-y_i\bar x)\]

6

\[=\sum y_i(x_i-\bar x)\]

The second numerator on Slides p.26.

7

\[=\sum y_i(x_i-\bar x)-\sum\bar y(x_i-\bar x)\]

The subtracted sum is 0: \(\sum\bar y(x_i-\bar x)=\bar y(\sum x_i-n\bar x)=0\). This is the "because" line on Slides p.26.

8

\[=\sum (y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)\]

9

\[=S_{xy}\]

Definition of \(S_{xy}\).

Denominator. The steps are the same, with \(x\) in place of \(y\):

1

\[\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2\]

The denominator on Slides p.25.

2

\[=\sum x_i^2-\bar x\,(n\bar x)\]

3

\[=\sum x_i^2-\bar x\sum x_i\]

Substitute \(n\bar x=\sum x_i\).

4

\[=\sum (x_ix_i-x_i\bar x)\]

5

\[=\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)\]

The second denominator on Slides p.26.

6

\[=\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)-\sum\bar x(x_i-\bar x)\]

The subtracted sum is 0: \(\sum\bar x(x_i-\bar x)=\bar x(\sum x_i-n\bar x)=0\). (Added)

7

\[=\sum (x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)\]

8

\[=\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2=S_{xx}\]

Definition of \(S_{xx}\).

The last chain puts the two results together:

1

\[\hat\beta_1^{LS}=\frac{\sum y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x}{\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2}\]

Result of Section 03.4.

2

\[=\frac{\sum(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}\]

Substitute the results of the two chains above.

3

\[=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\]

With Section 03.3: \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=\bar y-\hat\beta_1^{LS}\bar x\). ∎

The least squares estimators are thus \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=\bar y-\hat\beta_1^{LS}\bar x\). All later inference and prediction start from these two formulas.

### 03.6 The open question: why least squares Slides p.26

Slides p.26 ends with a question. This unit does not answer it.

Lecture 2 · p.26 But why minimize least squares? Why not some other objective function?

Objective function: the function that we make a minimum (or a maximum). In this unit, the objective function is \(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\).

The slide asks why we use the sum of squares and not a different objective function.

Unit 04 gives the answer. When the errors have a normal distribution, maximum likelihood estimation gives the same \(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1\) as least squares.

### 03.7 Practice Added

The three questions below practice three tasks: the short form, the long form, and one identity from the derivation.

**Q1.** Consider the data \((x_i,y_i)\): (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5). Calculate the least squares estimates \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}\) and \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}\) with \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).

Answer

Step 1: \(n=5\), \(\bar x=15/5=3\), \(\bar y=20/5=4\).

Step 2: The deviations \(x_i-\bar x\) are \(-2,-1,0,1,2\). The deviations \(y_i-\bar y\) are \(-2,0,1,0,1\).

Step 3: \(S_{xy}=(-2)(-2)+(-1)(0)+(0)(1)+(1)(0)+(2)(1)=4+0+0+0+2=6\).

Step 4: \(S_{xx}=4+1+0+1+4=10\).

Step 5: \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=6/10=0.6\).

Step 6: \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=4-0.6\times3=4-1.8=2.2\).

Check: \(2.2+0.6\times3=4=\bar y\). The point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is on the line.

**Q2.** For the same data, calculate \(\hat\beta_1\) again with \(\hat\beta_1=\dfrac{\sum y_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x}{\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2}\). Check that it agrees with Q1.

Answer

Step 1: \(\sum y_ix_i=2+8+15+16+25=66\).

Step 2: \(\sum x_i^2=1+4+9+16+25=55\).

Step 3: The numerator is \(66-5\times4\times3=66-60=6\).

Step 4: The denominator is \(55-5\times3^2=55-45=10\).

Step 5: \(\hat\beta_1=6/10=0.6\). This value agrees with Q1, because the numerator is \(S_{xy}\) and the denominator is \(S_{xx}\).

**Q3.** Show that \(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)=0\), and use it to show that \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2\).

Answer

1

\[\sum (x_i-\bar x)=\sum x_i-n\bar x\]

The sum of \(n\) copies of \(\bar x\) is \(n\bar x\).

2

\[=n\bar x-n\bar x=0\]

Substitute \(\sum x_i=n\bar x\).

3

\[\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2=\sum (x_i-\bar x)x_i-\sum (x_i-\bar x)\bar x\]

Write one factor \(x_i-\bar x\) as \(x_i\) minus \(\bar x\).

4

\[=\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar x\sum (x_i-\bar x)\]

5

\[=\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar x\cdot0=\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)\]

Substitute the result of line 2. ∎

This identity is the reason that \(\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)\) and \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\) are equal on Slides p.26.

This unit gives the least squares estimators \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=\bar y-\hat\beta_1^{LS}\bar x\). For all 236 brainhead observations, the estimates are 0.2608207 and 335.4323150 (Slides p.38). Unit 04 explains why least squares uses the sum of squares.

## 04 · Maximum likelihood estimation and its equality to least squares

This unit uses a second method to estimate \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). The method is maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). The result is this: with normal errors, MLE gives the same \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\) as least squares. This result answers the question on Slides p.26: "But why minimize least squares?"

Plan · Slides p.27–29

Step 1 (Slides p.27): Write the likelihood \(L\) from the model. Then take the log to get the log-likelihood \(\ell\).

Step 2 (Slides p.28): Find the partial derivatives of \(\ell\) for \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma^2\). This gives (⋆), (⋆⋆) and a third equation.

Step 3 (Slides p.29): Set (⋆) and (⋆⋆) to 0. Show that this is the same problem as "minimize the sum of squares". Thus \(\hat\beta^{LS}=\hat\beta^{ML}\).

Start point (results of Units 02–03) · Added

Model: \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\). This is the same as \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\).

In words: each \(y_i\) has a normal distribution. Its mean is the line height \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\). Its variance is \(\sigma^2\). The \(y_i\) are independent.

Least squares (LS) minimizes the sum of squares \(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\). The result is \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=\bar y-\hat\beta_1^{LS}\bar x\) (Slides p.26).

Data from the slides: in the brainhead data, \(x\) is head size (cm³) and \(y\) is brain weight (g). Slides p.10 shows \((x_1,y_1)=(4512,1530)\) and \((x_2,y_2)=(3738,1297)\). Slides p.38 shows \(\hat\beta_0=335.4323150\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\), and the fitted values 1512.255 and 1310.380 for observations 1 and 2.

Small data set (Added): \((x_i,y_i)\) = (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 6), so \(n=4\). Examples that need all \(n\) observations use this data set. You can do every step by hand.

### 04.1 Likelihood and log-likelihood Slides p.27

This section writes a function that gives the probability density of the data for given parameter values. This function is the likelihood. Then it takes the log to get the log-likelihood, which is easier to use.

**What** Slides p.27

Maximum Likelihood Estimation · Lecture 2 · p.27 Recall: \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\)
We can write the likelihood: \[L(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2|y)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\left(-\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\] It's more convenient to work with the log-likelihood: \[\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2|y)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

Normal density: the PDF of \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(f(y)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{(y-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\). It has its largest value at \(y=\mu\). It decreases when \(y\) moves away from \(\mu\).

\(\exp(a)=e^a\), with \(e\approx2.718\). In this course, \(\log\) is the natural log (base \(e\)).

\(\prod_{i=1}^n a_i=a_1\times a_2\times\cdots\times a_n\) is a product. \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\) is a sum.

Likelihood \(L(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2|y)\): the joint density of the data, used as a function of the parameters \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2\). The data \(y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\) stay fixed. The bar "\(|y\)" means "the data \(y\) are given".

Log-likelihood \(\ell=\log L\): the natural log of the likelihood.

Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): use the parameter values that make \(L\) largest. These values also make \(\ell\) largest. We write them \(\hat\beta_0^{ML},\hat\beta_1^{ML}\).

The density of observation \(i\) is a normal density with mean \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\). The \(y_i\) are independent. Thus the joint density of all observations is the product of the single densities. This product is \(L\). The log is an increasing function, so \(L\) and \(\ell\) have their largest values at the same point. The log changes the product into a sum, and a sum is easier to differentiate.

This section gives the function \(\ell\) that we must maximize. The How steps below calculate \(\ell\) for data.

**How** Added

Write \(\ell\) and calculate its value at given parameters

- **Write one density.** Put the model \(y_i\sim N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\) into the normal density. Replace \(\mu\) with \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\).
- **Multiply to get \(L\).** The \(y_i\) are independent, so multiply the \(n\) densities.
- **Take the log to get \(\ell\).** The result always has three terms: \(-\frac n2\log(2\pi)\), \(-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)\), and \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\).
- **Find each difference.** Calculate \(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i]\) for each \(i\).
- **Add the squares.** Square each difference. Add the squares.
- **Calculate the three terms.** Put \(n\), \(\sigma^2\), and the sum of squares into the three terms of step 3.
- **Add the three terms.** The result is the value of \(\ell\).

**Self-check:** ① The first term uses only \(n\). ② The second term uses only \(n\) and \(\sigma^2\). ③ The third term is minus "sum of squares divided by \(2\sigma^2\)", so it is always \(\le0\). ④ For one observation, the contribution to \(\ell\) must equal the log of its density.

**Example 1 · Density of one brainhead observation** Added

This example uses the slide numbers for observation 1. It calculates the normal density of \(y_1\) and its contribution to \(\ell\). We use \(\beta_0=335.4323150\), \(\beta_1=0.2608207\) (Slides p.38) and \(\sigma^2=5000\).

The true \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. The value 5000 is only a fixed number for this example. Unit 06 shows how to estimate \(\sigma^2\).

1

Mean of observation 1 How step 1

\[x_1=4512,\quad y_1=1530\]

\[\beta_0+\beta_1x_1=335.4323150+0.2608207\times4512=335.4323150+1176.8230=1512.255\]

\[y_1-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_1]=1530-1512.255=17.745\]

Slides p.10 gives \(x_1,y_1\). Slides p.38 gives the value 1512.255.

2

Constant in front of the exponential How step 1

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\times5000}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{31415.93}}=\frac{1}{177.2454}=0.005641896\]

3

Exponential part How step 1

\[\frac{(17.745)^2}{2\times5000}=\frac{314.8850}{10000}=0.03148850\]

\[\exp(-0.03148850)=0.9690021\]

4

Density How step 1

\[f(y_1)=0.005641896\times0.9690021=0.005467009\]

5

Contribution to \(\ell\) How steps 6–7

\[-\frac12\log(2\pi)-\frac12\log(5000)-0.03148850\]

\[=-0.9189385-4.2585966-0.0314885=-5.2090236\]

Check: \(\log(0.005467009)=-5.209024\). The two values agree (self-check ④). ▲

One observation adds about \(-5.21\) to \(\ell\). \(L\) multiplies \(n\) small densities such as 0.005467, so \(L\) becomes very small for large \(n\). \(\ell\) adds terms such as \(-5.21\), so the size of \(\ell\) increases only in proportion to \(n\).

**Example 2 · \(\ell\) for the small data set** Added

This example calculates \(\ell\) for all four observations of the small data set. We use \(\beta_0=0.5\), \(\beta_1=1.4\) and \(\sigma^2=1\). Example 3 in Section 04.3 shows that 0.5 and 1.4 are the LS estimates.

1

Line heights How step 4

\[0.5+1.4\times1=1.9,\quad0.5+1.4\times2=3.3,\quad0.5+1.4\times3=4.7,\quad0.5+1.4\times4=6.1\]

2

Differences \(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i]\) How step 4

\[2-1.9=0.1,\quad3-3.3=-0.3,\quad5-4.7=0.3,\quad6-6.1=-0.1\]

3

Sum of squares How step 5

\[0.1^2+(-0.3)^2+0.3^2+(-0.1)^2=0.01+0.09+0.09+0.01=0.2\]

4

Three terms How step 6

\[-\frac42\log(2\pi)=-2\times1.837877=-3.675754\]

\[-\frac42\log(1)=-2\times0=0\]

\[-\frac{1}{2\times1}\times0.2=-0.1\]

5

Add How step 7

\[\ell(0.5,\,1.4,\,1\,|\,y)=-3.675754+0-0.1=-3.775754\]

▲

\(\ell=-3.775754\) at \((\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)=(0.5,1.4,1)\). Section 04.3 compares this value with \(\ell\) at another line.

**Why · From \(L\) to \(\ell\)** Slides p.27

First, this derivation changes the product in \(L\) into the second form on the slide. Then it takes the log to get \(\ell\).

1

\[L=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\left(-\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

**Independence:** joint density = product of the densities.

2

\[=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\right)\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\exp\left(-\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\right)\]

3

\[=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\right)^n\prod_{i=1}^n\exp\left(-\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

4

\[=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\prod_{i=1}^n\exp\left(-\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

**Exponent rules:** \(1/\sqrt{a}=a^{-1/2}\) and \((a^{-1/2})^n=a^{-n/2}\).

5

\[=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

**Exponent rule:** \(e^{a_1}e^{a_2}\cdots e^{a_n}=e^{a_1+\cdots+a_n}\). This is the second form on the slide.

6

\[\ell=\log L=\log\left[(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\right]+\log\left[\exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\right]\]

**Log rule:** \(\log(ab)=\log a+\log b\).

7

\[=-\frac n2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\]

**Log rules:** \(\log(a^k)=k\log a\) and \(\log(e^b)=b\).

8

\[=-\frac n2\left[\log(2\pi)+\log(\sigma^2)\right]-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\]

**Log rule:** \(\log(ab)=\log a+\log b\).

9

\[=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2}{2\sigma^2}\]

10

\[=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

\(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\) does not change with \(i\), so it moves out of the sum. This is \(\ell\) on Slides p.27. ∎

\(\ell\) has three terms. Only the third term contains \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), and it is the sum of squares times \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\). Section 04.2 finds the partial derivatives of \(\ell\).

### 04.2 The three partial derivatives of the log-likelihood Slides p.28

This section finds the derivatives of \(\ell\) for the three parameters. At the maximum, these derivatives are 0. Thus they give the equations for the MLE.

**What** Slides p.28

Maximum Likelihood Estimation · Lecture 2 · p.28 \[\max\left[-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\right]\] \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_0}=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])\right)\qquad(\star)\] \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_1}=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])x_i\right)\qquad(\star\star)\] \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2}=-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\] Setting \((\star)\) and \((\star\star)\) to 0 and solving

Partial derivative \(\partial\ell/\partial\beta_0\): the derivative of \(\ell\) when only \(\beta_0\) changes. \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma^2\) stay constant. The other two partial derivatives work in the same way.

\(\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2\): the derivative for \(\sigma^2\) as one variable. It is not the derivative for \(\sigma\).

"max": find the parameter values that make the expression in the brackets largest. At the maximum of a smooth function, all partial derivatives are 0.

The bracket in (⋆) is the sum of the differences \(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i]\). The bracket in (⋆⋆) multiplies each difference by \(x_i\) before the sum. The third equation is for \(\sigma^2\). This unit uses only (⋆) and (⋆⋆). Unit 06 sets the third equation to 0 and solves for \(\sigma^2\) (Slides p.34).

Thus, to find \(\hat\beta_0^{ML}\) and \(\hat\beta_1^{ML}\), we solve the two equations (⋆) = 0 and (⋆⋆) = 0.

**How** Added

Calculate (⋆) and (⋆⋆) at given parameters

- **Find each difference.** Calculate \(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i]\) for \(i=1,\dots,n\).
- **Calculate (⋆).** Add the differences. Divide the sum by \(\sigma^2\).
- **Calculate (⋆⋆).** Multiply each difference by its \(x_i\). Add the products. Divide the sum by \(\sigma^2\).
- **Decide.** If both values are 0, the point is a stationary point of \(\ell\) for \(\beta_0,\beta_1\). A stationary point is a point where all partial derivatives are 0.

**Self-check:** \(\sigma^2>0\). Thus (⋆) = 0 only when \(\sum(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])=0\). For the decision, you can look only at the sum in the bracket.

**Example · (⋆) and (⋆⋆) for the small data set** Added

This example calculates (⋆) and (⋆⋆) at two lines, with \(\sigma^2=1\). Line A is \(\beta_0=0.5,\ \beta_1=1.2\). Line B is \(\beta_0=0.5,\ \beta_1=1.4\).

1

Line A: differences How step 1

\[0.5+1.2\times1=1.7,\quad0.5+1.2\times2=2.9,\quad0.5+1.2\times3=4.1,\quad0.5+1.2\times4=5.3\]

\[2-1.7=0.3,\quad3-2.9=0.1,\quad5-4.1=0.9,\quad6-5.3=0.7\]

2

Line A: (⋆) and (⋆⋆) How steps 2–3

\[(\star)=\frac{0.3+0.1+0.9+0.7}{1}=2\]

\[(\star\star)=\frac{0.3\times1+0.1\times2+0.9\times3+0.7\times4}{1}=\frac{0.3+0.2+2.7+2.8}{1}=6\]

The two values are not 0, so line A is not the maximum (How step 4).

3

Line B: differences How step 1

\[0.1,\quad-0.3,\quad0.3,\quad-0.1\]

These are the differences from Example 2, step 2.

4

Line B: (⋆) and (⋆⋆) How steps 2–4

\[(\star)=\frac{0.1-0.3+0.3-0.1}{1}=0\]

\[(\star\star)=\frac{0.1\times1-0.3\times2+0.3\times3-0.1\times4}{1}=\frac{0.1-0.6+0.9-0.4}{1}=0\]

Both values are 0, so line B is a stationary point of \(\ell\). ▲

Line B makes (⋆) and (⋆⋆) equal to 0. Section 04.3 shows that this line is also the least squares line.

**Why · Derivation of the three partial derivatives** Slides p.28

The derivation differentiates \(\ell\) one term at a time. Only the third term contains \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). The chain rule is \(\frac{d}{du}g(h(u))=g'(h(u))\,h'(u)\).

(a) For \(\beta_0\):

1

\[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_0}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_0}\left[-\frac n2\log(2\pi)\right]+\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_0}\left[-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)\right]+\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_0}\left[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\right]\]

2

\[=0+0-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_0}(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

The first two terms do not contain \(\beta_0\).

3

\[=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n2(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])(-1)\]

**Chain rule:** the derivative of \(u^2\) is \(2u\). The derivative of \(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i\) for \(\beta_0\) is \(-1\).

4

\[=\frac{2}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])\]

5

\[=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])\right)\qquad(\star)\]

∎

(b) For \(\beta_1\):

1

\[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_1}=0+0-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_1}(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

The first two terms do not contain \(\beta_1\).

2

\[=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n2(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])(-x_i)\]

**Chain rule:** the derivative of \(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i\) for \(\beta_1\) is \(-x_i\).

3

\[=\frac{2}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])x_i\]

4

\[=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])x_i\right)\qquad(\star\star)\]

∎

(c) For \(\sigma^2\): treat \(\sigma^2\) as one variable. Only the second and third terms of \(\ell\) contain \(\sigma^2\).

1

\[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2}=0-\frac n2\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma^2}-\frac{\partial}{\partial\sigma^2}\left(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\right)\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

**Derivative rule:** the derivative of \(\log(\sigma^2)\) for \(\sigma^2\) is \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\). The sum does not contain \(\sigma^2\), so it is a constant factor.

2

\[=-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}-\left(-\frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}\right)\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

**Derivative rule:** the derivative of \(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\) for \(\sigma^2\) is \(-\frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}\).

3

\[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2}=-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

This is the third line on Slides p.28. Unit 06 sets it to 0. ∎

All three partial derivatives are now derived. (⋆) and (⋆⋆) both start with the positive constant \(1/\sigma^2\). Section 04.3 uses this fact.

### 04.3 MLE and LS give the same estimates (\(\hat\beta^{LS}=\hat\beta^{ML}\)) Slides p.29

This section shows that two problems are the same. Problem 1 solves (⋆) = 0 and (⋆⋆) = 0. Problem 2 minimizes the sum of squares \(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\). Thus the two methods give the same estimates.

**What** Slides p.29

Maximum Likelihood Estimation · Lecture 2 · p.29 Setting \((\star)\) and \((\star\star)\) to 0 and solving is equivalent to minimizing the sum of squares!
• That is \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=\hat\beta_0^{ML}\) and \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=\hat\beta_1^{ML}\)
• Here on out we will call the LS/MLE estimators \(\hat\beta\).

Equivalent: the two problems have the same solution.

\(\hat\beta\): from this point, \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\) are the LS estimators. They are also the MLE. The slides do not use the labels LS or ML after this point.

In \(\ell\), \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) occur only in the third term \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\). \(\sigma^2>0\), so \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\) is negative. Thus a smaller \(S\) gives a larger \(\ell\). With normal errors, least squares is the same as maximum likelihood.

This section answers the question on Slides p.26: we minimize least squares because, in the normal model, it gives the MLE.

**How** Added

Find the MLE of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)

- **Check the model.** The model must be \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\). The errors must be normal and independent, with one constant variance.
- **Calculate the inputs.** Calculate \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(S_{xx}\), and \(S_{xy}\).
- **Calculate the LS slope.** Calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).
- **Calculate the LS intercept.** Calculate \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).
- **Use them as the MLE.** \(\hat\beta_0^{ML}=\hat\beta_0^{LS}\) and \(\hat\beta_1^{ML}=\hat\beta_1^{LS}\).

**Self-check:** ① At \(\hat\beta\), \(\sum(y_i-[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i])=0\). This is (⋆) = 0. ② At \(\hat\beta\), \(\sum(y_i-[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i])x_i=0\). This is (⋆⋆) = 0. ③ \(\ell\) at \(\hat\beta\) must be larger than \(\ell\) at another line, for each \(\sigma^2\).

**Example 3 · MLE for the small data set** Added

This example finds the MLE for the small data set (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 6). It uses the LS formulas. Then it does the three self-checks.

1

Check the model How step 1

We use the model \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\) for these data.

2

Means How step 2

\[\bar x=\frac{1+2+3+4}{4}=\frac{10}{4}=2.5,\qquad\bar y=\frac{2+3+5+6}{4}=\frac{16}{4}=4\]

3

\(S_{xx}\) and \(S_{xy}\) How step 2

\[x_i-\bar x:\ -1.5,\ -0.5,\ 0.5,\ 1.5\qquad y_i-\bar y:\ -2,\ -1,\ 1,\ 2\]

\[S_{xx}=(-1.5)^2+(-0.5)^2+0.5^2+1.5^2=2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25=5\]

\[S_{xy}=(-1.5)(-2)+(-0.5)(-1)+(0.5)(1)+(1.5)(2)=3+0.5+0.5+3=7\]

4

Estimates How steps 3–5

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac75=1.4\]

\[\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=4-1.4\times2.5=4-3.5=0.5\]

\[\hat\beta_0^{ML}=\hat\beta_0^{LS}=0.5,\qquad\hat\beta_1^{ML}=\hat\beta_1^{LS}=1.4\]

5

Self-checks ① and ② Section 04.2 example, step 4

The example in Section 04.2 found (⋆) = 0 and (⋆⋆) = 0 at \((0.5,1.4)\). Both checks pass.

6

Self-check ③ with \(\sigma^2=1\) How steps 4–7 of Section 04.1

\[S(0.5,1.4)=0.2\quad\Rightarrow\quad\ell=-3.675754-0-\frac{0.2}{2}=-3.775754\]

\[S(0.5,1.2)=0.3^2+0.1^2+0.9^2+0.7^2=0.09+0.01+0.81+0.49=1.4\]

\[\ell(0.5,1.2,1\,|\,y)=-3.675754-0-\frac{1.4}{2}=-4.375754\]

\(-3.775754>-4.375754\). The least squares line has the larger \(\ell\). ▲

[figure]
Figure 4-1 (Added) · The small data set, with \(\beta_0\) fixed at \(\hat\beta_0=0.5\). Only \(\beta_1\) changes. Top (blue): the sum of squares \(S\), with its minimum \(S=0.2\) at \(\hat\beta_1=1.4\). Bottom (green): the log-likelihood \(\ell\) with \(\sigma^2=1\), with its maximum \(\ell=-3.775754\) at the same \(\hat\beta_1=1.4\) (orange dashed line). The purple points show line A (\(\beta_1=1.2\)): \(S=1.4\) and \(\ell=-4.375754\).

For the small data set, the MLE is \(\hat\beta_0=0.5\), \(\hat\beta_1=1.4\). This is the same as the least squares line. Figure 4-1 shows that the minimum of \(S\) and the maximum of \(\ell\) are at the same point. The reason: the bottom curve is the top curve times \(-\frac12\), plus a constant.

**Why · (⋆) = 0 and (⋆⋆) = 0 are the same as "minimize \(S\)"** Slides p.29

The proof has two parts. Part (a) compares the objective functions. Part (b) compares the equations.

(a) Objective functions: start from the full \(\ell\). Then write it with the definition of \(S\).

1

\[\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2|y)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

Slides p.27.

2

\[=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\]

**Substitute** \(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\) (Slides p.21).

3

\[=c-k\,S(\beta_0,\beta_1),\qquad c=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2),\quad k=\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}>0\]

For a fixed \(\sigma^2\), \(c\) and \(k\) do not contain \(\beta_0,\beta_1\). \(k>0\), so a smaller \(S\) gives a larger \(\ell\). The minimum of \(S\) is the maximum of \(\ell\). ∎

(b) Equations: write the two LS equations (Slides p.23, p.25). Then compare them with (⋆) and (⋆⋆).

1

\[\frac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_0}=\sum_{i=1}^n2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)(-1)=-2\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])\]

Slides p.23.

2

\[(\star)=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_0}\]

**Substitute** step 1: \(\sum(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])=-\frac12\,\partial S/\partial\beta_0\).

3

\[\frac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_1}=\sum_{i=1}^n2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)(-x_i)=-2\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])x_i\]

Slides p.25.

4

\[(\star\star)=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])x_i=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_1}\]

**Substitute** step 3.

5

\[(\star)=0\iff\frac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_0}=0,\qquad(\star\star)=0\iff\frac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_1}=0\]

The reason is \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\neq0\). The two pairs of equations are the same, so they have the same solution: \(\hat\beta_0^{ML}=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=\hat\beta_0^{LS}\) and \(\hat\beta_1^{ML}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}=\hat\beta_1^{LS}\). ∎

For \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), \(\ell\) is \(S\) times a negative number, plus a constant. Thus \(\hat\beta^{ML}=\hat\beta^{LS}\), and the slides call both \(\hat\beta\). Unit 05 uses \(\hat\beta\) to calculate fitted values and residuals.

Under \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\), the log-likelihood is \(\ell=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\). Setting (⋆) and (⋆⋆) to 0 is the same as minimizing \(S\). Thus \(\hat\beta_0^{LS}=\hat\beta_0^{ML}\) and \(\hat\beta_1^{LS}=\hat\beta_1^{ML}\). Unit 06 solves \(\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2=0\).

### 04.4 Practice Added

These three questions use the formulas of this unit. The answers use slide numbers or the small data set.

**Q1.** In the brainhead data, observation 2 has \(x_2=3738\) and \(y_2=1297\) (Slides p.10). Its fitted value is 1310.380 (Slides p.38). Use \(\sigma^2=5000\). Calculate (a) the normal density of \(y_2\), and (b) its contribution to the log-likelihood \(\ell\).

Answer

(a) Fitted value: \(335.4323150+0.2608207\times3738=335.4323150+974.9478=1310.380\). Difference: \(1297-1310.380=-13.380\). Square: \((-13.380)^2=179.0244\).

Exponent: \(179.0244/(2\times5000)=0.01790244\). Then \(\exp(-0.01790244)=0.9822569\).

Constant: \(1/\sqrt{2\pi\times5000}=0.005641896\) (Example 1, step 2).

Density: \(0.005641896\times0.9822569=0.005541791\).

(b) The contribution of one observation to \(\ell\) is \(-\frac12\log(2\pi)-\frac12\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{(y_2-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_2])^2}{2\sigma^2}\):

\[-0.9189385-4.2585966-0.0179024=-5.1954375\]

Check: \(\log(0.005541791)=-5.195438\). The two values agree.

**Q2.** Start from \((\star)\). Show that \(\partial\ell/\partial\beta_0=0\) gives \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).

Answer

1

\[0=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i])\right)\]

Set (⋆) = 0.

2

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)\]

\(\sigma^2>0\).

3

\[0=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i-n\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\]

4

\[n\hat\beta_0=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\]

5

\[\hat\beta_0=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ny_i-\hat\beta_1\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\]

This is the LS result on Slides p.23. ∎

**Q3.** True or false: under the model \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\), the maximum likelihood estimates of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) depend on the value of \(\sigma^2\). Use the log-likelihood to justify your answer.

Answer

False.

\(\ell=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\). For each fixed \(\sigma^2>0\), the first two terms do not contain \(\beta_0,\beta_1\). The factor \(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\) is negative. Thus the \(\beta_0,\beta_1\) that make \(\ell\) largest are always the values that make \(S\) smallest.

Numbers for the small data set with \(\sigma^2=2\): \(-\frac42\log(2)=-2\times0.693147=-1.386294\).

At \((0.5,1.4)\): \(\ell=-3.675754-1.386294-\frac{0.2}{4}=-5.112048\).

At \((0.5,1.2)\): \(\ell=-3.675754-1.386294-\frac{1.4}{4}=-5.412048\).

The least squares line \((0.5,1.4)\) has the larger \(\ell\) again, as for \(\sigma^2=1\) in Example 3.

This unit showed that, in the normal model, maximum likelihood and least squares give the same \(\hat\beta\). Unit 05 uses \(\hat\beta\) to define fitted values and residuals. Unit 06 uses \(\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2=0\) to estimate \(\sigma^2\).

## 05 · Fitted values and residuals

This unit defines two new quantities: the fitted value \(\hat y_i\) and the residual \(e_i\). Unit 06 uses the residuals to estimate \(\sigma^2\) with \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2/(n-2)\). Thus, this unit calculates fitted values and residuals first.

Plan · Slides p.30–32

Step 1: Read the section page "Fitted Values & Residuals" (Slides p.30).

Step 2: Define and calculate the fitted values \(\hat y_i\) (Slides p.31).

Step 3: Define and calculate the residuals \(e_i\) (Slides p.31).

Step 4: Compare the residuals \(e_i\) with the errors \(\epsilon_i\) (Slides p.31).

Step 5: Show the data, the fitted line, and the residuals in one figure (Slides p.32).

Data for this unit · Added

Small data set: \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\), so \(n=5\). Practice Q1 of Unit 03 found \(\hat\beta_0=2.2\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) for these data.

Brainhead data: Slides p.38 gives \(\hat\beta_0=335.4323150\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\) for all 236 observations. Slides p.10 gives the first six pairs \((x_i,y_i)\).

### 05.1 Section page Slides p.30

This page gives only the name of the new part of the lecture.

Slides p.30 is the section page "Fitted Values & Residuals". Slides p.31–32 belong to this part.

The next section starts with the fitted values on Slides p.31.

### 05.2 Fitted values Slides p.31

This section defines the fitted value. A fitted value is the height of the least squares line at one observed \(x_i\).

**What** Slides p.31

Fitted Values and Residuals · Lecture 2 · p.31 Define the fitted values: \[\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\]

The list below defines each symbol in the statement.

\(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\) are the least squares estimates: \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\) (Slides p.26).

The fitted line is the line \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x\). It is the least squares line.

The fitted value \(\hat y_i\) ("y hat i") is the height of the fitted line at \(x=x_i\). It has the same unit as \(y_i\).

Each observation has one fitted value. Thus, \(n\) observations have \(n\) fitted values.

**How** Added

Calculate the fitted value \(\hat y_i\)

- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).
- Find \(x_i\) of observation \(i\). Do not use \(y_i\).
- Calculate the product \(\hat\beta_1x_i\).
- Add \(\hat\beta_0\) to the product. The result is \(\hat y_i\).

**Self-check:** \(\hat y_i\) has the unit of \(y\). The point \((x_i,\hat y_i)\) is on the fitted line.

**Example 1 · The small data set** Added

This example applies the four steps to the five observations. Step 1 uses the estimates from Unit 03, Practice Q1.

1

\(\hat\beta_0=2.2,\quad \hat\beta_1=0.6\)

Unit 03, Practice Q1

2

\(\hat\beta_1x_i:\ 0.6(1),\ 0.6(2),\ 0.6(3),\ 0.6(4),\ 0.6(5)=0.6,\ 1.2,\ 1.8,\ 2.4,\ 3.0\)

3

\(\hat y_i:\ 2.2+0.6,\ 2.2+1.2,\ 2.2+1.8,\ 2.2+2.4,\ 2.2+3.0\)

4

\(\hat y_i:\ 2.8,\ 3.4,\ 4.0,\ 4.6,\ 5.2\)

Thus, at \(x=1\) the fitted line has the height 2.8, and at \(x=5\) it has the height 5.2.

**Example 2 · Observation 4 of the brainhead data** Added

This example uses only numbers that the slides print. Slides p.10 gives \((x_4,y_4)=(3777,1282)\).

1

\(\hat\beta_0=335.4323150,\quad \hat\beta_1=0.2608207\)

Slides p.38

2

\(\hat\beta_1x_4=0.2608207\times3777=985.1198\)

3

\(\hat y_4=335.4323150+985.1198\)

4

\(\hat y_4=1320.5521\)

Self-check: rounded to 3 decimals, \(\hat y_4=1320.552\) g. This is the fourth fitted value on Slides p.38.

Thus, for a head size of 3777 cm³, the fitted line gives a brain weight of 1320.552 g.

**Why** Added

The chain below shows what \(\hat y_i\) estimates. It starts from the mean line of Section 02.5: \(E[y_i|x_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\).

1

\(E[y_i|x_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\)

Section 02.5; \(E[\epsilon_i]=0\)

2

\(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\)

replace \(\beta_0,\beta_1\) with the estimates

3

\(=\hat y_i\)

definition, Slides p.31

∎ Thus, \(\hat y_i\) is the estimate of the mean \(E[y_i|x_i]\). The next section uses \(\hat y_i\) to find the distance of each point from the fitted line.

### 05.3 Residuals Slides p.31

This section defines the residual. A residual is the vertical distance from an observed point to the fitted line, with a sign.

**What** Slides p.31

Fitted Values and Residuals · Lecture 2 · p.31 Define the residuals: \[e_i=y_i-\hat y_i=y_i-(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i)\]

The residual \(e_i\) is the observed value \(y_i\) minus its fitted value \(\hat y_i\). It has the same unit as \(y_i\).

When \(e_i>0\), the point \((x_i,y_i)\) is above the fitted line.

When \(e_i<0\), the point \((x_i,y_i)\) is below the fitted line.

The size \(|e_i|\) is the vertical distance from the point to the fitted line.

The second equals sign in the statement only substitutes the definition of \(\hat y_i\).

**How** Added

Calculate the residual \(e_i\)

- Calculate the fitted value \(\hat y_i\) with the steps of Section 05.2.
- Find \(y_i\) of the same observation.
- Calculate \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). Subtract the fitted value from the observed value.
- Read the sign: plus means above the line, minus means below the line.

**Self-check:** \(\hat y_i+e_i\) must be equal to \(y_i\).

**Example 1 · The small data set** Added

This example uses the fitted values from Section 05.2, Example 1.

1

\(e_i:\ 2-2.8,\ 4-3.4,\ 5-4.0,\ 4-4.6,\ 5-5.2\)

2

\(e_i:\ -0.8,\ 0.6,\ 1.0,\ -0.6,\ -0.2\)

Self-check: \(2.8+(-0.8)=2\), \(3.4+0.6=4\), \(4.0+1.0=5\), \(4.6+(-0.6)=4\), \(5.2+(-0.2)=5\). Each sum is \(y_i\).

Points 2 and 3 are above the fitted line. Points 1, 4, and 5 are below it.

Unit 06 uses these five residuals to estimate \(\sigma^2\).

**Example 2 · Observations 4 and 5 of the brainhead data** Added

This example uses Slides p.10 for \(y_i\) and Slides p.38 for \(\hat y_i\).

1

\(e_4=y_4-\hat y_4=1282-1320.552\)

\(\hat y_4\) from Section 05.2, Example 2

2

\(e_4=-38.552\)

3

\(e_5=y_5-\hat y_5=1590-1424.880\)

\(y_5\): Slides p.10; \(\hat y_5\): Slides p.38

4

\(e_5=165.120\)

Person 4 has a brain weight 38.552 g below the fitted line.

Person 5 has a brain weight 165.120 g above the fitted line.

Figure 5-1 shows observation 5 with its fitted value and its residual.

[figure]
Figure 5-1 (Added) · Observation 5. The purple point is the observed value \((x_5,y_5)=(4177,1590)\). The blue line is the fitted line. The open blue point is the fitted value \(\hat y_5=1424.880\) at the same \(x_5=4177\). The orange vertical segment is the residual \(e_5=165.120\). The purple point is above the line, so \(e_5\) is positive.

**Why** Added

The chain below connects the residuals to least squares. It starts from the sum of squares \(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\) of Slides p.21.

1

\(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\)

Slides p.21

2

\(S(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)^2\)

substitute the estimates

3

\(=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i)\big)^2\)

4

\(=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\)

definition of \(\hat y_i\)

5

\(=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\)

definition of \(e_i\)

∎ Thus, the least squares line is the line with the smallest sum of squared residuals \(\sum e_i^2\). Unit 06 uses the same \(\sum e_i^2\) to estimate \(\sigma^2\).

### 05.4 Residuals and errors Slides p.31

This section compares two quantities with a similar form: the residual \(e_i\) and the error \(\epsilon_i\). The difference is the line that each one subtracts.

**What** Slides p.31

Fitted Values and Residuals · Lecture 2 · p.31 Note the residuals \(e_i\) are different from the errors: \(\epsilon_i=y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\)

The error \(\epsilon_i\) is \(y_i\) minus the mean line \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\) of Section 02.6. Slides p.13 calls it an "unobserved random error term".

The residual \(e_i\) is \(y_i\) minus the fitted line \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\). It uses only the data and the estimates, so we can calculate it.

The two formulas have the same form. \(\epsilon_i\) uses the parameters \(\beta_0,\beta_1\). \(e_i\) uses the estimates \(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1\).

Thus, the residual \(e_i\) is a value that we can calculate. We use it in place of the error \(\epsilon_i\), which we cannot observe.

**How** Added

Identify a residual or an error

- Look at the coefficients of the subtracted line.
- Call the quantity a residual \(e_i\) when the coefficients have hats (\(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1\)).
- Call the quantity an error \(\epsilon_i\) when the coefficients have no hats (\(\beta_0,\beta_1\)).
- Calculate \(e_i\) when you need a number. The parameters \(\beta_0,\beta_1\) are unknown.

**Self-check:** A quantity with a numeric value contains only data and estimates. Thus, it is a residual.

**Example · Observation 4 of the brainhead data** Added

This example writes both quantities for \((x_4,y_4)=(3777,1282)\) from Slides p.10.

1

\(e_4=1282-(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\times3777)\)

How step 2: hats

2

\(e_4=1282-1320.552\)

Section 05.2, Example 2

3

\(e_4=-38.552\)

1

\(\epsilon_4=1282-(\beta_0+\beta_1\times3777)\)

How step 3: no hats; \(\beta_0,\beta_1\) are unknown, so the chain stops here

Thus, \(e_4=-38.552\) is a number. The error \(\epsilon_4\) stays an expression with unknown parameters.

**Why** Added

The chain below subtracts the two definitions. It shows where the difference comes from.

1

\(\epsilon_i-e_i=\big[y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\big]-\big[y_i-(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i)\big]\)

the two definitions, Slides p.31

2

\(=y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i-y_i+\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\)

3

\(=-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i+\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\)

4

\(=(\hat\beta_0-\beta_0)+(\hat\beta_1-\beta_1)x_i\)

∎ The difference comes only from \(\hat\beta_0-\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1-\beta_1\). These two differences are unknown, so \(\epsilon_i\) is also unknown. The next section shows the residuals of the brainhead data in one figure.

### 05.6 Practice Added

The three questions below check the fitted values, the residuals, and one property of the residuals.

This unit defined the fitted value \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\) and the residual \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). We can calculate the residual, and we use it in place of the unobserved error \(\epsilon_i\). Unit 06 uses \(\sum e_i^2\) to estimate \(\sigma^2\).

## 06 · Estimating \(\sigma^2\): the MLE and the unbiased estimator

This unit estimates the last unknown parameter of the model: the error variance \(\sigma^2\). First, it finds the maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\sum e_i^2/n\). Then it gives the estimator that the course uses, \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum e_i^2/(n-2)\), and shows why the course uses it. Last, it calculates \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), and \(\hat\sigma\) together by hand.

Plan · Slides p.33–38

Step 1: Section title page (Slides p.33).

Step 2: Set \(\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2=0\) and solve for the maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\) (Slides p.34).

Step 3: Give the estimator that the course uses, \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum e_i^2/(n-2)\) (Slides p.35).

Step 4: Show that \(\hat\sigma^2\) is unbiased with a chi-squared result (Slides p.36).

Step 5: Calculate \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), and \(\hat\sigma\) in the order that the slide gives (Slides p.37).

Step 6: Read the estimates and the fitted values for the brainhead data (Slides p.38).

Start point (results of Units 02–05) · Added

Model: \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\). This is the same as \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\ \sigma^2)\).

The error variance \(\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}[\epsilon_i]\) tells how far the points spread around the mean line \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\). Its square root \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the errors. \(\sigma\) has the same unit as \(y\).

Estimates: \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\). The least squares method and maximum likelihood give the same values (Slides p.26–29).

The fitted value is \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\). The residual is \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\) (Slides p.31).

\(\sum e_i^2\) is the sum of squared residuals: square each of the \(n\) residuals, then add them. In this unit, \(\sum\) without limits means \(\sum_{i=1}^n\).

With this notation, the unit starts at the section title page.

### 06.1 Section page Slides p.33

This page gives only the name of the new part.

Slides p.33 is the section page "Estimating \(\sigma^2\)". Slides p.34–38 are in this part.

The earlier units estimated \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). The model still has one unknown parameter, \(\sigma^2\), and this part estimates it.

### 06.2 The maximum likelihood estimate of \(\sigma^2\) Slides p.34

This section estimates \(\sigma^2\) with maximum likelihood. The method is the same as for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\): take a partial derivative of the log-likelihood and set it to 0.

**What** Slides p.34

Maximum Likelihood Estimation Continued · Lecture 2 · p.34 \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2}=0\] \[-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2=0\] \[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i])^2}{n}=\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\] or equivalently \[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n}\]

The statement uses these terms.

Log-likelihood \(\ell\): the natural log of the likelihood. Unit 04 found it from Slides p.27: \(\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2|y)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\).

Subscript \(ML\): this mark shows that the estimate comes from maximum likelihood.

\(\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2\): the partial derivative of \(\ell\). It treats the full quantity \(\sigma^2\) as one variable.

Set the partial derivative of \(\ell\) with respect to \(\sigma^2\) to 0. The solution is \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\). It is the mean of the squared residuals: add the \(n\) values \(e_i^2\), then divide by \(n\).

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\) from data

- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).
- For each \(i\), calculate the fitted value \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\).
- For each \(i\), calculate the residual \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\).
- Square each \(e_i\). Add the squares to get \(\sum e_i^2\).
- Divide by \(n\): \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\sum e_i^2/n\).

**Self-check:** \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\ge0\), because it is a mean of squares. Its unit is the unit of \(y\), squared. The residuals must add to 0. If they do not, an estimate \(\hat\beta\) is incorrect.

**Example · The small data set of Unit 05** Added

This example applies the five steps to the small data set of Unit 05: \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\), so \(n=5\).

Step 1: \(\hat\beta_0=2.2\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) (Unit 03, Practice Q1).

Step 2: the fitted values are 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2 (Section 05.2, Example 1).

Step 3: the residuals are \(-0.8,\ 0.6,\ 1.0,\ -0.6,\ -0.2\) (Section 05.3, Example 1).

Step 4: the squares are 0.64, 0.36, 1.00, 0.36, 0.04. Thus, \(\sum e_i^2=0.64+0.36+1.00+0.36+0.04=2.4\).

Step 5: \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=2.4/5=0.48\). The square root is \(\hat\sigma_{ML}=\sqrt{0.48}=0.693\).

Self-check: \(-0.8+0.6+1.0-0.6-0.2=0\). The residuals add to 0.

The figure below shows the five residuals at their \(x\) positions Added. An estimate of \(\sigma\) measures the usual distance of these points from the line \(e=0\).

[figure]
Figure 6-1 (Added) · The five residuals \(e_i\) of the small data set (orange). The blue line is \(e=0\). The green band is \(\pm\hat\sigma=\pm0.894\), the estimate from Section 06.3. Four of the five residuals are in the band.

The example gives \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=0.48\). The derivation below shows where the formula comes from.

**Why** Slides p.34

The derivation starts from the log-likelihood of Slides p.27. It uses the partial derivative from Section 04.2, sets it to 0, and solves for \(\sigma^2\).

1

\[\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2|y)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

log-likelihood, Slides p.27

2

\[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2}=-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i])^2\]

Section 04.2 (c); third line on Slides p.28

3

\[-\frac{n}{2\hat\sigma^2_{ML}}+\frac{1}{2(\hat\sigma^2_{ML})^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i])^2=0\]

set to 0 (Slides p.34); the other two equations give \(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1\) (Slides p.29)

4

\[-n\hat\sigma^2_{ML}+\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i])^2=0\]

5

\[n\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i])^2\]

6

\[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i])^2}{n}\]

Slides p.34, third line

7

\[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n}\]

substitute \(e_i=y_i-(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i)\); Slides p.34, last line ∎

Result: \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\) is the mean of the squared residuals. The next section changes the denominator from \(n\) to \(n-2\).

### 06.3 The estimator \(\hat\sigma^2\) that the course uses Slides p.35

This section gives the estimator of \(\sigma^2\) that the course uses. It is different from \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\) only in the denominator.

**What** Slides p.35

Maximum Likelihood Estimation Continued · Lecture 2 · p.35 However we typically adopt a different estimator: \[\hat\sigma^2=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\qquad\text{Why?}\]

The course usually does not use \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\). It uses \(\hat\sigma^2\). The numerator is the same sum of squared residuals. The denominator is \(n-2\), not \(n\).

\(\hat\sigma^2\) has no subscript. In the rest of the course, \(\hat\sigma^2\) always means this estimator. Its square root \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2}\) estimates \(\sigma\). Slides p.35 asks "Why?", and Slides p.36 gives the answer.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat\sigma^2\) and \(\hat\sigma\) from data

- Do steps 1–4 of Section 06.2 to get \(\sum e_i^2\).
- Calculate \(n-2\).
- Divide the sum by \(n-2\): \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum e_i^2/(n-2)\).
- Take the square root: \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2}\).

**Self-check:** \(\hat\sigma^2\) is larger than \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\). The ratio \(\hat\sigma^2/\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\) is exactly \(n/(n-2)\).

**Example · The same small data set** Added

Section 06.2 found \(\sum e_i^2=2.4\) with \(n=5\).

Step 2: \(n-2=5-2=3\).

Step 3: \(\hat\sigma^2=2.4/3=0.8\).

Step 4: \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{0.8}=0.894\).

Self-check: \(\hat\sigma^2/\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=0.8/0.48=1.667\), and \(n/(n-2)=5/3=1.667\). The two values agree.

Result: for this data set, \(\hat\sigma^2=0.8\) and \(\hat\sigma=0.894\). With only 5 points, \(\hat\sigma^2\) is 5/3 times \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\). The next section answers the "Why?" of Slides p.35.

### 06.4 The unbiased estimator Slides p.36

This section shows why the denominator is \(n-2\): with \(n-2\), the estimator is unbiased. The slide gives only the intuition. It uses a chi-squared result and does not prove that result.

**What** Slides p.36

Unbiased Estimator · Lecture 2 · p.36 Why do we use this \(\hat\sigma^2\) instead of \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\)? \[E\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\right]=\sigma^2\] Intuition: \[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\quad\text{and}\quad E[\chi^2_\nu]=\nu\] \[\Longrightarrow E\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\right]=\sigma^2E\left[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\right]=\frac{\sigma^2}{(n-2)}E\left[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\right]=\sigma^2\] Often doesn't matter when \(n\ge50\)

The statement uses these terms.

Unbiased: an estimator is unbiased when its expectation is equal to the parameter. For \(\sigma^2\), this means \(E[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2\).

In words: collect many new data sets and calculate \(\hat\sigma^2\) for each. The mean of these values is \(\sigma^2\).

Chi-squared distribution \(\chi^2_\nu\): a distribution with only positive values. Lecture 1 p.26: if \(Z_1,\dots,Z_\nu\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1)\), then \(\sum Z_i^2\sim\chi^2_\nu\), and \(E[\chi^2_\nu]=\nu\).

Degrees of freedom \(\nu\): the parameter of the chi-squared distribution. It is also the mean. Here \(\nu=n-2\).

\(\sim\): "has the distribution". The random quantity on the left has the distribution on the right.

Slides p.36 gives two facts. First, the expectation of \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum e_i^2/(n-2)\) is exactly \(\sigma^2\), so \(\hat\sigma^2\) is unbiased. The reason: \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum e_i^2\) has a \(\chi^2_{(n-2)}\) distribution with mean \(n-2\). The division by \(n-2\) cancels this mean. Second, when \(n\ge50\), the values \(n\) and \(n-2\) are almost equal, so the choice usually does not change a conclusion.

The figure below shows the chi-squared density for \(\nu=3\) and marks the mean \(\nu\) Added.

[figure]
Figure 6-2 (Added) · The density curve of \(\chi^2_3\) (blue). The density is above 0 only for positive values. The purple dashed line is the mean \(E[\chi^2_3]=3\).

The curve has a long right tail, but its mean is exactly the degrees of freedom. The intuition on Slides p.36 uses this mean.

**How** Added

Find if an estimator of \(\sigma^2\) is unbiased, and find if the denominator is important

- Write the estimator in the form \(c\cdot\sum e_i^2\). Find the constant \(c\).
- Use \(E\left[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum e_i^2\right]=n-2\). This gives \(E\left[\sum e_i^2\right]=(n-2)\sigma^2\).
- Calculate \(E[c\sum e_i^2]=c(n-2)\sigma^2\).
- Compare \(c(n-2)\) with 1. When \(c(n-2)=1\), the estimator is unbiased.
- Look at \(n\). If \(n\ge50\), the ratio \(n/(n-2)\) is near 1, and the difference is usually small.

**Self-check:** only \(c=1/(n-2)\) gives \(c(n-2)=1\). The denominator must be equal to the degrees of freedom \(n-2\).

**Example · Two sample sizes** Added

This example does the five steps for the small data set (\(n=5\)) and for \(n=50\).

Step 1: for \(\hat\sigma^2\), \(c=1/(n-2)\). For \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\), \(c=1/n\).

Steps 2–3 with \(n=5\): \(E[\hat\sigma^2]=\frac13\cdot3\sigma^2=\sigma^2\). \(E[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}]=\frac15\cdot3\sigma^2=0.6\sigma^2\).

Step 4: \(\hat\sigma^2\) is unbiased. With \(n=5\), \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\) is too low by 40% on average.

Step 5 with \(n=50\): \(E[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}]=\frac{1}{50}\cdot48\sigma^2=0.96\sigma^2\). The ratio is \(n/(n-2)=50/48=1.042\). The difference is only 4%.

Result: the denominator \(n-2\) makes the estimator unbiased. When \(n\) is small, the denominator is important. When \(n\ge50\), it changes the estimate by less than 5%.

**Why** Slides p.36

The derivation writes out the chain of equations on Slides p.36, one change per line. The only input without proof is \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum e_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\). The slide uses this result as known.

1

\[E\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\right]\]

2

\[=E\left[\sigma^2\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\right]\]

\(\sigma^2\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma^2}=1\)

3

\[=\sigma^2E\left[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\right]\]

linearity of \(E\); \(\sigma^2\) is a constant

4

\[=\frac{\sigma^2}{(n-2)}E\left[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\right]\]

linearity of \(E\); \(\frac{1}{n-2}\) is a constant

5

\[=\frac{\sigma^2}{(n-2)}\cdot(n-2)\]

\(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum e_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\) and \(E[\chi^2_\nu]=\nu\)

6

\[=\sigma^2\]

∎

Result: the division by \(n-2\) cancels the chi-squared mean \(n-2\), so \(\hat\sigma^2\) is unbiased. The next section uses \(\hat\sigma^2\) in the full calculation.

### 06.5 Data example: all three estimates in order Slides p.37

This section puts all the formulas of Lecture 2 in one order. Slides p.37 shows this order as code. This section gives only the statistical steps.

**What** Slides p.37

Data Example · Lecture 2 · p.37 (statistical content of the slide) Prepare \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(S_{xy}=\sum(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)\), \(S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\), and \(n\) (number of observations).
\(\beta_1\) estimate (MLE): \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).
\(\beta_0\) estimate (MLE): \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).
Fitted values: \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\). Residuals: \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\).
\(\sigma\) (unbiased estimate): \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum e_i^2/(n-2)}\).

Each line is one formula from this lecture.

\(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) are the sample means. \(S_{xy}\) and \(S_{xx}\) are the sums of products and of squares of the deviations from the means.

A note on the slide gives a second way to get \(\hat\beta_1\). Divide the sample covariance of \(y\) and \(x\) by the sample variance of \(x\). Both have the denominator \(n-1\), so it cancels and the result is \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).

\(\hat\sigma\) is the square root of the unbiased estimator \(\hat\sigma^2\) of Section 06.4. It is not the square root of \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\).

**How** Added

Get the three point estimates \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), \(\hat\sigma\)

- Calculate \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), and \(n\).
- Calculate \(S_{xy}\) and \(S_{xx}\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).
- Calculate each fitted value \(\hat y_i\) and each residual \(e_i\).
- Calculate \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum e_i^2/(n-2)}\).

**Self-check:** the residuals add to 0. The point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is on the line: \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\bar x=\bar y\).

**Example · A data set with six points** Added

This example does the six steps for \(x=(1,2,3,4,5,6)\) and \(y=(3,5,4,8,7,9)\).

Step 1: \(n=6\). \(\bar x=21/6=3.5\). \(\bar y=36/6=6\).

Step 2, deviations: \(x_i-\bar x=(-2.5,-1.5,-0.5,0.5,1.5,2.5)\). \(y_i-\bar y=(-3,-1,-2,2,1,3)\).

Step 2, sums: \(S_{xy}=7.5+1.5+1+1+1.5+7.5=20\). \(S_{xx}=6.25+2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25+6.25=17.5\).

Step 3: \(\hat\beta_1=20/17.5=1.1429\) (exactly \(8/7\)).

Step 4: \(\hat\beta_0=6-\frac87\times3.5=6-4=2\).

Step 5, fitted values: \(\hat y_i=2+\frac87x_i\) gives 3.143, 4.286, 5.429, 6.571, 7.714, 8.857.

Step 5, residuals: \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\) gives \(-0.143,\ 0.714,\ -1.429,\ 1.429,\ -0.714,\ 0.143\).

Step 6: \(\sum e_i^2=0.0204+0.5102+2.0408+2.0408+0.5102+0.0204=5.1429\).

Step 6: \(\hat\sigma^2=5.1429/(6-2)=5.1429/4=1.2857\). \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{1.2857}=1.134\).

Self-check: the residuals add to 0. Also \(2+\frac87\times3.5=2+4=6=\bar y\).

Result: the three point estimates are \(\hat\beta_0=2\), \(\hat\beta_1=1.1429\), and \(\hat\sigma=1.134\). The next section reads the same estimates for the brainhead data on the slide.

### 06.6 Estimates and fitted values for the brainhead data Slides p.38

This section reads the statistical results that Slides p.38 prints for the brainhead data. Then it checks two fitted values by hand.

**What** Slides p.38

Data Example · Lecture 2 · p.38 (statistical results printed on the slide) Regression coefficients: \(\hat\beta_0=335.4323150\) (intercept), \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\).
Fitted values of observations 1–6: 1512.255, 1310.380, 1446.789, 1320.552, 1424.880, 1270.475.

The data come from Slides p.10. The covariate \(x\) is head size in cm³. The outcome \(y\) is brain weight in grams.

Intercept: the value \(\hat\beta_0\). It is the estimated mean of \(y\) at \(x=0\). Here \(\hat\beta_0=335.4323\) g.

Slope: the value \(\hat\beta_1\). One more cm³ of head size gives an estimated mean brain weight that is 0.2608 g larger.

The six fitted values are \(\hat y_1,\dots,\hat y_6\). They are on the fitted line at the head sizes of the first six people.

**How** Added

Check a fitted value and find its residual

- Find \(x_i\) and \(y_i\) of observation \(i\) on Slides p.10.
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1x_i\).
- Add \(\hat\beta_0\) to get \(\hat y_i\).
- Compare \(\hat y_i\) with the value on Slides p.38.
- Calculate \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\).

**Self-check:** your \(\hat y_i\), rounded to 3 decimals, is equal to the value on Slides p.38.

**Example · Observations 3 and 5** Added

Slides p.10 gives \((x_3,y_3)=(4261,1335)\) and \((x_5,y_5)=(4177,1590)\).

Observation 3, Step 2: \(\hat\beta_1x_3=0.2608207\times4261=1111.3570\).

Observation 3, Step 3: \(\hat y_3=335.4323150+1111.3570=1446.7893\).

Observation 3, Step 4: rounded, this is 1446.789, the third value on Slides p.38.

Observation 3, Step 5: \(e_3=1335-1446.789=-111.789\) g. This person has a brain weight 111.789 g below the fitted line.

Observation 5, Step 2: \(\hat\beta_1x_5=0.2608207\times4177=1089.4481\).

Observation 5, Step 3: \(\hat y_5=335.4323150+1089.4481=1424.8804\). Rounded, this is 1424.880, the fifth value on Slides p.38.

Observation 5, Step 5: \(e_5=1590-1424.880=165.120\) g. This person has a brain weight 165.120 g above the fitted line.

Result: the slide's \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\) give the slide's fitted values. To get \(\hat\sigma\) for these data, use all 236 residuals in step 6 of Section 06.5.

Summary of this unit

\(\sigma^2\) has two estimators. Maximum likelihood gives \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\sum e_i^2/n\). The course uses the unbiased \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum e_i^2/(n-2)\), because \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum e_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\) has mean \(n-2\). For the small data set, \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=0.48\) and \(\hat\sigma^2=0.8\). For \(n\ge50\), the two values are almost equal. The confidence intervals and tests of Lecture 3 use \(\hat\sigma\).

### 06.7 Practice Added

These questions practice the calculations and the derivation of this unit.

**Q1.** Consider the data \(x=(0,1,2,3)\) and \(y=(1,3,2,6)\). Calculate \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), the residuals, \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\), \(\hat\sigma^2\), and \(\hat\sigma\).

Answer

Step 1: \(n=4\). \(\bar x=6/4=1.5\). \(\bar y=12/4=3\).

Step 2: \(x_i-\bar x=(-1.5,-0.5,0.5,1.5)\). \(y_i-\bar y=(-2,0,-1,3)\).

Step 2: \(S_{xy}=3+0-0.5+4.5=7\). \(S_{xx}=2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25=5\).

Step 3: \(\hat\beta_1=7/5=1.4\).

Step 4: \(\hat\beta_0=3-1.4\times1.5=3-2.1=0.9\).

Step 5: \(\hat y_i=0.9+1.4x_i\) gives 0.9, 2.3, 3.7, 5.1. The residuals are \(0.1,\ 0.7,\ -1.7,\ 0.9\). Their sum is 0.

Step 6: \(\sum e_i^2=0.01+0.49+2.89+0.81=4.2\).

\(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=4.2/4=1.05\).

\(\hat\sigma^2=4.2/(4-2)=4.2/2=2.1\). \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{2.1}=1.449\).

Here \(n=4\), so the ratio \(n/(n-2)=4/2=2\). The unbiased estimate is two times the MLE.

**Q2.** Use \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\) to find \(E[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}]\). Is \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\) unbiased? Give the factor for \(n=5\) and for \(n=50\).

Answer

1

\[E[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}]=E\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n}\right]\]

2

\[=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}E\left[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\right]\]

linearity of \(E\)

3

\[=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}(n-2)\]

\(E[\chi^2_{(n-2)}]=n-2\)

4

\[=\frac{n-2}{n}\sigma^2\]

∎

The factor \(\frac{n-2}{n}\) is less than 1. Thus \(E[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}]\ne\sigma^2\), and \(\hat\sigma^2_{ML}\) is not unbiased. On average, it is too low. For \(n=5\), the factor is \(3/5=0.6\). For \(n=50\), the factor is \(48/50=0.96\).

**Q3.** Use the six fitted values on Slides p.38 and the six values \(y_i\) on Slides p.10. Calculate \(e_1,\dots,e_6\) and their sum. Can you use these six residuals to calculate \(\hat\sigma\) for the brainhead data?

Answer

Step 1: \(e_1=1530-1512.255=17.745\), \(e_2=1297-1310.380=-13.380\), \(e_3=1335-1446.789=-111.789\).

Step 2: \(e_4=1282-1320.552=-38.552\), \(e_5=1590-1424.880=165.120\), \(e_6=1300-1270.475=29.525\).

Step 3: \(17.745-13.380-111.789-38.552+165.120+29.525=48.669\).

The sum is not 0. This is correct, because the property \(\sum e_i=0\) applies to all \(n=236\) residuals together, not to six of them.

No. The estimate \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum e_i^2/(n-2)}\) uses all 236 residuals and \(n-2=234\). The slides do not print the other 230 residuals.

This unit is complete: the course estimates \(\sigma^2\) with the unbiased \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum e_i^2/(n-2)\). Lecture 3 uses \(\hat\sigma\) in the standard errors, the confidence intervals, and the tests.
