STAT 331 · Lecture 3 · Simple Linear Regression: Inference

# Lecture 3: Simple Linear Regression: Inference

This lecture finds the distributions of \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\beta_0\) and uses them for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests (Lecture 3 · p.1–49).

Contents
01 · Recap: the SLR model, least squares, and the estimate of \(\sigma^2\) 02 · Sampling distribution and unbiasedness of \(\hat\beta_1\) 03 · Variance and distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\beta_0\) 04 · Confidence interval for \(\beta_1\): known \(\sigma\), unknown \(\sigma\) (t distribution), and standard error 05 · Interval estimation example and interpretation 06 · Hypothesis tests for \(\beta_1\): p-value, coefficient table, and one-sided tests

## 01 · Recap: the SLR model, least squares, and the estimate of \(\sigma^2\)

This unit reviews four items from Lecture 2: the model, the meaning of \(\beta_1\), the least squares estimates, and the estimate of \(\sigma^2\). Units 02–06 build intervals and tests from these estimates. Thus, this unit calculates \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), and \(\hat\sigma\) by hand first.

Plan · Slides p.1–8

Step 1: Read the title page and the section page (Slides p.1–2).

Step 2: Write the simple linear regression model and its four assumptions (Slides p.3–4).

Step 3: Interpret \(\beta_1\) (Slides p.5).

Step 4: Calculate \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\) with least squares (Slides p.6–7).

Step 5: Calculate the fitted values, the residuals, and \(\hat\sigma^2\) (Slides p.8).

Data for this unit · Added

Small data set: \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\), so \(n=5\). This unit does all hand calculations on these data.

Brainhead data: \(n=236\) persons. The response \(y\) is brain weight in g. The explanatory variable \(x\) is head size in cm³.

Slides p.45 prints the brainhead results: \(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\), \(\hat\sigma=72.35\), and 234 degrees of freedom.

### 01.1 Title page and section page Slides p.1–2

These two pages give only names. They have no new mathematics.

Slides p.1 is the title page: "Lecture 3: Simple Linear Regression: Inference".

Inference is the use of sample data to make statements about unknown population parameters. Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are two types of inference.

Slides p.2 is the section page "Recap". Slides p.3–8 belong to this part.

The next section starts with the model on Slides p.3.

### 01.2 The simple linear regression model and its assumptions Slides p.3–4

This section writes the base model of the course. All inference results in this lecture are correct only when the four assumptions are true.

**What** Slides p.3–4

Simple Linear Regression · Lecture 3 · p.3–4 \[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i,\quad \epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\] Or: \[y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\] Assumptions:
1. Linearity
2. Independence
3. Normality
4. Equal variance (homoskedasticity)

The list below defines each symbol in the statement.

Simple linear regression (SLR) is a model in which the mean of a response \(y\) is a straight-line function of one explanatory variable \(x\).

The response \(y_i\) is the result value of observation \(i\). In the brainhead data, \(y_i\) is brain weight in g.

The explanatory variable \(x_i\) is the input value of observation \(i\). The model treats \(x_i\) as a known constant. In the brainhead data, \(x_i\) is head size in cm³.

The index \(i\) is the observation number, \(i=1,\dots,n\). The sample size \(n\) is the number of observations.

The intercept \(\beta_0\) and the slope \(\beta_1\) are two unknown constants of the population line. An unknown constant of a model is a parameter.

The error \(\epsilon_i\) is the difference between \(y_i\) and the population line \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\). It is random, and nobody can observe it.

\(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is the Normal distribution: a bell-shaped distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).

The mean is the center of a distribution. The variance is the mean squared distance of the values from the mean.

\(\sigma^2\) is the error variance. It is the third unknown parameter. Its square root \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation.

"iid" means independent and identically distributed. Each \(\epsilon_i\) has the same distribution, and the value of one \(\epsilon_i\) does not change the distribution of another.

"indep" means independent. The second form does not say "identically distributed", because the mean \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\) changes with \(x_i\).

The list below gives the meaning of each assumption.

1. Linearity: the mean of \(y\) is the straight-line function \(\beta_0+\beta_1x\).

2. Independence: the errors of different observations are independent.

3. Normality: each error has a Normal distribution.

4. Equal variance (homoskedasticity): the errors have the same variance \(\sigma^2\) at each value of \(x\).

The two forms give the same model. The first form writes "line plus error". The second form writes the distribution of \(y_i\).

**How** Added

Write a data set as an SLR model

- Find the response \(y\). It is the variable that the question explains or predicts.
- Find the explanatory variable \(x\). It is the variable that the question uses to explain \(y\).
- Write \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\) with \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,\dots,n\).
- List the three unknown parameters: \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\), \(\sigma^2\).
- For the second form, put the mean \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\) and the variance \(\sigma^2\) into \(N(\cdot,\cdot)\).

**Self-check:** The only Greek letters in the model are \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\), \(\sigma^2\), and \(\epsilon_i\). The values \(x_i\) and \(y_i\) are data. The number \(n\) is equal to the number of data pairs.

**Example 1 · The small data set** Added

This example writes the model for the five pairs \((1,2),(2,4),(3,5),(4,4),(5,5)\).

Step 1–2: \(y\) is the second value of each pair. \(x\) is the first value. \(n=5\).

Step 3: \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,\dots,5\).

Observation 3 gives the equation \(5=\beta_0+\beta_1\cdot3+\epsilon_3\). The values \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\), and \(\epsilon_3\) are unknown.

Step 5: \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\). For observation 3, \(y_3\sim N(\beta_0+3\beta_1,\sigma^2)\).

Thus, the model has three unknown parameters. Section 01.4 estimates \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), and Section 01.5 estimates \(\sigma^2\).

**Example 2 · The brainhead data** Added

This example writes the model for the course data. The question is how head size explains brain weight.

Step 1: the response \(y_i\) is the brain weight of person \(i\), in g.

Step 2: the explanatory variable \(x_i\) is the head size of person \(i\), in cm³.

Step 3: \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,\dots,236\).

Self-check: Slides p.45 gives 234 degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom are \(n-2\), so \(n=234+2=236\).

Thus, the brainhead model has the same form and the same three parameters as the small model.

**Why · The two forms are the same** Added

The chain below finds the mean and the variance of \(y_i\) from the first form. Here \(x_i\), \(\beta_0\), and \(\beta_1\) are constants.

1

\(E[y_i]=E[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i]\)

2

\(=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+E[\epsilon_i]\)

linearity of expectation

3

\(=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+0\)

\(\epsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\)

4

\(\mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\mathrm{Var}[\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i]\)

5

\(=\mathrm{Var}[\epsilon_i]\)

a constant does not change the variance

6

\(=\sigma^2\)

A Normal variable plus a constant is also Normal. Thus, \(y_i\sim N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\). The \(\epsilon_i\) are independent, so the \(y_i\) are also independent. ∎

This section gives a model with three unknown parameters and four assumptions. The next section explains the most important parameter, \(\beta_1\).

### 01.3 The interpretation of \(\beta_1\) Slides p.5

This section gives the meaning of \(\beta_1\) in a real problem. The intervals and tests in Units 04–06 all give information about this quantity.

**What** Slides p.5

Interpretations · Lecture 3 · p.5 \[\beta_1=E[y|x=x^*+1]-E[y|x=x^*]\] \(\beta_1\) is the mean difference comparing a population with \(x\) to a population with \(x\) a unit lower
\(\hat\beta_1\) is an estimate of this mean difference

The conditional expectation \(E[y|x=x^*]\) is the mean of \(y\) in the group of units that has \(x=x^*\).

\(x^*\) is any fixed value of \(x\).

A population is the set of all possible units. Here "a population with \(x\)" is all units that have the same value of \(x\).

An estimate is a value that we calculate from the sample data. The hat symbol "^" shows that a quantity comes from the data. Thus, \(\hat\beta_1\) is the estimate of \(\beta_1\).

Compare two populations. The \(x\) of the first population is 1 unit higher than the \(x\) of the second. The difference between their mean values of \(y\) is \(\beta_1\).

**How** Added

Interpret \(\hat\beta_1\) in one sentence

- Find the unit of \(x\) and the unit of \(y\).
- Write: "Compare two populations whose \(x\) differs by 1 (unit of \(x\))."
- Continue: "The estimated mean of \(y\) differs by \(\hat\beta_1\) (unit of \(y\))."
- Use the sign of \(\hat\beta_1\) to say "higher" or "lower" for the population with the larger \(x\).
- For a difference of \(k\) units in \(x\), use the mean difference \(k\hat\beta_1\).

**Self-check:** The sentence contains the word "mean". It compares two populations. It gives the two units.

**Example 1 · The small data set** Added

Section 01.4 calculates \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) for the small data set. This example uses that value. The data have no units.

Step 2–4: compare two populations whose \(x\) differs by 1. The estimated mean of \(y\) is 0.6 higher in the population with the larger \(x\).

Step 5: for \(x=5\) and \(x=1\), \(k=5-1=4\). The mean difference is \(4\times0.6=2.4\).

Thus, \(\hat\beta_1\) gives the change of the estimated mean for each unit of \(x\).

**Example 2 · The brainhead data** Added

This example uses \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) from Slides p.45.

Step 1: \(x\) is in cm³. \(y\) is in g.

Step 2–4: compare two populations whose head sizes differ by 1 cm³. The estimated mean brain weight is 0.26082 g higher in the population with the larger head size.

Step 5: for a difference of 100 cm³, the mean difference is \(100\times0.26082=26.082\) g.

This number is a difference of means. It does not give the brain weight change of one person.

**Why** Added

Section 01.2 gives \(E[y|x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x\). The chain below puts in two values of \(x\) and subtracts.

1

\(E[y|x=x^*+1]-E[y|x=x^*]=\big(\beta_0+\beta_1(x^*+1)\big)-\big(\beta_0+\beta_1x^*\big)\)

put in \(E[y|x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x\)

2

\(=\beta_0+\beta_1x^*+\beta_1-\beta_0-\beta_1x^*\)

3

\(=\beta_1\)

∎ The result does not contain \(x^*\). Thus, the comparison gives the same \(\beta_1\) at each value of \(x\). The next section calculates \(\hat\beta_1\) from the data.

### 01.4 Least squares estimation Slides p.6–7

This section calculates \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\) from the data. The method selects the line with the smallest sum of squared vertical distances from the points.

**What** Slides p.6–7

Least Squares Estimation · Lecture 3 · p.6 Minimize the sum of squares: \[S(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\] \[\Longrightarrow\ \frac{\partial S(\beta_0,\beta_1)}{\partial\beta_0}=0,\qquad \frac{\partial S(\beta_0,\beta_1)}{\partial\beta_1}=0\]

Estimates · Lecture 3 · p.7 So the least squares estimators are: \[\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.\] OLS=MLE under the assumption of Normality
OLS well defined even without Normality, but only equal to MLE under Normality

The sum of squares \(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)\) is a function of a candidate line. For each point, it squares the vertical difference \(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i\). Then it adds the squares.

The partial derivative \(\partial S/\partial\beta_0\) is the derivative of \(S\) with respect to \(\beta_0\), with \(\beta_1\) held constant. At the minimum, both partial derivatives are 0.

Least squares (OLS, ordinary least squares) uses the values of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) that make \(S\) smallest.

An estimator is a formula that changes the data into an estimate. An example is \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).

The sample means are \(\bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) and \(\bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\).

\(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\) is the sum of squared deviations of \(x\). \(S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\) is the sum of cross products of deviations.

The maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) uses the parameter values that make the probability density of the observed data largest.

OLS needs only the sum of squares. Thus, OLS is defined without the Normality assumption. With the Normality assumption, OLS also gives the MLE.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\beta_0\)

- Calculate \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\).
- Calculate the deviations \(x_i-\bar x\) and \(y_i-\bar y\) for each observation.
- Calculate \(S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\).
- Calculate \(S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).

**Self-check:** \(S_{xx}>0\). The sign of \(\hat\beta_1\) is the sign of \(S_{xy}\). The point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is on the fitted line: \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\bar x=\bar y\).

**Example 1 · The small data set** Added How steps 1–6

This example applies the six steps to \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\).

Step 1: the sample means.

1

\(\bar x=\dfrac{1+2+3+4+5}{5}=\dfrac{15}{5}=3\)

2

\(\bar y=\dfrac{2+4+5+4+5}{5}=\dfrac{20}{5}=4\)

Step 2: the deviations.

\(x_i-\bar x\): \(1-3,\ 2-3,\ 3-3,\ 4-3,\ 5-3=-2,\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 2\).

\(y_i-\bar y\): \(2-4,\ 4-4,\ 5-4,\ 4-4,\ 5-4=-2,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1\).

Step 3–4: the two sums.

1

\(S_{xx}=(-2)^2+(-1)^2+0^2+1^2+2^2\)

2

\(=4+1+0+1+4=10\)

3

\(S_{xy}=(-2)(-2)+(-1)(0)+(0)(1)+(1)(0)+(2)(1)\)

4

\(=4+0+0+0+2=6\)

Step 5–6: the slope and the intercept.

1

\(\hat\beta_1=\dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\dfrac{6}{10}=0.6\)

2

\(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=4-0.6\times3\)

3

\(=4-1.8=2.2\)

Self-check: \(S_{xx}=10>0\). \(S_{xy}=6\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) are both positive. \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\bar x=2.2+0.6\times3=2.2+1.8=4=\bar y\).

Thus, the fitted line for the small data set is \(\hat y=2.2+0.6x\).

**Example 2 · The brainhead data** Slides p.45

The brainhead data have 236 observations, so this unit does not calculate the sums by hand. Slides p.45 prints the two estimates.

\(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\) g and \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) g per cm³.

The fitted line is \(\hat y=335.43231+0.26082x\).

Figure 1-1 shows the 236 points and this fitted line. The green point is \((\bar x,\bar y)\). It is on the line, as the self-check says.

[figure]
Figure 1-1 · The brainhead data (blue points, \(n=236\)) and the least squares line from Slides p.45 (orange line). The line goes through the point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) (green point).

Results for later units

Small data set: \(n=5\), \(\bar x=3\), \(\bar y=4\), \(S_{xx}=10\), \(S_{xy}=6\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\), \(\hat\beta_0=2.2\).

Brainhead data (Slides p.45): \(n=236\), \(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\).

**Why** Added

The chains below set the two partial derivatives of Slides p.6 to 0 and solve. The first chain solves for \(\hat\beta_0\).

1

\(\dfrac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_0}=\sum_{i=1}^n2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)(-1)\)

chain rule

2

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)\)

set to 0, divide by \(-2\)

3

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i-n\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\)

4

\(n\hat\beta_0=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\)

5

\(\hat\beta_0=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ny_i-\hat\beta_1\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\)

6

\(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\)

definition of \(\bar x,\bar y\)

The second chain solves for \(\hat\beta_1\). It puts in the result for \(\hat\beta_0\).

1

\(\dfrac{\partial S}{\partial\beta_1}=\sum_{i=1}^n2(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)(-x_i)\)

chain rule

2

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)x_i\)

set to 0, divide by \(-2\)

3

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^ny_ix_i-\hat\beta_0n\bar x-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2\)

\(\sum x_i=n\bar x\)

4

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^ny_ix_i-(\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x)n\bar x-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2\)

put in \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\)

5

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^ny_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x+\hat\beta_1n\bar x^2-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2\)

6

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^ny_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x+\hat\beta_1\Big(n\bar x^2-\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2\Big)\)

7

\(\hat\beta_1=\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^ny_ix_i-n\bar y\bar x}{\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2-n\bar x^2}\)

The last two chains show that the denominator is \(S_{xx}\) and the numerator is \(S_{xy}\). The first chain is for the denominator.

1

\(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\)

2

\(=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2-2\bar x\sum_{i=1}^nx_i+n\bar x^2\)

3

\(=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2-2n\bar x^2+n\bar x^2\)

\(\sum x_i=n\bar x\)

4

\(=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2-n\bar x^2\)

The second chain is for the numerator.

1

\(S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\)

2

\(=\sum_{i=1}^nx_iy_i-\bar y\sum_{i=1}^nx_i-\bar x\sum_{i=1}^ny_i+n\bar x\bar y\)

3

\(=\sum_{i=1}^nx_iy_i-n\bar x\bar y-n\bar x\bar y+n\bar x\bar y\)

\(\sum x_i=n\bar x,\ \sum y_i=n\bar y\)

4

\(=\sum_{i=1}^nx_iy_i-n\bar x\bar y\)

∎ Thus, \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).

Check on the small data set: \(\sum x_i^2=55\), so \(\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2=55-5\times3^2=55-45=10=S_{xx}\).

Check on the small data set: \(\sum x_iy_i=66\), so \(\sum x_iy_i-n\bar x\bar y=66-5\times3\times4=66-60=6=S_{xy}\).

This section gives \(\hat\beta_0=2.2\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) for the small data set. The next section uses them to calculate the residuals and \(\hat\sigma^2\).

### 01.5 Fitted values, residuals, and \(\hat\sigma^2\) Slides p.8

This section estimates the third parameter, \(\sigma^2\). First, it calculates the residual of each point. Then it adds the squared residuals and divides by \(n-2\). Units 04–06 use \(\hat\sigma\) in the standard error and in the \(t\) statistic.

**What** Slides p.8

Fitted Values, Residuals, and σ̂² · Lecture 3 · p.8 Fitted values: \[\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\] Residuals: \[e_i=y_i-\hat y_i=y_i-(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i)\] • Note: \(e_i\) are different from errors, \(\epsilon_i=y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\), and have different properties
Estimate of \(\sigma^2\) is: \[\hat\sigma^2=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{n-2}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2}{n-2}\] • This is not the MLE—instead it is an unbiased estimate of \(\sigma^2\)

The fitted value \(\hat y_i\) is the height of the fitted line at \(x=x_i\).

The residual \(e_i\) is the observed value minus the fitted value: \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). It uses the fitted line, so we can calculate it.

The error \(\epsilon_i\) is the observed value minus the population line. The population line is unknown, so we cannot calculate \(\epsilon_i\). The residual \(e_i\) is the calculable replacement for \(\epsilon_i\).

The sum of squared residuals \(\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2\) is the minimum value of \(S\). It occurs at the least squares line.

An estimator is unbiased when its expected value is equal to the parameter. Here, \(E[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2\).

\(\hat\sigma\) is the square root of \(\hat\sigma^2\). It has the same unit as \(y\).

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat y_i\), \(e_i\), and \(\hat\sigma^2\)

- Calculate each fitted value \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\).
- Calculate each residual \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\).
- Square each residual. Add the squares to get \(\sum e_i^2\).
- Divide the sum by \(n-2\). The result is \(\hat\sigma^2\).
- Take the square root of \(\hat\sigma^2\). The result is \(\hat\sigma\).

**Self-check:** \(\sum e_i=0\), with a small rounding difference. \(\hat\sigma^2>0\). The denominator is \(n-2\), not \(n\).

**Example 1 · The small data set** Added How steps 1–5

This example uses \(\hat\beta_0=2.2\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) from Section 01.4.

Step 1: the fitted values.

1

\(\hat\beta_1x_i:\ 0.6(1),\ 0.6(2),\ 0.6(3),\ 0.6(4),\ 0.6(5)=0.6,\ 1.2,\ 1.8,\ 2.4,\ 3.0\)

2

\(\hat y_i:\ 2.2+0.6,\ 2.2+1.2,\ 2.2+1.8,\ 2.2+2.4,\ 2.2+3.0\)

3

\(\hat y_i:\ 2.8,\ 3.4,\ 4.0,\ 4.6,\ 5.2\)

Step 2: the residuals.

1

\(e_i:\ 2-2.8,\ 4-3.4,\ 5-4.0,\ 4-4.6,\ 5-5.2\)

2

\(e_i:\ -0.8,\ 0.6,\ 1.0,\ -0.6,\ -0.2\)

Self-check: \(-0.8+0.6+1.0-0.6-0.2=0\).

Figure 1-2 shows the five points, the fitted line, and the residuals.

[figure]
Figure 1-2 (Added) · The small data set. The blue points are the observations \((x_i,y_i)\). The orange points are the fitted values \((x_i,\hat y_i)\) on the fitted line. The length of each purple segment is \(|e_i|\). A point above the line has \(e_i>0\). A point below the line has \(e_i<0\).

Step 3–5: the squared residuals and \(\hat\sigma^2\).

1

\(e_i^2:\ (-0.8)^2,\ 0.6^2,\ 1.0^2,\ (-0.6)^2,\ (-0.2)^2=0.64,\ 0.36,\ 1.00,\ 0.36,\ 0.04\)

2

\(\sum_{i=1}^5e_i^2=0.64+0.36+1.00+0.36+0.04=2.4\)

3

\(\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{2.4}{5-2}=\dfrac{2.4}{3}=0.8\)

4

\(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{0.8}=0.8944\)

Thus, the points of the small data set are at a typical vertical distance of about 0.89 from the fitted line.

**Example 2 · The brainhead data** Slides p.45

Slides p.45 prints \(\hat\sigma=72.35\) g with 234 degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom are the denominator \(n-2\).

1

\(n-2=236-2=234\)

2

\(\hat\sigma^2=72.35^2=5234.52\ \text{g}^2\)

from the rounded \(\hat\sigma\)

Thus, at a fixed head size, brain weight has a typical distance of about 72.35 g from the fitted line.

Results for later units (continued)

Small data set: \(\sum e_i^2=2.4\), \(\hat\sigma^2=0.8\), \(\hat\sigma=0.8944\), \(n-2=3\).

Brainhead data (Slides p.45): \(\hat\sigma=72.35\), \(n-2=234\).

**Why · \(\sum e_i=0\) and the denominator \(n-2\)** Added

The first chain explains the self-check \(\sum e_i=0\). It starts from line 2 of the \(\hat\beta_0\) chain in Section 01.4.

1

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)\)

Section 01.4, \(\hat\beta_0\) chain, line 2

2

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat y_i)\)

definition of \(\hat y_i\)

3

\(0=\sum_{i=1}^ne_i\)

definition of \(e_i\)

The second chain explains the denominator \(n-2\). It uses the chi-squared distribution \(\chi^2_\nu\). This is a distribution of non-negative values with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom and mean \(E[\chi^2_\nu]=\nu\). The course gives \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\).

1

\(E[\hat\sigma^2]=E\left[\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2}{n-2}\right]\)

2

\(=\sigma^2E\left[\dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2}{n-2}\right]\)

3

\(=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n-2}E\left[\dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2\right]\)

linearity of expectation

4

\(=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n-2}(n-2)\)

mean of \(\chi^2_{(n-2)}\) is \(n-2\)

5

\(=\sigma^2\)

∎ Thus, the denominator \(n-2\) makes \(\hat\sigma^2\) unbiased. The "2" is the number of estimated line parameters, \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). Slides p.8 states that this estimate is not the MLE.

This section gives \(\hat\sigma=0.8944\) for the small data set and \(\hat\sigma=72.35\) for the brainhead data. Unit 02 uses \(S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\sigma\) to study the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\).

**Q1.** A data set has \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\). The least squares line is \(\hat y=2.2+0.6x\). Calculate the fitted value \(\hat y_3\) and the residual \(e_3\). Is point 3 above or below the fitted line?

Answer

1

\(\hat y_3=2.2+0.6\times3\)

\(=2.2+1.8=4.0\)

\(e_3=y_3-\hat y_3=5-4.0=1.0\)

\(e_3>0\). Thus, point 3 is above the fitted line.

**Q2.** For the brainhead data, \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) (Slides p.45). Interpret \(\hat\beta_1\). Then estimate the difference in mean brain weight between a population with head size 4000 cm³ and a population with head size 3000 cm³.

Answer

Compare two populations whose head sizes differ by 1 cm³. The estimated mean brain weight is 0.26082 g higher in the population with the larger head size.

1

\(k=4000-3000=1000\)

2

\(k\hat\beta_1=1000\times0.26082\)

Section 01.3, How step 5

3

\(=260.82\) g

Thus, the estimated mean brain weight is 260.82 g higher for the 4000 cm³ population.

**Q3.** For the small data set, \(\sum_{i=1}^5e_i^2=2.4\). Calculate \(\hat\sigma^2\) and \(\hat\sigma\). Why is the denominator \(n-2\)?

Answer

1

\(\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{2.4}{5-2}=\dfrac{2.4}{3}\)

2

\(=0.8\)

3

\(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{0.8}=0.8944\)

The denominator \(n-2\) makes \(\hat\sigma^2\) unbiased. The quantity \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum e_i^2\) has a \(\chi^2_{(n-2)}\) distribution with mean \(n-2\). Thus, \(E[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2\).

This unit gives the model, the meaning of \(\beta_1\), and three estimates: \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), and \(\hat\sigma\). Unit 02 treats \(\hat\beta_1\) as a random variable and finds its sampling distribution.

## 02 · Sampling distribution and unbiasedness of \(\hat\beta_1\)

This unit shows how \(\hat\beta_1\) changes from one sample to a different sample. It has three steps. First, we write \(\hat\beta_1\) as a weighted sum of the \(y_i\). Then we find its distribution. Last, we show that its mean is \(\beta_1\).

Plan · Slides p.9–18

Step 1: The title page starts the new material (Slides p.9).

Step 2: Different samples give different estimates (Slides p.10).

Step 3: Read the section page "Properties of LS Estimator" (Slides p.11).

Step 4: Write \(\hat\beta_1\) as \(\sum w_iy_i\) (Slides p.12).

Step 5: Find the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) (Slides p.13).

Step 6: Show that \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\), so \(\hat\beta_1\) is unbiased (Slides p.14–18).

### 02.1 Title page Slides p.9

Page 9 repeats the title page of Lecture 3. The recap (p.1–8) stops here, and the new material starts.

Title: Lecture 3: Simple Linear Regression: Inference.

This page has no formulas. The next section starts with the question on p.10.

### 02.2 Why we need inference Slides p.10

This section shows one fact: an estimate changes when the sample changes. All later sections of this lecture measure the size of this change.

**What** Slides p.10

Inference for \(\beta\) · Lecture 3 · p.10 (slide 7/25) In two different samples, we will get different estimates of β.
How do we acknowledge this variability?
How do we characterize uncertainty in our estimates?
• Standard errors
• Confidence intervals
• Hypothesis tests

The slide uses these technical names.

Sample: the \(n\) data pairs \((x_i,y_i)\) that we have. The brainhead data have \(n=236\) pairs.

One sample gives one estimate. Example: \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\) for the brainhead data (Lecture 2 · p.38).

Variability: the estimate changes when we use a different sample.

Uncertainty: we do not know the distance between the estimate and the true value \(\beta_1\).

Standard errors, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests are three tools that describe uncertainty. Later units of this lecture teach them.

All three tools need one fact first: the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) over different samples. This unit finds that distribution.

**How** Added

Compare the estimates from two samples

- Divide the data into two samples.
- For each sample, calculate \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\).
- For each sample, calculate \(S_{xy}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)\) and \(S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\).
- For each sample, calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).
- Compare the two values of \(\hat\beta_1\).

**Self-check:** Keep each \(x_i\) with its own \(y_i\). Each pair must stay in the same sample.

**Example · Two samples of three observations** Added

This example uses the first six observations of the brainhead data (Lecture 2 · p.10). Here, \(x\) is head size (cm³) and \(y\) is brain weight (g).

Observations 1–6: \((4512,1530)\), \((3738,1297)\), \((4261,1335)\), \((3777,1282)\), \((4177,1590)\), \((3585,1300)\).

Sample A is observations 1–3. Sample B is observations 4–6.

Sample A, step 2:

1

\[\bar x=\frac{4512+3738+4261}{3}=\frac{12511}{3}=4170.333\]

2

\[\bar y=\frac{1530+1297+1335}{3}=\frac{4162}{3}=1387.333\]

Sample A, step 3. The deviations are \(x_i-\bar x=341.667,\ -432.333,\ 90.667\) and \(y_i-\bar y=142.667,\ -90.333,\ -52.333\).

1

\[S_{xy}=(142.667)(341.667)+(-90.333)(-432.333)+(-52.333)(90.667)\]

2

\[=48744.444+39054.111-4744.889\]

3

\[=83053.667\]

4

\[S_{xx}=341.667^2+(-432.333)^2+90.667^2\]

5

\[=116736.111+186912.111+8220.444\]

6

\[=311868.667\]

Sample A, step 4:

1

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{83053.667}{311868.667}=0.2663\]

Sample B, step 2:

1

\[\bar x=\frac{3777+4177+3585}{3}=\frac{11539}{3}=3846.333\]

2

\[\bar y=\frac{1282+1590+1300}{3}=\frac{4172}{3}=1390.667\]

Sample B, step 3. The deviations are \(x_i-\bar x=-69.333,\ 330.667,\ -261.333\) and \(y_i-\bar y=-108.667,\ 199.333,\ -90.667\).

1

\[S_{xy}=(-108.667)(-69.333)+(199.333)(330.667)+(-90.667)(-261.333)\]

2

\[=7534.222+65912.889+23694.222\]

3

\[=97141.333\]

4

\[S_{xx}=(-69.333)^2+330.667^2+(-261.333)^2\]

5

\[=4807.111+109340.444+68295.111\]

6

\[=182442.667\]

Sample B, step 4:

1

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{97141.333}{182442.667}=0.5324\]

Step 5 compares the results.

Sample A gives \(\hat\beta_1=0.2663\). Sample B gives \(\hat\beta_1=0.5324\).

All 236 observations give \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\) (Lecture 2 · p.38).

The three values are different. We do not know which value is nearest to the true \(\beta_1\).

This example shows that \(\hat\beta_1\) changes from sample to sample.

**Why** Added

We calculate \(\hat\beta_1\) from \(y_1,\dots,y_n\). The model is \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\). The error \(\epsilon_i\) is random. A different sample has different \(\epsilon_i\), thus different \(y_i\), thus a different \(\hat\beta_1\).

Thus \(\hat\beta_1\) is a random variable. A random variable is a quantity whose value comes from a random outcome. The next sections find its distribution.

### 02.3 Section page: properties of the LS estimator Slides p.11

Page 11 is a section page with the title "Properties of LS Estimator".

LS estimator (least squares estimator): the formula that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. For the slope, it is \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).

The estimator is a function of the random \(y_i\). Thus it is a random variable. One data set gives one estimate.

This section studies the properties of this estimator. It starts with \(\hat\beta_1\).

### 02.4 Write \(\hat\beta_1\) as a linear combination of the \(y_i\) Slides p.12

This section writes \(\hat\beta_1\) as \(\sum w_iy_i\). With this form, we can get the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) from the distribution of the \(y_i\).

**What** Slides p.12

Properties of \(\hat\beta_1\) · Lecture 3 · p.12 (slide 8/25) Recall: \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\) \[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}=\frac{\sum_i y_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i\] where \(w_i=\frac{(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\) are fixed with respect to \(y\).
Hence \(\hat\beta_1\) is a linear combination of independent Normals!

The slide uses these symbols and names.

\(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\): each \(y_i\) has a Normal distribution with mean \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). The \(y_i\) are independent of each other.

Independent: the value of one \(y_i\) gives no information about the value of a different \(y_i\).

\(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\): the sample means of \(x\) and \(y\).

The denominator \(\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\) is \(S_{xx}\). Its index is \(j\), so that it is different from the index \(i\) in the numerator.

Weight \(w_i\): the number that multiplies \(y_i\) in \(\hat\beta_1\).

Fixed with respect to \(y\): \(w_i\) uses only \(x_1,\dots,x_n\). The model treats each \(x_i\) as a known constant, so \(w_i\) is a constant.

Linear combination: a sum of quantities, each multiplied by a constant, for example \(a_1y_1+a_2y_2+\dots+a_ny_n\). Here the constants are the \(w_i\).

Thus p.12 says: \(\hat\beta_1\) is a sum of independent Normal variables \(y_i\), each multiplied by a constant \(w_i\).

**How** Added

Calculate the \(w_i\) and use them to get \(\hat\beta_1\)

- Calculate \(\bar x\).
- Calculate \(S_{xx}=\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\).
- For each \(i\), calculate \(w_i=(x_i-\bar x)/S_{xx}\).
- Calculate \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i\).
- Compare the result of step 4 with \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).

**Self-check:** (1) \(\sum w_iy_i\) must equal \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\). (2) \(\sum w_i\) must equal 0. (3) \(\sum w_ix_i\) must equal 1.

(4) If \(x_i>\bar x\), then \(w_i>0\). If \(x_i<\bar x\), then \(w_i<0\). Section 02.6 shows the reasons for (2) and (3).

**Example · Six observations of the brainhead data** Added

This example does the five steps on the six observations from Lecture 2 · p.10. It also does all four self-checks.

Step 1:

1

\[\bar x=\frac{4512+3738+4261+3777+4177+3585}{6}\]

2

\[=\frac{24050}{6}\]

3

\[=4008.333\]

Step 2. The deviations \(x_i-\bar x\) are \(503.667,\ -270.333,\ 252.667,\ -231.333,\ 168.667,\ -423.333\).

1

\[S_{xx}=503.667^2+(-270.333)^2+252.667^2+(-231.333)^2+168.667^2+(-423.333)^2\]

2

\[=253680.111+73080.111+63840.444+53515.111+28448.444+179211.111\]

3

\[=651775.333\]

Step 3 divides each deviation by \(S_{xx}=651775.333\).

\(w_1=503.667/651775.333=7.7276\times10^{-4}\)

\(w_2=-270.333/651775.333=-4.1476\times10^{-4}\)

\(w_3=252.667/651775.333=3.8766\times10^{-4}\)

\(w_4=-231.333/651775.333=-3.5493\times10^{-4}\)

\(w_5=168.667/651775.333=2.5878\times10^{-4}\)

\(w_6=-423.333/651775.333=-6.4951\times10^{-4}\)

Step 4 multiplies each \(w_i\) by its \(y_i\) and adds the products.

1

\[\sum w_iy_i=(7.7276\times10^{-4})(1530)+(-4.1476\times10^{-4})(1297)+\dots+(-6.4951\times10^{-4})(1300)\]

2

\[=1.18232-0.53795+0.51752-0.45502+0.41146-0.84436\]

3

\[=0.2740\]

The sum of the rounded terms is 0.27397. The unrounded sum is 0.27398.

Step 5 calculates \(S_{xy}\) in the usual way. Here \(\bar y=8334/6=1389\), so \(y_i-\bar y=141,\ -92,\ -54,\ -107,\ 201,\ -89\).

1

\[S_{xy}=(141)(503.667)+(-92)(-270.333)+\dots+(-89)(-423.333)\]

2

\[=71017+24870.667-13644+24752.667+33902+37676.667\]

3

\[=178575\]

4

\[\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac{178575}{651775.333}=0.2740\]

The self-checks give these results.

Check (1): \(\sum w_iy_i=0.2740\) and \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}=0.2740\). The two values are equal.

Check (2): \(\sum w_i=(503.667-270.333+252.667-231.333+168.667-423.333)/651775.333=0/651775.333=0\).

Check (3): \(\sum w_ix_i=3.48670-1.55039+1.65182-1.34056+1.08093-2.32849=1.00001\). The exact value is 1. The extra 0.00001 comes from rounding.

Check (4): observations 1, 3, 5 have \(x_i>\bar x=4008.333\) and \(w_i>0\). Observations 2, 4, 6 have \(x_i<\bar x\) and \(w_i<0\).

The figure below shows the 236 weights \(w_i\) of the full brainhead data against \(x_i\). It shows that \(w_i\) is a straight-line function of \(x_i\).

[figure]
Figure 2-1 (Added): the 236 weights \(w_i\) of the brainhead data against \(x_i\). The orange dashed line is \(\bar x\). The grey dashed line is \(w=0\). All points are on one straight line through \((\bar x,0)\) with slope \(1/S_{xx}\). To the right of \(\bar x\), the weights are positive. To the left of \(\bar x\), the weights are negative. A point far from \(\bar x\) has a large \(|w_i|\).

This example confirms the equation on p.12. The value of \(\hat\beta_1\) is \(\sum w_iy_i\), and each \(w_i\) comes only from the \(x\) values.

**Why** Slides p.12

The first equals sign on p.12 removes \(\bar y\) from the numerator. The slide does not give the reason. First we show \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\). Then we use it for this equals sign.

Helper result: the deviations add to 0.

1

\[\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-\sum_{i=1}^n\bar x\]

2

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar x\]

The sum adds the constant \(\bar x\) \(n\) times.

3

\[=n\bar x-n\bar x\]

Substitute \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=n\bar x\), from \(\bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).

4

\[=0\]

The numerator:

1

\[\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[y_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar y(x_i-\bar x)\right]\]

2

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(x_i-\bar x)-\sum_{i=1}^n\bar y(x_i-\bar x)\]

3

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar y\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)\]

\(\bar y\) has no index \(i\).

4

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar y\cdot0\]

Helper result \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\).

5

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(x_i-\bar x)\]

The six observations confirm this. The terms \(y_i(x_i-\bar x)\) are \(770610-350622.333+337310-296569.333+268180-550333.333\). Their sum is \(178575\), which is equal to \(S_{xy}\).

The split into \(\sum w_iy_i\):

1

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

2

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{y_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

The denominator has no index \(i\).

3

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\,y_i\]

4

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i\]

Definition of \(w_i\). ∎

These three chains together give the full line on p.12. The next section uses \(\hat\beta_1=\sum w_iy_i\) to find the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\).

### 02.5 The sampling distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) Slides p.13

This section gives the full distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\). It uses the result of Section 02.4: \(\hat\beta_1\) is a linear combination of independent Normal variables.

**What** Slides p.13

Properties of \(\hat\beta_1\) · Lecture 3 · p.13 (slide 8/25) Hence \(\hat\beta_1\) is a linear combination of independent Normals! \[\Longrightarrow\ \hat\beta_1\sim N\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i),\ \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\Big)\]

Sampling distribution: the distribution of the values of an estimator over all possible samples. Here the estimator is \(\hat\beta_1\).

Expectation \(E[\cdot]\): the mean value of a random variable over many repeated samples. The expectation of \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is \(\mu\).

The variance \(\mathrm{Var}[\cdot]\) measures spread (Section 01.2). The variance of \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is \(\sigma^2\).

Thus p.13 says: \(\hat\beta_1\) is Normal, with expectation \(\sum w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\) and variance \(\sigma^2\sum w_i^2\).

This step uses one rule. A linear combination of independent Normal variables is also Normal. If \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)\) and each \(a_i\) is a constant, then \(\sum a_iy_i\sim N(\sum a_i\mu_i,\ \sum a_i^2\sigma_i^2)\).

**How** Added

Write the distribution of a linear combination

- Write the estimator as \(\sum a_iy_i\). Make sure that no \(a_i\) contains \(y\). Here \(a_i=w_i\).
- Make sure that the \(y_i\) are independent and Normal. Here the model gives this.
- Write the mean \(\mu_i\) and the variance \(\sigma_i^2\) of each \(y_i\). Here \(\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\) and \(\sigma_i^2=\sigma^2\).
- Calculate the mean \(\sum a_i\mu_i\).
- Calculate the variance \(\sum a_i^2\sigma_i^2\).
- Write the result as \(N(\text{mean},\ \text{variance})\).

**Self-check:** The variance uses squared constants (\(w_i^2\)). The mean uses the constants without squares (\(w_i\)). The variance must be positive.

**Example · Six head sizes with supposed parameters** Added

The true \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma\) are unknown. For this example, we suppose that the true values are the brainhead estimates from the slides.

\(\beta_0=335.4323150\) and \(\beta_1=0.2608207\) (Lecture 2 · p.38).

\(\sigma=72.35\), the value of \(\hat\sigma\) on Slides p.45.

The \(x_i\) are the six head sizes of Section 02.4. The weights \(w_i\) are the six weights of Section 02.4.

Steps 1–3: \(a_i=w_i\). The model makes the \(y_i\) independent and Normal. Each mean is \(\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\). For observation 1:

1

\[\mu_1=335.4323150+0.2608207\times4512\]

2

\[=335.4323150+1176.8229984\]

3

\[=1512.2553\]

The same calculation gives \(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_6=1512.2553,\ 1310.3801,\ 1446.7893,\ 1320.5521,\ 1424.8804,\ 1270.4745\). These are the fitted values on Lecture 2 · p.38.

Step 4 calculates the mean:

1

\[\sum w_i\mu_i=(7.7276\times10^{-4})(1512.2553)+\dots+(-6.4951\times10^{-4})(1270.4745)\]

2

\[=1.16861-0.54350+0.56086-0.46870+0.36873-0.82518\]

3

\[=0.26082\]

Step 5 calculates the variance:

1

\[\sum w_i^2=5.9716\times10^{-7}+1.7203\times10^{-7}+1.5028\times10^{-7}+1.2597\times10^{-7}+0.66967\times10^{-7}+4.2186\times10^{-7}\]

2

\[=1.5343\times10^{-6}\]

3

\[\sigma^2\sum w_i^2=72.35^2\times1.5343\times10^{-6}\]

4

\[=5234.5225\times1.5343\times10^{-6}\]

5

\[=0.00803\]

Step 6:

For these six head sizes, \(\hat\beta_1\sim N(0.26082,\ 0.00803)\).

The mean 0.26082 is equal to the supposed \(\beta_1=0.2608207\). Section 02.6 shows that this is always true.

The figure below shows a sampling distribution. It comes from a computer simulation with all 236 head sizes and the same supposed \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma\). The simulation made 10000 new sets of \(y\) values from the model. For each set, it calculated \(\hat\beta_1=\sum w_iy_i\).

Figure 2-2 (Added): histogram of 10000 simulated values of \(\hat\beta_1\). The height of each bar is the number of values in that interval. The shape is a bell, which is the shape of a Normal distribution. The centre is near the orange line, which is the supposed \(\beta_1\).

Each sample gives one \(\hat\beta_1\). Together, the values make the bell-shaped sampling distribution of p.13. The next unit simplifies the variance \(\sigma^2\sum w_i^2\).

**Why** Slides p.13

The Normal shape comes from the rule above. The two chains below give the mean and the variance on p.13.

The mean:

1

\[E[\hat\beta_1]=E\Big[\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i\Big]\]

Section 02.4: \(\hat\beta_1=\sum w_iy_i\).

2

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iE[y_i]\]

Linearity of expectation; each \(w_i\) is a constant.

3

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\]

Model: \(E[y_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\).

The variance:

1

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i\Big]\]

2

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{Var}[w_iy_i]\]

The \(y_i\) are independent.

3

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\,\mathrm{Var}[y_i]\]

\(\mathrm{Var}[aY]=a^2\mathrm{Var}[Y]\).

4

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\sigma^2\]

Model: \(\mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\sigma^2\).

5

\[=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\]

∎

These two chains give the two parameters on p.13. The next section simplifies the mean to \(\beta_1\).

### 02.6 The mean of \(\hat\beta_1\): unbiasedness Slides p.14–18

This section simplifies the mean \(\sum w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\) from Section 02.5. The result is \(\beta_1\). Thus, on average, \(\hat\beta_1\) is equal to the true value.

**What** Slides p.14–18

Mean of \(\hat\beta_1\) · Lecture 3 · p.14–18 (slide 9/25) \[\begin{aligned}E[\hat\beta_1]&=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\\&=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\\&=\beta_0\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}+\beta_1\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\\&=0+\beta_1\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\\&=\beta_1\end{aligned}\] Hence it is unbiased.

Section 01.5 defines an unbiased estimator: its expectation is equal to the parameter. Here \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\).

In plain words: repeat the sampling many times and calculate \(\hat\beta_1\) each time. The mean of these values is the true \(\beta_1\).

One single \(\hat\beta_1\) can still be different from \(\beta_1\).

Pages 14–18 are five build steps of one slide. Each page adds one line. Page 18 is the full slide, and the quote above copies it.

**How** Added

Show that the linear estimator \(\sum w_iy_i\) is unbiased

- Write \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\sum w_iE[y_i]=\sum w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\).
- Split the sum into two terms: \(\beta_0\sum w_i+\beta_1\sum w_ix_i\).
- Show that \(\sum w_i=0\). Use \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)=0\) in the numerator.
- Show that \(\sum w_ix_i=1\). Show that the numerator \(\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)\) equals the denominator \(\sum(x_j-\bar x)^2\).
- Substitute: \(\beta_0\cdot0+\beta_1\cdot1=\beta_1\).

**Self-check:** The final result must not contain \(\beta_0\) or any \(x_i\).

**Example · Six head sizes with supposed parameters** Added

This example does steps 2–5 for the six observations of Section 02.4. It uses the same supposed \(\beta_0=335.4323150\) and \(\beta_1=0.2608207\) as Section 02.5.

Step 3: \(\sum w_i=0\) (check (2) in Section 02.4). Thus \(\beta_0\sum w_i=335.4323150\times0=0\).

Step 4: \(\sum w_ix_i=1\) (check (3) in Section 02.4). Thus \(\beta_1\sum w_ix_i=0.2608207\times1=0.2608207\).

Step 5: \(\sum w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)=0+0.2608207=0.2608207\). This is the supposed \(\beta_1\).

Section 02.5 calculated the same mean term by term and got 0.26082. The two results agree.

The simulation of Figure 2-2 gives a mean of 0.26063 for the 10000 values. This is near \(\beta_1=0.2608207\).

This example confirms that the mean of \(\hat\beta_1\) is \(\beta_1\) for these six head sizes.

**Why** Slides p.14–18

Slides p.18 does not give reasons for two steps. One step is "\(=0\)". The other step changes \(\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)\) to \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)\). First we show the second step. Then we write the full chain.

Helper result: \(\sum x_i(x_i-\bar x)=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\).

1

\[\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[x_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar x(x_i-\bar x)\right]\]

2

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar x\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)\]

\(\bar x\) has no index \(i\).

3

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar x\cdot0\]

Helper result of Section 02.4: \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\).

4

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)\]

The six observations confirm this. The terms \(x_i(x_i-\bar x)\) are \(2272544-1010506+1076612.667-873746+704520.667-1517650\). Their sum is \(651775.333\), which is equal to \(S_{xx}\).

The main chain (the five lines of p.18):

1

\[E[\hat\beta_1]=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\]

Mean from Section 02.5. p.14.

2

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\]

Definition of \(w_i\). p.15.

3

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\beta_0(x_i-\bar x)+\beta_1x_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

4

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\beta_0(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\beta_1x_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

5

\[=\beta_0\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}+\beta_1\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\), and the denominator have no index \(i\). p.16.

6

\[=\beta_0\frac{0}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}+\beta_1\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

Helper result of Section 02.4.

7

\[=0+\beta_1\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

8

\[=0+\beta_1\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

Helper result above. p.17.

9

\[=\beta_1\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

10

\[=\beta_1\]

The numerator and the denominator are the same sum with a different index letter. p.18. ∎

Thus \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\), and \(\hat\beta_1\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\beta_1\). With Section 02.5, the result of p.13 becomes \(\hat\beta_1\sim N(\beta_1,\ \sigma^2\sum w_i^2)\). The next unit simplifies the variance \(\sigma^2\sum w_i^2\).

### 02.7 Practice Added

These three questions test the three parts of this unit: the weights \(w_i\), their two properties, and the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\).

**Q1.** A data set has three pairs: \((x_i,y_i)=(1,2),\ (3,3),\ (5,7)\). Calculate \(w_1,w_2,w_3\). Then calculate \(\hat\beta_1=\sum w_iy_i\) and compare it with \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).

Answer

Step 1: \(\bar x=(1+3+5)/3=9/3=3\).

Step 2: \(x_i-\bar x=-2,\ 0,\ 2\). Thus \(S_{xx}=(-2)^2+0^2+2^2=4+0+4=8\).

Step 3: \(w_1=-2/8=-0.25\), \(w_2=0/8=0\), \(w_3=2/8=0.25\).

Step 4: \(\sum w_iy_i=(-0.25)(2)+(0)(3)+(0.25)(7)=-0.5+0+1.75=1.25\).

Step 5: \(\bar y=(2+3+7)/3=12/3=4\), so \(y_i-\bar y=-2,\ -1,\ 3\). Then \(S_{xy}=(-2)(-2)+(-1)(0)+(3)(2)=4+0+6=10\). Thus \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}=10/8=1.25\).

Self-check: \(\sum w_i=-0.25+0+0.25=0\). \(\sum w_ix_i=(-0.25)(1)+(0)(3)+(0.25)(5)=-0.25+0+1.25=1\).

This question uses the procedure of Section 02.4.

**Q2.** Let \(w_i=\frac{(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\). Show that \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_ix_i=1\).

Answer

1

\[\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

The denominator has no index \(i\).

2

\[=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar x}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

3

\[=\frac{n\bar x-n\bar x}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

\(\sum x_i=n\bar x\).

4

\[=0\]

1

\[\sum_{i=1}^n w_ix_i=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

2

\[=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar x\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

The new term is \(\bar x\cdot0=0\).

3

\[=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

4

\[=1\]

These two chains are steps 3 and 4 of the procedure in Section 02.6.

**Q3.** Use the three \(x\) values of Q1. Suppose that \(\beta_0=1\), \(\beta_1=1\), and \(\sigma=2\). Write the sampling distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\). Which two parts of the model make \(\hat\beta_1\) exactly Normal?

Answer

Means: \(\mu_i=1+x_i\), so \(\mu_1=2\), \(\mu_2=4\), \(\mu_3=6\).

Mean of \(\hat\beta_1\): \(\sum w_i\mu_i=(-0.25)(2)+(0)(4)+(0.25)(6)=-0.5+0+1.5=1\). This is equal to \(\beta_1=1\).

\(\sum w_i^2=0.0625+0+0.0625=0.125\).

Variance of \(\hat\beta_1\): \(\sigma^2\sum w_i^2=4\times0.125=0.5\).

Result: \(\hat\beta_1\sim N(1,\ 0.5)\).

Two parts of the model make \(\hat\beta_1\) Normal: (1) each \(y_i\) is Normal, and (2) the \(y_i\) are independent. The \(w_i\) are constants, so \(\sum w_iy_i\) is a linear combination of independent Normals.

This question uses the results of Sections 02.5 and 02.6.

This unit wrote \(\hat\beta_1\) as \(\sum w_iy_i\), showed that it is Normal, and showed that \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\). The next unit simplifies the variance \(\sigma^2\sum w_i^2\) and gives the distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\).
