This unit calculates the variance of \(\hat\beta_1\). Then it states the full distributions of \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\beta_0\). The next unit uses these distributions to make a confidence interval for \(\beta_1\).

Plan · Slides p.19–24

Step 1: Calculate \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\) (Slides p.19–23). The slides show one equation chain in 5 parts.

Step 2: Put the mean and the variance together. State the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) (Slides p.24, top).

Step 3: State the distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\) (Slides p.24, bottom). The slides give only the result.

Step 4: Practice questions (Added).

First, this unit repeats the results that it uses from Units 01–02.

Model (Slides p.12): \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\ \sigma^2)\), \(i=1,\dots,n\).

Weight \(w_i=\dfrac{x_i-\bar x}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\). Thus \(\hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i\) (Slides p.12). Each \(w_i\) uses only the \(x\) values. Thus \(w_i\) is a fixed constant with respect to \(y\).

Two results from Unit 02: \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\) (Slides p.13), and \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\) (Slides p.18).

The examples in this unit use six head sizes. Added

The data are the first 6 brainhead observations (Lecture 2 · p.10). \(x\) is the head size in cm³. \(y\) is the brain weight in g.

| \(i\) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6

| \(x_i\) (cm³) | 4512 | 3738 | 4261 | 3777 | 4177 | 3585

The formulas in this unit use only \(x\) and \(\sigma\). They do not use the \(y\) values.

The true \(\sigma\) is not known. For the examples, this unit supposes \(\sigma=72.35\) g, the value of \(\hat\sigma\) on Slides p.45. Thus \(\sigma^2=72.35^2=5234.5225\). Unit 02 supposes the same value. Unit 04 shows the method when \(\sigma\) is not known.

### 03.1 Variance of \(\hat\beta_1\) Slides p.19–23

This section tells how much \(\hat\beta_1\) changes from sample to sample. The answer is a formula that uses only \(\sigma^2\) and the \(x\) values.

\(S_{xx}=\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\): the sum of the squared distances between each \(x_j\) and \(\bar x\). It uses only the \(x\) values.

**What** Slides p.19–23

Variance of \(\hat\beta_1\) · Lecture 3 · p.19–23 \[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]&=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\\ &=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\frac{(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\right]^2\\ &=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{\left[\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\right]^2}\\ &=\sigma^2\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}{\left[\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\right]^2}\\ &=\sigma^2\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} \end{aligned}\]

On Slides p.23, the denominator of the last line is \(\sum_{j=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\). The sum index is \(j\). Thus the term must be \(x_j\). The block above uses \(x_j\).

The variance of \(\hat\beta_1\) is equal to the error variance \(\sigma^2\) divided by \(S_{xx}\).

When \(\sigma^2\) increases, the points are farther from the line. Then the variance of \(\hat\beta_1\) increases.

When \(S_{xx}\) increases, the \(x\) values have a larger spread. Then the variance of \(\hat\beta_1\) decreases.

\(S_{xx}\) is a sum of \(n\) terms, and each term is 0 or more. An added observation cannot make \(S_{xx}\) smaller.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]\)

- Calculate \(\bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).
- Calculate each distance \(x_j-\bar x\).
- Square each distance. Add the squares to get \(S_{xx}\).
- Get \(\sigma^2\) from the question.
- Calculate \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\).
- For the standard deviation, take the square root: \(\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

**Self-check:** Calculate each \(w_i=(x_i-\bar x)/S_{xx}\). The sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\) must be equal to \(1/S_{xx}\).

Standard deviation: the square root of the variance. It has the same unit as the random variable.

**Example · Six head sizes** Added

This example uses the 6 observations and \(\sigma=72.35\). It also does the self-check.

1

Mean of \(x\) Step 1

\[\bar x=\frac{4512+3738+4261+3777+4177+3585}{6}=\frac{24050}{6}=4008.3333\]

2

Distances from \(\bar x\) Step 2

\[503.6667,\quad -270.3333,\quad 252.6667,\quad -231.3333,\quad 168.6667,\quad -423.3333\]

For example, \(x_1-\bar x=4512-4008.3333=503.6667\).

3

Squares and their sum Step 3

\[253680.1111,\quad 73080.1111,\quad 63840.4444,\quad 53515.1111,\quad 28448.4444,\quad 179211.1111\]

\[S_{xx}=253680.1111+73080.1111+63840.4444+53515.1111+28448.4444+179211.1111=651775.3333\]

The rounded squares give 651775.3332. The exact value is 651775.3333.

4

Weights and the self-check Self-check

\[w_1=\frac{503.6667}{651775.3333}=7.7276\times10^{-4},\qquad w_1^2=5.9716\times10^{-7}\]

\[w_2^2=1.7203\times10^{-7},\ w_3^2=1.5028\times10^{-7},\ w_4^2=1.2597\times10^{-7},\ w_5^2=6.6967\times10^{-8},\ w_6^2=4.2186\times10^{-7}\]

\[\sum_{i=1}^6 w_i^2=1.5343\times10^{-6},\qquad \frac{1}{S_{xx}}=\frac{1}{651775.3333}=1.5343\times10^{-6}\]

**Self-check:** The two values are equal. The equation chain of Slides p.19–23 is correct for these data.

5

Variance Steps 4–5

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}=\frac{5234.5225}{651775.3333}=0.0080312\]

6

Standard deviation Step 6

\[\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=\sqrt{0.0080312}=0.089617\]

Thus, with 6 observations, the standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\) is 0.089617 g/cm³. Unit 02 got the same variance, 0.00803, from \(\sigma^2\sum w_i^2\). ▲

Slides p.45 uses all 236 observations. There, the printed estimate of this standard deviation is 0.01307. Slides p.45

The full data have a much larger \(S_{xx}\). Thus their value is much smaller than 0.089617.

Slides p.45 uses \(\hat\sigma=72.35\) in place of \(\sigma\). Unit 04 calls this value the standard error, \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

**Why** Slides p.19–23

The derivation starts at the first line of Slides p.19. Unit 02 derived this line. \(\hat\beta_1=\sum w_iy_i\) and the \(y_i\) are independent. Thus \(\mathrm{Var}[\sum w_iy_i]=\sum w_i^2\mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\sigma^2\sum w_i^2\). Each line below makes one change.

1

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\]

Slides p.19. Derived in Unit 02.

2

\[=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\frac{(x_i-\bar x)}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\right]^2\]

Put in the definition of \(w_i\). Slides p.20.

3

\[=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{\left[\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\right]^2}\]

Square the numerator and the denominator. Slides p.21.

4

\[=\sigma^2\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}{\left[\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\right]^2}\]

The denominator does not contain \(i\). Move it out of \(\sum_i\). Slides p.22.

5

\[=\sigma^2\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}{\left[\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\right]^2}\]

The name of the sum index has no effect: \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2\).

6

\[=\sigma^2\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\]

Cancel one factor. Slides p.23.

7

\[=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\]

\(S_{xx}=\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2\). ∎

This section gives \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\). The next section puts it together with \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\) to state the full distribution.

### 03.2 Distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) Slides p.24

This section puts three results into one statement: \(\hat\beta_1\) is Normal, with mean \(\beta_1\) and variance \(\sigma^2/S_{xx}\).

**What** Slides p.24

Distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) · Lecture 3 · p.24 So the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) is: \[\hat\beta_1\sim N\Big(\beta_1,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\Big)\]

Take many samples, and calculate \(\hat\beta_1\) for each sample. The values then have a bell-shaped curve. The center of the curve is the true value \(\beta_1\). The variance of the curve is \(\sigma^2/S_{xx}\).

The symbol \(\sim\) means "has the distribution". The random variable on the left has the distribution on the right.

In \(N(\cdot,\cdot)\), the second item is the variance. It is not the standard deviation.

**How** Added

Write the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\)

- Write \(\beta_1\) as the mean. The reason is \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\).
- Calculate \(S_{xx}\) with the steps of Section 03.1.
- Write \(\sigma^2/S_{xx}\) as the variance.
- Write \(N\) as the distribution family. The reason is on Slides p.12–13.

**Self-check:** The unit of the variance is the square of the unit of \(\hat\beta_1\). Here \(\hat\beta_1\) has the unit g/cm³. Thus the variance has the unit (g/cm³)².

**Example · Six head sizes** Added

For the 6 observations, \(S_{xx}=651775.3333\) and \(\sigma^2=5234.5225\). Put these values in the formula:

\[\hat\beta_1\sim N\Big(\beta_1,\ \frac{5234.5225}{651775.3333}\Big)=N\big(\beta_1,\ 0.0080312\big)\]

The standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.0080312}=0.089617\). Thus 95% of the values of \(\hat\beta_1\) are within \(1.96\times0.089617=0.175649\) of \(\beta_1\). ▲

Figure 3-1 shows a sampling distribution with the numbers of Slides p.45. Added · Slides p.45

Slides p.45 prints \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) and the estimated standard deviation 0.01307 for all 236 observations.

The tick marks are \(0.26082+k\times0.01307\), for \(k=-3,\dots,3\). For example, \(0.26082-3\times0.01307=0.26082-0.03921=0.22161\).

[figure]
Figure 3-1 (Added): the estimated sampling distribution \(N(0.26082,\ 0.01307^2)\) of \(\hat\beta_1\) for all 236 brainhead observations (numbers from Slides p.45). The orange dashed line is the center. The green line shows 1 standard deviation on each side. Almost all of the area is between 0.22 and 0.30. This range is far from 0.

**Why** Added

1

\[\hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i,\qquad y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\]

Slides p.12.

2

\[\hat\beta_1\sim N\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i),\ \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\Big)\]

A linear combination of independent Normals is Normal. Slides p.13.

3

\[\hat\beta_1\sim N\Big(\beta_1,\ \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2\Big)\]

Put in \(\sum w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)=\beta_1\). Slides p.18.

4

\[\hat\beta_1\sim N\Big(\beta_1,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\Big)\]

Put in \(\sigma^2\sum w_i^2=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\) from Section 03.1. ∎

This section gives the full distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\). Unit 04 uses it to make a confidence interval for \(\beta_1\).

### 03.3 Distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\) Slides p.24

Slides p.24 then asks: "what about \(\hat\beta_0\)?" This section gives the answer and calculates the values for the 6 observations.

**What** Slides p.24

Distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\) · Lecture 3 · p.24 Question: what about \(\hat\beta_0\)? \[\hat\beta_0\sim N\Big(\beta_0,\ \sigma^2\Big(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\Big)\Big)\]

\(\hat\beta_0\) is also Normal and unbiased. Its mean is the true value \(\beta_0\). Its variance is \(\sigma^2\) multiplied by the sum of two terms.

The first term is \(\frac1n\). When the sample size increases, this term decreases.

The second term is \(\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\). When \(\bar x\) is farther from 0, this term increases.

The intercept \(\beta_0\) is the mean of \(y\) at \(x=0\). When the data are far from \(x=0\), the estimate of \(\beta_0\) is less precise.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_0]\)

- Calculate \(n\), \(\bar x\), and \(S_{xx}\) with the steps of Section 03.1.
- Calculate \(\frac1n\).
- Calculate \(\bar x^2\). Then calculate \(\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\).
- Add the two terms to get the factor \(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\).
- Multiply the factor by \(\sigma^2\) to get the variance.
- Take the square root to get the standard deviation.

**Self-check:** The factor must be larger than \(\frac1n\), because \(\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\geq0\).

**Example · Six head sizes** Added

This example uses the 6 observations and \(\sigma=72.35\).

1

Basic values Step 1

\[n=6,\qquad \bar x=4008.3333,\qquad S_{xx}=651775.3333\]

2

First term Step 2

\[\frac1n=\frac16=0.166667\]

3

Second term Step 3

\[\bar x^2=4008.3333^2=16066736.1111\]

\[\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}=\frac{16066736.1111}{651775.3333}=24.650727\]

4

Sum Step 4

\[\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}=0.166667+24.650727=24.817394\]

**Self-check:** 24.817394 is larger than \(\frac1n=0.166667\).

5

Multiply by \(\sigma^2\) Step 5

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_0]=5234.5225\times24.817394=129907.21\]

6

Square root Step 6

\[\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}}=\sqrt{129907.21}=360.43\]

Here \(\bar x=4008.3333\) is far from 0. Thus the second term 24.650727 is almost all of the factor 24.817394. The standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_0\) is 360.43 g. ▲

For all 236 observations, Slides p.45 prints the estimated standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_0\) as 47.77644. Slides p.45 This value uses \(\hat\sigma\) in place of \(\sigma\). Unit 04 calls it the standard error of \(\hat\beta_0\).

**Why** Added

The slides give only the result. They do not give a derivation. The reason for the mean \(\beta_0\) and for Normality is the same as for \(\hat\beta_1\). \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\) is also a linear combination of the \(y_i\). Its coefficients use only the \(x\) values. The block below shows the source of the variance formula.

Optional — not on the slides

This block gives only an outline. For the exam, use the result on the slides.

Covariance: \(\mathrm{Cov}[U,V]=E[(U-E[U])(V-E[V])]\). It shows how two random variables change together.

For two random variables, \(\mathrm{Var}[U-V]=\mathrm{Var}[U]+\mathrm{Var}[V]-2\mathrm{Cov}[U,V]\).

\(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\bar x\,\hat\beta_1\). Thus \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_0]=\mathrm{Var}[\bar y]+\bar x^2\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]-2\bar x\,\mathrm{Cov}[\bar y,\hat\beta_1]\).

\(\mathrm{Var}[\bar y]=\sigma^2/n\), and \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\).

\(\mathrm{Cov}[\bar y,\hat\beta_1]=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n w_i\sigma^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=0\), because \(\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)=0\).

Put these together: \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_0]=\sigma^2\big(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\big)\). ∎

This section gives the distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\). It has the same form as the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\). Unit 04 uses the same method to make a confidence interval for \(\beta_0\).

### 03.4 Practice Added

These three questions test the three results of this unit: the variance formula, the effect of \(S_{xx}\), and the parts of \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_0]\).

**Q1.** Use the model \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\), with \(\hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i\) and \(w_i=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{\sum_{j=1}^n(x_j-\bar x)^2}\). Show that \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\). Tell where the derivation uses independence.

Answer

\(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\mathrm{Var}[\sum w_iy_i]=\sum\mathrm{Var}[w_iy_i]\). This step uses independence. For independent \(y_i\), the variance of the sum is equal to the sum of the variances.

\(=\sum w_i^2\mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\sigma^2\sum w_i^2\).

\(=\sigma^2\sum_i\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{[\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2]^2}=\sigma^2\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}{[\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2]^2}=\sigma^2\frac{1}{\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\).

**Q2.** For the 6 observations, \(S_{xx}=651775.3333\) and \(\sigma=72.35\). A second study measures the same 6 head sizes again. The combined data have each \(x_i\) two times, so \(n=12\). (a) Calculate the new \(S_{xx}\). (b) Calculate the new standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\).

Answer

(a) Each \(x_i\) occurs two times. Thus \(\bar x\) does not change: it is 4008.3333. Each square \((x_i-\bar x)^2\) occurs two times. Thus the new \(S_{xx}=2\times651775.3333=1303550.6667\).

(b) \(\sigma^2/S_{xx}=5234.5225/1303550.6667=0.0040156\). The square root is \(\sqrt{0.0040156}=0.063369\).

This value is equal to the old value divided by \(\sqrt2\): \(0.089617/1.41421=0.063369\). When \(S_{xx}\) doubles, the variance is half.

**Q3.** For the 6 observations, \(n=6\), \(\bar x=4008.3333\), and \(S_{xx}=651775.3333\). (a) Calculate the factor \(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\). (b) Which term gives the larger part of \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_0]\)? Give the reason in one sentence.

Answer

(a) \(\frac1n=0.166667\). \(\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}=16066736.1111/651775.3333=24.650727\). The factor is \(0.166667+24.650727=24.817394\).

(b) The second term gives the larger part: \(24.650727/24.817394=0.99328\), or about 99%. The reason: the mean head size 4008.3333 is far from \(x=0\), and the intercept is the value at \(x=0\).

This unit gives two distributions: \(\hat\beta_1\sim N(\beta_1,\sigma^2/S_{xx})\) and \(\hat\beta_0\sim N\big(\beta_0,\sigma^2(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}})\big)\). Unit 04 uses them when \(\sigma\) is not known, with the t distribution and the standard error.

## 04 · Confidence interval for \(\beta_1\): known \(\sigma\), unknown \(\sigma\) (t distribution), and standard error

This unit makes an interval estimate for the unknown slope \(\beta_1\). It starts from the Normal distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\). First it uses a known \(\sigma\) and the number 1.96. Then it replaces \(\sigma\) with \(\hat\sigma\), and 1.96 changes to a t quantile. At the end, it gives the name "standard error".

Plan · Slides p.25–35

Step 1 (Slides p.25–26): Standardize \(\hat\beta_1\) to get a quantity \(Z\) with distribution \(N(0,1)\).

Step 2 (Slides p.27–30): With known \(\sigma\), start from \(P(-1.96\le Z\le1.96)=0.95\). Solve for \(\beta_1\) to get the 95% confidence interval.

Step 3 (Slides p.31–33): With unknown \(\sigma\), use \(\hat\sigma\). Show that the new quantity has the distribution \(t_{(n-2)}\).

Step 4 (Slides p.34): Replace 1.96 with the t quantile \(q=t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\). This gives the interval that we use in practice.

Step 5 (Slides p.35): Define \(\mathrm{SD}(\hat\beta_1)\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\). Write the interval as \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\).

Unit 05 calculates the full brainhead interval from Slides p.36–37.

Start point (results of Units 01–03) · Added

Model (Slides p.3): \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,\dots,n\). Here \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the errors.

SD means standard deviation (Section 03.1).

Result of Unit 03 (Slides p.24): \(\hat\beta_1\sim N\!\left(\beta_1,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\), with \(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\).

Estimate of \(\sigma^2\) (Slides p.8): \(\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2\). The residual is \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\), and the fitted value is \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\).

\(N(0,1)\) is the standard Normal distribution: a Normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1.

Brainhead data: \(x\) is head size (cm³) and \(y\) is brain weight (g). Lecture 2 · p.38 gives \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\). Slides p.45 give \(\hat\sigma=72.35\) on 234 degrees of freedom, so \(n-2=234\) and \(n=236\). The same slide gives \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\).

Four-point data set (Added): \((x_i,y_i)\) = (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 6), so \(n=4\). Here \(\bar x=10/4=2.5\) and \(\bar y=16/4=4\). The deviations are \(x_i-\bar x=-1.5,-0.5,0.5,1.5\) and \(y_i-\bar y=-2,-1,1,2\). Thus \(S_{xy}=3+0.5+0.5+3=7\) and \(S_{xx}=2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25=5\). The estimates are \(\hat\beta_1=7/5=1.4\) and \(\hat\beta_0=4-1.4\times2.5=0.5\).

### 04.1 Standardize \(\hat\beta_1\) Slides p.25–26

This section changes \(\hat\beta_1\) into a quantity \(Z\) with the fixed distribution \(N(0,1)\). All the confidence intervals in this unit start from this \(Z\).

Slides p.25 is the section page "Confidence Interval for \(\beta_1\)". It has no formulas.

**What** Slides p.26

Confidence interval for β1 · Lecture 3 · p.26 \[\hat\beta_1\sim N\!\left(\beta_1,\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim N(0,1)\]

Confidence interval (CI): an interval that we calculate from the data. The method makes the interval contain the unknown parameter with a given probability, for example 95%.

Standardize: subtract the mean of a random variable, then divide by its standard deviation. The result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

The standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\) is \(\sqrt{\sigma^2/S_{xx}}=\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). Thus the slide subtracts the mean \(\beta_1\) and divides by \(\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

The distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) contains the unknown values \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma\). After we standardize, the distribution is \(N(0,1)\). This distribution contains no unknown values. Thus we can use known probabilities of \(N(0,1)\) to make statements about \(\beta_1\).

This section gives \(Z=\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim N(0,1)\). The How steps below calculate each part of \(Z\) from data.

**How** Added

Write \(Z\) for a data set

- **Get the mean.** The mean of \(\hat\beta_1\) is \(\beta_1\) (Unit 02, unbiased).
- **Get the standard deviation.** Take the square root of the variance \(\sigma^2/S_{xx}\). The result is \(\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).
- **Calculate \(\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).** ① Calculate \(\bar x\). ② Calculate each \((x_i-\bar x)^2\). ③ Add them to get \(S_{xx}\). ④ Take the square root.
- **Write \(Z\).** The numerator is \(\hat\beta_1-\beta_1\). The denominator is \(\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

Self-check: the denominator contains \(\sqrt{S_{xx}}\), not \(S_{xx}\). The denominator is a standard deviation, not a variance.

**Example · Four-point data set** Added

This example calculates the part of the denominator of \(Z\) that comes from the data.

1

Mean of \(x\) How step 3 ①

\[\bar x=\frac{1+2+3+4}{4}=\frac{10}{4}=2.5\]

2

Squared distances How step 3 ②

\[(1-2.5)^2=2.25,\quad(2-2.5)^2=0.25,\quad(3-2.5)^2=0.25,\quad(4-2.5)^2=2.25\]

3

\(S_{xx}\) and its square root How step 3 ③④

\[S_{xx}=2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25=5,\qquad\sqrt{S_{xx}}=\sqrt5=2.236068\]

4

Standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\) How step 2

\[\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=\frac{\sigma}{2.236068}=0.447214\,\sigma\]

5

Write \(Z\) How step 4

\[Z=\frac{1.4-\beta_1}{0.447214\,\sigma}\sim N(0,1)\]

\(Z\) still contains \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma\). \(\beta_1\) is the value that we want to estimate. Section 04.3 removes \(\sigma\). ▲

For these data, the standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\) is 0.447214 times \(\sigma\).

**Why** Added

The derivation uses one fact: a linear transformation of a Normal variable is also Normal. A linear transformation multiplies by a constant and adds a constant. Then the derivation calculates the mean and the variance of \(Z\).

1

\[Z=\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}{\sigma}\hat\beta_1-\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}{\sigma}\beta_1\]

**Linear transformation:** \(Z=a\hat\beta_1+b\) with constants \(a=\sqrt{S_{xx}}/\sigma\) and \(b=-\sqrt{S_{xx}}\beta_1/\sigma\). Thus \(Z\) is Normal.

2

\[E[Z]=\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}{\sigma}E[\hat\beta_1]-\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}{\sigma}\beta_1\]

**Expectation rule:** \(E[aW+b]=aE[W]+b\). The expectation is the mean.

3

\[=\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}{\sigma}\beta_1-\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}{\sigma}\beta_1=0\]

**Substitute** \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\).

4

\[\mathrm{Var}[Z]=\left(\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}{\sigma}\right)^2\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]\]

**Variance rule:** \(\mathrm{Var}[aW+b]=a^2\mathrm{Var}[W]\).

5

\[=\frac{S_{xx}}{\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\]

**Substitute** \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\).

6

\[=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Z\sim N(0,1)\]

Normal, mean 0, variance 1. ∎

The result is \(Z\sim N(0,1)\). Section 04.2 uses the probabilities of \(Z\) to get an interval for \(\beta_1\).

### 04.2 95% CI for \(\beta_1\) with known \(\sigma\) Slides p.27–30

This section uses a known \(\sigma\). It starts from \(P(-1.96\le Z\le1.96)=0.95\) and changes the inequality until \(\beta_1\) is alone in the middle. The result is the 95% confidence interval.

**What** Slides p.27–30

95% CI for β1 — Known σ · Lecture 3 · p.27–30 Suppose \(\sigma\) is known. \[0.95=P(-1.96\le Z\le1.96)\] \[0.95=P\!\left(\hat\beta_1-1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\] So a 95% CI for \(\beta_1\) is \(\hat\beta_1\pm1.96\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\)
I.e. the random interval \(\hat\beta_1\pm1.96\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\) will cover the true \(\beta_1\) 95% of the time.

\(P(A)\): the probability of the event \(A\). It is a number from 0 to 1.

Quantile: for a random variable \(W\) and a probability \(p\), the quantile is the number \(q\) with \(P(W\le q)=p\).

1.96 is the 0.975 quantile of \(N(0,1)\): \(P(Z\le1.96)=0.975\). The more exact value is 1.959964.

\(\pm\): "plus or minus". \(a\pm b\) is the interval from \(a-b\) to \(a+b\).

Random interval: its end points come from the random value \(\hat\beta_1\), so the interval changes with the data. \(\beta_1\) is a fixed number.

\(N(0,1)\) is symmetric about 0. Each tail outside \(\pm1.96\) has area 0.025, so the center has area 0.95. We put the definition of \(Z\) into the inequality and solve for \(\beta_1\). "95%" is a property of the method. With many new samples and one interval per sample, about 95% of the intervals contain \(\beta_1\).

This section gives the formula \(\hat\beta_1\pm1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). The How steps below use it.

**How** Added

95% CI with known σ

- **Get the quantile.** Use 1.96, the 0.975 quantile of \(N(0,1)\).
- **Calculate \(\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).** Divide the known \(\sigma\) by \(\sqrt{S_{xx}}\) from the data.
- **Calculate the half-width.** Half-width \(=1.96\times\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).
- **Write the interval.** Lower end \(=\hat\beta_1-\) half-width. Upper end \(=\hat\beta_1+\) half-width.

Self-check: the center of the interval is \(\hat\beta_1\). The two ends have the same distance from \(\hat\beta_1\). The area of \(N(0,1)\) between \(-1.96\) and 1.96 is 0.950004.

**Example · Four-point data set with a supposed \(\sigma\)** Added

In practice, \(\sigma\) is not known. For this example only, we suppose that \(\sigma=0.3\) is known.

1

Quantile How step 1

\[q=1.96\]

2

Standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\) How step 2

\[\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=\frac{0.3}{2.236068}=0.134164\]

\(\sqrt{S_{xx}}=2.236068\) comes from the example in Section 04.1.

3

Half-width How step 3

\[1.96\times0.134164=0.262962\]

4

Interval How step 4

\[1.4-0.262962=1.137038,\qquad1.4+0.262962=1.662962\]

\[1.4\pm0.262962=(1.137038,\ 1.662962)\]

The center is \(\hat\beta_1=1.4\). Each end is 0.262962 from the center. ▲

With known \(\sigma\), the interval needs only 1.96, \(\sigma\), \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(S_{xx}\). Unit 05 shows the meaning of "95% of the time" with the figure on Slides p.39.

**Why** Slides p.27–30

The derivation changes the inequality inside the probability until \(\beta_1\) is alone in the middle. Each step does the same operation on all three parts, so the probability stays 0.95.

1

\[0.95=P(-1.96\le Z\le1.96)\]

**Quantile of \(N(0,1)\):** \(P(Z\le1.96)=0.975\), and \(N(0,1)\) is symmetric.

2

\[0.95=P\!\left(-1.96\le\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le1.96\right)\]

**Substitute** the definition of \(Z\) (Section 04.1).

3

\[0.95=P\!\left(-1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\hat\beta_1-\beta_1\le1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

\(\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}>0\), so the inequality signs stay the same.

4

\[0.95=P\!\left(-1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1-\hat\beta_1\le1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

Multiply by \(-1\). The signs change direction. The two bounds are symmetric, so the form stays the same.

5

\[0.95=P\!\left(\hat\beta_1-1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

This is the last line of Slides p.30. ∎

With known \(\sigma\), the 95% CI is \(\hat\beta_1\pm1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). In practice \(\sigma\) is unknown, and Section 04.3 solves this problem.

### 04.3 Unknown \(\sigma\): use \(\hat\sigma\) and get the t distribution Slides p.31–33

This section replaces \(\sigma\) in \(Z\) with \(\hat\sigma\) from the data. The new quantity does not have the distribution \(N(0,1)\). It has a t distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom. This distribution is fully known, so we can still make an interval.

**What** Slides p.31–33

95% CI for β1 — Unknown σ · Lecture 3 · p.31–33 In practice, \(\sigma\) is unknown and must be estimated. We have:
1. \(Z=\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim N(0,1)\)
2. \(V=\dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\)
3. It can be shown that \(Z\) and \(V\) are independent
Note that for independent \(Z\sim N(0,1)\) and \(V\sim\chi^2_\nu\), \(\Longrightarrow\dfrac{Z}{\sqrt{V/\nu}}\sim t_\nu\) \[\Longrightarrow\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/\nu}}=\frac{\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2/(n-2)}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\] \[\frac{\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{1/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2/(n-2)}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\] \[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\]

The chi-squared distribution \(\chi^2_\nu\) (Section 01.5) is the distribution of a sum of \(\nu\) squared independent \(N(0,1)\) variables.

Degrees of freedom (df) \(\nu\): the parameter of a \(\chi^2\) or t distribution. It sets the shape. Here \(\nu=n-2\), the same as the denominator of \(\hat\sigma^2\).

t distribution \(t_\nu\): the distribution of \(Z/\sqrt{V/\nu}\), with independent \(Z\sim N(0,1)\) and \(V\sim\chi^2_\nu\).

The t distribution is bell-shaped and symmetric about 0. Its tails are thicker than the tails of \(N(0,1)\). When \(\nu\) increases, it comes nearer to \(N(0,1)\).

The slides state item 3 (independence of \(Z\) and \(V\)) without proof.

We cannot calculate \(Z\) from data, because \(Z\) contains the unknown \(\sigma\). We replace \(\sigma\) with \(\hat\sigma\). Then the denominator is also random, and the distribution changes from \(N(0,1)\) to \(t_{(n-2)}\). The final quantity \(\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\) does not contain \(\sigma\). Its distribution \(t_{(n-2)}\) contains no unknown values.

This section gives the quantity \(\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\), which we can use with data. The How steps below calculate it.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\) and the degrees of freedom

- **Fit the line.** Calculate \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\). Then calculate the fitted values \(\hat y_i\).
- **Calculate the residual sum of squares.** ① Calculate \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). ② Square each \(e_i\). ③ Add them to get \(\sum e_i^2\).
- **Get the degrees of freedom.** \(\nu=n-2\).
- **Calculate \(\hat\sigma\).** Calculate \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum e_i^2/(n-2)\). Then take the square root.
- **Calculate the denominator.** Divide \(\hat\sigma\) by \(\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). Then \((\hat\beta_1-\beta_1)/(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}})\sim t_{(n-2)}\).

Self-check: divide by \(n-2\), not by \(n\). The degrees of freedom are the same number \(n-2\). The residuals must add to 0.

**Example · Four-point data set** Added

This example does all How steps for the four-point data set. It gives the denominator and the degrees of freedom of the t quantity.

1

Fitted values How step 1

\[\hat y_i=0.5+1.4x_i:\quad0.5+1.4=1.9,\quad0.5+2.8=3.3,\quad0.5+4.2=4.7,\quad0.5+5.6=6.1\]

2

Residuals How step 2 ①

\[e_1=2-1.9=0.1,\quad e_2=3-3.3=-0.3,\quad e_3=5-4.7=0.3,\quad e_4=6-6.1=-0.1\]

Self-check: \(0.1-0.3+0.3-0.1=0\).

3

Residual sum of squares How step 2 ②③

\[\sum_{i=1}^4e_i^2=0.01+0.09+0.09+0.01=0.2\]

4

Degrees of freedom How step 3

\[\nu=n-2=4-2=2\]

5

\(\hat\sigma\) How step 4

\[\hat\sigma^2=\frac{0.2}{2}=0.1,\qquad\hat\sigma=\sqrt{0.1}=0.316228\]

6

t quantity How step 5

\[\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=\frac{0.316228}{2.236068}=0.141421\]

\[\frac{1.4-\beta_1}{0.141421}\sim t_{(2)}\]

Now \(\beta_1\) is the only unknown value. ▲

For the brainhead data, Slides p.45 give \(\hat\sigma=72.35\) on 234 degrees of freedom. Thus the brainhead t quantity has the distribution \(t_{(234)}\).

**Why** Slides p.31–33

The derivation starts from the definition \(Z/\sqrt{V/\nu}\) of the t distribution. It puts in \(Z\) and \(V\) with \(\nu=n-2\). Then it shows that \(\sigma\) cancels.

1

\[\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-2)}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\]

**Definition of t:** items 1–3 on the slide give \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), \(V\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\), and independence.

2

\[\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-2)}}=\frac{\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2/(n-2)}}\]

**Substitute** the definitions of \(Z\) and \(V\).

3

\[=\frac{\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}}{\frac{1}{\sigma}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2/(n-2)}}\]

\(\sqrt{\frac{1}{\sigma^2}A}=\frac{1}{\sigma}\sqrt{A}\) because \(\sigma>0\).

4

\[=\frac{\sigma\cdot\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2/(n-2)}}\]

5

\[=\frac{\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{1/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2/(n-2)}}\]

\(\sigma\) cancels here. This is the second line of Slides p.32.

6

\[=\frac{\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{1/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}}{\hat\sigma}\]

**Substitute** \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2/(n-2)}\) (Slides p.8).

7

\[=\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\]

This is the last line of Slides p.33. ∎

\(\sigma\) cancels, so we can use \(\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\) with data. Section 04.4 uses its quantile to make the interval.

### 04.4 Make the interval with a t quantile \(q=t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\) Slides p.34

This section does the same inequality steps as Section 04.2. The difference: 1.96 changes to a quantile \(q\) of \(t_{(n-2)}\), and \(\sigma\) changes to \(\hat\sigma\).

**What** Slides p.34

95% CI for β1 — Unknown σ · Lecture 3 · p.34 So we can find some quantile \(q\) such that \[0.95=P\!\left(-q\le\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le q\right)\] \[0.95=P\!\left(\hat\beta_1-q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\] and construct a 95% CI for \(\beta_1\) is \(\hat\beta_1\pm q\dfrac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\)
Often written \(t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\), as in: \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\dfrac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\)

\(\alpha\) (alpha): the probability that the interval does not contain the true value. The confidence level is \(1-\alpha\). A 95% CI has \(\alpha=0.05\).

\(t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\): the \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile of \(t_{(n-2)}\). Thus \(P(T\le t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2})=1-\alpha/2\), and the right tail has area \(\alpha/2\). Here \(T\) is a \(t_{(n-2)}\) variable.

For a 95% CI, \(\alpha/2=0.025\). Thus \(q\) is the 0.975 quantile \(t_{0.975,n-2}\). We get it from a t table or from statistical software.

The t distribution is also symmetric about 0. Each tail outside \(\pm q\) has area \(\alpha/2\), so the center has area \(1-\alpha\). The t tails are thicker than the Normal tails. Thus \(q\) is a little larger than 1.96, and the interval is a little wider.

This section gives the interval for practice: \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\,\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). The How steps below find \(q\).

**How** Added

Find \(t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\) and write the interval

- **Get \(\alpha\).** \(\alpha=1-\) confidence level. For 95%, \(\alpha=0.05\).
- **Get the degrees of freedom.** df \(=n-2\).
- **Get \(q\).** Find the \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile of \(t_{(n-2)}\) in a t table or with software.
- **Write the interval.** \(\hat\beta_1\pm q\,\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

Self-check: ① For 95%, \(q\) is larger than 1.96. When df increases, \(q\) comes nearer to 1.96. ② The left tail area \(P(T\le-q)\) must equal \(\alpha/2\).

**Example 1 · Brainhead data: compare \(q\) with 1.96** Added

This example finds \(q\) for a 95% interval for the brainhead data (\(n=236\), df = 234). Then it compares \(q\) with the Normal value 1.959964.

1

\(\alpha\) and df How steps 1–2

\[\alpha=1-0.95=0.05,\qquad\alpha/2=0.025,\qquad\text{df}=236-2=234\]

2

t quantile How step 3

\[q=t_{0.975,234}=1.970154\]

3

Compare with the Normal value Self-check ①

\[1.970154-1.959964=0.010190\]

\(q\) is larger than 1.96 by about 0.0102, because the t tails are thicker. df = 234 is large, so the difference is small.

4

Tail area Self-check ②

\[P(T\le-1.970154)=0.025\]

The left tail is 0.025, the right tail is 0.025, and the center is 0.95. ▲

The values of \(t_{0.975,\nu}\) below show the effect of df:

df = 2: \(q=4.302653\). df = 5: \(q=2.570582\). df = 10: \(q=2.228139\).

df = 30: \(q=2.042272\). df = 234: \(q=1.970154\). When df increases, \(q\) comes nearer to 1.959964.

The two figures below show the same result. The first figure shows the full curves. The second figure shows the right boundary at a larger scale.

Figure 4-1. Densities of \(N(0,1)\) (blue solid line) and \(t_{(234)}\) (orange dashed line). The largest difference in height between the two lines is 0.00058. The green area is the area of \(t_{(234)}\) between \(-q\) and \(q\), and it equals 0.95, and each tail has 0.025. At this scale, the difference between \(q=1.970\) and 1.96 is too small to see. [figure]
Figure 4-2. The interval from 1.85 to 2.10 at a larger scale. The orange dashed line (t) is above the blue solid line (Normal). Thus the t tail has more area. To keep the right tail area at 0.025, the t boundary moves to the right, from 1.960 to 1.970.

**Example 2 · Four-point data set: 95% CI with unknown σ** Added

This example makes the full 95% interval for the four-point data set. It uses \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}=0.141421\) from the example in Section 04.3.

1

\(\alpha\) and df How steps 1–2

\[\alpha=0.05,\qquad\alpha/2=0.025,\qquad\text{df}=4-2=2\]

2

t quantile How step 3

\[q=t_{0.975,2}=4.302653\]

3

Half-width How step 4

\[q\,\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=4.302653\times0.1414214=0.608487\]

4

Interval How step 4

\[1.4-0.608487=0.791513,\qquad1.4+0.608487=2.008487\]

\[1.4\pm0.608487=(0.791513,\ 2.008487)\]

With only 2 df, \(q=4.302653\) is much larger than 1.96. Thus this interval is wide. ▲

For a small \(n\), the t quantile is much larger than 1.96. For the brainhead data, it is only 0.0102 larger.

**Why** Slides p.34

The derivation is the same as in Section 04.2. Each step does the same operation on all three parts until \(\beta_1\) is alone. The only changes are \(q\) for 1.96 and \(\hat\sigma\) for \(\sigma\).

1

\[0.95=P\!\left(-q\le\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le q\right)\]

**t quantile:** \(q=t_{0.975,n-2}\), and \(t_{(n-2)}\) is symmetric about 0 (Section 04.3).

2

\[0.95=P\!\left(-q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\hat\beta_1-\beta_1\le q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

\(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}>0\), so the inequality signs stay the same.

3

\[0.95=P\!\left(-q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1-\hat\beta_1\le q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

Multiply by \(-1\). The bounds are symmetric, so the form stays the same.

4

\[0.95=P\!\left(\hat\beta_1-q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

For a general level \(1-\alpha\), replace 0.95 with \(1-\alpha\) and \(q\) with \(t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\). ∎

With unknown \(\sigma\), the \(1-\alpha\) CI is \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\,\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). Section 04.5 gives a name to \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

### 04.5 Standard deviation and standard error: \(\mathrm{SD}(\hat\beta_1)\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\) Slides p.35

This section names two quantities. The first is the true standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\), which contains \(\sigma\). The second is its estimate, the standard error, which contains \(\hat\sigma\). The interval uses the standard error.

**What** Slides p.35

Standard Errors · Lecture 3 · p.35 Standard error of \(\hat\beta_1\) is the estimated standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\) \[\mathrm{SD}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\] \[\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\] Can write a CI as \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\)

\(\mathrm{SD}(\hat\beta_1)\): the standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\). It shows the usual distance of \(\hat\beta_1\) from \(\beta_1\) over many samples. It contains the unknown \(\sigma\), so we cannot calculate it.

Standard error \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\): the estimate of \(\mathrm{SD}(\hat\beta_1)\) with \(\hat\sigma\) in place of \(\sigma\). We can calculate it from data.

In the interval of Section 04.4, \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\) is \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\). Thus the interval has the form "estimate ± t quantile × standard error".

This section gives the form on the slide: \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\). The How steps below calculate SE.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\)

- **Calculate \(\hat\sigma\).** \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum e_i^2/(n-2)}\) (Section 04.3, How steps 2–4).
- **Calculate \(\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).** Use Section 04.1, How step 3.
- **Divide.** \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

Self-check: SE has the same unit as \(\hat\beta_1\). SE uses \(\hat\sigma\), not \(\sigma\).

**Example · Four-point data set and brainhead data** Added

This example calculates \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\) for the four-point data set. Then it reads the brainhead SE from the slides and checks it.

1

\(\hat\sigma\) for the four-point data set How step 1

\[\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{0.2}{4-2}}=\sqrt{0.1}=0.316228\]

2

\(\sqrt{S_{xx}}\) for the four-point data set How step 2

\[\sqrt{S_{xx}}=\sqrt5=2.236068\]

3

Divide How step 3

\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{0.316228}{2.236068}=0.141421\]

4

Brainhead SE Slides p.45

\[\hat\sigma=72.35,\qquad\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\]

\[\sqrt{S_{xx}}=\frac{\hat\sigma}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)}=\frac{72.35}{0.01307}=5535.6\]

The slide values are rounded, so this \(\sqrt{S_{xx}}\) is approximate.

5

Put into the interval form Slides p.35

\[\hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,234}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.2608207\pm1.970154\times0.01307\]

Unit 05 does this multiplication and compares the result with Slides p.36–37. ▲

For the brainhead data, \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\). Over many samples, \(\hat\beta_1\) is usually about 0.013 from the true \(\beta_1\).

**Why** Added

The derivation starts from the variance in Unit 03. The square root gives SD. Then \(\hat\sigma\) in place of \(\sigma\) gives SE.

1

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\]

**Result of Unit 03** (Slides p.23–24).

2

\[\mathrm{SD}(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]}=\sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}}\]

**Definition:** the standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

3

\[=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\]

4

\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\]

**Definition (Slides p.35):** SE is the estimate of SD, with \(\hat\sigma\) in place of \(\sigma\). ∎

SD contains the unknown \(\sigma\), and SE is its estimate from data. Unit 05 calculates the interval \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\) for the brainhead data.

### 04.6 Practice Added

The three questions below practice the three procedures of this unit: find a t quantile, derive the interval, and calculate SE.

**Q1.** The brainhead data have \(n=236\). Do this for a 90% CI and for a 99% CI. Give \(\alpha\), \(\alpha/2\), df and the name of the quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\). The values are \(t_{0.95,234}=1.651391\) and \(t_{0.995,234}=2.597002\). Compare each value with the \(N(0,1)\) quantiles 1.644854 and 2.575829.

Answer

df \(=236-2=234\).

90%: \(\alpha=0.10\) and \(\alpha/2=0.05\). The quantile is \(t_{0.95,234}=1.651391\). The Normal 0.95 quantile is 1.644854. The difference is \(1.651391-1.644854=0.006537\).

99%: \(\alpha=0.01\) and \(\alpha/2=0.005\). The quantile is \(t_{0.995,234}=2.597002\). The Normal 0.995 quantile is 2.575829. The difference is \(2.597002-2.575829=0.021173\).

At both levels, the t quantile is a little larger than the Normal quantile, because the t tails are thicker. A higher confidence level gives a larger \(q\) and a wider interval.

**Q2.** Suppose \(\sigma\) is unknown. Start from \(1-\alpha=P\!\left(-t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\le\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)}\le t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\right)\). Derive the \(1-\alpha\) CI for \(\beta_1\).

Answer

Write \(t=t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\) and \(\mathrm{SE}=\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\).

1

\[1-\alpha=P\!\left(-t\le\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\mathrm{SE}}\le t\right)\]

2

\[1-\alpha=P\!\left(-t\,\mathrm{SE}\le\hat\beta_1-\beta_1\le t\,\mathrm{SE}\right)\]

\(\mathrm{SE}>0\).

3

\[1-\alpha=P\!\left(-t\,\mathrm{SE}\le\beta_1-\hat\beta_1\le t\,\mathrm{SE}\right)\]

Multiply by \(-1\). The bounds are symmetric.

4

\[1-\alpha=P\!\left(\hat\beta_1-t\,\mathrm{SE}\le\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+t\,\mathrm{SE}\right)\]

Thus the \(1-\alpha\) CI is \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\). ∎

**Q3.** Use the small data set of Unit 01: \((x_i,y_i)\) = (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5). Section 01.4 and Section 01.5 give \(S_{xx}=10\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\), and \(\sum e_i^2=2.4\). Calculate \(\hat\sigma\), \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\), and df. Then make the 95% CI for \(\beta_1\). Use \(t_{0.975,3}=3.182446\).

Answer

\(n=5\). df \(=5-2=3\).

\(\hat\sigma^2=2.4/3=0.8\) and \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{0.8}=0.894427\).

\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.894427/\sqrt{10}=0.894427/3.162278=0.2828427\).

Half-width: \(3.182446\times0.2828427=0.900132\).

95% CI: \(0.6-0.900132=-0.300132\) and \(0.6+0.900132=1.500132\). The interval is \((-0.300132,\ 1.500132)\).

This unit started from \(\hat\beta_1\sim N(\beta_1,\sigma^2/S_{xx})\). With known \(\sigma\), it gave \(\hat\beta_1\pm1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). With unknown \(\sigma\), it used \(t_{(n-2)}\) and gave \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\). For the brainhead data, \(q=1.970154\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\). Unit 05 puts these values into the interval and explains its meaning.

## 05 · Interval estimation example and interpretation

This unit calculates the 95% confidence intervals for \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_0\) in the brainhead data. Then it shows what "95%" means.

Plan · Slides p.36–39

Step 1: Calculate the two intervals by hand (Slides p.36).

Step 2: Check the printed intervals and read the question on Slides p.37–38.

Step 3: Answer the question with repeated samples (Slides p.39).

Step 4: Practice questions (Added).

Start point · Added

The brainhead data have \(n=236\) persons. \(x_i\) is the head size of person \(i\) (cm³). \(y_i\) is the brain weight of person \(i\) (g).

Model: \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\). \(\beta_0\) is the intercept and \(\beta_1\) is the slope. Both are fixed numbers that we do not know.

Least squares estimates: \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}=0.2608207\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=335.4323150\) (Lecture 2 · p.38).

The estimate of \(\sigma\) is \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2/(n-2)}=72.35\), with \(n-2=234\) (Slides p.45).

Two more values come from the course data file brainhead.csv (Added): the sample mean \(\bar x=3637.8644\) and \(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2=30647233.66\). The more exact value of \(\hat\sigma\) from the same file is 72.35066.

### 05.1 Calculate the confidence intervals for \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_0\) Slides p.36

This section calculates two 95% intervals from the brainhead numbers. The results are [0.235, 0.287] for \(\beta_1\) and [241.305, 429.559] for \(\beta_0\).

**What** Slides p.36

Example: interval estimation · Lecture 3 · p.36 (results only) 95% CI for \(\beta_1\): [0.235, 0.287]
95% CI for \(\beta_0\): [241.305, 429.559]

Section 04.5 gives the form of the interval for \(\beta_1\): \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\).

The 95% level gives \(\alpha=0.05\) and \(1-\alpha/2=0.975\). The degrees of freedom are \(n-2\).

Slides p.36 also calculates an interval for \(\beta_0\). The only change is the standard error. Slides p.24 gives the distribution \(\hat\beta_0\sim N\big(\beta_0,\ \sigma^2(1/n+\bar x^2/S_{xx})\big)\). We replace \(\sigma\) with \(\hat\sigma\) in its standard deviation:

\(\beta_1\): \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\), with \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\dfrac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\)

\(\beta_0\): \(\hat\beta_0\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)\), with \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)=\hat\sigma\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n}+\dfrac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}}\)

Both intervals have the form "estimate ± quantile × standard error".

**How** Added

Calculate the confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) or \(\beta_0\)

- Find the quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\).
- Calculate the standard error. For \(\beta_1\), use \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). For \(\beta_0\), use \(\hat\sigma\sqrt{1/n+\bar x^2/S_{xx}}\).
- Multiply the quantile by the standard error. The result is the half-width.
- Subtract the half-width from the estimate. This is the lower limit.
- Add the half-width to the estimate. This is the upper limit.

Self-check: ① The midpoint of the interval must equal the estimate. ② At 95% with large \(n\), the quantile is near 1.96. For \(n=236\), it is 1.970. ③ The two standard errors must agree with the values on Slides p.45: 0.01307 and 47.77644.

**Example 1 · CI for \(\beta_1\) in the brainhead data** Added

This example applies the five How steps to \(\beta_1\). The start values are \(n=236\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\), \(\hat\sigma=72.35066\) and \(S_{xx}=30647233.66\).

1

Quantile How step 1

\[t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}=t_{1-0.05/2,\,236-2}\]

\[=t_{0.975,\,234}\]

\[=1.970154\]

Value from the t distribution with 234 degrees of freedom.

2

Standard error How step 2

\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=\frac{72.35066}{\sqrt{30647233.66}}\]

\[=\frac{72.35066}{5535.994}\]

\[=0.01306914\]

Slides p.45 print 0.01307.

3

Half-width How step 3

\[t_{0.975,\,234}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=1.970154\times0.01306914\]

\[=0.0257482\]

4

Lower and upper limits How steps 4–5

\[\hat\beta_1\pm0.0257482=0.2608207\pm0.0257482\]

\[=(0.2608207-0.0257482,\ \ 0.2608207+0.0257482)\]

\[=(0.2350725,\ \ 0.2865689)\]

To 3 decimal places, this is [0.235, 0.287]. This agrees with Slides p.36.

**Example 2 · CI for \(\beta_0\) in the brainhead data** Added

This example applies the same steps to \(\beta_0\). Only step 2 is different. The start values are \(n=236\), \(\hat\beta_0=335.4323150\), \(\hat\sigma=72.35066\), \(\bar x=3637.8644\) and \(S_{xx}=30647233.66\).

1

Quantile How step 1

\[t_{0.975,\,234}=1.970154\]

The value of \(\alpha\) and the value of \(n-2\) are the same as in Example 1. Thus the quantile is the same.

2

Standard error How step 2

\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)=\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}}=72.35066\sqrt{\frac{1}{236}+\frac{3637.8644^2}{30647233.66}}\]

\[=72.35066\sqrt{\frac{1}{236}+\frac{13234057.39}{30647233.66}}\]

\[=72.35066\sqrt{0.0042373+0.4318190}\]

\[=72.35066\sqrt{0.4360563}\]

\[=72.35066\times0.6603456\]

\[=47.77644\]

Slides p.45 print 47.77644.

3

Half-width How step 3

\[t_{0.975,\,234}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)=1.970154\times47.77644\]

\[=94.12694\]

4

Lower and upper limits How steps 4–5

\[\hat\beta_0\pm94.12694=335.43232\pm94.12694\]

\[=(335.43232-94.12694,\ \ 335.43232+94.12694)\]

\[=(241.30538,\ \ 429.55926)\]

To 3 decimal places, this is [241.305, 429.559]. This agrees with Slides p.36.

\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)=47.78\) is much larger than \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.0131\). The cause is the term \(\bar x^2/S_{xx}=0.4318\). The value \(\bar x=3637.8644\) is far from \(x=0\). Thus the line must go far past the data to give the intercept.

**Why** Added

This derivation shows that the interval for \(\beta_0\) has the same form as the interval for \(\beta_1\). It uses the same steps as Slides p.33–34, with the variance of \(\hat\beta_0\).

1

\[\hat\beta_0\sim N\Big(\beta_0,\ \sigma^2\Big(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\Big)\Big)\]

Distribution from Slides p.24.

2

\[\frac{\hat\beta_0-\beta_0}{\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}}}\sim N(0,1)\]

Standardize: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation.

3

\[\frac{\hat\beta_0-\beta_0}{\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\]

Replace \(\sigma\) with \(\hat\sigma\). The reason is the same as for \(\hat\beta_1\) on Slides p.33.

4

\[0.95=P\Big(-t_{0.975,\,n-2}\le\frac{\hat\beta_0-\beta_0}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)}\le t_{0.975,\,n-2}\Big)\]

Write \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)=\hat\sigma\sqrt{1/n+\bar x^2/S_{xx}}\).

5

\[0.95=P\big(-t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)\le\hat\beta_0-\beta_0\le t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)\big)\]

6

\[0.95=P\big(-t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)\le\beta_0-\hat\beta_0\le t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)\big)\]

7

\[0.95=P\big(\hat\beta_0-t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)\le\beta_0\le\hat\beta_0+t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)\big)\]

Thus the 95% CI for \(\beta_0\) is \(\hat\beta_0\pm t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)\). ∎ This section gives \(\beta_1\in[0.235,0.287]\) and \(\beta_0\in[241.305,429.559]\). The next section checks the same two intervals with more decimal places.

### 05.2 The printed intervals and the question Slides p.37–38

This section checks the two intervals that Slides p.37 prints. Then it states the question on Slides p.38: what does "95%" mean?

**What** Slides p.37–38

Example: interval estimation · Lecture 3 · p.37–38 (results only) 95% CI for \(\beta_0\): from 241.3053884 to 429.5592416
95% CI for \(\beta_1\): from 0.2350725 to 0.2865689
Does this mean \(P(0.235\le\beta_1\le0.287)=95\%\)? No!

Slides p.37 gives the same two intervals as Slides p.36, with more decimal places.

The lower limit is the 2.5% point and the upper limit is the 97.5% point. The area between the two limits is the central 95%.

**How** Added

Check a printed interval

- Add the two limits and divide by 2. The result must equal the estimate.
- Subtract the lower limit from the upper limit and divide by 2. The result is the half-width.
- Divide the half-width by the standard error. The result must equal \(t_{0.975,\,n-2}\).

Self-check: For the brainhead data, step 3 must give \(t_{0.975,\,234}=1.970154\).

**Example 3 · Check the printed intervals** Added

This example applies the three How steps to the two intervals. Then it compares them with Examples 1 and 2.

\(\beta_1\), step 1: \((0.2350725+0.2865689)/2=0.2608207=\hat\beta_1\).

\(\beta_1\), step 2: \((0.2865689-0.2350725)/2=0.0257482\). Example 1 gives the same half-width.

\(\beta_1\), step 3: \(0.0257482/0.01306914=1.97015\). This is \(t_{0.975,\,234}=1.970154\), rounded.

\(\beta_0\), step 1: \((241.3053884+429.5592416)/2=335.432315=\hat\beta_0\).

\(\beta_0\), step 2: \((429.5592416-241.3053884)/2=94.1269266\). Example 2 gives 94.12694. The small difference comes from rounding.

\(\beta_0\), step 3: \(94.1269266/47.77644=1.97015\). This is also \(t_{0.975,\,234}\), rounded.

Thus the printed intervals use the formulas of Section 05.1.

Slides p.38 asks if [0.235, 0.287] contains \(\beta_1\) with probability 95%. The answer on the slide is "No!". The next section gives the correct meaning of 95%.

### 05.3 Interpretation of the confidence interval Slides p.39

This section shows what "95%" describes. The answer: it describes the **method** that makes the interval. It does not describe one interval that we already calculated.

**What** Slides p.39

Interval interpretation · Lecture 3 · p.39 If we were to draw samples repeatedly and construct intervals in the same way, any given interval may or may not cover the truth. On average, 95% will cover the truth.

\(\beta_1\) is a fixed number. It does not change from sample to sample. It has no probability distribution.

Before we take the sample, the limits \(L=\hat\beta_1-t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\) and \(U=\hat\beta_1+t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\) come from the random \(y_i\). Thus \(L\) and \(U\) are random variables.

An interval covers \(\beta_1\) when \(L\le\beta_1\le U\).

"95%" means \(P(L\le\beta_1\le U)=0.95\). Over many samples, 95% of the intervals cover the true \(\beta_1\).

After we take the sample, \(L=0.235\) and \(U=0.287\) are fixed numbers. This one interval covers \(\beta_1\), or it does not cover \(\beta_1\).

We say that we have 95% confidence in [0.235, 0.287]. This means that the interval comes from a method that covers \(\beta_1\) in 95% of samples.

**How** Added

Write the interpretation of a confidence interval

- State the parameter and its unit.
- State the interval and the confidence level.
- Say that the 95% describes the method. Use repeated samples and the same method.

Self-check: ① In your sentence, "95%" must describe the intervals or the method. It must not describe \(\beta_1\). ② The limits in your sentence must agree with Slides p.36–37.

**Example 4 · Interpretation for \(\beta_1\) in the brainhead data** Added

This example applies the three How steps.

Interpretation · brainhead \(\beta_1\)

Step 1: \(\beta_1\) is the change in mean brain weight (g) for each 1 cm³ increase in head size.

Step 2: The 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is [0.235, 0.287] g per cm³.

Step 3: Draw many samples of 236 persons. Make an interval \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,\,234}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\) from each sample. Then about 95% of these intervals cover the true \(\beta_1\).

**Example 5 · Simulation of coverage** Added

In real data, \(\beta_1\) is unknown. Thus we cannot check if one interval covers it. A simulation solves this problem. We set the true values, make many samples, and count the intervals that cover the true \(\beta_1\).

Simulation settings

True values: \(\beta_0=2\), \(\beta_1=1\), \(\sigma=2\).

Fixed \(x\) values: \(1,2,\dots,10\). Thus \(n=10\), \(\bar x=5.5\) and \(S_{xx}=82.5\).

Each sample: make \(y_i=2+1\cdot x_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\epsilon_i\sim N(0,2^2)\).

Each interval: use the method of Section 05.1 for \(\beta_1\). The quantile is \(t_{0.975,\,8}=2.306004\).

The settings give \(S_{xx}\) by hand: the values \(x_i-\bar x\) are \(\pm0.5,\pm1.5,\pm2.5,\pm3.5,\pm4.5\). Their squares add to \(2(0.25+2.25+6.25+12.25+20.25)=2\times41.25=82.5\).

Figure 5-1 shows the first 20 intervals. The text after the figure gives the result for 10000 intervals.

[figure]
Figure 5-1 · The 95% CIs from 20 simulated samples (Added). Each horizontal line is one interval. The dot is the \(\hat\beta_1\) of that sample. The red vertical line is the true value \(\beta_1=1.0\). The 19 blue intervals cover the true value. Interval 1 (orange, [0.061, 0.941]) does not cover it.

The figure shows three facts:

The red line does not move. \(\beta_1=1\) is fixed.

The intervals move. Each sample gives a different \(\hat\beta_1\) and a different \(\hat\sigma\). Thus the center and the width of each interval change.

The fraction is near 95%. In 20 intervals, 19 cover the true value: \(19/20=0.95\). In 10000 intervals, 9497 cover it: \(9497/10000=0.9497\).

Thus "95%" is the fraction of intervals that cover the true value when we use the method many times. This is the statement on Slides p.39.

**Why** Added

This derivation shows why the 95% probability belongs to the interval and not to \(\beta_1\). It starts from the t result on Slides p.33.

1

\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\]

Slides p.33. \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\sigma\) are random because they come from the random \(y_i\).

2

\[0.95=P\Big(-t_{0.975,\,n-2}\le\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le t_{0.975,\,n-2}\Big)\]

Definition of the quantile.

3

\[0.95=P\Big(\hat\beta_1-t_{0.975,\,n-2}\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+t_{0.975,\,n-2}\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\Big)\]

Slides p.34.

4

\[0.95=P(L\le\beta_1\le U)\]

\(L\) and \(U\) are random variables. \(\beta_1\) is a constant.

5

\[L=0.235,\quad U=0.287\]

Put in the one brainhead sample. No random quantity remains.

Line 4 is a property of the method before we take the sample. Line 5 is one result of the method. ∎ Thus 95% is the success rate of the method. The parameter \(\beta_1\) is fixed, and the interval is random. The next unit uses the same t statistic for hypothesis tests.

(A) There is a 95% probability that \(\beta_1\) lies in [0.235, 0.287].

(B) Draw many samples of size 236 and make an interval the same way from each. About 95% of these intervals cover the true \(\beta_1\).

**(B)**. \(\beta_1\) is a fixed number. The limits \(L\) and \(U\) are random. The 95% is the fraction of intervals from the same method that cover \(\beta_1\) (Slides p.39).
