## 06 · Hypothesis tests for \(\beta_1\): p-value, coefficient table, and one-sided tests

This unit shows how to use data to test a claim that \(\beta_1\) is equal to a given number. The tools are a test statistic and a p-value.

Plan · Slides p.40–49

Step 1: Write the null hypothesis, the alternative hypothesis, and the test statistic (Slides p.40–41).

Step 2: Define the p-value and show it as an area under the t density (Slides p.42).

Step 3: Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) on the brainhead data (Slides p.43–44).

Step 4: Read the coefficient table on Slides p.45.

Step 5: Interpret the p-value and define the Type-I error rate (Slides p.46–47).

Step 6: Do one-sided tests (Slides p.48–49).

Step 7: Practice questions (Added).

First, this unit repeats the results that it uses from Units 01–05.

Model and estimates (Unit 01): \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\). Also \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2/(n-2)}\).

Standard error (Unit 04): \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

Unit 04 result (Slides p.33–35): \(\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\).

Brainhead data (Unit 05): \(n=236\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\), \(\hat\sigma=72.35066\), \(S_{xx}=30647233.66\). \(x\) is the head size in cm³. \(y\) is the brain weight in g.

With these results, the next section makes a test.

### 06.1 Hypothesis test setup and test statistic Slides p.40–41

This section writes the two claims to test. Then it finds a quantity with a fully known distribution when the null hypothesis is true.

Slides p.40 is the section page "Hypothesis Tests for \(\beta_1\)". It has no formulas.

Hypothesis test: a method that uses data to measure the evidence against a claim about a parameter.

Null hypothesis \(H_0\): the claim that we test, for example \(H_0:\beta_1=\theta_0\). The test starts with the assumption that \(H_0\) is true.

\(\theta_0\): a specified number from the question. The most frequent value is \(\theta_0=0\). Then \(H_0\) says that the mean of \(y\) has no linear relation with \(x\).

Alternative hypothesis \(H_1\): the claim against \(H_0\), for example \(H_1:\beta_1\ne\theta_0\).

Test statistic: a number that we calculate from the data. Its distribution under \(H_0\) is known. Thus we can tell if its value is "extreme".

**What** Slides p.40–41

Hypothesis Testing · Lecture 3 · p.41 Want to test a null hypothesis \(H_0:\beta_1=\theta_0\) vs. some alternative hypothesis \(H_1:\beta_1\ne\theta_0\).
• E.g., often want to test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\).
Goal is to characterize how much evidence we have against \(H_0\)
• How “extreme” are our data relative to \(H_0\)?
• I.e. If \(H_0\) really were true, would these data be really surprising?
Under \(H_0\): \[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\]

The test does not prove that \(H_0\) is true or false. The test measures how much evidence the data give against \(H_0\). We assume that \(H_0\) is true. Then we ask if the observed data are rare under that assumption.

The test statistic \(\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\) gives the distance from \(\hat\beta_1\) to \(\theta_0\) in units of standard errors. A larger distance shows that the data agree less with \(H_0\).

Notation: \(T\) is the random test statistic. \(t\) is its observed value from our data (Slides p.42).

**How** Added

Calculate the observed test statistic \(t\)

- Write \(H_0:\beta_1=\theta_0\). Get \(\theta_0\) from the question.
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).
- Calculate \(\hat\sigma\). Then calculate \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).
- Calculate \(t=\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\).
- Write the reference distribution \(t_{(n-2)}\). The degrees of freedom are \(n-2\).

**Self-check:** When \(\hat\beta_1>\theta_0\), \(t\) must be positive. When \(\hat\beta_1<\theta_0\), \(t\) must be negative. The denominator \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\) must be positive.

**Example · Brainhead data** Slides p.43

This example tests \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) on the brainhead data. The numbers come from Unit 05. Slides p.43 prints the result \(t=19.957\).

1

Hypotheses How step 1

\[H_0:\beta_1=0\quad\text{vs.}\quad H_1:\beta_1\ne0,\qquad \theta_0=0\]

2

Slope estimate How step 2

\[\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\]

3

Standard error How step 3

\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=0.01306914\]

Section 05.1, Example 1 shows this division. Slides p.45 prints 0.01307.

4

Observed value How step 4

\[t=\frac{0.2608207-0}{0.01306914}=\frac{0.2608207}{0.01306914}=19.957\]

5

Reference distribution How step 5

\[n-2=236-2=234,\qquad T\sim t_{(234)}\ \text{under}\ H_0\]

**Self-check:** \(\hat\beta_1=0.26>0=\theta_0\). Thus \(t\) must be positive, and it is positive.

This example shows that \(\hat\beta_1\) is about 20 standard errors from 0. The next section changes this distance into a probability. ▲

**Why** Slides p.41

This part shows why the test statistic has the \(t_{(n-2)}\) distribution under \(H_0\). We put \(H_0\) into the Unit 04 result.

1

\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\]

Unit 04 result (Slides p.33–35). It is true for each true value \(\beta_1\).

2

\[\beta_1=\theta_0\]

The true value when \(H_0\) is true.

3

\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\quad\text{under }H_0\]

Line 2 put into line 1.

∎ Under \(H_0\), the distribution of the test statistic has no unknown parameter. The next section uses this distribution to calculate a probability.

### 06.2 The p-value Slides p.42

This section changes the observed test statistic into a probability, the p-value. A smaller p-value shows less support for \(H_0\).

p-value: the probability, under \(H_0\), that the test statistic is as extreme as the observed value or more extreme.

Extreme: in a two-sided test, a large \(|T|\). Thus \(T\) is far from 0 in either direction.

Probability density function (PDF): a curve. The area under the curve over an interval is the probability that the random variable is in that interval.

**What** Slides p.42

Hypothesis Testing – p value · Lecture 3 · p.42 Under \(H_0\): \(\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\)
• What’s the probability under the null of a test statistic as extreme or more than what we observe? \[P(|T|\ge|t|)=2P(T\ge|t|)=2[1-P(T\le|t|)]\quad\text{(last term corrected)}\]

Correction: on Slides p.42, the last term is \(2[1-P(T\le-|t|)]\). This is a typing error. The correct form is \(2[1-P(T\le|t|)]\). The block above uses the correct form. The Why part below shows each step.

Slides p.42 says "DRAW PLOT". Figure 6-1 is that plot.

[figure]
Figure 6-1. The \(t_{(234)}\) density curve (blue). The two orange areas are the tails \(T\ge|t|\) and \(T\le-|t|\). Their total area is the two-sided p-value. The figure uses the demonstration value \(|t|=2\). The brainhead value 19.957 is far past the right edge, and its tail area is too small to show. For \(|t|=2\), each tail has area 0.02332811. The two tails together have area 0.04665622.

**How** Added

Calculate the two-sided p-value

- Calculate the observed value \(t\) with the procedure in Section 06.1. Find the degrees of freedom \(n-2\).
- Take the absolute value \(|t|\).
- Find the right-tail area \(P(T\ge|t|)\) for \(T\sim t_{(n-2)}\). Use a t table or software.
- Multiply this area by 2. The result is \(P(|T|\ge|t|)\).

**Self-check:** The p-value must be between 0 and 1. The left-tail area \(P(T\le-|t|)\) times 2 must give the same result.

**Example · Demonstration value and brainhead data** Added

First, this example uses the demonstration value \(|t|=2\) from Figure 6-1. Then it uses the brainhead value \(t=19.957\). The brainhead p-value is on Slides p.43.

1

Demonstration value: right tail How step 3

\[P(T\ge2)=0.02332811,\qquad T\sim t_{(234)}\]

2

Demonstration value: multiply by 2 How step 4

\[P(|T|\ge2)=2\times0.02332811=0.04665622\]

3

Brainhead: right tail How step 3

\[P(T\ge t)=1.015856\times10^{-52}\]

The unrounded \(t\) from the full data (brainhead.csv) is 19.956998.

4

Brainhead: multiply by 2 How step 4

\[P(|T|\ge|t|)=2\times1.015856\times10^{-52}=2.031713\times10^{-52}\]

**Self-check:** Slides p.43 prints the same p-value, \(2.031713\times10^{-52}\).

This example shows that \(|t|=2\) gives a p-value of about 0.047. The value \(|t|=19.957\) gives a p-value near \(10^{-52}\). A larger \(|t|\) gives a smaller p-value. ▲

**Why** Slides p.42

This part shows the equation chain on Slides p.42. It uses two facts. The two tails do not overlap. The t distribution is symmetric about 0.

1

\[P(|T|\ge|t|)=P(T\ge|t|)+P(T\le-|t|)\]

The event \(|T|\ge|t|\) is two separate events: the right tail or the left tail.

2

\[P(T\le-|t|)=P(T\ge|t|)\]

The t distribution is symmetric about 0.

3

\[P(|T|\ge|t|)=2P(T\ge|t|)\]

Line 2 put into line 1.

4

\[P(T\ge|t|)=1-P(T<|t|)\]

Complement event.

5

\[P(T<|t|)=P(T\le|t|)\]

\(T\) is continuous. Thus \(P(T=|t|)=0\).

6

\[P(|T|\ge|t|)=2[1-P(T\le|t|)]\]

Lines 4 and 5 put into line 3.

∎ Lines 2 and 3 also give \(P(|T|\ge|t|)=2P(T\le-|t|)\). This section gives the formula for the p-value. The next section uses it to make a decision.

### 06.3 Example: test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) Slides p.43–44

This section uses the two previous sections together. It finds the p-value for the brainhead data and makes a decision at the 5% level.

Significance level \(\alpha\): a limit that we set before the test. When the p-value is less than \(\alpha\), we reject \(H_0\). This course uses \(\alpha=0.05\).

Reject \(H_0\): the data give sufficient evidence against \(H_0\).

**What** Slides p.43–44

Example: Testing a Hypothesis · Lecture 3 · p.43–44 The pval < 0.05. Hence we reject the null hypothesis at the 5% level.
What if pval > 0.05? Would we accept the null? No! Simply would not have enough evidence to reject.

When the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level. When the p-value is more than 0.05, we do not have enough evidence to reject \(H_0\). This result does not show that \(H_0\) is true.

**How** Added

Make a decision at level \(\alpha\)

- Write \(H_0\), \(H_1\), and \(\alpha\). The default is \(\alpha=0.05\).
- Calculate \(t\) and the p-value with the procedures in Sections 06.1 and 06.2.
- If the p-value is less than \(\alpha\), write "reject \(H_0\) at the \(100\alpha\%\) level".
- If the p-value is more than \(\alpha\), write "not enough evidence to reject \(H_0\)".
- Write the result as one sentence in the words of the question.

**Self-check:** The result sentence uses only one of two phrases: "reject" or "not enough evidence to reject".

**Example · Brainhead data** Slides p.43

Slides p.43 gives \(t=19.957\) and the p-value \(2.031713\times10^{-52}\). This example uses them in the procedure.

1

Hypotheses and level How step 1

\[H_0:\beta_1=0,\quad H_1:\beta_1\ne0,\quad \alpha=0.05\]

2

Statistic and p-value How step 2

\[t=19.957,\qquad \text{p-value}=2\times1.015856\times10^{-52}=2.031713\times10^{-52}\]

3

Compare How step 3

\[2.031713\times10^{-52}<0.05\ \Rightarrow\ \text{reject }H_0\text{ at the 5\% level}\]

4

Result sentence How step 5

The data give very strong evidence that the mean brain weight changes linearly with head size (\(\beta_1\ne0\)).

This section gives the brainhead result: we reject \(H_0:\beta_1=0\). ▲ The next section shows a table that gives the same numbers for each coefficient.

### 06.4 Read the coefficient table Slides p.45

This section reads the coefficient table on Slides p.45. Each row of the table is a test of \(H_0:\text{coefficient}=0\).

**What** Slides p.45

Example: Testing a Hypothesis · Lecture 3 · p.45 (numbers only) Intercept row: estimate 335.43231, standard error 47.77644, t value 7.021, p-value \(2.37\times10^{-11}\).
Slope row: estimate 0.26082, standard error 0.01307, t value 19.957, p-value less than \(2\times10^{-16}\).
\(\hat\sigma\): 72.35 on 234 degrees of freedom.

Each row of the table is one coefficient. The intercept row is \(\beta_0\). The slope row is \(\beta_1\).

**Estimate**: the point estimate. Here \(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\).

**Standard error**: for the slope row, \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}=0.01307\). For the intercept row, \(\hat\sigma\sqrt{1/n+\bar x^2/S_{xx}}=47.77644\).

**t value**: the observed \(t\) for \(H_0:\text{coefficient}=0\). It is equal to the estimate divided by the standard error.

**p-value**: the two-sided p-value \(P(|T|\ge|t|)\), with \(T\sim t_{(n-2)}\).

The table gives the slope p-value only as less than \(2\times10^{-16}\). Slides p.43 gives the exact value \(2.031713\times10^{-52}\).

**\(\hat\sigma\)**: 72.35, with \(n-2=234\) degrees of freedom.

Slides p.45 also gives a summary of the 236 residuals: minimum −174.88, first quartile −49.03, median −2.40, third quartile 46.72, and maximum 242.41.

Slides p.45 also prints \(R^2=0.6299\), adjusted \(R^2=0.6283\), and an F statistic of 398.3 on 1 and 234 degrees of freedom. Lecture 3 does not explain these values. Later lectures use them.

**How** Added

Read one test from the coefficient table

- Select the row. For \(\beta_1\), use the slope row. For \(\beta_0\), use the intercept row.
- Use \(H_0:\text{coefficient}=0\) and the two-sided \(H_1:\text{coefficient}\ne0\). The table is only for \(\theta_0=0\).
- Read the t value and the p-value.
- Compare the p-value with \(\alpha=0.05\) with the procedure in Section 06.3. Write the result.

**Self-check:** The estimate divided by the standard error must be equal to the t value, to the last digit of rounding. The degrees of freedom must be 234.

**Example · Brainhead data** Slides p.45

This example checks the t values in the table by hand.

1

Intercept row: t value Self-check

\[t=\frac{335.43231}{47.77644}=7.020873\approx7.021\]

2

Intercept row: p-value Section 06.2

\[2P(T\ge7.020873)=2.371264\times10^{-11}\approx2.37\times10^{-11}\]

3

Slope row: t value Self-check

\[t=\frac{0.26082}{0.01307}=19.9556\]

The table divides the unrounded numbers: \(0.2608207/0.01306914=19.957\). The rounded numbers give a small difference in the third decimal.

4

Slope row: p-value Section 06.3

\[2.031713\times10^{-52}<2\times10^{-16}\]

**Self-check:** This is the same p-value as in Section 06.3.

This example shows that both rows reject their \(H_0:\text{coefficient}=0\) at the 5% level. ▲ The next section shows how to interpret a p-value in words.

### 06.5 Interpret the p-value Slides p.46–47

This section gives the correct interpretation of a p-value. Then it defines the Type-I error rate.

Type-I error: \(H_0\) is true, but the test rejects \(H_0\).

Type-I error rate: the probability that the test rejects \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true.

**What** Slides p.46–47

Interpreting P-Values · Lecture 3 · p.46–47 Does this mean pval \(=P(\beta_1=0)\)? No! Instead, it means that under the null hypothesis (i.e. assuming \(\beta_1=0\)) the probability of a test statistic as extreme as the one observed is pval. That’s why a small p-value is evidence against the null, since it would be particularly “rare” under the null (and hence surprising).

If we reject the null whenever we get a p-value below 5%, then if the null is true and we repeat the experiment over and over then we will only reject the null incorrectly 5% of the time. This is called the Type-I error rate.

We calculate the p-value with the assumption \(\beta_1=0\). The p-value tells how rare the observed test statistic is. \(\beta_1\) is a fixed constant. Thus the p-value is a probability about the data, not about \(\beta_1\).

Use the rule "reject when the p-value is below 5%". Assume that \(H_0\) is true and that we repeat the experiment many times. Then 5% of the tests reject \(H_0\) incorrectly.

**How** Added

Interpret a p-value in one sentence

- Write the condition: "Assuming \(H_0\) is true (\(\beta_1=\theta_0\)), …".
- Write the event: "… the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed \(t\) …".
- Write the value: "… is p-value = …".
- Write the result: a small p-value shows rare data under \(H_0\). Thus it is evidence against \(H_0\).

**Self-check:** The sentence must contain the condition "assuming \(H_0\)". The probability must be about the test statistic.

**Example · Brainhead data** Added

This example interprets the p-value of the brainhead slope with the procedure.

1

Condition How step 1

Assuming \(\beta_1=0\) (head size has no linear effect on mean brain weight),

2

Event and value How steps 2–3

the probability of \(|T|\ge19.957\) is \(2.031713\times10^{-52}\).

3

Result How step 4

This value is very rare under \(H_0\). Thus the data give very strong evidence against \(\beta_1=0\).

This example gives one sentence that you can write in an answer. ▲

**Why · The Type-I error rate is 5%** Slides p.47

This part shows that the rule "reject when the p-value is below 0.05" rejects with probability 0.05 when \(H_0\) is true. It uses the quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\).

Section 04.4 defines the quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\). For the brainhead data, \(t_{0.975,\,234}=1.970154\).

1

\[P(\text{reject}\mid H_0)=P(\text{p-value}<0.05\mid H_0)\]

The decision rule.

2

\[\text{p-value}<0.05\iff 2P(T\ge|t|)<0.05\]

Section 06.2: \(P(|T|\ge|t|)=2P(T\ge|t|)\).

3

\[2P(T\ge|t|)<0.05\iff P(T\ge|t|)<0.025\]

4

\[P(T\ge|t|)<0.025\iff |t|>t_{0.975,\,n-2}\]

The right-tail area decreases when \(|t|\) increases. The area 0.025 is at the point \(t_{0.975,\,n-2}\).

5

\[P(\text{reject}\mid H_0)=P(|T|>t_{0.975,\,n-2})\]

Under \(H_0\), \(T\sim t_{(n-2)}\).

6

\[P(|T|>t_{0.975,\,n-2})=0.025+0.025=0.05\]

Each tail has area 0.025 (symmetry).

∎ Thus the limit 5% gives a Type-I error rate of 5%. All tests so far are two-sided. The next section gives one-sided tests.

### 06.6 One-sided tests Slides p.48–49

This section uses an alternative hypothesis in one direction only. The test statistic does not change. The p-value uses only one tail.

Two-sided alternative: \(H_1:\beta_1\ne\theta_0\). Evidence for \(\beta_1>\theta_0\) and evidence for \(\beta_1<\theta_0\) both count against \(H_0\).

One-sided alternative: for example \(H_1:\beta_1>\theta_0\). Only evidence that \(\beta_1\) is larger than \(\theta_0\) counts.

**What** Slides p.48–49

One-sided hypothesis tests · Lecture 3 · p.48–49 Above we conducted a hypothesis test of the null \(H_0:\beta_1=\theta_0\) vs the two-sided alternative \(H_1:\beta_1\ne\theta_0\)
• Evidence against the null (and in favour of the alternative) is evidence that either \(\beta_1>\theta_0\) or \(\beta_1<\theta_0\)
Sometimes we are interested in evidence one direction: e.g., \(H_1:\beta_1>\theta_0\)
• Evidence against the null in favour of \(H_1\) is evidence that the true \(\beta_1\) is larger than \(\theta_0\)
• How do we compute a p-value here?
◦ Consider the test statistic: \(\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{(n-2)}\)
◦ Evidence against the null and in favour of \(H_1\) is evidence that \(\beta_1>\theta_0\).
◦ So large values of \(\hat\beta_1-\theta_0\) indicate evidence against the null in favour of \(H_1\)
◦ \(\Longrightarrow\) large values of \(\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\) indicate evidence in favour of \(H_1\)
◦ I.e. p-value only includes one tail

Note: Slides p.48 writes the two-sided alternative as \(H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0\). The meaning is \(H_1:\beta_1\ne\theta_0\). The block above uses this form.

For \(H_1:\beta_1>\theta_0\), only large positive values of \(t\) support \(H_1\). Thus "as extreme or more extreme" means only the right side. The p-value is \(P(T\ge t)\). Do not take the absolute value. Do not multiply by 2.

[figure]
Figure 6-2. The p-value for the one-sided test with \(H_1:\beta_1>\theta_0\). It uses only the right tail \(T\ge t\) (green). The axes are the same as in Figure 6-1, with the demonstration value \(t=2\). The right-tail area is 0.02332811. This is half of the two-sided p-value 0.04665622 in Figure 6-1.

**How** Added

One-sided test of \(H_0:\beta_1=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\beta_1>\theta_0\)

- Calculate \(t=\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\) with the procedure in Section 06.1. Keep the sign.
- Find the right-tail area \(P(T\ge t)\) for \(T\sim t_{(n-2)}\).
- Do not multiply by 2. This area is the p-value.
- Compare the p-value with \(\alpha\) with the procedure in Section 06.3. Write the result.

**Self-check:** When \(t>0\), the one-sided p-value must be half of the two-sided p-value.

**Example · Brainhead data** Added

This example tests \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) vs. \(H_1:\beta_1>0\) on the brainhead data. \(H_1\) says that a larger head gives a larger mean brain weight. The slides do not calculate this example.

1

Statistic How step 1

\[t=\frac{0.2608207-0}{0.01306914}=19.957\]

2

Right tail How steps 2–3

\[\text{p-value}=P(T\ge19.957)=1.015856\times10^{-52}\]

**Self-check:** \(2.031713\times10^{-52}/2=1.015856\times10^{-52}\). The two values agree.

3

Decision How step 4

\[1.015856\times10^{-52}<0.05\ \Rightarrow\ \text{reject }H_0\text{ in favour of }\beta_1>0\]

This example shows very strong evidence that \(\beta_1>0\). ▲

**Why · The p-value uses one tail** Slides p.49

This part shows why the one-sided p-value is \(P(T\ge t)\). It follows the arrow chain on Slides p.49.

1

\[H_1:\beta_1>\theta_0\]

Evidence for \(H_1\) is evidence that \(\beta_1\) is larger than \(\theta_0\).

2

\[\hat\beta_1-\theta_0\ \text{large}\]

\(\hat\beta_1\) is unbiased for \(\beta_1\). Thus \(\beta_1>\theta_0\) usually gives large positive \(\hat\beta_1-\theta_0\).

3

\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\ \text{large}\]

The denominator is positive. It does not change the direction.

4

\[\text{p-value}=P(T\ge t)\quad\text{under }H_0,\ T\sim t_{(n-2)}\]

"As extreme or more extreme" includes only values larger than \(t\): the right tail.

∎ When \(t>0\), the symmetry in Section 06.2 gives \(P(T\ge t)=\tfrac12P(|T|\ge|t|)\). This section gives the one-sided p-value: the area of the right tail.

### 06.7 Practice Added

These three questions check this unit: a two-sided test with nonzero \(\theta_0\), a one-sided test, and the coefficient table. All numbers come from the brainhead data.

**Q1.** For the brainhead data, \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\), \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}=0.01306914\), and \(n=236\). Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0.25\) vs. \(H_1:\beta_1\ne0.25\) at the 5% level. Give the test statistic, the p-value, and the result.

Answer

\(t=\dfrac{0.2608207-0.25}{0.01306914}=\dfrac{0.0108207}{0.01306914}=0.8280\).

The reference distribution is \(t_{(234)}\). The right tail is \(P(T\ge0.8280)=0.2043\). The p-value is \(2\times0.2043=0.4085\).

\(0.4085>0.05\). We do not have enough evidence to reject \(H_0:\beta_1=0.25\) at the 5% level.

**Q2.** Use the same data. A researcher says that the slope is larger than 0.24. Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0.24\) vs. \(H_1:\beta_1>0.24\) at the 5% level. Also give the two-sided p-value for \(H_1:\beta_1\ne0.24\).

Answer

\(t=\dfrac{0.2608207-0.24}{0.01306914}=\dfrac{0.0208207}{0.01306914}=1.5931\).

The one-sided p-value is \(P(T\ge1.5931)=0.05624\), with \(T\sim t_{(234)}\).

\(0.05624>0.05\). We do not have enough evidence to reject \(H_0\) in favour of \(\beta_1>0.24\) at the 5% level.

The two-sided p-value is \(2\times0.05624=0.1125\). The one-sided p-value is half of it.

**Q3.** On Slides p.45, the intercept row shows estimate 335.43231, standard error 47.77644, t value 7.021, and p-value \(2.37\times10^{-11}\). (a) Write the hypotheses for this row. (b) Check the t value. (c) Interpret the p-value in one sentence.

Answer

(a) \(H_0:\beta_0=0\) vs. \(H_1:\beta_0\ne0\).

(b) \(335.43231/47.77644=7.020873\approx7.021\).

(c) Assuming \(\beta_0=0\), the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as \(|t|=7.021\) is \(2.37\times10^{-11}\). This value is very rare under \(H_0\). Thus it is strong evidence against \(\beta_0=0\), and we reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level.

This unit gives the full test procedure for \(\beta_1\). Calculate \(t=\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\). Find the two-tail or one-tail area under \(t_{(n-2)}\) as the p-value. Then compare it with 5%. The coefficient table gives the same result for each coefficient when \(\theta_0=0\).
