STAT 331 · Lecture 4 · Simple Linear Regression: Prediction

# Lecture 4: Simple Linear Regression: Prediction

This lecture estimates the mean response at a given \(x_0\), gives a confidence interval for it, and gives a prediction interval for a new response (Lecture 4 · p.1–43).

Contents
01 · Recap: the model, the estimators, and inference for \(\beta_1\) 02 · Point estimate of the mean response and its distribution 03 · Confidence interval for the mean response 04 · Predicting a new response: the prediction interval 05 · Prediction intervals over a range of \(x\) values 06 · Practice questions Q1 and Q2

## 01 · Recap: the model, the estimators, and inference for \(\beta_1\)

This unit reviews four tools from Lectures 2–3: the model, the estimators, the confidence interval, and the hypothesis test. The prediction methods in the rest of Lecture 4 use these four tools. Thus, this unit uses each tool again with numbers.

Plan · Slides p.1–7

Step 1: Read the title page and the section page (Slides p.1–2).

Step 2: Write the simple linear regression model and its four assumptions (Slides p.3).

Step 3: Calculate the least squares estimators and write the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) (Slides p.4).

Step 4: Use this distribution to make a confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) (Slides p.5).

Step 5: Use the same distribution to test a hypothesis about \(\beta_1\) (Slides p.6).

Step 6: Find the results of Steps 3–5 in the numbers that Slides p.7 prints.

Data for this unit · Added

Small data set: \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\), so \(n=5\). This unit does the full hand calculations on these data.

Brainhead data: the response \(y\) is brain weight in g. The covariate \(x\) is head size in cm³.

Slides p.7 prints the brainhead results. Examples in this unit use only these printed numbers.

### 01.1 Title page and section page Slides p.1–2

These two pages give only names. They have no new mathematics.

Slides p.1 is the title page: "Lecture 4: Simple Linear Regression: Prediction".

Prediction is the use of a fitted model to give a value for a new response. Unit 04 of this lecture teaches it.

Slides p.2 is the section page "Recap". Slides p.3–7 belong to this part.

The next section starts with the model on Slides p.3.

### 01.2 The simple linear regression model and its assumptions Slides p.3

This section writes the model. This unit gets all distribution results from this model.

**What** Slides p.3

Simple Linear Regression · Lecture 4 · p.3 \[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i,\qquad \epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\] Or: \[y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\ \sigma^2)\] Assumptions:
1. Linearity
2. Independence
3. Normality
4. Equal variance (homoskedasticity)

The list below defines each symbol in the statement.

Simple linear regression (SLR) is a model in which the mean of a response \(y\) is a straight-line function of one covariate \(x\).

The response \(y_i\) is the value that we want to explain for observation \(i\). The index \(i\) goes from 1 to \(n\).

The sample size \(n\) is the number of observations.

The covariate \(x_i\) is the value that we use to explain \(y_i\). The model treats \(x_i\) as a known constant.

The intercept \(\beta_0\) is the mean of \(y\) when \(x=0\).

The slope \(\beta_1\) is the change in the mean of \(y\) when \(x\) increases by 1 unit.

A parameter is an unknown constant of the model. \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are parameters.

The error \(\epsilon_i\) is the random difference between \(y_i\) and the line \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\).

\(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is the normal distribution: a bell-shaped distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).

The expectation \(E[\cdot]\) is the long-run average value of a random variable. The variance \(\mathrm{Var}[\cdot]\) is the expected squared distance from the expectation.

\(\sigma^2\) is the error variance. It is the third unknown parameter. Its square root \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the errors.

"iid" means independent and identically distributed. All \(\epsilon_i\) have the same distribution, and one \(\epsilon_i\) does not change the distribution of another.

"indep" means independent. The second form does not say "identically distributed", because the mean \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\) changes with \(x_i\).

The list below gives the meaning of each assumption.

1. Linearity

The mean of \(y_i\) is a straight-line function of \(x_i\): \(E[y_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\).

2. Independence

The errors \(\epsilon_i\) of different observations are independent.

3. Normality

Each error \(\epsilon_i\) has a normal distribution.

4. Equal variance (homoskedasticity)

Each error \(\epsilon_i\) has the same variance \(\sigma^2\). This variance does not change with \(x_i\).

The two forms give the same model. The first form writes "line plus error". The second form writes the distribution of \(y_i\).

**How** Added

Write a data set as an SLR model

- Find the response \(y\). It is the variable that the question explains or predicts.
- Find the covariate \(x\). It is the variable that the question uses to explain \(y\).
- Count the observations to get \(n\).
- Write \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,\dots,n\).
- Write the second form \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\). List the four assumptions.

**Self-check:** The model has three unknown parameters: \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\), \(\sigma^2\). The data give the values \(x_i\), \(y_i\), and \(n\).

**Example 1 · The small data set** Added

This example writes the model for the five pairs \((1,2),(2,4),(3,5),(4,4),(5,5)\).

Step 1: \(y\) is the second value of each pair.

Step 2: \(x\) is the first value of each pair.

Step 3: There are five pairs, so \(n=5\).

Step 4: \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,\dots,5\).

Step 5: \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\). For observation 3, \(y_3\sim N(\beta_0+3\beta_1,\sigma^2)\).

**Example 2 · The brainhead data** Slides p.7

This example writes the model for the course data set.

Step 1: \(y_i\) is the brain weight of person \(i\), in g.

Step 2: \(x_i\) is the head size of person \(i\), in cm³.

Step 3: Slides p.7 prints 234 degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom are \(n-2\), so \(n=234+2=236\).

Step 4: \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(i=1,\dots,236\).

Step 5: \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\ \sigma^2)\), with the four assumptions.

[figure]
Figure 1-1. The 236 brainhead points (blue) and the fitted line \(\hat y=335.43+0.26082\,x\) (orange). The points are near a straight line. The vertical spread is almost the same at each \(x\). This agrees with the linearity and equal variance assumptions.

Thus, each data set gives a model with three unknown parameters. Section 01.3 estimates them.

**Why · The two forms are equal** Added

This derivation starts from the first form and gets the second form. It uses only the rules for the mean and the variance.

1

\[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\]

2

\[E[y_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+E[\epsilon_i]\]

\(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\) is a constant.

3

\[E[y_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\]

\(\epsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) has mean 0.

4

\[\mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\mathrm{Var}[\epsilon_i]\]

A constant does not change the variance.

5

\[\mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\sigma^2\]

6

\[y_i\sim N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\ \sigma^2)\]

A Normal variable plus a constant is normal.

7

\[y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\ \sigma^2)\]

Each \(y_i\) is a constant plus an independent \(\epsilon_i\). ∎

Thus, the second form is the distribution of \(y_i\). Section 01.3 uses this distribution to get the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\).

### 01.3 The least squares estimators and the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) Slides p.4

This section gives the formulas for the estimates of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). Then it gives the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\), which the interval and the test use.

**What** Slides p.4

Recap: Estimates · Lecture 4 · p.4 So the least squares estimators are: \[\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.\] \[\hat\beta_1\sim N\!\left(\beta_1,\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim N(0,1)\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

The list below defines each new symbol.

An estimator is a formula that uses the data to give a value for an unknown parameter. The hat \(\hat{\ }\) marks an estimator, for example \(\hat\beta_1\) for \(\beta_1\).

Least squares (LS) chooses \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\) to make \(\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)^2\) as small as possible.

The sample means are \(\bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) and \(\bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\).

\(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\) is the sum of squared distances of \(x_i\) from \(\bar x\).

\(S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)\) is the sum of the products of the two distances.

The fitted value is \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\). The residual is \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\).

\(\hat\sigma\) is the estimate of \(\sigma\). Its square is \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2/(n-2)\).

The standard error is \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). It is the estimate of the standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\).

\(N(0,1)\) is the standard normal distribution: the normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1.

\(t_{n-2}\) is the \(t\) distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom. It is bell-shaped and symmetric about 0, with wider tails than \(N(0,1)\).

The chain on the slide has three parts. The first part gives the distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\). The second part standardizes it. The third part puts \(\hat\sigma\) in place of the unknown \(\sigma\), and the distribution changes to \(t_{n-2}\).

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), \(\hat\sigma\), and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\)

- Calculate \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\).
- Calculate \(S_{xx}\) and \(S_{xy}\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).
- Calculate each fitted value \(\hat y_i\) and each residual \(e_i\).
- Calculate \(\hat\sigma^2=\sum e_i^2/(n-2)\) and \(\hat\sigma\).
- Calculate \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).

**Self-check:** The residuals add to 0. The line contains the point \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

**Example 3 · The small data set** Added

This example does the seven steps on \(x=(1,2,3,4,5)\), \(y=(2,4,5,4,5)\).

Step 1: \(\bar x=(1+2+3+4+5)/5=15/5=3\). \(\bar y=(2+4+5+4+5)/5=20/5=4\).

Step 2: The values \(x_i-\bar x\) are \(-2,-1,0,1,2\). The values \(y_i-\bar y\) are \(-2,0,1,0,1\).

Step 2 (cont.): \(S_{xx}=4+1+0+1+4=10\).

Step 2 (cont.): \(S_{xy}=(-2)(-2)+(0)(-1)+(1)(0)+(0)(1)+(1)(2)=4+0+0+0+2=6\).

Step 3: \(\hat\beta_1=6/10=0.6\).

Step 4: \(\hat\beta_0=4-0.6\times3=4-1.8=2.2\).

Step 5: \(\hat y_i=2.2+0.6x_i\) gives \(2.8,\ 3.4,\ 4.0,\ 4.6,\ 5.2\).

Step 5 (cont.): \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\) gives \(-0.8,\ 0.6,\ 1.0,\ -0.6,\ -0.2\).

Step 6: \(\sum e_i^2=0.64+0.36+1.00+0.36+0.04=2.4\).

Step 6 (cont.): \(\hat\sigma^2=2.4/(5-2)=2.4/3=0.8\), and \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{0.8}=0.894427\).

Step 7: \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.894427/\sqrt{10}=0.894427/3.162278=0.282843\).

Self-check: \(-0.8+0.6+1.0-0.6-0.2=0\), and \(2.2+0.6\times3=4=\bar y\). For these data, the slide's chain gives this result with \(n-2=3\):
\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=\frac{0.6-\beta_1}{0.282843}\sim t_{3}.\]
**Example 4 · The brainhead data** Slides p.7

For the brainhead data, Slides p.7 prints the results of the seven steps.

\(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\).

\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\).

\(\hat\sigma=72.35\), with \(n-2=234\) degrees of freedom.

Interpretation: when head size increases by 1 cm³, the estimated mean brain weight increases by 0.26082 g. The chain gives this result:
\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}=\frac{0.26082-\beta_1}{0.01307}\sim t_{234}.\]
Thus, we have the estimates and the standard error for both data sets. Sections 01.4 and 01.5 use these numbers.

**Why · The distribution chain** Added

This derivation follows Lecture 3. It writes \(\hat\beta_1\) as a weighted sum of the \(y_i\). Then it finds the mean and the variance.

1

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\]

2

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i y_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar y\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\]

3

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i y_i(x_i-\bar x)-\bar y\cdot 0}{S_{xx}}\]

\(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=n\bar x-n\bar x=0\).

4

\[\hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i,\qquad w_i=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\]

Each \(w_i\) uses only \(x\), so it is a constant.

5

\[\hat\beta_1\sim N\!\left(\sum_i w_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i),\ \sigma^2\sum_i w_i^2\right)\]

A weighted sum of independent normal variables is normal.

6

\[E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_0\sum_i w_i+\beta_1\sum_i w_ix_i\]

7

\[E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_0\cdot0+\beta_1\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)x_i}{S_{xx}}\]

\(\sum_i w_i=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)/S_{xx}=0\).

8

\[E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\]

\(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\bar x=0\).

9

\[E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\frac{S_{xx}}{S_{xx}}=\beta_1\]

10

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2\sum_i\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}\]

11

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2\frac{S_{xx}}{S_{xx}^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\]

12

\[\hat\beta_1\sim N\!\left(\beta_1,\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

The first result on Slides p.4.

13

\[Z=\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim N(0,1)\]

Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation.

14

\[V=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)},\quad Z,V\text{ independent}\]

Lecture 3 states this result ("It can be shown"). \(\chi^2_\nu\) is the chi-squared distribution.

15

\[\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-2)}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

Rule: independent \(Z\sim N(0,1)\) and \(V\sim\chi^2_\nu\) give \(Z/\sqrt{V/\nu}\sim t_\nu\).

16

\[\frac{(\hat\beta_1-\beta_1)\big/(\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}})}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_i e_i^2/(n-2)}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

17

\[\frac{(\hat\beta_1-\beta_1)\big/(1/\sqrt{S_{xx}})}{\sqrt{\sum_i e_i^2/(n-2)}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

18

\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

\(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum_i e_i^2/(n-2)}\). ∎

Thus, the \(t_{n-2}\) result has only one unknown, \(\beta_1\). Section 01.4 solves it for \(\beta_1\). Section 01.5 puts \(\beta_1=\theta_0\) into it.

### 01.4 The confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) Slides p.5

This section uses the \(t_{n-2}\) result of Section 01.3 to make an interval for \(\beta_1\). The interval gives a range of values for \(\beta_1\).

**What** Slides p.5

Confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) · Lecture 4 · p.5 95% CI for \(\beta_1\) is \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,n-2}\times\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}}\)
or \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,n-2}\times \mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\).
If we were to collect a new sample, we would obtain a different estimate and a different 95% CI

- 95% of such intervals will cover the true \(\beta_1\)
More generally a \(100\times(1-\alpha)\%\) CI is: \(\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\times \mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\)

A confidence interval (CI) is an interval that we calculate from the data with a fixed rule.

The confidence level \(100\times(1-\alpha)\%\) is the proportion of such intervals that cover the true parameter over many samples. For 95%, \(\alpha=0.05\).

The quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\) is the point with area \(1-\alpha/2\) to its left under the \(t_{n-2}\) curve.

For 95%, the quantile is \(t_{0.975,n-2}\). The area to its right is 0.025.

\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\), from Section 01.3.

The interval changes from sample to sample. The true \(\beta_1\) does not change. Over many samples, 95% of the intervals contain \(\beta_1\).

**How** Added

Calculate a \(100\times(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\beta_1\)

- Get \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\) from Section 01.3.
- Calculate the degrees of freedom \(n-2\).
- Find the quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\) in a \(t\) table or with statistical software.
- Calculate the half-width \(t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\times\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\).
- Calculate the lower limit \(\hat\beta_1-\text{half-width}\) and the upper limit \(\hat\beta_1+\text{half-width}\).

**Self-check:** The midpoint of the interval is equal to \(\hat\beta_1\). A higher confidence level gives a wider interval.

**Example 5 · 95% CI for the small data set** Added

This example uses the results of Example 3.

Step 1: \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.282843\).

Step 2: \(n-2=5-2=3\).

Step 3: The \(t\) table gives \(t_{0.975,3}=3.182446\).

Step 4: Half-width \(=3.182446\times0.282843=0.900132\).

Step 5: \(0.6-0.900132=-0.300132\) and \(0.6+0.900132=1.500132\).

The 95% CI is \([-0.300132,\ 1.500132]\). It is wide because \(n=5\) is small and \(t_{0.975,3}\) is large.

**Example 6 · 95% CI for the brainhead data** Slides p.7

This example uses the numbers on Slides p.7.

Step 1: \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\).

Step 2: \(n-2=236-2=234\).

Step 3: The \(t\) table gives \(t_{0.975,234}=1.970154\).

Step 4: Half-width \(=1.970154\times0.01307=0.025750\).

Step 5: \(0.26082-0.025750=0.235070\) and \(0.26082+0.025750=0.286570\).

The hand result is \([0.235070,\ 0.286570]\). Slides p.7 prints \([0.2350725,\ 0.2865689]\). The rounded inputs cause the small difference. Interpretation: we are 95% confident that 1 cm³ more head size increases the mean brain weight by 0.2351 g to 0.2866 g.

[figure]
Figure 1-2. The density curve of \(t_{234}\). The blue center area is 0.95. Each orange tail area is 0.025. The right boundary is \(t_{0.975,234}=1.970154\). The half-width of the 95% CI is this quantile times \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\).

**Why · The interval formula** Added

This derivation solves the \(t_{n-2}\) result for \(\beta_1\). Let \(q=t_{0.975,n-2}\) and \(T\sim t_{n-2}\).

1

\[0.95=P(-q\le T\le q)\]

The \(t\) distribution is symmetric. Each tail has area 0.025.

2

\[0.95=P\!\left(-q\le\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le q\right)\]

Put in the \(t_{n-2}\) result of Section 01.3.

3

\[0.95=P\!\left(-q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\hat\beta_1-\beta_1\le q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

4

\[0.95=P\!\left(-q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1-\hat\beta_1\le q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

5

\[0.95=P\!\left(\hat\beta_1-q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\le\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+q\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\right)\]

6

\[\hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,n-2}\times\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\]

\(\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}=\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\). Put \(1-\alpha/2\) in place of 0.975 for the general form. ∎

In line 5, the random values are \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\sigma\), not \(\beta_1\). Thus, 0.95 is the probability that the interval covers \(\beta_1\). Section 01.5 uses the same \(t_{n-2}\) result for a test.

### 01.5 The hypothesis test for \(\beta_1\) Slides p.6

This section uses the same \(t_{n-2}\) result to test if \(\beta_1\) is equal to a given value.

**What** Slides p.6

Hypothesis Testing · Lecture 4 · p.6 Want to test \(H_0:\beta_1=\theta_0\) vs \(H_1:\beta_1\neq\theta_0\).
Under \(H_0\): \(\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{n-2}\)

- P-value: What's the probability under the null of observing a test statistic as or more extreme than the one we observed?

- I.e. for \(T\sim t_{n-2}\) and our observed test statistic \(t^{obs}\): \(P(|T|\ge|t^{obs}|)\)

A hypothesis test is a procedure that uses the data to decide if a statement about a parameter agrees with the data.

The null hypothesis \(H_0:\beta_1=\theta_0\) is the statement that we test. \(\theta_0\) is a given number. The usual value is 0, which means "no linear relation".

The alternative hypothesis \(H_1:\beta_1\neq\theta_0\) is the statement for the case where \(H_0\) is false. The sign \(\neq\) makes the test two-sided.

The test statistic is \(\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\). Under \(H_0\), it has the \(t_{n-2}\) distribution.

\(t^{obs}\) is the value of the test statistic for our data.

The p-value is the probability, when \(H_0\) is true, of a test statistic as extreme as \(t^{obs}\) or more extreme. It is \(P(|T|\ge|t^{obs}|)\).

A small p-value shows that the data do not agree with \(H_0\).

**How** Added

Test \(H_0:\beta_1=\theta_0\) vs \(H_1:\beta_1\neq\theta_0\)

- Write \(H_0\) and \(H_1\). Find \(\theta_0\).
- Get \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\).
- Calculate \(t^{obs}=(\hat\beta_1-\theta_0)/\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\).
- Calculate the p-value \(2P(T\ge|t^{obs}|)\), with \(T\sim t_{n-2}\).
- Compare the p-value with the significance level \(\alpha\), usually 0.05.
- If the p-value is less than \(\alpha\), reject \(H_0\). If not, do not reject \(H_0\).

**Self-check:** For \(\theta_0=0\), the 95% CI does not contain 0 exactly when the p-value is less than 0.05.

**Example 7 · Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) for the small data set** Added

This example uses the results of Example 3.

Step 1: \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) vs \(H_1:\beta_1\neq0\), so \(\theta_0=0\).

Step 2: \(\hat\beta_1=0.6\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.282843\).

Step 3: \(t^{obs}=(0.6-0)/0.282843=2.121320\).

Step 4: Software gives \(2P(T\ge2.121320)=0.124027\), with \(T\sim t_3\).

Step 5–6: \(0.124027>0.05\), so we do not reject \(H_0\).

This agrees with Example 5: the 95% CI \([-0.300132,\ 1.500132]\) contains 0.

**Example 8 · Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) for the brainhead data** Slides p.7

This example tests if head size and brain weight have no linear relation.

Step 1: \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) vs \(H_1:\beta_1\neq0\), so \(\theta_0=0\).

Step 2: \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\).

Step 3: \(t^{obs}=(0.26082-0)/0.01307=19.956\). Slides p.7 prints 19.957, from inputs with more digits.

Step 4: Software gives \(2P(T\ge19.957)=2.03\times10^{-52}\), with \(T\sim t_{234}\).

Step 4 (cont.): Slides p.7 prints only that this p-value is less than \(2\times10^{-16}\).

Step 5–6: The p-value is much less than 0.05, so we reject \(H_0\).

[figure]
Figure 1-3. Under \(H_0\), the test statistic \(T\) has the \(t_{234}\) distribution. Almost all of its area is between \(-4\) and 4. The value \(t^{obs}=19.957\) is far to the right of the plot. The p-value is the area of both tails beyond \(\pm19.957\), which is too small to see.

Conclusion: the data do not agree with \(\beta_1=0\). Head size and brain weight have a linear relation. This agrees with the 95% CI \([0.2351,\ 0.2866]\), which does not contain 0.

**Why · The test statistic has the \(t_{n-2}\) distribution** Added

This derivation starts from the result of Section 01.3. It puts in \(H_0\), and then it writes the p-value as one tail.

1

\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_1}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

Section 01.3, line 18. It is true for each value of \(\beta_1\).

2

\[\frac{\hat\beta_1-\theta_0}{\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\sim t_{n-2}\quad\text{under }H_0\]

\(H_0\) gives \(\beta_1=\theta_0\).

3

\[P(|T|\ge|t^{obs}|)=P(T\ge|t^{obs}|)+P(T\le-|t^{obs}|)\]

4

\[P(|T|\ge|t^{obs}|)=2P(T\ge|t^{obs}|)\]

The \(t\) distribution is symmetric about 0. ∎

Thus, the test and the interval use the same \(t_{n-2}\) result. The interval solves for \(\beta_1\), and the test puts in \(\beta_1=\theta_0\).

### 01.6 The brainhead results on Slides p.7 Slides p.7

This section lists the statistical numbers that Slides p.7 prints. Then it connects each number to a formula of Sections 01.3–01.5.

**What** Slides p.7

Slides p.7 shows the fitted SLR model for the brainhead data. The list below gives its numbers.

Intercept: estimate \(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\), standard error 47.77644, \(t\) value 7.021, p-value \(2.37\times10^{-11}\).

Slope: estimate \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\), standard error 0.01307, \(t\) value 19.957, p-value less than \(2\times10^{-16}\).

\(\hat\sigma=72.35\) on 234 degrees of freedom.

95% CI for \(\beta_0\): \([241.3053884,\ 429.5592416]\).

95% CI for \(\beta_1\): \([0.2350725,\ 0.2865689]\).

Slides p.7 also prints the numbers below. Later lectures explain them. This unit does not use them.

Residuals: minimum \(-174.88\), first quartile \(-49.03\), median \(-2.40\), third quartile 46.72, maximum 242.41.

\(R^2=0.6299\) and adjusted \(R^2=0.6283\).

F-statistic 398.3 on 1 and 234 degrees of freedom, with a p-value less than \(2.2\times10^{-16}\).

**How** Added

Connect the printed numbers to the formulas

- Match each estimate to \(\hat\beta_0\) or \(\hat\beta_1\).
- Match the slope standard error to \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).
- Divide each estimate by its standard error. The result is \(t^{obs}\) for \(\theta_0=0\).
- Match each p-value to \(P(|T|\ge|t^{obs}|)\) with \(T\sim t_{n-2}\).
- Add 2 to the degrees of freedom to get \(n\).
- Calculate the midpoint of each CI. Compare it with the estimate.

**Self-check:** Each \(t\) value is equal to the estimate divided by its standard error, to rounding.

**Example 9 · Check each number** Slides p.7

This example does the six steps on the numbers of Slides p.7.

Step 1: \(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\).

Step 2: \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\).

Step 3: Slope: \(0.26082/0.01307=19.956\). The printed value is 19.957, from inputs with more digits.

Step 3 (cont.): Intercept: \(335.43231/47.77644=7.021\). This is equal to the printed value.

Step 4: Software gives \(2P(T\ge7.021)=2.37\times10^{-11}\) with \(T\sim t_{234}\). This is equal to the printed intercept p-value.

Step 5: \(n=234+2=236\).

Step 6: Slope CI midpoint: \((0.2350725+0.2865689)/2=0.5216414/2=0.2608207\). This rounds to 0.26082.

Step 6 (cont.): Intercept CI midpoint: \((241.3053884+429.5592416)/2=670.8646300/2=335.432315\). This rounds to 335.43231.

Thus, the formulas of Sections 01.3–01.5 give each coefficient number on Slides p.7.

This unit reviewed the SLR model, the result \(\hat\beta_1\sim N(\beta_1,\sigma^2/S_{xx})\), the \(t_{n-2}\) result, and the CI and test that it gives. Unit 02 uses the same method to estimate the mean response \(\mu_0\) at a given value \(x_0\).

### 01.7 Practice Added

The three questions below use only the numbers on Slides p.7.

**Q1.** Using the results on Slides p.7, calculate a 90% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\). You may use \(t_{0.95,234}=1.651391\). Interpret the interval.

Answer

Step 1: \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.01307\).

Step 2: \(\alpha=0.10\), so \(1-\alpha/2=0.95\). The quantile is \(t_{0.95,234}=1.651391\).

Step 3: Half-width \(=1.651391\times0.01307=0.021584\).

Step 4: \(0.26082-0.021584=0.239236\) and \(0.26082+0.021584=0.282404\).

The 90% CI is \([0.239236,\ 0.282404]\). We are 90% confident that 1 cm³ more head size increases the mean brain weight by 0.2392 g to 0.2824 g. It is narrower than the 95% CI, because 1.651391 is less than 1.970154.

**Q2.** Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0.25\) vs \(H_1:\beta_1\neq0.25\) at the 5% level. Report \(t^{obs}\), the p-value, and your conclusion.

Answer

Step 1: \(\theta_0=0.25\).

Step 2: \(t^{obs}=(0.26082-0.25)/0.01307=0.01082/0.01307=0.82785\).

Step 3: Software gives \(2P(T\ge0.82785)=0.4086\), with \(T\sim t_{234}\).

Step 4: \(0.4086>0.05\), so we do not reject \(H_0\). The data agree with \(\beta_1=0.25\).

This agrees with the 95% CI \([0.2351,\ 0.2866]\), which contains 0.25.

**Q3.** Using the results on Slides p.7, verify the 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_0\). Use \(t_{0.975,234}=1.970154\).

Answer

Step 1: \(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\), and its standard error is 47.77644.

Step 2: Half-width \(=1.970154\times47.77644=94.1269\).

Step 3: \(335.43231-94.1269=241.3054\) and \(335.43231+94.1269=429.5592\).

The result \([241.3054,\ 429.5592]\) agrees with the interval \([241.3053884,\ 429.5592416]\) on Slides p.7. The formula is the same as for \(\beta_1\): estimate \(\pm\ t_{0.975,n-2}\times\) standard error.

These three questions practice the three operations of this unit: make a CI, do a \(t\) test, and check a printed interval.

## 02 · Point estimate of the mean response and its distribution

This unit estimates the mean of \(y\) at a given value \(x_0\). It then finds the expectation, the variance and the distribution of this estimator. The next unit uses these three results to make a confidence interval for the mean response.

Plan · Slides p.8–18

Step 1 (Slides p.10–13): Write the mean response \(\mu_0\) and its estimator \(\hat\mu_0\). Then write \(\hat\mu_0\) as \(\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\).

Step 2 (Slides p.14–15): Show that \(\hat\mu_0\) is unbiased, that is, \(E[\hat\mu_0]=\mu_0\).

Step 3 (Slides p.16–17): Find \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]\) one line at a time.

Step 4 (Slides p.18): Put the expectation and the variance together. Write the normal distribution of \(\hat\mu_0\).

Slides p.8 Page 8 repeats the Lecture 4 title page (Simple Linear Regression: Prediction).

Slides p.9 Page 9 is a section page with the title "Estimating Mean Response". The content of this unit starts on page 10.

Model and notation from earlier · Slides p.3–4 (unit 01 defines each item)

Model: \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\). The same model in a second form is \(y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\).

Least squares estimators: \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\). Here \(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\) and \(S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)\).

An estimator is a random quantity that we calculate from the data. An estimate is the number that we get from one data set.

Each step in this unit uses only this notation.

Example data · Slides p.7 and Added

The examples use the brainhead data. The data have \(n=236\) persons. \(x_i\) is the head size of person \(i\) (cm³). \(y_i\) is the brain weight of person \(i\) (g).

Slides p.7 prints the estimates \(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) and \(\hat\sigma=72.35\), with \(n-2=234\).

The course data file brainhead.csv gives four more values (Added): \(\bar x=3637.864\), \(\bar y=1284.263\), \(S_{xx}=30647233.66\) and \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\) to more digits.

### 02.1 The mean response \(\mu_0\) and its point estimate \(\hat\mu_0\) Slides p.10–13

This section gives the mean of \(y\) at a new value \(x_0\). It also shows how to estimate this mean from the data.

**What** Slides p.10

Lecture 4 · p.10 Recall the mean response is \(E[y_i\mid x_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\).
For an arbitrary \(x_0\), the mean outcome is \(\mu_0:=E[y_0\mid x_0]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0\).
We can estimate this as \[\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\]

The expectation \(E[\cdot]\) of a random variable is its long-run average value.

The conditional expectation \(E[y\mid x]\) is the long-run average of \(y\) when \(x\) has one fixed value.

The mean response is the conditional expectation \(E[y\mid x]\). In this model, it is the height \(\beta_0+\beta_1x\) of the true line, because \(E[\epsilon]=0\).

\(x_0\) is one value of the covariate that we want to study. It does not have to be in the data. \(y_0\) is the response at \(x_0\).

The symbol \(:=\) means "is defined as". Thus \(\mu_0:=E[y_0\mid x_0]\) gives the name \(\mu_0\) to \(E[y_0\mid x_0]\).

A point estimate is one number that estimates an unknown quantity. Here \(\hat\mu_0\) is the point estimate of \(\mu_0\).

\(\mu_0\) is the height of the true line at \(x_0\). We do not know \(\mu_0\), because we do not know \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). \(\hat\mu_0\) is the height of the fitted line at \(x_0\). We can calculate \(\hat\mu_0\) from the data.

Lecture 4 · p.11–13 \[\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0=\left(\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\right)+\hat\beta_1x_0=\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\] Intuition?
• What happens at \(\bar x\)?

Slides p.11–12 write \(\hat\mu_0\) in a second form. The second form starts at the center point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) of the data. Then it moves along the fitted line by the horizontal distance \(x_0-\bar x\). For each unit of distance, the height changes by \(\hat\beta_1\).

Slides p.13 asks about \(x_0=\bar x\). At this point the horizontal distance is 0. Thus \(\hat\mu_0=\bar y\).

The two forms give the same number. At \(x_0=\bar x\), the result is \(\bar y\).

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat\mu_0\)

- Calculate \(n\), \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(S_{xx}\) and \(S_{xy}\) from the data.
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\). Then calculate \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).
- Form 1 (Slides p.10): put \(x_0\) into \(\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\).
- Form 2 (Slides p.12): calculate the distance \(x_0-\bar x\).
- Calculate \(\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\).

**Self-check:** ① Form 1 and form 2 must give the same result, except for rounding. ② At \(x_0=\bar x\), the result must equal \(\bar y\). ③ When \(\hat\beta_1>0\) and \(x_0>\bar x\), the result must be larger than \(\bar y\).

These steps change any \(x_0\) into one number \(\hat\mu_0\). The next example applies them to the course data.

**Example 1 · The brainhead data at \(x_0=4000\) cm³** Added

This example estimates the mean brain weight of persons with a head size of 4000 cm³. It also calculates \(\hat\mu_0\) at \(x_0=\bar x\).

1

Start values How step 1

\[n=236,\quad \bar x=3637.864,\quad \bar y=1284.263,\quad S_{xx}=30647233.66\]

Values from brainhead.csv (Added).

2

Coefficients How step 2

\[\hat\beta_1=0.2608207,\qquad \hat\beta_0=335.4323\]

Basis: \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\) (Slides p.4). Slides p.7 prints the same values, 335.43231 and 0.26082.

3

Form 1 How step 3 · Slides p.10

\[\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\]

\[\hat\mu_0=335.4323+0.2608207\times4000\]

\[\hat\mu_0=335.4323+1043.2828=1378.7151\]

4

Form 2 How steps 4–5 · Slides p.12

\[x_0-\bar x=4000-3637.864=362.136\]

\[\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)=0.2608207\times362.136=94.452\]

\[\hat\mu_0=\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)=1284.263+94.452=1378.715\]

**Self-check:** Both forms give 1378.715. Here \(x_0>\bar x\) and \(\hat\beta_1>0\). The result is larger than \(\bar y=1284.263\). This agrees with self-check ③.

5

At \(x_0=\bar x\) Slides p.13

\[\hat\mu_0=\bar y+\hat\beta_1(\bar x-\bar x)=\bar y+\hat\beta_1\times0=\bar y=1284.263\]

[figure]
Figure 2-1. The blue points are the brainhead data. The orange line is the fitted line. The purple point is the center \((\bar x,\bar y)\). The fitted line always contains this point. The green point is \(\hat\mu_0=1378.715\) at \(x_0=4000\). From the purple point, move right by \(x_0-\bar x=362.1\). The height increases by \(\hat\beta_1\times362.1=94.45\).

Result of the example: at a head size of 4000 cm³, the estimate of the mean brain weight is \(\hat\mu_0=1378.715\) g. At \(x_0=\bar x\), the estimate is \(\bar y=1284.263\) g.

**Why · The two forms are equal** Slides p.10–13

The chain below changes the form on p.10 into the form on p.12. It uses only \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).

1

\[\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\]

Definition, Slides p.10.

2

\[=\left(\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\right)+\hat\beta_1x_0\]

Substitute \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\) (Slides p.4, p.11).

3

\[=\bar y+\hat\beta_1x_0-\hat\beta_1\bar x\]

4

\[=\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\]

Slides p.12. ∎

At \(x_0=\bar x\) (Slides p.13):

1

\[\hat\mu_0=\bar y+\hat\beta_1(\bar x-\bar x)\]

Substitute \(x_0=\bar x\).

2

\[=\bar y+\hat\beta_1\times0\]

3

\[=\bar y\]

Thus the fitted line always contains the point \((\bar x,\bar y)\). ∎

\(\hat\mu_0\) equals the center height \(\bar y\) plus the slope times the distance from the center. The next section finds the expectation of \(\hat\mu_0\).

### 02.2 \(\hat\mu_0\) is unbiased Slides p.14–15

This section shows that the average of \(\hat\mu_0\) over repeated samples equals the true value \(\mu_0\).

**What** Slides p.15

Lecture 4 · p.15 \[E[\hat\mu_0]=E[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0]=E[\hat\beta_0]+E[\hat\beta_1]x_0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0\]

An estimator is unbiased when its expectation equals the parameter that it estimates. Here \(E[\hat\mu_0]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0=\mu_0\).

Repeated sampling means this: keep \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) the same, get a new set of \(y_1,\dots,y_n\), and calculate \(\hat\mu_0\) again.

Each new sample gives a different \(\hat\mu_0\). The long-run average of these values is \(E[\hat\mu_0]\). One value of \(\hat\mu_0\) can be too high or too low. But \(\hat\mu_0\) has no systematic error in one direction.

**How** Added

Find \(E[\hat\mu_0]\)

- Write \(\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\).
- Use linearity of expectation: \(E[aU+bV]=aE[U]+bE[V]\) when \(a\) and \(b\) are constants.
- Treat \(x_0\) as a constant.
- Substitute the Lecture 3 results \(E[\hat\beta_0]=\beta_0\) and \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\).

**Self-check:** The result must not contain a quantity with a hat. The result must be \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_0\), which is \(\mu_0\).

**Example 2 · A small data set with known parameters** Added

We do not know the true \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) for real data. Thus this example uses a small data set and gives the parameters values. It calculates \(E[\hat\mu_0]\) by hand and compares it with \(\mu_0\).

Data and parameters: \(n=3\), \(x=(1,2,3)\), \(\beta_0=2\), \(\beta_1=0.5\), and \(x_0=4\).

The example writes \(\hat\mu_0\) as \(\sum_{i=1}^n c_iy_i\). Section 02.3 (line 6 of the chain) shows that the weight is \(c_i=\frac1n+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\).

1

Center and spread of \(x\)

\[\bar x=\frac{1+2+3}{3}=\frac{6}{3}=2\]

\[S_{xx}=(1-2)^2+(2-2)^2+(3-2)^2=1+0+1=2\]

\[x_0-\bar x=4-2=2\]

2

Weights \(c_i\)

\[c_1=\frac13+\frac{(1-2)(2)}{2}=\frac13-1=-\frac23\]

\[c_2=\frac13+\frac{(2-2)(2)}{2}=\frac13+0=\frac13\]

\[c_3=\frac13+\frac{(3-2)(2)}{2}=\frac13+1=\frac43\]

3

Expected responses

\[E[y_1]=2+0.5\times1=2.5,\quad E[y_2]=2+0.5\times2=3,\quad E[y_3]=2+0.5\times3=3.5\]

Model: \(E[y_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\) (Slides p.3).

4

Expectation of \(\hat\mu_0\)

\[E[\hat\mu_0]=c_1E[y_1]+c_2E[y_2]+c_3E[y_3]\]

\[=-\frac23\times2.5+\frac13\times3+\frac43\times3.5\]

\[=-\frac53+1+\frac{14}3=\frac{-5+3+14}{3}=\frac{12}{3}=4\]

5

True mean response

\[\mu_0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0=2+0.5\times4=2+2=4\]

**Self-check:** \(E[\hat\mu_0]=4=\mu_0\). The estimator is unbiased in this example.

The example shows \(E[\hat\mu_0]=\mu_0\) with numbers. Section 02.3 uses the same small data set to check the variance.

**Why · \(\hat\mu_0\) is unbiased** Slides p.14–15

1

\[E[\hat\mu_0]=E[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0]\]

Definition \(\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\), Slides p.10.

2

\[=E[\hat\beta_0]+E[\hat\beta_1x_0]\]

Linearity of expectation.

3

\[=E[\hat\beta_0]+E[\hat\beta_1]x_0\]

\(x_0\) is a constant.

4

\[=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0\]

Lecture 3: \(E[\hat\beta_0]=\beta_0\) and \(E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\).

5

\[=\mu_0\]

Definition \(\mu_0:=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0\), Slides p.10. ∎

\(\hat\mu_0\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\mu_0\), so its distribution has its center at \(\mu_0\). The next section finds the spread of this distribution, which is the variance.

### 02.3 The variance of \(\hat\mu_0\) Slides p.16–17

This section finds \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]\). The result shows how the precision of \(\hat\mu_0\) changes with \(x_0\).

**What** Slides p.17

Lecture 4 · p.17 \[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}\right)\]

The variance of a random variable is the expected squared distance from its expectation.

The denominator \(\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\) is \(S_{xx}\).

The first term, \(\sigma^2/n\), does not change with \(x_0\). It is the variance at the center \(\bar x\).

The second term, \(\sigma^2(x_0-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}\), increases when \(x_0\) moves away from \(\bar x\).

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance. It has the same unit as \(y\).

The variance is smallest at \(x_0=\bar x\), where it equals \(\sigma^2/n\). Away from the center, the distance multiplies the error in \(\hat\beta_1\). Thus the variance increases.

**How** Added

Calculate \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]\)

- Calculate \(1/n\).
- Calculate \((x_0-\bar x)^2\). Divide it by \(S_{xx}\).
- Add the two results. This gives the factor \(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\).
- Multiply the factor by \(\sigma^2\).
- To get a number, replace \(\sigma\) with \(\hat\sigma\). Then take the square root.

**Self-check:** ① The factor is always at least \(1/n\). ② At \(x_0=\bar x\), the factor equals \(1/n\). ③ Two values of \(x_0\) at the same distance from \(\bar x\) give the same variance.

\(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2/(n-2)}\) is the estimate of \(\sigma\) from Lecture 2. Here \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\) is the residual. Slides p.7 prints \(\hat\sigma=72.35\). The next unit uses \(\hat\sigma\) to make a confidence interval.

**Example 3 · The brainhead data at \(x_0=4000\) and \(x_0=\bar x\)** Added

This example calculates the factor at two values of \(x_0\). Then it uses \(\hat\sigma=72.35\) (Slides p.7) to get the estimated standard deviation.

1

\(x_0=4000\): the two terms How steps 1–2

\[\frac1n=\frac1{236}=0.004237288\]

\[(x_0-\bar x)^2=362.1356^2=131142.19\]

\[\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}=\frac{131142.19}{30647233.66}=0.004279087\]

2

\(x_0=4000\): the factor How step 3

\[\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}=0.004237288+0.004279087=0.008516375\]

3

\(x_0=4000\): multiply by \(\sigma^2\) How steps 4–5

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\sigma^2\times0.008516375\]

\[\sqrt{0.008516375}=0.09228421\]

\[\hat\sigma\sqrt{0.008516375}=72.35\times0.09228421=6.677\]

4

\(x_0=\bar x\)

\[\frac1n+\frac{(\bar x-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}=\frac1n+0=0.004237288\]

\[\sqrt{236}=15.36229\]

\[\hat\sigma\sqrt{1/n}=\frac{72.35}{15.36229}=4.710\]

**Self-check:** At \(\bar x\) the factor is exactly \(1/n\). Also, 4.710 is smaller than 6.677. The estimate is most precise at the center.

[figure]
Figure 2-2. The curve shows \(\hat\sigma\sqrt{1/n+(x_0-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}}\) for the brainhead data. The horizontal axis is the same as in Figure 2-1. The lowest point is at \(x_0=\bar x\), with the value \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt n=4.710\). At \(x_0=4000\) the value is 6.677. The curve increases with the distance from \(\bar x\).

Result of Example 3: at \(x_0=4000\), \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\sigma^2\times0.008516375\). At \(\bar x\), \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\sigma^2/236\). With \(\hat\sigma\) in place of \(\sigma\), the standard deviations are 6.677 and 4.710.

**Example 4 · The small data set of Example 2** Added

This example calculates \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]\) in two ways for \(x=(1,2,3)\) and \(x_0=4\). The two results must agree.

1

Formula from Slides p.17

\[\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}=\frac13+\frac{2^2}{2}=\frac13+2=\frac73\]

2

Sum of squared weights

\[\sum_{i=1}^3c_i^2=\left(-\frac23\right)^2+\left(\frac13\right)^2+\left(\frac43\right)^2=\frac49+\frac19+\frac{16}9=\frac{21}9=\frac73\]

Example 2 gives the weights \(c_i\). Line 7 of the chain below gives \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\sigma^2\sum c_i^2\).

**Self-check:** Both ways give \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\frac73\sigma^2\).

**Why · The chain for the variance** Slides p.16–17

The chain below follows Slides p.17 line by line. First it writes \(\hat\mu_0\) as a sum of constants times \(y_i\). Then it uses the variance rules for independent variables. When one slide line makes more than one change, this chain shows each change on its own line.

The chain uses four facts:

Fact A (model): \(y_1,\dots,y_n\) are independent, and \(\mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\sigma^2\).

Fact B (Lecture 2): \(\mathrm{Var}(aY)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(Y)\). For independent \(X\) and \(Y\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)\).

Fact C: \(\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar x=n\bar x-n\bar x=0\).

Fact D (Lecture 3): \(\hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iy_i\), with \(w_i=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\). Each \(w_i\) is a fixed number, not a random variable.

1

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0]\]

Definition, Slides p.10.

2

\[=\mathrm{Var}[(\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x)+\hat\beta_1x_0]\]

Substitute \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\).

3

\[=\mathrm{Var}[\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)]\]

The same change as in Section 02.1.

4

\[=\mathrm{Var}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n y_i\right)+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\right]\]

Substitute \(\bar y=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n y_i\). (Added: one slide line split in two.)

5

\[=\mathrm{Var}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n y_i\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}y_i\right)(x_0-\bar x)\right]\]

Fact D: substitute \(\hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}y_i\).

6

\[=\mathrm{Var}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)y_i\right]\]

The two sums have the same index, so we join them. The constant \(x_0-\bar x\) goes inside the sum.

7

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)^2\mathrm{Var}[y_i]\]

Facts A and B: the \(y_i\) are independent. Each constant moves out of the variance as its square. (Added: split.)

8

\[=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)^2\sigma^2\]

Fact A: \(\mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\sigma^2\).

9

\[=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac1{n^2}+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}+2\,\frac1n\,\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

Move \(\sigma^2\) out of the sum. Expand the square with \((a+b)^2=a^2+b^2+2ab\).

10

\[=\sigma^2\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1{n^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}+2\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n\,\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

Split the sum into three sums.

11

\[=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}+2\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n\,\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

\(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1{n^2}=n\cdot\frac1{n^2}=\frac1n\). (Added: split.)

12

\[=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2+2\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n\,\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

The factor \(\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}\) does not change with \(i\). Move it out of the sum. (Added: split.)

13

\[=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}S_{xx}+2\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n\,\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

Definition: \(\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2=S_{xx}\). (Added: split.)

14

\[=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}S_{xx}+2\,\frac1n\,\frac{(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)\right)\]

The factor \(\frac1n\frac{x_0-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\) does not change with \(i\). Move it out of the sum. This is the second-last line on Slides p.17.

15

\[=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}S_{xx}+2\,\frac1n\,\frac{(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\cdot0\right)\]

Fact C: \(\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)=0\). (Added: split.)

16

\[=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

The cross term is 0. Also \(S_{xx}/S_{xx}^2=1/S_{xx}\). (Added: split.)

17

\[=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}\right)\]

Definition: \(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\). This is the last line on Slides p.17. ∎

Number check (Added): the three sums in line 10 for the small data set \(x=(1,2,3)\), \(x_0=4\), with \(\bar x=2\), \(S_{xx}=2\) and \(x_0-\bar x=2\).

First sum: \(\sum_{i=1}^3\frac1{3^2}=3\times\frac19=\frac13\). This equals \(1/n\).

Second sum: \(\frac{(1)(4)+(0)(4)+(1)(4)}{2^2}=\frac{8}{4}=2\). This equals \((x_0-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}=4/2=2\).

Third sum: \(2\times\frac13\times\frac{(-1)(2)+(0)(2)+(1)(2)}{2}=2\times\frac13\times\frac{0}{2}=0\).

Total: \(\frac13+2+0=\frac73\). This agrees with Example 4.

\(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]\) has two parts. The first part is the variance \(\sigma^2/n\) of \(\bar y\). The second part is the slope error multiplied by the distance \(x_0-\bar x\). The cross term is 0 because \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)=0\). The next section uses this variance in the distribution of \(\hat\mu_0\).

### 02.4 The distribution of \(\hat\mu_0\) Slides p.18

This section puts the expectation and the variance together. The result is the full distribution of \(\hat\mu_0\).

**What** Slides p.18

Lecture 4 · p.18 \[\Longrightarrow\ \hat\mu_0\sim N\!\left[\mu_0,\ \sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}\right)\right]\qquad\text{(why?)}\]

The symbol \(\sim\) means "has the distribution".

A linear combination is a quantity of the form \(\sum_{i=1}^n c_iy_i\), where each \(c_i\) is a fixed number.

\(\hat\mu_0\) has a normal distribution. Its mean is the true value \(\mu_0\). Its variance is the result of Section 02.3.

**How** Added

Write the distribution of \(\hat\mu_0\)

- Family: Confirm that \(\hat\mu_0\) is a linear combination of independent normal \(y_i\). Thus \(\hat\mu_0\) is normal.
- Mean: write \(E[\hat\mu_0]=\mu_0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0\) (Section 02.2).
- Variance: write \(\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\) (Section 02.3).
- Put in the values of \(n\), \(\bar x\), \(S_{xx}\) and \(x_0\).

**Self-check:** The mean must not contain a hat. The variance must contain only one unknown, \(\sigma^2\). All other parts are numbers.

**Example 5 · The brainhead data at \(x_0=4000\)** Added

This example puts the numbers from Sections 02.1–02.3 into the result on Slides p.18.

1

Family How step 1

\[\hat\mu_0=\sum_{i=1}^{236}\left(\frac1{236}+\frac{(x_i-3637.864)(362.136)}{30647233.66}\right)y_i\]

The weights are fixed numbers. The \(y_i\) are independent and normal. Thus \(\hat\mu_0\) is normal.

2

Mean How step 2

\[E[\hat\mu_0]=\mu_0=\beta_0+4000\,\beta_1\]

3

Variance How steps 3–4

\[\hat\mu_0\sim N\!\left[\beta_0+4000\,\beta_1,\ \sigma^2\times0.008516375\right]\]

Example 3 gives the factor 0.008516375. This data set gives one value of the estimator, \(\hat\mu_0=1378.715\).

Result of the example: at \(x_0=4000\), \(\hat\mu_0\) is normal with mean \(\beta_0+4000\beta_1\) and variance \(0.008516375\,\sigma^2\).

**Why · \(\hat\mu_0\) is normal (the "why?" on Slides p.18)** Slides p.18

1

\[\hat\mu_0=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)(x_0-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\right)y_i\]

Section 02.3, line 6. Each weight contains only \(n\), \(x_i\), \(\bar x\), \(x_0\) and \(S_{xx}\). Thus each weight is a fixed number.

2

\[y_i\overset{indep}{\sim}N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)\]

Model assumption, Slides p.3.

3

\[\hat\mu_0\ \text{is a linear combination of independent normals}\ \Longrightarrow\ \hat\mu_0\ \text{is normal}\]

Lecture 3 uses the same rule for \(\hat\beta_1=\sum w_iy_i\): a linear combination of independent normal variables is normal.

4

\[E[\hat\mu_0]=\mu_0\]

Section 02.2 (Slides p.15).

5

\[\hat\mu_0\sim N\!\left[\mu_0,\ \sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}\right)\right]\]

Section 02.3 (Slides p.17) gives the variance. ∎

The mean and the variance fully specify a normal distribution. Thus the three results give the full distribution of \(\hat\mu_0\).

**Unit summary:** At any \(x_0\), \(\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0=\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\mu_0\). Its distribution is \(\hat\mu_0\sim N\!\left[\mu_0,\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right]\).

### 02.5 Practice Added

These three questions use the formulas of this unit and the brainhead numbers.

**Q1.** Use the brainhead data: \(n=236\), \(\bar x=3637.864\), \(\bar y=1284.263\), \(\hat\beta_0=335.4323\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207\). Calculate \(\hat\mu_0\) at \(x_0=3000\) cm³ in two ways: (a) \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\); (b) \(\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\).

Answer

(a) \(0.2608207\times3000=782.4621\). Then \(\hat\mu_0=335.4323+782.4621=1117.894\).

(b) \(x_0-\bar x=3000-3637.864=-637.864\).

\(\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)=0.2608207\times(-637.864)=-166.368\).

\(\hat\mu_0=1284.263-166.368=1117.895\). The two ways agree to rounding (1117.894).

Here \(x_0\) is smaller than \(\bar x\) and \(\hat\beta_1>0\). Thus the result is smaller than \(\bar y\).

**Q2.** Show that \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]\) is smallest at \(x_0=\bar x\). Give its value at \(x_0=\bar x\) in terms of \(\sigma^2\) and \(n\).

Answer

The formula is \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\).

The term \(\sigma^2/n\) does not change with \(x_0\). Also \((x_0-\bar x)^2\geq0\) and \(S_{xx}>0\). Thus the second term is at least 0. It equals 0 only at \(x_0=\bar x\).

Put in \(x_0=\bar x\):

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(\bar x-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right)=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+0\right)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\]

At this point \(\hat\mu_0=\bar y\). The result agrees with \(\mathrm{Var}[\bar y]=\sigma^2/n\).

**Q3.** Use the brainhead data with \(S_{xx}=30647233.66\). Calculate the factor \(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\) at \(x_0=3000\) and at \(x_0=4500\). At which \(x_0\) is the estimate of \(\mu_0\) more precise? Use the distance to \(\bar x\) in your answer.

Answer

\(x_0=3000\): \(x_0-\bar x=-637.8644\). Then \((x_0-\bar x)^2=406871.0\) and \(406871.0/30647233.66=0.01327595\). The factor is \(0.004237288+0.01327595=0.01751323\).

\(x_0=4500\): \(x_0-\bar x=862.1356\). Then \((x_0-\bar x)^2=743277.8\) and \(743277.8/30647233.66=0.02425269\). The factor is \(0.004237288+0.02425269=0.02848998\).

0.01751323 is smaller than 0.02848998. Thus the variance is smaller at \(x_0=3000\), and the estimate is more precise there.

The distance from 3000 to \(\bar x\) is 637.9. The distance from 4500 to \(\bar x\) is 862.1. The variance increases with \((x_0-\bar x)^2\).

This unit gave the calculation, the expectation, the variance and the normal distribution of \(\hat\mu_0\). The next unit (03) uses them to make a confidence interval for the mean response.

## 03 · Confidence interval for the mean response

This unit makes an interval for the mean response \(\mu_0\). The interval has its center at \(\hat\mu_0\). The quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\) and the standard error set its width. The unit has six steps. Step 1 (Slides p.19) standardizes \(\hat\mu_0\) and gets a quantity with a \(t_{n-2}\) distribution. Step 2 (Slides p.20) changes this quantity into the interval.

Step 3 (Slides p.21–22) calculates the interval at many values of \(x_0\) and draws the result. Steps 4 and 5 (Slides p.23–24) answer two questions from the slides. Step 4 shows why the intervals become wider at the edges. Step 5 shows why most points are outside the lines. Step 6 (Slides p.25) shows why we also need a prediction interval.

Start point · Slides p.3, p.7, p.10–18

Model (Slides p.3): \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\). Here \(\beta_0\) is the intercept and \(\beta_1\) is the slope.

The data are the brainhead data with \(n=236\) persons. \(x_i\) is the head size of person \(i\) (cm³). \(y_i\) is the brain weight of person \(i\) (g).

The sample mean of the \(x_i\) is \(\bar x\). The sum of squares of \(x\) is \(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\).

A residual \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\) is the observed value minus the fitted value. The estimate of \(\sigma\) is \(\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2/(n-2)}\).

The mean response at a value \(x_0\) is \(\mu_0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0\). It is the mean of \(y\) for all persons with \(x=x_0\). Its estimator is \(\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\) (Slides p.10).

Slides p.7 prints \(\hat\beta_0=335.43231\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.26082\) and \(\hat\sigma=72.35\) on 234 degrees of freedom. This unit uses more digits from the course data file brainhead.csv (Added): \(\hat\beta_0=335.432315\), \(\hat\beta_1=0.2608207153\), \(\hat\sigma=72.35066237\), \(\bar x=3637.864407\) and \(S_{xx}=30647233.66\).

The start result is the distribution of \(\hat\mu_0\) from Slides p.18:
\[\hat\mu_0\sim N\!\left(\mu_0,\ \sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}\right)\right)\]
With this notation, the unit starts with the standardization.

### 03.1 Standardize: from \(N(0,1)\) to \(t_{n-2}\) Slides p.19

This section makes a quantity with a fully known distribution. We need a known distribution to find quantiles and to make an interval.

**What** Slides p.19

Lecture 4 · p.19 So \[\frac{\hat\mu_0-\mu_0}{\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}}}\sim N(0,1)\] And by the same logic as before: \[\frac{\hat\mu_0-\mu_0}{\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

The standard deviation of a random quantity is the square root of its variance.

To standardize a normal quantity, subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation. The result has the standard normal distribution \(N(0,1)\).

The denominator of the first line contains \(\sigma\). We do not know \(\sigma\). Thus we cannot calculate the first line from data.

The second line replaces \(\sigma\) with \(\hat\sigma\). After this change, the distribution is the t distribution \(t_{n-2}\).

The t distribution is a symmetric distribution with more area in its tails than \(N(0,1)\). Its degrees of freedom here are \(n-2\).

The standard error (SE) of \(\hat\mu_0\) is the estimate of its standard deviation: \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}}\).

**How** Added

Calculate the standard error of \(\hat\mu_0\)

- Calculate \(n\), \(\bar x\) and \(S_{xx}\).
- Calculate \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), the residuals \(e_i\) and \(\hat\sigma\).
- Calculate \(x_0-\bar x\) and square it.
- Divide the square by \(S_{xx}\).
- Add \(1/n\) to the result.
- Take the square root of the sum.
- Multiply the square root by \(\hat\sigma\).

**Self-check:** ① The standard error has the same unit as \(y\) (here, g). ② For the brainhead data, the sum in step 5 is much less than 1. Thus the standard error must be much less than \(\hat\sigma\).

**Example 1 · Standard error at \(x_0=4000\)** Added

This example calculates \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)\) at a head size of \(x_0=4000\) cm³. It starts at How step 3, because the start point gives the step 1–2 values. The next section uses the result.

1

Distance from \(\bar x\) How step 3

\[x_0-\bar x=4000-3637.864407=362.1355932\]

\[(x_0-\bar x)^2=362.1355932^2=131142.1879\]

2

Divide by \(S_{xx}\) How step 4

\[\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}=\frac{131142.1879}{30647233.66}=0.004279087285\]

3

Add \(1/n\) How step 5

\[\frac1n=\frac1{236}=0.004237288136\]

\[0.004237288136+0.004279087285=0.008516375421\]

4

Square root How step 6

\[\sqrt{0.008516375421}=0.09228421003\]

5

Multiply by \(\hat\sigma\) How step 7

\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=72.35066237\times0.09228421003=6.676823721\]

At \(x_0=4000\), the standard error of \(\hat\mu_0\) is 6.676823721 g. This is much less than \(\hat\sigma=72.35066237\) g, as the self-check requires. ▲

**Why** Added

This derivation shows why the change from \(\sigma\) to \(\hat\sigma\) gives \(t_{n-2}\). It uses the same logic as Lecture 3 p.31 for \(\hat\beta_1\). The only change is \(\hat\mu_0\) in place of \(\hat\beta_1\). We write \(c_0=\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\) to make the lines shorter.

1

\[\hat\mu_0\sim N\!\left(\mu_0,\ \sigma^2c_0\right)\]

Slides p.18.

2

\[\hat\mu_0-\mu_0\sim N\!\left(0,\ \sigma^2c_0\right)\]

3

\[Z=\frac{\hat\mu_0-\mu_0}{\sigma\sqrt{c_0}}\sim N(0,1)\]

First line of Slides p.19.

4

\[V=\frac1{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\sim\chi^2_{(n-2)}\]

Lecture 3 p.31, items 2 and 3: \(Z\) and \(V\) are independent.

5

\[\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-2)}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

Lecture 3 p.31: independent \(Z\sim N(0,1)\) and \(V\sim\chi^2_\nu\) give \(Z/\sqrt{V/\nu}\sim t_\nu\).

6

\[\sqrt{\frac{V}{n-2}}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{\sigma^2(n-2)}}=\frac{\hat\sigma}{\sigma}\]

7

\[\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-2)}}=\frac{\hat\mu_0-\mu_0}{\sigma\sqrt{c_0}}\cdot\frac{\sigma}{\hat\sigma}\]

8

\[\frac{\hat\mu_0-\mu_0}{\hat\sigma\sqrt{c_0}}\sim t_{n-2}\]

Second line of Slides p.19. ∎

Two independent random quantities are quantities where the value of one gives no information about the other.

The chi-squared distribution \(\chi^2_\nu\) is the distribution of a sum of \(\nu\) squared independent \(N(0,1)\) quantities.

This section gives a quantity with a known distribution and a denominator that we can calculate from data. The next section uses its quantiles to make the interval.

### 03.2 The \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_0\) Slides p.20

This section changes the \(t_{n-2}\) quantity of Section 03.1 into an interval for \(\mu_0\).

**What** Slides p.20

Lecture 4 · p.20 \[\Longrightarrow\ 1-\alpha=P\!\left(-t_{1-\frac\alpha2,\,n-2}\le\frac{\hat\mu_0-\mu_0}{\hat\sigma\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}\right)^{1/2}}\le t_{1-\frac\alpha2,\,n-2}\right)\] and a 100(1-α)% CI is: \[\hat\mu_0\pm t_{1-\frac\alpha2,\,n-2}\,\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}}\]

A confidence interval (CI) is an interval that we calculate from the data. With repeated samples, \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) of these intervals contain the true \(\mu_0\).

The value \(\alpha\) is the probability that the interval does not contain the true value. A 95% interval has \(\alpha=0.05\).

The quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\) is the point of the \(t_{n-2}\) distribution with area \(1-\alpha/2\) on its left side.

The interval has the form "center ± quantile × standard error". The center is \(\hat\mu_0\).

The half-width is the quantile multiplied by the standard error: \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\times\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)\).

**How** Added

Calculate the CI for \(\mu_0\) at a value \(x_0\)

- Calculate \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)\) with the How of Section 03.1.
- Calculate the center \(\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\).
- Find the quantile \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\) of the t distribution.
- Multiply the quantile by \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)\). The result is the half-width.
- Subtract the half-width from \(\hat\mu_0\). This is the lower limit \(L\).
- Add the half-width to \(\hat\mu_0\). This is the upper limit \(U\).

**Self-check:** ① The midpoint \((L+U)/2\) must equal \(\hat\mu_0\). ② At 95% with \(n=236\), the quantile is near 1.96. Its value is 1.970.

**Example 2 · 95% CI for the mean brain weight at \(x_0=4000\)** Added

This example finds the 95% CI for the mean brain weight of persons with head size \(x_0=4000\) cm³. It starts at How step 2. Example 1 gives the How step 1 value \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=6.676823721\).

1

Center How step 2

\[\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0=335.432315+0.2608207153\times4000\]

\[=335.432315+1043.282861\]

\[=1378.715176\]

2

Quantile How step 3

\[\alpha=0.05,\quad 1-\frac\alpha2=0.975,\quad n-2=236-2=234\]

\[t_{0.975,\,234}=1.970153643\]

Value from the t distribution with 234 degrees of freedom.

3

Half-width How step 4

\[t_{0.975,\,234}\times\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=1.970153643\times6.676823721=13.15436858\]

Basis: Example 1 gives \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=6.676823721\).

4

Lower limit How step 5

\[L=1378.715176-13.15436858=1365.560808\]

5

Upper limit How step 6

\[U=1378.715176+13.15436858=1391.869545\]

Self-check: \((1365.560808+1391.869545)/2=1378.715176\), which equals \(\hat\mu_0\).

Result: for persons with a head size of 4000 cm³, the 95% CI for the mean brain weight is (1365.561, 1391.870) g. ▲

**Why** Added

This derivation shows how the probability statement on Slides p.20 gives the form \(\hat\mu_0\pm\ldots\). It isolates \(\mu_0\) in the inequality. We write \(t=t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\) and \(\mathrm{SE}=\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}}\).

1

\[1-\alpha=P\!\left(-t\le\frac{\hat\mu_0-\mu_0}{\mathrm{SE}}\le t\right)\]

Section 03.1: the quantity has the \(t_{n-2}\) distribution. The distribution is symmetric, so each tail has area \(\alpha/2\).

2

\[1-\alpha=P\!\left(-t\,\mathrm{SE}\le\hat\mu_0-\mu_0\le t\,\mathrm{SE}\right)\]

\(\mathrm{SE}>0\).

3

\[1-\alpha=P\!\left(-\hat\mu_0-t\,\mathrm{SE}\le-\mu_0\le-\hat\mu_0+t\,\mathrm{SE}\right)\]

4

\[1-\alpha=P\!\left(\hat\mu_0-t\,\mathrm{SE}\le\mu_0\le\hat\mu_0+t\,\mathrm{SE}\right)\]

Multiply by \(-1\); the inequality signs change direction.

5

\[\text{CI}=\hat\mu_0\pm t_{1-\frac\alpha2,\,n-2}\,\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}}\]

∎

This section gives the interval formula at one value \(x_0\). The next section uses the formula at many values of \(x_0\).

### 03.3 Confidence intervals at a range of \(x_0\) values Slides p.21–22

This section applies the formula of Section 03.2 at each \(x_0\) from the smallest \(x\) to the largest \(x\). Then it draws the limits as two curves.

**What** Slides p.21–22

Lecture 4 · p.22 Estimating mean outcomes and report corresponding CIs at a range of x0 values

Slides p.21 shows only computer code. The code does the steps of Section 03.2 at many values of \(x_0\).

The values of \(x_0\) form a grid. A grid is a list of values with equal spaces between them.

The grid on Slides p.21 starts at the smallest \(x\), stops at the largest \(x\), and has a step of 1.

The level is 95%. Thus every interval uses the quantile \(t_{0.975,\,234}\).

Slides p.22 plots the data, the fitted line, and the lower and upper limits at each grid value.

A confidence band is the pair of curves that join the limits \(L\) and \(U\) of all grid values.

**How** Added

Draw the confidence band for the mean response

- Find the smallest \(x\) and the largest \(x\) in the data.
- Make the grid of \(x_0\) values between them, with a step of 1.
- At each grid value, calculate \(L\) and \(U\) with the How of Section 03.2.
- Plot the data points and the fitted line \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x\).
- Join all lower limits with a curve.
- Join all upper limits with a second curve.

**Self-check:** ① The number of grid values is (largest \(x\) − smallest \(x\)) + 1. ② At \(x_0=4000\), the limits must equal the Example 2 result (1365.561, 1391.870).

\[(4747-2773)+1=1974+1=1975\]

2

\[x_0-\bar x=2773-3637.864407=-864.8644068\]

\[\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}=\frac{747990.4421}{30647233.66}=0.02440645868\]

3

Standard error 03.1 How steps 5–7

\[0.004237288136+0.02440645868=0.02864374682\]

\[\sqrt{0.02864374682}=0.169244636\]

\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=72.35066237\times0.169244636=12.24496152\]

4

Center 03.2 How step 2

\[\hat\mu_0=335.432315+0.2608207153\times2773\]

\[=335.432315+723.2558436=1058.688159\]

5

Half-width 03.2 How step 4

\[1.970153643\times12.24496152=24.12445554\]

\[L=1058.688159-24.12445554=1034.563703\]

\[U=1058.688159+24.12445554=1082.812614\]

Figure 3-1 · Slides p.22, drawn again from the data. The grey dots are the 236 observations. The blue line is the fitted line \(\hat\mu_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0\). The orange curves are the 95% limits \(L\) and \(U\) at each \(x_0\). The purple dashed line is \(\bar x\). The two orange curves are nearest at \(\bar x\). They become farther apart toward the edges.

This section gives the confidence band. The next two sections use Figure 3-1 to answer the two questions on the slides.

### 03.4 Why the intervals become wider toward the edges Slides p.23

This section answers the first question on the slides. The answer is in the term \((x_0-\bar x)^2\) of the standard error.

**What** Slides p.23

Lecture 4 · p.23 Why do the CIs get wider toward the edges?

The half-width is \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\,\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}}\).

For one data set, \(t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\), \(\hat\sigma\), \(n\), \(\bar x\) and \(S_{xx}\) are fixed numbers.

Only the term \((x_0-\bar x)^2\) changes with \(x_0\).

When \(x_0\) moves farther from \(\bar x\), this term increases. Thus the interval becomes wider.

At \(x_0=\bar x\), this term is 0. Thus the interval is narrowest at \(\bar x\).

**How** Added

Compare the interval widths at different values of \(x_0\)

- For each \(x_0\), calculate \(|x_0-\bar x|\).
- Calculate the half-width with the How of Section 03.2.
- Multiply the half-width by 2. The result is the width.
- Sort the \(x_0\) values by \(|x_0-\bar x|\), from small to large.
- Make sure that the widths increase in the same order.

**Self-check:** ① At \(x_0=\bar x\), \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)\) must equal \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt n\). ② The ratio of two widths depends only on the ratio of the two sums under the square root.

**Example 4 · Widths at four values of \(x_0\)** Added

This example compares the 95% intervals at \(x_0=\bar x\), 4000, 2773 (smallest \(x\)) and 4747 (largest \(x\)). All four use \(t_{0.975,\,234}=1.970153643\), \(\hat\sigma=72.35066237\), \(1/n=0.004237288136\) and \(S_{xx}=30647233.66\).

\(x_0=\bar x=3637.864407\) · \(|x_0-\bar x|=0\)

\(\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}=0\). Sum \(=0.004237288136\). Square root \(=0.06509445549\).

\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=72.35066237\times0.06509445549=4.709626971\). Half-width \(=1.970153643\times4.709626971=9.278688732\).

\(\hat\mu_0=335.432315+948.8303969=1284.262712\). CI \(=(1274.984,\ 1293.541)\). Width \(=2\times9.278688732=18.557\).

Self-check: \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt n=72.35066237\times0.06509445549=4.709626971\). This equals \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)\).

\(x_0=4000\) · \(|x_0-\bar x|=362.1355932\)

Example 1 and Example 2 give these values.

\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=6.676823721\). Half-width \(=13.15436858\).

CI \(=(1365.561,\ 1391.870)\). Width \(=2\times13.15436858=26.309\).

\(x_0=2773\) (smallest \(x\)) · \(|x_0-\bar x|=864.8644068\)

Example 3 gives these values.

\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=12.24496152\). Half-width \(=24.12445554\).

\(x_0=4747\) (largest \(x\)) · \(|x_0-\bar x|=1109.135593\)

\(\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}=\frac{1230181.764}{30647233.66}=0.0401400589\). Sum \(=0.04437734703\). Square root \(=0.2106593151\).

\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)=72.35066237\times0.2106593151=15.24134098\). Half-width \(=1.970153643\times15.24134098=30.02778345\).

\(\hat\mu_0=335.432315+1238.115936=1573.548251\). CI \(=(1543.520,\ 1603.576)\). Width \(=2\times30.02778345=60.056\).

The four widths increase in the order of \(|x_0-\bar x|\): 18.557, 26.309, 48.249, 60.056. The width at the largest \(x\) is \(\sqrt{0.04437734703/0.004237288136}=3.236209805\) times the width at \(\bar x\). ▲

[figure]
Figure 3-2 · The half-width \(t_{0.975,\,234}\times\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu_0)\) of the 95% interval at each \(x_0\) (Added). The curve is lowest at \(\bar x\) (purple dashed line). It increases with the distance from \(\bar x\). The blue dots are the four values of \(x_0\) in Example 4.

**Why** Added

This part shows why the variance contains \((x_0-\bar x)^2\). Slides p.17 derives the variance line by line. Here we read only its structure:
\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\mathrm{Var}[\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)]=\underbrace{\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}_{\text{from }\bar y}+\underbrace{\frac{\sigma^2(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}}_{\text{from }\hat\beta_1}\]
The first equal sign uses \(\hat\mu_0=\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\) from Slides p.12. The second equal sign is the result of Slides p.17. In that chain, the cross term contains \(\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)=0\), so it is 0. ∎

The form \(\bar y+\hat\beta_1(x_0-\bar x)\) shows that the fitted line always contains the point \((\bar x,\bar y)\). The error in \(\bar y\) is the same at each \(x_0\). It gives the term \(\frac1n\). The distance \(x_0-\bar x\) multiplies the error in the slope \(\hat\beta_1\). It gives the term \(\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\).

Thus the interval is narrowest at \(\bar x\) and becomes wider toward the edges. The next section answers the second question on the slides.

### 03.5 Why most points are outside the lines Slides p.24

This section answers the second question on the slides. The answer: the target of the interval is the mean \(\mu_0\), not one observation \(y\).

**What** Slides p.24

Lecture 4 · p.24 Why do most of the points fall outside the lines?

The interval of Section 03.2 tells where the mean \(\mu_0\) of \(y\) at \(x_0\) is.

Each observation is \(y_i=\mu_i+\epsilon_i\), with \(\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i\).

The error \(\epsilon_i\) has standard deviation \(\sigma\). Its estimate is \(\hat\sigma=72.35066237\) g.

The largest half-width of the band is 30.02778345 g, at \(x_0=4747\) (Example 4).

Thus most observations are farther from the line than the half-width of the band.

**How** Added

Find if an observation is inside the band

- Use the value \(x_i\) of the observation as \(x_0\).
- Calculate \(L_i\) and \(U_i\) with the How of Section 03.2.
- Compare \(y_i\) with \(L_i\) and \(U_i\).
- If \(L_i\le y_i\le U_i\), record the point as inside the band. If not, record it as outside the band.
- Do steps 1–4 for all \(n\) observations and count the two groups.

**Self-check:** the number inside plus the number outside must equal \(n=236\).

**Why** Added

This derivation compares the variance of one observation with the variance of \(\hat\mu_0\). The variance of a random quantity is the expected squared distance from its expectation.

1

\[y_i=\mu_i+\epsilon_i,\qquad \mathrm{Var}[y_i]=\sigma^2\]

Model, Slides p.3.

2

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]

Slides p.17.

3

\[\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\le0.04437734703\quad\text{for }2773\le x_0\le4747\]

Example 4: the largest value is at \(x_0=4747\).

4

\[\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_0]\le0.04437734703\,\sigma^2\]

The variance of \(\hat\mu_0\) is less than 5% of the variance of one \(y_i\). ∎

The width of the interval shows only the error of \(\hat\mu_0\) as an estimate of \(\mu_0\). When \(n\) increases, \(\frac1n\) and \(\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\) decrease, and the interval becomes narrower. The spread \(\sigma\) of each point about \(\mu_i\) does not decrease with \(n\). Thus this interval cannot contain most single observations. The next section states the new problem that this result gives.

### 03.6 When we want to predict a new observation Slides p.25

This section only states the problem. The next unit gives the answer.

Lecture 4 · p.25 What if we don't just care about the mean, but predictions? I.e. even if we got the mean absolutely perfect—the new points wouldn't fall directly on this line!

Suppose that we know \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) exactly. Then \(\hat\mu_0=\mu_0\), and the mean has no estimation error.

A new observation is still \(\mu_0\) plus an error \(\epsilon\), with \(\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\).

In the brainhead data, \(\hat\sigma=72.35066237\) g. Thus new points are still at a distance from the line.

An interval for a new observation must include two errors: the error of the mean estimate and the new error \(\epsilon\).

A prediction interval is an interval that we make to contain a new observation. Unit 04 gives this interval.

Summary of this unit

The \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for the mean response is \(\hat\mu_0\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-2}\,\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}}\).

The interval is narrowest at \(\bar x\). It contains the mean, not single observations. For one new observation, use the prediction interval of the next unit.
