Step 2: \[E[\mathbf{z}]=\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\mu=\left[\begin{array}{c}1(3637.864)+0(1284.263)\\1(3637.864)-1(1284.263)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}3637.864\\2353.601\end{array}\right]\]

Step 3: \(\mathbf{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&1\\0&-1\end{array}\right]\). Then \[\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}130413.76(1)+34014.61(0)&130413.76(1)+34014.61(-1)\\34014.61(1)+14084.06(0)&34014.61(1)+14084.06(-1)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}130413.76&96399.15\\34014.61&19930.55\end{array}\right]\]

Step 4: row 1 of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \((1,0)\), so row 1 of the result is row 1 of \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T\). Row 2 of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \((1,-1)\), so row 2 is row 1 minus row 2. \[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}130413.76&96399.15\\130413.76-34014.61&96399.15-19930.55\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}130413.76&96399.15\\96399.15&76468.60\end{array}\right]\]

Self-check: the two entries off the diagonal are both 96399.15, so the result is symmetric. \(Var(z_1)=130413.76=var(y_1)\), which agrees with \(z_1=y_1\).

Self-check: Section 04.5 with \(\mathbf{b}=(1,-1)^T\) gives \(\mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{b}=(1)(96399.15)+(-1)(19930.55)=76468.60\). This agrees with \(Var(z_2)\).

Thus \(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T\) give all means, variances and covariances of the \(k\) linear combinations in one calculation. ▲

**Why (1) · \(E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{A}E[\mathbf{y}]\)** Slides p.32–33

The derivation multiplies \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\) row by row. Each row is a sum, and the expectation goes into each sum. The slides use a square \(n\times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\). The same steps apply for \(k\) rows.

1

\[E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}]=E\left[\left[\begin{array}{cccc}a_{11}&a_{12}&\dots&a_{1n}\\a_{21}&a_{22}&\dots&a_{2n}\\ \vdots&&&\\a_{n1}&a_{n2}&\dots&a_{nn}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1\\y_2\\ \vdots\\y_n\end{array}\right]\right]\]

2

\[=E\left[\begin{array}{c}\sum_ia_{1i}y_i\\ \sum_ia_{2i}y_i\\ \vdots\\ \sum_ia_{ni}y_i\end{array}\right]\]

Matrix times vector: row \(r\) gives the sum of products with \(\mathbf{y}\).

3

\[=\left[\begin{array}{c}\sum_ia_{1i}E[y_i]\\ \sum_ia_{2i}E[y_i]\\ \vdots\\ \sum_ia_{ni}E[y_i]\end{array}\right]\]

Entry rule (p.22), then linearity of expectation in each entry.

4

\[=\mathbf{A}E[\mathbf{y}]\]

Step 3 is \(\mathbf{A}\) times the column \((E[y_1],\dots,E[y_n])^T\), row by row.

Thus the expectation moves through the constant matrix \(\mathbf{A}\). The next proof uses this result. ∎

**Why (2) · \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{A}Var(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{A}^T\)** Slides p.34–35

The proof uses the transpose rule for a product (Lecture 5 · p.11): \((\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^T=\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T\). The transpose of a product is the product of the transposes in the opposite order.

Small check with the matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) of the example in Section 04.6 and \(\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{y}\): \((\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})^T=(y_1,\ y_1-y_2)\).

Also \(\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{A}^T=(y_1,\ y_2)\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&1\\0&-1\end{array}\right]=(y_1,\ y_1-y_2)\). The two results are equal.

1

\[Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})=E[(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}])(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}])^T]\]

Definition of p.23, with \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\) in place of \(\mathbf{y}\).

2

\[=E[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{y}])(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{y}]))^T]\]

Substitute \(E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{A}E[\mathbf{y}]\) from Why (1). Then take out the factor \(\mathbf{A}\).

3

\[=E[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{y}])(\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{y}])^T\mathbf{A}^T]\]

\((\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^T=\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T\), with \(\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{y}]\).

4

\[=\mathbf{A}E[(\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{y}])(\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{y}])^T]\mathbf{A}^T\]

A constant matrix moves out of the expectation on each side. Each entry is a weighted sum with constant weights.

5

\[=\mathbf{A}Var(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{A}^T\]

The middle part is \(var(\mathbf{y})\) of p.23.

Thus the variance of \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\) is \(\mathbf{A}Var(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{A}^T\). ∎

A linear transformation \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\) has mean \(\mathbf{A}E[\mathbf{y}]\) and variance \(\mathbf{A}Var(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{A}^T\). Later units write the estimator \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) as a constant matrix times \(\mathbf{y}\) and use these two formulas.

### 04.7 Practice Added

The three questions use the same \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) as the examples. They practice a linear combination, a linear transformation, and a proof.

In all three questions, let \(\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2)^T\) with \(\boldsymbol\mu=E[\mathbf{y}]=(3637.864,\ 1284.263)^T\) and \(\mathbf{V}=var(\mathbf{y})=\left[\begin{array}{cc}130413.76&34014.61\\34014.61&14084.06\end{array}\right]\).

**Q1.** Let \(z=y_1+y_2\). Write \(z=\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y}\). Then calculate \(E[z]\) and \(Var(z)\).

Answer

Step 1: \(\mathbf{a}=(1,\ 1)^T\).

Step 2: \(E[z]=\mathbf{a}^T\boldsymbol\mu=3637.864+1284.263=4922.127\).

Step 3: \(Var(z)=\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{V}_{11}+2\mathbf{V}_{12}+\mathbf{V}_{22}=130413.76+2(34014.61)+14084.06\).

Step 4: \(130413.76+68029.22+14084.06=212527.04\).

**Self-check:** the result is \(\ge0\).

**Q2.** Let \(z_1=y_1+y_2\) and \(z_2=y_2\). Write \(\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\). Then calculate \(E[\mathbf{z}]\) and \(Var(\mathbf{z})\). What is \(cov(z_1,z_2)\)?

Answer

Step 1: \(\mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&1\\0&1\end{array}\right]\) and \(\mathbf{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&0\\1&1\end{array}\right]\).

Step 2: \(E[\mathbf{z}]=\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\mu=(3637.864+1284.263,\ 1284.263)^T=(4922.127,\ 1284.263)^T\).

Step 3: \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}130413.76+34014.61&34014.61\\34014.61+14084.06&14084.06\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}164428.37&34014.61\\48098.67&14084.06\end{array}\right]\).

Step 4: row 1 of \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T\) is the sum of the two rows of step 3. Row 2 is row 2 of step 3. \[Var(\mathbf{z})=\left[\begin{array}{cc}164428.37+48098.67&34014.61+14084.06\\48098.67&14084.06\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}212527.04&48098.67\\48098.67&14084.06\end{array}\right]\]

Step 5: \(cov(z_1,z_2)=[Var(\mathbf{z})]_{12}=48098.67\).

**Self-check:** the matrix is symmetric. \(Var(z_1)=212527.04\) agrees with Q1. \(Var(z_2)=14084.06=var(y_2)\) agrees with \(z_2=y_2\).

**Q3.** Show that \(Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{a}^TVar(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{a}\) (p.29) is a special case of \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{A}Var(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{A}^T\) (p.31).

Answer

1

\[\text{Let } k=1,\ \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{a}^T\ (1\times n)\]

One linear combination gives a matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) with one row.

2

\[Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{a}^TVar(\mathbf{y})(\mathbf{a}^T)^T\]

Substitute into p.31.

3

\[=\mathbf{a}^TVar(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{a}\]

Two transposes give the original vector: \((\mathbf{a}^T)^T=\mathbf{a}\).

The result is \(1\times1\), which is one number. This agrees with p.29. ∎

A random vector \(\mathbf{y}\) has mean vector \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and covariance matrix \(\mathbf{V}\), which is symmetric and positive semi-definite. A linear transformation \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\) has mean \(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\mu\) and variance \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T\). Unit 05 uses these results for the multivariate normal distribution.

## 05 · Multivariate normal distribution: definition and properties

This unit defines the multivariate normal distribution and gives its four properties. Later units write the error vector of the regression model \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\) as multivariate normal. Thus later units use these four properties to find the distributions of the estimators.

Plan · Slides p.36–40

Step 1: Make \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\) from an i.i.d. standard normal vector \(\mathbf{z}\). Find its mean and covariance matrix (Slides p.36).

Step 2: Write the joint density of \(\mathbf{y}\) and calculate its value at one point (Slides p.36).

Step 3: Property 1. A linear transformation of an MVN vector is MVN (Slides p.37).

Step 4: Property 2. A marginal distribution is MVN (Slides p.38).

Step 5: Property 3. A conditional distribution is MVN (Slides p.39).

Step 6: Property 4. Zero covariance gives independence (Slides p.40).

All sections use one two-dimensional example: \(\mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&0\\1&1\end{array}\right]\) and \(\boldsymbol\mu=\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\2\end{array}\right]\). All calculations are by hand.

### 05.1 Definition: construction from a standard normal vector Slides p.36

This section gives the construction of a multivariate normal vector. Then it finds the mean vector and the covariance matrix of that vector.

**What** Slides p.36

Multivariate Normal Distribution · Lecture 5 · p.36 Let \(\mathbf{z}=(z_1,\dots,z_n)^T\) be a random vector of i.i.d standard normal random variables, i.e. \(z_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1)\).
Then \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\) has multivariate normal distribution, i.e.: \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) where

- \(E[\mathbf{y}]=\boldsymbol\mu\) and
- \(Var(\mathbf{y})=\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T\).

First, we define each symbol in the statement.

The standard normal distribution \(N(0,1)\) is the normal distribution (Section 01.2) with mean 0 and variance 1.

i.i.d. means "independent and identically distributed" (Section 01.2). The symbol \(\overset{iid}{\sim}\) reads "are i.i.d. with distribution".

\(\mathbf{A}\) is a fixed matrix of constants. It is not random. \(\boldsymbol\mu\) is a fixed \(n\times1\) vector of constants.

The multivariate normal distribution (MVN) is the distribution of a random vector made as \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\). In \(MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\), the first parameter is the mean vector and the second parameter is the covariance matrix.

Unit 04 defines the mean vector \(E[\mathbf{y}]\) and the covariance matrix \(Var(\mathbf{y})\). Here the slides use \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) (capital sigma) for the covariance matrix.

Thus an MVN vector is an i.i.d. standard normal vector, multiplied by a matrix, plus a constant vector.

**How** Added

Find the distribution of \(\mathbf{y}\) from \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol\mu\)

- Write the mean: \(E[\mathbf{y}]=\boldsymbol\mu\).
- Find \(\mathbf{A}^T\). Write row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) as column \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}^T\).
- Find \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T\). For entry \((i,j)\), multiply row \(i\) and row \(j\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) term by term. Then add the products.
- Write \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\).

**Self-check:** \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) must be symmetric, so \(\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}\). Each diagonal entry is a variance, so it must be \(\ge 0\). \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) is \(n\times n\), and \(\boldsymbol\mu\) has length \(n\).

**Example** Added

This example makes a two-dimensional MVN vector with the construction on p.36. We use \(n=2\) and these constants:
\[\mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&0\\1&1\end{array}\right],\qquad \boldsymbol\mu=\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\2\end{array}\right]\]
Step 1: \(E[\mathbf{y}]=\boldsymbol\mu=(1,2)^T\).

Step 2: Row 1 of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \((2,0)\). Row 2 of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \((1,1)\). Thus \(\mathbf{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&1\\0&1\end{array}\right]\).

Step 3: \(\Sigma_{11}=2\cdot2+0\cdot0=4\). \(\Sigma_{12}=2\cdot1+0\cdot1=2\). \(\Sigma_{21}=1\cdot2+1\cdot0=2\). \(\Sigma_{22}=1\cdot1+1\cdot1=2\).

Thus \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{cc}4&2\\2&2\end{array}\right]\).

Step 4: \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN\left(\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\2\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{cc}4&2\\2&2\end{array}\right]\right)\).

Self-check: \(\Sigma_{12}=\Sigma_{21}=2\), so \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) is symmetric. The diagonal entries 4 and 2 are positive.

Figure 05.1 shows what this distribution looks like. A random draw is one value that the random vector gets when the random process runs one time. The left panel shows 400 random draws of \(\mathbf{y}\), made with \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\).

[figure]
Figure 05.1 · The left panel shows 400 random draws of \(\mathbf{y}\). The orange point is the mean \(\boldsymbol\mu=(1,2)^T\). The cloud of points slopes up to the right because \(\Sigma_{12}=2>0\): a large \(y_1\) tends to come with a large \(y_2\). The cloud is wider than it is tall because \(\Sigma_{11}=4>\Sigma_{22}=2\). Both axes use the same scale, and Section 05.6 uses the right panel.

Thus the example gives \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) with mean \((1,2)^T\) and covariance matrix \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T\).

**Why** Added

The proof uses two rules for random vectors from Section 04.6, with a constant vector added. Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be a matrix of constants, \(\mathbf{b}\) a vector of constants, and \(\mathbf{z}\) a random vector.

Rule E: \(E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{b}]=\mathbf{A}\,E[\mathbf{z}]+\mathbf{b}\).

Rule V: \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{b})=\mathbf{A}\,Var(\mathbf{z})\,\mathbf{A}^T\). The constant vector \(\mathbf{b}\) only shifts the vector. It does not change the covariance matrix.

The proof also needs \(E[\mathbf{z}]\) and \(Var(\mathbf{z})\).

Each \(z_i\sim N(0,1)\), so \(E[z_i]=0\). Thus \(E[\mathbf{z}]=\mathbf{0}\), the vector of zeros.

On the diagonal, \(Var(z_i)=1\). Off the diagonal, \(z_i\) and \(z_j\) with \(i\ne j\) are independent, so \(cov(z_i,z_j)=0\).

Thus \(Var(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{I}\), the identity matrix (Section 02.4).

First, we find the mean.

1

\[E[\mathbf{y}]=E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu]\]

2

\[=\mathbf{A}\,E[\mathbf{z}]+\boldsymbol\mu\]

Rule E with \(\mathbf{b}=\boldsymbol\mu\).

3

\[=\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{0}+\boldsymbol\mu\]

\(E[\mathbf{z}]=\mathbf{0}\).

4

\[=\boldsymbol\mu\]

∎

Next, we find the covariance matrix.

1

\[Var(\mathbf{y})=Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu)\]

2

\[=\mathbf{A}\,Var(\mathbf{z})\,\mathbf{A}^T\]

Rule V.

3

\[=\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{I}\,\mathbf{A}^T\]

\(Var(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{I}\).

4

\[=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T=\boldsymbol\Sigma\]

A product with \(\mathbf{I}\) does not change a matrix. ∎

Thus the two MVN parameters \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) are the mean vector and the covariance matrix of \(\mathbf{y}\). The next section writes the density of \(\mathbf{y}\).

### 05.2 Density function Slides p.36

This section gives the joint density of \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\). Then it calculates the density at one point.

**What** Slides p.36

MVN density · Lecture 5 · p.36 \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\), if: \[f(\mathbf{y})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{\frac n2}|\boldsymbol\Sigma|^{\frac12}}\exp\left\{-\frac12(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)\right\}\]

First, we define the symbols in the formula.

The joint density \(f(\mathbf{y})\) is the density of all \(n\) components together. The probability that \(\mathbf{y}\) falls in a small region near a point is about \(f(\mathbf{y})\) times the volume of that region.

The determinant \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|\) is one number that we calculate from a square matrix. For a \(2\times2\) matrix, it is \(ad-bc\) (the optional block in Section 02.4).

The inverse \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\) (Section 02.4) gives \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}=\mathbf{I}\). The examples use the \(2\times2\) formula from the optional block in Section 02.4.

\(\exp\{x\}=e^x\), where \(e\approx2.71828\).

The quadratic form \((\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)\) is a \(1\times n\) vector times an \(n\times n\) matrix times an \(n\times1\) vector. The result is one number.

This number measures the distance from \(\mathbf{y}\) to \(\boldsymbol\mu\), with a scale that comes from \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\).

The density uses only \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\). Thus these two parameters give the full distribution \(MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\).

**How** Added

Calculate \(f(\mathbf{y})\) at a point \(\mathbf{y}\)

- Calculate the difference vector \(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu\).
- Calculate the determinant \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|\).
- Calculate the inverse \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\).
- Calculate \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)\).
- Calculate \(q=(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)\). Multiply the result of step 4 by \(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu\) term by term, then add.
- Put the values into \(f=\dfrac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}|\boldsymbol\Sigma|^{1/2}}e^{-q/2}\).

**Self-check:** \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|>0\). \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}=\mathbf{I}\). \(q\ge0\). When \(\mathbf{y}=\boldsymbol\mu\), \(q=0\) and the density has its largest value.

**Example** Added

We use \(\boldsymbol\mu=(1,2)^T\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{cc}4&2\\2&2\end{array}\right]\) from Section 05.1. We calculate the density at the point \(\mathbf{y}=(2,3)^T\), with \(n=2\).

Step 1: \(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu=(2-1,\ 3-2)^T=(1,1)^T\).

Step 2: \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|=4\cdot2-2\cdot2=8-4=4\).

Step 3: \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}=\frac14\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&-2\\-2&4\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}0.5&-0.5\\-0.5&1\end{array}\right]\).

Step 4: \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(1,1)^T=(0.5-0.5,\ -0.5+1)^T=(0,\ 0.5)^T\).

Step 5: \(q=1\cdot0+1\cdot0.5=0.5\).

Step 6: \((2\pi)^{n/2}=(2\pi)^1=2\pi\). \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|^{1/2}=4^{1/2}=2\). The denominator is \(2\pi\cdot2=4\pi=12.566371\).

Step 7: \(e^{-q/2}=e^{-0.25}=0.778801\).

Step 8: \(f=\dfrac{0.778801}{12.566371}=0.061975\).

Self-check: \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|=4>0\) and \(q=0.5\ge0\). Also \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\) has entry \((1,1)\) equal to \(4\cdot0.5+2\cdot(-0.5)=1\).

Thus the MVN density at \((2,3)^T\) is 0.061975.

**Why** Added

This part shows that for \(n=1\), the MVN density is the usual normal density. Let \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\sigma^2\) (a \(1\times1\) matrix), \(\mathbf{y}=y\), and \(\boldsymbol\mu=\mu\).

1

\[f(y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{\frac12}|\sigma^2|^{\frac12}}\exp\left\{-\frac12(y-\mu)^T(\sigma^2)^{-1}(y-\mu)\right\}\]

Put in \(n=1\).

2

\[=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\left\{-\frac12(y-\mu)^T(\sigma^2)^{-1}(y-\mu)\right\}\]

The determinant of a \(1\times1\) matrix is its one entry, so \(|\sigma^2|^{1/2}=\sigma\).

3

\[=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\left\{-\frac12(y-\mu)\frac{1}{\sigma^2}(y-\mu)\right\}\]

The transpose of a number is the same number. \((\sigma^2)^{-1}=1/\sigma^2\).

4

\[=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\left\{-\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}\]

This is the density of \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). ∎

Thus the MVN density extends the normal density: \(\sigma^2\) becomes \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\), and division by \(\sigma^2\) becomes multiplication by \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\). The next four sections give the four MVN properties.

### 05.3 Property 1: linearity Slides p.37

This section shows that a linear transformation of an MVN vector is MVN. It also gives the new mean and covariance matrix.

**What** Slides p.37

Properties of \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) · Lecture 5 · p.37 Linearity: If \(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{d}\), then: \[\mathbf{u}\sim MVN(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d},\ \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T)\]

A linear transformation multiplies by a constant matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) and then adds a constant vector \(\mathbf{d}\).

If \(\mathbf{C}\) is \(m\times n\), then \(\mathbf{d}\) is \(m\times1\) and \(\mathbf{u}\) is \(m\times1\).

The property gives two facts. First, \(\mathbf{u}\) is normal. Second, Rule E and Rule V give its two parameters.

**How** Added

Find the distribution of \(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{d}\)

- Write \(\mathbf{C}\) (\(m\times n\)) and \(\mathbf{d}\) (\(m\times1\)).
- Calculate the mean \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d}\).
- Calculate \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\).
- Multiply the result of step 3 on the right by \(\mathbf{C}^T\).
- Write \(\mathbf{u}\sim MVN(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d},\ \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T)\). When \(m=1\), this is a univariate normal \(N(\cdot,\cdot)\).

**Self-check:** The mean has length \(m\). The covariance matrix is \(m\times m\), symmetric, and has diagonal entries \(\ge0\).

**Example** Added

We use \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN\left(\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\2\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{cc}4&2\\2&2\end{array}\right]\right)\) from Section 05.1. Let \(\mathbf{C}=(1,\ -1)\) (\(1\times2\)) and \(\mathbf{d}=3\). Then \(u=y_1-y_2+3\).

Step 1: \(\mathbf{C}=(1,-1)\), so \(m=1\). \(\mathbf{d}=3\).

Step 2: \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d}=1\cdot1+(-1)\cdot2+3=2\).

Step 3: \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma=(1\cdot4-1\cdot2,\ 1\cdot2-1\cdot2)=(2,\ 0)\).

Step 4: \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T=2\cdot1+0\cdot(-1)=2\).

Step 5: \(u\sim N(2,\ 2)\).

Self-check: The mean has length 1 and the variance 2 is positive.

Thus \(u=y_1-y_2+3\) is normal with mean 2 and variance 2.

**Why** Added

The proof writes \(\mathbf{u}\) in the form of p.36: a matrix times \(\mathbf{z}\), plus a constant vector.

1

\[\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{d}\]

2

\[=\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu)+\mathbf{d}\]

Put in \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\) from p.36.

3

\[=(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A})\mathbf{z}+(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d})\]

This has the form of p.36. \(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}\) is the matrix and \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d}\) is the shift. Thus \(\mathbf{u}\) is MVN with mean \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d}\).

4

\[Var(\mathbf{u})=(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A})(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A})^T\]

p.36: the covariance matrix is the matrix times its transpose.

5

\[=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{C}^T\]

Transpose rule \((\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A})^T=\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{C}^T\).

6

\[=\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T\]

\(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T=\boldsymbol\Sigma\). ∎

Thus a linear transformation keeps the vector normal and changes only the parameters, by Rule E and Rule V. The next section uses linearity to get the marginal distribution.

### 05.4 Property 2: marginal distribution Slides p.38

This section shows that a subset of the components of an MVN vector is also MVN.

**What** Slides p.38

Properties of \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) · Lecture 5 · p.38 Marginal Distribution: If \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}=(y_1,\dots,y_m)^T\subset\mathbf{y}\) is a vector subset of \(\mathbf{y}\), then \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\) is MVN-distributed.

A marginal distribution is the distribution of some components when we ignore all other components.

A vector subset \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\subset\mathbf{y}\) is a vector of \(m\) components taken from \(\mathbf{y}\), with \(m\le n\). The slides take the first \(m\) components.

The slides state only that \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\) is MVN. Linearity gives its parameters (see Why below). The mean holds the matching entries of \(\boldsymbol\mu\). The covariance matrix holds the matching rows and columns of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\).

**How** Added

Find the distribution of \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\)

- List the indices of the components that you keep, for example \(\{1,\dots,m\}\).
- For the mean, take the entries of \(\boldsymbol\mu\) with these indices.
- For the covariance matrix, take the entries of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) where these rows and these columns cross.
- Write \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\sim MVN(\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu},\tilde{\boldsymbol\Sigma})\). For one component \(y_i\), write \(y_i\sim N(\mu_i,\Sigma_{ii})\).

**Self-check:** \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\Sigma}\) is \(m\times m\). Its diagonal entries are equal to the matching variances in \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\).

**Example** Added

We use \(\mathbf{y}\) from Section 05.1 and keep only \(y_1\), so \(m=1\).

Step 1: Keep the index set \(\{1\}\).

Step 2: \(\mu_1=1\).

Step 3: \(\Sigma_{11}=4\).

Step 4: \(y_1\sim N(1,4)\). The standard deviation is \(\sqrt4=2\).

Next, we use the p.36 density with \(n=1\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=4\) to find the density of \(y_1\) at the point 2.

Step 5: \(y_1-\mu_1=2-1=1\). \(q=1\cdot\frac14\cdot1=0.25\).

Step 6: \((2\pi)^{1/2}\cdot4^{1/2}=2.506628\cdot2=5.013257\).

Step 7: \(e^{-q/2}=e^{-0.125}=0.882497\).

Step 8: \(f(2)=\dfrac{0.882497}{5.013257}=0.176033\).

Figure 05.2 compares random draws of \(y_1\) with this \(N(1,4)\) density curve. Here the histogram (Section 04.5) uses a density scale: the total area of the bars is 1.

[figure]
Figure 05.2 · The blue histogram shows many random draws of \(y_1\), made with \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\). The height is density: frequency divided by bin width. The orange curve is the \(N(1,4)\) density. The two shapes agree, so \(y_1\) alone has the distribution \(N(\mu_1,\Sigma_{11})\).

Thus a marginal distribution needs only the matching entries of \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and the matching block of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\).

**Why** Added

To take the first \(m\) components is a linear transformation with a special \(\mathbf{C}\). Let \(\mathbf{C}=[\,\mathbf{I}_m\ \ \mathbf{0}\,]\) and \(\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0}\). \(\mathbf{C}\) is \(m\times n\). Its left part is the \(m\times m\) identity matrix, and its right part is all zeros.

1

\[\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\dots,y_m)^T=\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\]

Row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{C}\) has 1 only in column \(i\).

2

\[\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\sim MVN(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu,\ \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T)\]

Linearity (p.37) with \(\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0}\).

3

\[\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)^T\]

4

\[\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T=\text{the top-left }m\times m\text{ block of }\boldsymbol\Sigma\]

\(\mathbf{C}\) on the left keeps the first \(m\) rows. \(\mathbf{C}^T\) on the right keeps the first \(m\) columns. ∎

In the example, \(\mathbf{C}=(1,0)\). Then \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu=1\) and \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T=\Sigma_{11}=4\), the same values as above. The next section looks at one part of \(\mathbf{y}\) when we know the other part.

### 05.5 Property 3: conditional distribution Slides p.39

This section shows that if we split \(\mathbf{y}\) into two parts, the first part given the second part is MVN.

**What** Slides p.39

Properties of \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) · Lecture 5 · p.39 Conditional Distribution: If \(\mathbf{y}=(\mathbf{y}_1^T,\mathbf{y}_2^T)^T\), then \(\mathbf{y}_1|\mathbf{y}_2\) is MVN-distributed.

A partition \(\mathbf{y}=(\mathbf{y}_1^T,\mathbf{y}_2^T)^T\) cuts \(\mathbf{y}\) into a top part and a bottom part. Bold \(\mathbf{y}_1\) is the top sub-vector. Bold \(\mathbf{y}_2\) is the bottom sub-vector.

The conditional distribution \(\mathbf{y}_1|\mathbf{y}_2\) is the distribution of \(\mathbf{y}_1\) when \(\mathbf{y}_2\) has a known, fixed value. The bar \(|\) reads "given".

The slides give only the result "is MVN". They do not give formulas for the conditional mean or the conditional covariance matrix. This unit also does not give them.

**How** Added

Identify the type of a conditional distribution

- Confirm that \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\).
- State which components make \(\mathbf{y}_1\) and which components make \(\mathbf{y}_2\).
- Conclude that \(\mathbf{y}_1|\mathbf{y}_2\) is MVN. If \(\mathbf{y}_1\) has one component, the conditional distribution is univariate normal.

**Self-check:** Together, the components of \(\mathbf{y}_1\) and \(\mathbf{y}_2\) are all the components of \(\mathbf{y}\). No component is in both parts.

**Example** Added

We use \(\mathbf{y}\) from Section 05.1, which has two components.

Step 1: \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN\left(\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\2\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{cc}4&2\\2&2\end{array}\right]\right)\), so \(\mathbf{y}\) is MVN.

Step 2: \(\mathbf{y}_1=y_1\) and \(\mathbf{y}_2=y_2\). Each part has one component.

Step 3: By p.39, \(y_1|y_2\) is MVN. \(\mathbf{y}_1\) has one component, so \(y_1\) given \(y_2=3\) has a univariate normal distribution.

Self-check: \(\{y_1\}\) and \(\{y_2\}\) together give both components of \(\mathbf{y}\), with no overlap.

Figure 05.3 shows the shape. It keeps only the random draws with \(y_2\) within 0.05 of 3. Then it shows the histogram of \(y_1\) for those draws.

[figure]
Figure 05.3 · The purple histogram shows the values of \(y_1\) in the random draws with \(y_2\) near 3. The orange curve is a normal density with the same mean and standard deviation as these values. The histogram is bell-shaped and agrees with the curve. This agrees with p.39: \(y_1|y_2\) is normal.

Thus, when \(y_2\) is fixed, \(y_1\) still has a bell-shaped normal distribution.

**Why** Added

No proof on Slides p.39

Slide p.39 states the result only. It does not give a proof, and it does not give the conditional mean or covariance matrix. This unit stays in the scope of the slides and uses only the result "\(\mathbf{y}_1|\mathbf{y}_2\) is MVN".

Thus, to identify the type of a conditional distribution, cite p.39. The next section gives the last property: zero covariance gives independence.

### 05.6 Property 4: independence Slides p.40

This section shows that, for an MVN vector, zero covariance gives independence.

**What** Slides p.40

Properties of \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) · Lecture 5 · p.40 Independence: If \(\Sigma_{ij}=0\), then \(\mathbf{y}_i\) and \(\mathbf{y}_j\) are independent.

\(\Sigma_{ij}\) is the entry of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) in row \(i\), column \(j\). It is equal to \(cov(y_i,y_j)\).

Two variables are independent when the value of one variable does not change the distribution of the other variable.

For variables with a density, independence means that the joint density is the product of the marginal densities: \(f(y_i,y_j)=f_i(y_i)f_j(y_j)\).

This property is true only when \(\mathbf{y}\) is MVN.

**How** Added

Use \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) to find independent components

- Confirm that the vector is MVN.
- If the vector is \(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{d}\), use linearity to find its covariance matrix first.
- Read the off-diagonal entry \(\Sigma_{ij}\).
- If \(\Sigma_{ij}=0\), conclude that component \(i\) and component \(j\) are independent.

**Self-check:** \(\Sigma_{ij}\) and \(\Sigma_{ji}\) are equal. Both must be 0.

**Example** Added

In the Section 05.1 example, \(\Sigma_{12}=2\). Thus \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are not covered by this property. We first make a linear transformation with zero covariance.

Let \(\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{C}_2\mathbf{y}\), with \(\mathbf{C}_2=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&-1\\0&1\end{array}\right]\). Then \(\mathbf{w}=(y_1-y_2,\ y_2)^T\).

Step 1: \(\mathbf{y}\) is MVN, so by linearity \(\mathbf{w}\sim MVN(\mathbf{C}_2\boldsymbol\mu,\ \mathbf{C}_2\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}_2^T)\).

Step 2: \(\mathbf{C}_2\boldsymbol\mu=(1-2,\ 2)^T=(-1,\ 2)^T\).

Step 3: \(\mathbf{C}_2\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{cc}4-2&2-2\\2&2\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&0\\2&2\end{array}\right]\).

Step 4: \(\mathbf{C}_2^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&0\\-1&1\end{array}\right]\).

Step 5: \(\mathbf{C}_2\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}_2^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2-0&0+0\\2-2&0+2\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&0\\0&2\end{array}\right]\).

Step 6: The off-diagonal entries are 0.

Step 7: Thus \(w_1=y_1-y_2\) and \(w_2=y_2\) are independent.

The right panel of Figure 05.1 shows the same 400 random draws as \(\mathbf{w}\). The cloud of points does not slope. Its orange center point is the mean \((-1,2)^T\). This agrees with p.40: the two components are independent.

**Why** Added

We prove the property for \(n=2\). Let \(\Sigma_{12}=\Sigma_{21}=0\), so \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\Sigma_{11}&0\\0&\Sigma_{22}\end{array}\right]\). The goal is to write the joint density as a product of two univariate normal densities.

1

\[|\boldsymbol\Sigma|=\Sigma_{11}\Sigma_{22}-0\cdot0=\Sigma_{11}\Sigma_{22}\]

2

\[\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}=\frac{1}{\Sigma_{11}\Sigma_{22}}\left[\begin{array}{cc}\Sigma_{22}&0\\0&\Sigma_{11}\end{array}\right]\]

\(2\times2\) inverse formula (optional block, Section 02.4).

3

\[=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1/\Sigma_{11}&0\\0&1/\Sigma_{22}\end{array}\right]\]

4

\[(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)=\frac{(y_1-\mu_1)^2}{\Sigma_{11}}+\frac{(y_2-\mu_2)^2}{\Sigma_{22}}\]

5

\[f(\mathbf{y})=\frac{1}{2\pi(\Sigma_{11}\Sigma_{22})^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{(y_1-\mu_1)^2}{2\Sigma_{11}}-\frac{(y_2-\mu_2)^2}{2\Sigma_{22}}\right\}\]

The p.36 density. For \(n=2\), \((2\pi)^{n/2}=2\pi\).

6

\[=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt{\Sigma_{11}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{(y_1-\mu_1)^2}{2\Sigma_{11}}\right\}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt{\Sigma_{22}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{(y_2-\mu_2)^2}{2\Sigma_{22}}\right\}\]

\(e^{a+b}=e^ae^b\).

7

\[=f_1(y_1)\,f_2(y_2)\]

By the marginal property (p.38), \(y_1\sim N(\mu_1,\Sigma_{11})\) and \(y_2\sim N(\mu_2,\Sigma_{22})\). The two factors are their densities. ∎

The joint density is the product of the marginal densities, so \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are independent. Thus, for an MVN vector, a zero off-diagonal entry of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) gives independence.

This unit made \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T)\) from an i.i.d. standard normal vector and gave its density. It also gave four properties: linear, marginal, and conditional distributions are MVN, and zero covariance gives independence. Unit 06 uses these results to write multiple linear regression in MVN form.

### 05.7 Practice Added

The three questions below practice linearity, marginal distributions with independence, and the density calculation.

**Q1.** Let \(\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2)^T\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) with \(\boldsymbol\mu=\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\2\end{array}\right]\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{cc}4&2\\2&2\end{array}\right]\). Find the distribution of \(u=2y_1+y_2-1\).

Answer

Step 1: \(u=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{d}\), with \(\mathbf{C}=(2,\ 1)\) and \(\mathbf{d}=-1\).

Step 2: \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d}=2\cdot1+1\cdot2-1=3\).

Step 3: \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma=(2\cdot4+1\cdot2,\ 2\cdot2+1\cdot2)=(10,\ 6)\).

Step 4: \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T=10\cdot2+6\cdot1=26\).

Step 5: By linearity (p.37), \(u\sim N(3,\ 26)\).

**Q2.** Let \(\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2,y_3)^T\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) with \(\boldsymbol\mu=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\1\\-1\end{array}\right]\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}3&1&0\\1&2&0\\0&0&5\end{array}\right]\). (a) Give the distribution of \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}=(y_1,y_3)^T\). (b) Which pairs of components are independent by the Independence property?

Answer

(a) Step 1: Keep the index set \(\{1,3\}\).

(a) Step 2: \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\mu}=(\mu_1,\mu_3)^T=(0,\ -1)^T\).

(a) Step 3: Take rows 1 and 3 and columns 1 and 3: \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\Sigma}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\Sigma_{11}&\Sigma_{13}\\\Sigma_{31}&\Sigma_{33}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}3&0\\0&5\end{array}\right]\).

(a) Step 4: By the marginal property (p.38), \(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\sim MVN\left(\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\-1\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{cc}3&0\\0&5\end{array}\right]\right)\).

(b) \(\Sigma_{13}=\Sigma_{31}=0\), so \(y_1\) and \(y_3\) are independent (p.40).

(b) \(\Sigma_{23}=\Sigma_{32}=0\), so \(y_2\) and \(y_3\) are independent (p.40).

(b) \(\Sigma_{12}=1\), so the Independence property does not apply to \((y_1,y_2)\).

**Q3.** Let \(z_1,z_2\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1)\), \(\mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&0\\1&1\end{array}\right]\), \(\boldsymbol\mu=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\0\end{array}\right]\), and \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\). Find \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) and calculate the density \(f(\mathbf{y})\) at \(\mathbf{y}=(1,1)^T\).

Answer

Step 1: \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T\). \(\Sigma_{11}=1\cdot1+0\cdot0=1\). \(\Sigma_{12}=\Sigma_{21}=1\cdot1+0\cdot1=1\). \(\Sigma_{22}=1\cdot1+1\cdot1=2\).

Thus \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&1\\1&2\end{array}\right]\).

Step 2: \(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu=(1,1)^T\).

Step 3: \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|=1\cdot2-1\cdot1=1\).

Step 4: \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}=\frac11\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&-1\\-1&1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&-1\\-1&1\end{array}\right]\).

Step 5: \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(1,1)^T=(2-1,\ -1+1)^T=(1,\ 0)^T\).

Step 6: \(q=1\cdot1+1\cdot0=1\).

Step 7: The denominator is \((2\pi)^1\cdot1^{1/2}=2\pi=6.283185\).

Step 8: \(e^{-q/2}=e^{-0.5}=0.606531\).

Step 9: \(f=\dfrac{0.606531}{6.283185}=0.096532\).

These three questions cover the three calculations of this unit. Q1 finds the parameters after a linear transformation. Q2 finds a marginal distribution and independent pairs. Q3 finds \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) from \(\mathbf{A}\) and then the density.

## 06 · Exercises on the MVN, MLR as an MVN model, and practice

This unit uses the definition of the multivariate normal distribution in three exercises and two practice questions. It covers the last eight pages of Lecture 5.

Plan · Slides p.41–48

Step 1: Make a new variable \(X_2\) and show that it has the \(N(0,1)\) distribution (Slides p.41–42).

Step 2: Add \(X_2\) to \(X_1\). Show that the vector \((X_1,X_2)^T\) is not MVN (Slides p.43–44).

Step 3: Write the multiple linear regression model as one MVN statement (Slides p.45).

Step 4: Calculate mean vectors and covariance matrices in two practice questions (Slides p.46–48).

Step 5: Do two more practice questions.

This unit uses two results from unit 05. Section 05.1 gives the definition (Slides p.36): if \(z_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1)\), then \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T)\). Section 05.3 gives linearity (Slides p.37): \(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{d}\sim MVN(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf{d},\ \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{C}^T)\). When \(\mathbf{C}\) has one row, the result is a normal distribution of one variable.

The exercise on Slides p.41 uses these two facts. The next section starts it.

### 06.1 Exercise: \(X_2\) has a normal distribution Slides p.41–42

This section makes a new variable \(X_2\) from \(X_1\) and a coin. It shows that \(X_2\) has the \(N(0,1)\) distribution.

**What (1)** Slides p.41

Exercise · Lecture 5 · p.41 Let r.v.'s \(X_1\sim N(0,1)\) and \(B\sim Bernoulli(0.5)\), independent of \(X_1\). Now consider r.v. \(X_2=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}X_1 & \text{if } B=0\\ -X_1 & \text{if } B=1\end{array}\right.\)
\(X_2\) is clearly Normally distributed (we've just swapped half the signs to be opposite, and since it's symmetric, the distribution is unchanged.)

"r.v." means random variable (Section 01.2).

\(B\sim Bernoulli(0.5)\) means that \(B\) is 0 or 1, with \(P(B=0)=P(B=1)=0.5\). It is the result of one fair coin toss.

Independent (Section 05.6) means that the value of \(B\) does not change the distribution of \(X_1\).

Symmetric means that the \(N(0,1)\) density curve has the same shape on the left of 0 and on the right of 0. Thus \(X_1\) and \(-X_1\) have the same distribution.

The rule makes \(X_2\) from \(X_1\). If \(B=0\), \(X_2\) is \(X_1\). If \(B=1\), \(X_2\) is \(X_1\) with the opposite sign. The sign change does not change a symmetric distribution. Thus \(X_2\sim N(0,1)\).

**What (2) · the visual check** Slides p.42

Slides p.41–42 check this result with a simulation. A simulation makes many random draws (Section 05.1) with a computer. Then it shows their pattern.

A density curve is a curve whose area over an interval is the probability of that interval.

Slides p.42 shows a histogram (Section 04.5) of the random draws of \(X_2\) on a density scale. The \(N(0,1)\) density curve is on it.

On Slides p.42, the bars follow the curve. The highest bars are near 0, at a height of approximately 0.4.

The \(N(0,1)\) density at 0 is \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\approx0.3989\). This value agrees with the height on the slide.

**How** Added

A cumulative distribution function (CDF) gives \(P(X\le t)\) for each number \(t\). Two variables with the same CDF at all \(t\) have the same distribution. Let \(\Phi(t)=P(X_1\le t)\) be the CDF of \(N(0,1)\).

Find \(P(X_2\le t)\) for one value of \(t\)

- Divide the event into two cases: \(B=0\) and \(B=1\).
- In each case, put the rule for \(X_2\) in place of \(X_2\).
- Use independence to write each case as a product of two probabilities.
- Change \(P(-X_1\le t)\) to \(P(X_1\ge -t)\). Then use symmetry to change it to \(\Phi(t)\).
- Add the two cases.

**Self-check:** The two case probabilities \(P(B=0)\) and \(P(B=1)\) must add to 1. The result must equal \(\Phi(t)\).

**Example · \(t=1\)** Added

This example finds \(P(X_2\le1)\). The \(N(0,1)\) table value is \(\Phi(1)=0.8413\).

Step 1: \(P(X_2\le1)=P(X_2\le1,\ B=0)+P(X_2\le1,\ B=1)\).

Step 2: \(=P(X_1\le1,\ B=0)+P(-X_1\le1,\ B=1)\).

Step 3: \(=P(X_1\le1)\times0.5+P(-X_1\le1)\times0.5\).

Step 4: \(P(-X_1\le1)=P(X_1\ge-1)=1-\Phi(-1)=1-0.1587=0.8413\). This is equal to \(\Phi(1)\), as the figure below shows.

Step 5: \(P(X_2\le1)=0.8413\times0.5+0.8413\times0.5=0.42065+0.42065=0.8413\).

Self-check: \(0.5+0.5=1\), and the result \(0.8413\) is equal to \(\Phi(1)\).

[figure]
Figure 06.1 · The \(N(0,1)\) density. The area to the left of \(-1\) (blue) is 0.1587. The area to the right of \(1\) (orange) is also 0.1587. Because the two areas are equal, \(P(X_1\ge-1)=P(X_1\le1)\).

**Why** Added

The chain below does the How steps for a general \(t\).

1

\[P(X_2\le t)=P(X_2\le t,\ B=0)+P(X_2\le t,\ B=1)\]

\(B\) is 0 or 1.

2

\[=P(X_1\le t,\ B=0)+P(-X_1\le t,\ B=1)\]

The rule for \(X_2\).

3

\[=P(X_1\le t)P(B=0)+P(-X_1\le t)P(B=1)\]

\(B\) and \(X_1\) are independent.

4

\[=\tfrac12\,\Phi(t)+\tfrac12\,P(-X_1\le t)\]

5

\[=\tfrac12\,\Phi(t)+\tfrac12\,P(X_1\le t)\]

Symmetry: \(-X_1\) and \(X_1\) have the same distribution.

6

\[=\tfrac12\,\Phi(t)+\tfrac12\,\Phi(t)=\Phi(t)\]

Thus \(X_2\sim N(0,1)\). ∎

Result: \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) each have the \(N(0,1)\) distribution. The next section asks if the vector \((X_1,X_2)^T\) is MVN.

### 06.2 Exercise continued: \(Y=X_1+X_2\) is not normal Slides p.43–44

This section shows that normal components do not make an MVN vector. It uses the sum \(Y=X_1+X_2\).

**What** Slides p.43–44

Exercise continued · Lecture 5 · p.43–44 Now let \(Y=X_1+X_2\). Is \(Y\) Normal? No!
How do we know?
• \(P(Y=0)=P(B=1)=1/2\)
What's going on here?
• While \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are each normally distributed, \(\mathbf{x}=(X_1,X_2)^T\) is not multivariate normal.
• I.e. cannot find \(\mathbf{A}_{2\times k}\) s.t. \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}\) for \(\mathbf{z}=(Z_1,\dots,Z_k)^T\), \(Z_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1)\)

If \(B=1\), then \(X_2=-X_1\). Thus \(Y=X_1-X_1=0\). This case has probability 1/2.

A normal variable with a positive variance has probability 0 at each single value. A normal variable with variance 0 is a constant, so its probability at that value is 1.

\(P(Y=0)=1/2\) is not 0 and not 1. Thus \(Y\) is not normal.

A linear combination of \(\mathbf{x}\) is a sum of its components times constants. \(Y=(1,1)\,\mathbf{x}\) is a linear combination of \(\mathbf{x}\).

If \(\mathbf{x}\) is MVN, then linearity (p.37) makes \(Y\) normal. \(Y\) is not normal, so \(\mathbf{x}\) is not MVN.

"cannot find \(\mathbf{A}_{2\times k}\)" is the opposite of the p.36 definition. No constant \(2\times k\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) gives \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}\).

**How** Added

Use linearity to show that a vector \(\mathbf{x}\) is not MVN

- Select a constant row vector \(\mathbf{C}\). Let \(u=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}\). Here \(\mathbf{C}=(1,1)\) and \(u=X_1+X_2=Y\).
- Assume that \(\mathbf{x}\) is MVN. Then linearity (p.37, \(\mathbf{d}=0\)) makes \(u\) normal.
- Calculate one probability of \(u\). Here, calculate \(P(Y=0)\) for the cases \(B=0\) and \(B=1\).
- Compare the result with 0 and 1. If it is neither, the assumption in step 2 is false.

**Self-check:** \(\mathbf{C}\) must be constant. It must not contain \(B\) or \(X_1\). The case probabilities must add to 1: \(P(B=0)+P(B=1)=1\).

**Example · Six hand-made values** Added

This example uses six values of \(X_1\) and six coin results \(B\). These values are hand-made to show the pattern.

Data: \(X_1=(1.2,\ -0.5,\ 0.8,\ -1.5,\ 2.0,\ 0.3)\) and \(B=(0,\ 1,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0)\).

Step 1: \(\mathbf{C}=(1,1)\), so \(Y=X_1+X_2\).

Step 2: Assume that \(\mathbf{x}\) is MVN. Then \(Y\) is normal.

Step 3a, the rows with \(B=0\) (rows 1, 4, 6): \(X_2=X_1\). Thus \(Y=2X_1\): \(2\times1.2=2.4\), \(2\times(-1.5)=-3.0\), \(2\times0.3=0.6\).

Step 3b, the rows with \(B=1\) (rows 2, 3, 5): \(X_2=-X_1\), which gives \(0.5\), \(-0.8\), \(-2.0\). Thus \(Y\): \(-0.5+0.5=0\), \(0.8-0.8=0\), \(2.0-2.0=0\).

Step 3c: \(Y=(2.4,\ 0,\ 0,\ -3.0,\ 0,\ 0.6)\). Each row with \(B=1\) gives \(Y=0\) exactly.

Step 4: \(P(B=1)=1/2\), so the rows with \(B=1\) are one half of all rows on average. Thus \(P(Y=0)=1/2\). This is not 0 and not 1, so \(\mathbf{x}\) is not MVN.

[figure]
Figure 06.2 · The distribution of \(Y=X_1+X_2\). The purple bar is the probability 1/2 at the single value 0 (case \(B=1\)). The blue curve is the spread-out part from \(Y=2X_1\) (case \(B=0\)). A normal distribution has no probability at a single value.

**Why** Added

The first chain calculates \(P(Y=0)\). The second chain uses this result to show that no matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) exists.

1

\[P(Y=0)=P(Y=0,\ B=0)+P(Y=0,\ B=1)\]

\(B\) is 0 or 1.

2

\[=P(X_1+X_1=0,\ B=0)+P(X_1-X_1=0,\ B=1)\]

The rule for \(X_2\).

3

\[=P(2X_1=0,\ B=0)+P(0=0,\ B=1)\]

4

\[=P(X_1=0)P(B=0)+P(B=1)\]

Independence; \(0=0\) is always true.

5

\[=0\times\tfrac12+\tfrac12=\tfrac12\]

\(X_1\sim N(0,1)\) has probability 0 at one value. ∎

1

\[\text{Assume } \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z},\quad \mathbf{A}_{2\times k},\ Z_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1)\]

Then \(\mathbf{x}\sim MVN(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T)\) (p.36, \(\boldsymbol\mu=\mathbf{0}\)).

2

\[Y=(1,1)\,\mathbf{x}\]

3

\[Y\sim MVN\big((1,1)\mathbf{0},\ (1,1)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T(1,1)^T\big)\]

Linearity (p.37), \(\mathbf{C}=(1,1)\), \(\mathbf{d}=0\).

4

\[Y\sim N\big(0,\ (1,1)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T(1,1)^T\big)\]

An MVN with one component is normal.

5

\[P(Y=0)\in\{0,\ 1\}\]

0 for a positive variance; 1 for variance 0.

6

\[P(Y=0)=\tfrac12\notin\{0,\ 1\}\]

The first chain. The assumption in line 1 is false, so no \(\mathbf{A}_{2\times k}\) exists. ∎

Result: MVN is a property of the full vector, not of each component. Thus the regression model on the next page assumes that the full error vector is MVN.

### 06.3 Multiple linear regression as an MVN model Slides p.45

This section writes the multiple linear regression model as one MVN statement.

**What** Slides p.45

Multiple Linear Regression · Lecture 5 · p.45 \[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\dots+\beta_px_{ip}+\epsilon_i,\qquad \epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\] We can write this: \[\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1\\y_2\\\vdots\\y_n\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}1&x_{11}&x_{12}&\dots&x_{1p}\\1&x_{21}&x_{22}&\dots&x_{2p}\\\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\1&x_{n1}&x_{n2}&\dots&x_{np}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\vdots\\\beta_p\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c}\epsilon_1\\\epsilon_2\\\vdots\\\epsilon_n\end{array}\right]\] Or more simply: \[\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon,\quad \boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\quad\iff\quad \mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\]

The list below gives the new symbols.

Multiple linear regression (MLR) and the symbols \(\mathbf{y}\), \(\mathbf{X}\), \(\boldsymbol\beta\), \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) and \(\iff\) have their definitions in Sections 01.5 and 01.6. Page 45 repeats the matrix form of page 8 and adds the MVN statement.

\(\mathbf{I}\) is the \(n\times n\) identity matrix (Section 02.4).

\(\sigma^2\mathbf{I}\) has \(\sigma^2\) on the diagonal and 0 at other positions. Each error has variance \(\sigma^2\), and each pair of errors has covariance 0.

The errors \(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\) give \(\boldsymbol\epsilon=\sigma\mathbf{I}\mathbf{z}\), with \(\mathbf{z}\) i.i.d. standard normal. Thus \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) is MVN by the p.36 definition. \(\mathbf{y}\) is \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) plus the constant vector \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\). By linearity, \(\mathbf{y}\) is MVN with mean \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) and the same covariance matrix.

**How** Added

Write the distribution of \(\mathbf{y}\) from the distribution of \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\)

- Write \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\) and \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\).
- Write \(\mathbf{y}\) in the form \(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\epsilon+\mathbf{d}\), with \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{I}\) and \(\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\).
- Calculate the mean: \(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\).
- Calculate the covariance matrix: \(\mathbf{C}(\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{C}^T=\mathbf{I}\sigma^2\mathbf{I}\mathbf{I}=\sigma^2\mathbf{I}\).
- Write the result: \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\).

**Self-check:** \(\mathbf{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta\) are not random, so \(\mathbf{d}\) is constant. The mean is \(n\times1\). The covariance matrix is \(n\times n\), with \(\sigma^2\) on the diagonal and 0 at other positions.

**Example · A small data set** Added

This example uses \(n=3\) observations and \(p=2\) explanatory variables. The values are \((x_{i1},x_{i2})=(2,1),\ (3,0),\ (5,4)\).

Step 1: \(\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1\\y_2\\y_3\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1&2&1\\1&3&0\\1&5&4\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\beta_2\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c}\epsilon_1\\\epsilon_2\\\epsilon_3\end{array}\right]\), \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\).

Step 2: \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{I}\) (\(3\times3\)) and \(\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\).

Step 3: Multiply each row of \(\mathbf{X}\) by \(\boldsymbol\beta\): \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0+2\beta_1+1\beta_2\\\beta_0+3\beta_1+0\beta_2\\\beta_0+5\beta_1+4\beta_2\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0+2\beta_1+\beta_2\\\beta_0+3\beta_1\\\beta_0+5\beta_1+4\beta_2\end{array}\right]\).

Step 4: \(\sigma^2\mathbf{I}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\sigma^2&0&0\\0&\sigma^2&0\\0&0&\sigma^2\end{array}\right]\).

Step 5: \(\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1\\y_2\\y_3\end{array}\right]\sim MVN\left(\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0+2\beta_1+\beta_2\\\beta_0+3\beta_1\\\beta_0+5\beta_1+4\beta_2\end{array}\right],\ \left[\begin{array}{ccc}\sigma^2&0&0\\0&\sigma^2&0\\0&0&\sigma^2\end{array}\right]\right)\).

**Self-check:** the mean is \(3\times1\) and the covariance matrix is \(3\times3\).

**Self-check:** the marginal distribution property (p.38) says that a subset of an MVN vector is MVN. Use it to keep only \(y_1\).

Then \(y_1\sim N(\beta_0+2\beta_1+\beta_2,\ \sigma^2)\). This agrees with the model for one observation.

**Why** Added

The chain shows the direction "⟹" in lines 1–3 and the direction "⟸" in lines 4–6. Both directions use only linearity (p.37).

1

\[\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{I}\boldsymbol\epsilon+\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\quad \boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\]

2

\[\mathbf{y}\sim MVN\big(\mathbf{I}\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\ \mathbf{I}(\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{I}^T\big)\]

Linearity, \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\).

3

\[\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\ \sigma^2\mathbf{I})\]

\(\mathbf{I}\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}\), \(\mathbf{I}^T=\mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{I}\mathbf{I}=\mathbf{I}\). This gives ⟹.

4

\[\boldsymbol\epsilon=\mathbf{I}\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\quad \mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\]

5

\[\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN\big(\mathbf{I}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\ \mathbf{I}(\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{I}^T\big)\]

Linearity, \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{d}=-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\).

6

\[\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\mathbf{0},\ \sigma^2\mathbf{I})\]

This gives ⟸. ∎

Result: the full distribution assumption of MLR is one line, \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\). Later lectures use this line to find the distribution of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\).

### 06.4 Practice Q1: mean vectors and covariance matrices Slides p.46–47

This section does Practice Q1. It finds the mean and the variance of two linear transformations of \(\mathbf{y}\).

Slides p.46 is the title page "Practice". Slides p.47–48 give the two questions.

**What** Slides p.47

Practice Q1 · Lecture 5 · p.47 Let \(\mathbf{y}=(y_1,y_2,y_3)^T\) such that \(E[\mathbf{y}]=(1,2,2)^T\) and \(Var(\mathbf{y})=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}4&0&1\\0&3&-1\\1&-1&4\end{array}\right]\) and let \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,3)^T\) and \(\mathbf{A}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1&-1&0\\0&1&-1\\1&0&-1\\1&1&1\end{array}\right]\). Compute \(E[\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y}]\), \(E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}]\), \(Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})\), \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})\)

\(Var(\mathbf{y})\) is the covariance matrix of \(\mathbf{y}\) (Section 04.2).

\(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y}=y_1+2y_2+3y_3\) is one number (\(1\times3\) times \(3\times1\)).

\(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\) is a \(4\times1\) vector. Its component \(i\) is row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) times \(\mathbf{y}\).

The question uses four formulas from unit 04. Section 04.5 gives \(E[\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y}+b]=\mathbf{a}^TE[\mathbf{y}]+b\) and \(Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{a}^TVar(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{a}\) (Slides p.28–29). Section 04.6 gives \(E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{A}E[\mathbf{y}]\) and \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{A}Var(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{A}^T\) (Slides p.31).

**How** Added

Let \(\mathbf{V}=Var(\mathbf{y})\) in the steps below.

Practice Q1

- For \(E[\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y}]\), write \(\mathbf{a}^TE[\mathbf{y}]\) with \(b=0\). Multiply matching components and add.
- For \(E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}]\), write \(\mathbf{A}E[\mathbf{y}]\). Do step 1 with each row of \(\mathbf{A}\).
- For \(Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})\), calculate \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{a}\) first. This is a \(3\times1\) vector.
- Then calculate \(\mathbf{a}^T(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{a})\). This is one number.
- For \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})\), calculate \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\) (\(4\times3\)) first.
- Get row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\): add the rows of \(\mathbf{V}\), with row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) as weights.
- Then calculate \((\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V})\mathbf{A}^T\) (\(4\times4\)).
- Get entry \((i,j)\): multiply row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\) and row \(j\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) term by term. Add the products.

**Self-check:** \(Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})\ge0\), because \(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{a}\ge0\) (p.25). \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})\) must be symmetric (p.24: \(V_{ij}=V_{ji}\)). Its diagonal must be \(\ge0\).

**Example · the full calculation** Added

Answer: Practice Q1

Step 1: \(E[\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{a}^TE[\mathbf{y}]=1\times1+2\times2+3\times2=1+4+6=11\).

Step 2, row 1: \(1\times1+(-1)\times2+0\times2=1-2+0=-1\).

Step 2, row 2: \(0\times1+1\times2+(-1)\times2=0+2-2=0\).

Step 2, row 3: \(1\times1+0\times2+(-1)\times2=1+0-2=-1\).

Step 2, row 4: \(1\times1+1\times2+1\times2=1+2+2=5\). Thus \(E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}]=(-1,\ 0,\ -1,\ 5)^T\).

Step 3: \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{a}=\left[\begin{array}{c}4\times1+0\times2+1\times3\\0\times1+3\times2+(-1)\times3\\1\times1+(-1)\times2+4\times3\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}4+0+3\\0+6-3\\1-2+12\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}7\\3\\11\end{array}\right]\).

Step 4: \(Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{a}=1\times7+2\times3+3\times11=7+6+33=46\).

Step 5: Let the rows of \(\mathbf{V}\) be \(\mathbf{v}_1=(4,0,1)\), \(\mathbf{v}_2=(0,3,-1)\), \(\mathbf{v}_3=(1,-1,4)\).

Step 6, row 1 of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \((1,-1,0)\): \(\mathbf{v}_1-\mathbf{v}_2=(4-0,\ 0-3,\ 1+1)=(4,-3,2)\).

Step 6, row 2 of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \((0,1,-1)\): \(\mathbf{v}_2-\mathbf{v}_3=(0-1,\ 3+1,\ -1-4)=(-1,4,-5)\).

Step 6, row 3 of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \((1,0,-1)\): \(\mathbf{v}_1-\mathbf{v}_3=(4-1,\ 0+1,\ 1-4)=(3,1,-3)\).

Step 6, row 4 of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \((1,1,1)\): \(\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_2+\mathbf{v}_3=(4+0+1,\ 0+3-1,\ 1-1+4)=(5,2,4)\).

Steps 7–8, row \((4,-3,2)\) with the rows of \(\mathbf{A}\): \(4+3+0=7\); \(0-3-2=-5\); \(4+0-2=2\); \(4-3+2=3\).

Steps 7–8, row \((-1,4,-5)\): \(-1-4+0=-5\); \(0+4+5=9\); \(-1+0+5=4\); \(-1+4-5=-2\).

Steps 7–8, row \((3,1,-3)\): \(3-1+0=2\); \(0+1+3=4\); \(3+0+3=6\); \(3+1-3=1\).

Steps 7–8, row \((5,2,4)\): \(5-2+0=3\); \(0+2-4=-2\); \(5+0-4=1\); \(5+2+4=11\).
\[Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})=\left[\begin{array}{cccc}7&-5&2&3\\-5&9&4&-2\\2&4&6&1\\3&-2&1&11\end{array}\right]\]
Self-check: \(46\ge0\). The \(4\times4\) matrix is symmetric: for example, entries \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) are both \(-5\).

Self-check: the diagonal entries 7, 9, 6, 11 are all \(\ge0\).

**Why** Slides p.34–35

Section 04.6, Why (2), gives the derivation of \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{A}Var(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{A}^T\) from Slides p.34–35. \(Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})\) is the special case in which \(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{a}^T\) has one row (Section 04.7, Q3).

Result: the mean of \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\) is \(\mathbf{A}E[\mathbf{y}]\), and its variance is \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T\). The next question uses the same method for two different transformations.

### 06.5 Practice Q2: the cross-covariance matrix Slides p.48

This section finds the covariance matrix between two linear transformations \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}\).

**What** Slides p.48

Practice Q2 · Lecture 5 · p.48 Suppose \(\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_n)^T\) is a random vector with \(E[\mathbf{x}]=\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(var(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{V}\). Let \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}_{p\times n}\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{B}_{q\times n}\mathbf{x}\). Let \(\mathbf{C}\) denote the "cross-covariance" matrix, where \(\mathbf{C}_{ij}=cov(y_i,w_j)\). (You can think of this as the off-diagonal block of the variance matrix of \((\mathbf{y}^T,\mathbf{w}^T)^T\), where the diagonal blocks would be \(var(\mathbf{y})\) and \(var(\mathbf{w})\).) Write \(\mathbf{C}\) in terms of \(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf{V},\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\)

The cross-covariance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) is a \(p\times q\) matrix. Entry \((i,j)\) is the covariance of component \(i\) of \(\mathbf{y}\) and component \(j\) of \(\mathbf{w}\).

"Off-diagonal block": put \(\mathbf{y}\) above \(\mathbf{w}\) to make one \((p+q)\times1\) vector. Its covariance matrix has four blocks.

The top-left block is \(var(\mathbf{y})\). The bottom-right block is \(var(\mathbf{w})\). The top-right block is \(\mathbf{C}\).

The question uses one formula from Section 04.5 (Slides p.26): if \(z=\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y}+c\) and \(u=\mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{y}+d\), then \(cov(z,u)=\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{b}\). In Q2, the random vector is \(\mathbf{x}\). Thus put \(\mathbf{x}\) in place of the \(\mathbf{y}\) of p.26.

**How** Added

Practice Q2

- Let \(\mathbf{a}_i^T\) be row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\). Let \(\mathbf{b}_j^T\) be row \(j\) of \(\mathbf{B}\).
- Write \(y_i=\mathbf{a}_i^T\mathbf{x}\) and \(w_j=\mathbf{b}_j^T\mathbf{x}\).
- Use p.26 with \(c=d=0\): \(\mathbf{C}_{ij}=cov(y_i,w_j)=\mathbf{a}_i^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{b}_j\).
- Note that \(\mathbf{a}_i^T\) is row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\), and \(\mathbf{b}_j\) is column \(j\) of \(\mathbf{B}^T\).
- Write \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{B}^T\). Entry \((i,j)\) of this product is \(\mathbf{a}_i^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{b}_j\).

**Self-check:** The size is \((p\times n)(n\times n)(n\times q)=p\times q\), the size of \(\mathbf{C}\). The answer has no \(\boldsymbol\mu\). If \(\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{A}\), the answer is \(var(\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T\).

**Example · The numbers of Q1** Added

Use the random vector of Q1 as \(\mathbf{x}\), with \(n=3\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) from Q1. Use the \(4\times3\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) of Q1, so \(p=4\). Use \(\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{a}^T=(1,2,3)\), so \(q=1\).

Answer: Practice Q2 and a numerical example

General answer: \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{B}^T\). \(\boldsymbol\mu\) does not appear.

Step 1: \(\mathbf{B}^T=\mathbf{a}=(1,2,3)^T\). Thus \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{a}\), with size \(4\times1\).

Step 2: Q1 step 3 gives \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{a}=(7,3,11)^T\).

Step 3, row 1 of \(\mathbf{A}\), \((1,-1,0)\): \(7-3+0=4\).

Step 3, row 2, \((0,1,-1)\): \(0+3-11=-8\).

Step 3, row 3, \((1,0,-1)\): \(7+0-11=-4\).

Step 3, row 4, \((1,1,1)\): \(7+3+11=21\). Thus \(\mathbf{C}=(4,\ -8,\ -4,\ 21)^T\).

Step 4: put \(\mathbf{A}\) above \(\mathbf{a}^T\) to make a \(5\times3\) matrix \(\mathbf{S}\). Then \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{S}^T\) is the covariance matrix of \((\mathbf{y}^T,w)^T\).
\[\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{S}^T=\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}7&-5&2&3&4\\-5&9&4&-2&-8\\2&4&6&1&-4\\3&-2&1&11&21\\4&-8&-4&21&46\end{array}\right]\]
The top-left \(4\times4\) block is \(Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y})\) from Q1. The bottom-right entry 46 is \(Var(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y})\) from Q1.

The first four entries of column 5 are \((4,-8,-4,21)\). This is \(\mathbf{C}\), as the question says.

Self-check: the size is \(4\times1=p\times q\).

**Why · \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{B}^T\)** Added

The first chain works with one entry, as in the How steps. The second chain uses matrices and shows why \(\boldsymbol\mu\) does not appear.

1

\[\mathbf{C}_{ij}=cov(y_i,w_j)\]

2

\[=cov(\mathbf{a}_i^T\mathbf{x},\ \mathbf{b}_j^T\mathbf{x})\]

\(\mathbf{a}_i^T\) is row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\); \(\mathbf{b}_j^T\) is row \(j\) of \(\mathbf{B}\).

3

\[=\mathbf{a}_i^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{b}_j\]

p.26, \(c=d=0\).

4

\[=\sum_{k=1}^n\sum_{l=1}^n A_{ik}V_{kl}B_{jl}\]

5

\[=\sum_{k=1}^n\sum_{l=1}^n A_{ik}V_{kl}(B^T)_{lj}\]

\(B_{jl}=(B^T)_{lj}\).

6

\[=[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{B}^T]_{ij}\]

Definition of the matrix product. This is true for all \(i,j\). ∎

1

\[\mathbf{C}=E[(\mathbf{y}-E[\mathbf{y}])(\mathbf{w}-E[\mathbf{w}])^T]\]

Entry \((i,j)\) is \(cov(y_i,w_j)\).

2

\[=E[(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol\mu)^T]\]

\(E[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}]=\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol\mu\) (p.31).

3

\[=E[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\mathbf{B}^T]\]

4

\[=\mathbf{A}E[(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^T]\mathbf{B}^T\]

5

\[=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{B}^T\]

Line 3 subtracts \(\boldsymbol\mu\), so \(\boldsymbol\mu\) is not in the answer. ∎

Result: the covariance between two linear transformations is \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{B}^T\). It does not depend on \(\boldsymbol\mu\). If \(\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{A}\), it is the \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T\) of Q1.

### 06.6 Practice Added

The two questions below practice the two methods of this unit. P1 uses the MVN form of MLR. P2 uses the mean, variance, and covariance of linear combinations.

**P1.** Use the small data set of Section 06.3: \((x_{i1},x_{i2})=(2,1),\ (3,0),\ (5,4)\). Assume \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\), \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\). Find the distribution of \(y_1-y_2\).

Answer

Step 1: Section 06.3 gives \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\), with \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0+2\beta_1+\beta_2,\ \beta_0+3\beta_1,\ \beta_0+5\beta_1+4\beta_2)^T\).

Step 2: \(y_1-y_2=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}\), with \(\mathbf{C}=(1,-1,0)\) and \(\mathbf{d}=0\).

Step 3 (mean): \(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0+2\beta_1+\beta_2)-(\beta_0+3\beta_1)=(2-3)\beta_1+\beta_2=-\beta_1+\beta_2\).

Step 4 (variance): \(\mathbf{C}(\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{C}^T=\sigma^2(1^2+(-1)^2+0^2)=\sigma^2(1+1+0)=2\sigma^2\).

Result: \(y_1-y_2\sim N(-\beta_1+\beta_2,\ 2\sigma^2)\), by linearity (p.37). \(\beta_0\) cancels.

**P2.** Use \(\mathbf{y}\), \(E[\mathbf{y}]\), and \(Var(\mathbf{y})\) from Practice Q1. Let \(u=2y_1-y_2+1\). Calculate \(E[u]\), \(Var(u)\), and \(cov(u,y_3)\).

Answer

Step 1: \(u=\mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{y}+1\), with \(\mathbf{b}=(2,-1,0)^T\).

Step 2: \(E[u]=\mathbf{b}^T\boldsymbol\mu+1=2\times1+(-1)\times2+0\times2+1=2-2+0+1=1\).

Step 3: \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{b}=(4\times2+0\times(-1)+1\times0,\ 0\times2+3\times(-1)+(-1)\times0,\ 1\times2+(-1)\times(-1)+4\times0)^T=(8,-3,3)^T\).

Step 4: \(Var(u)=\mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{b}=2\times8+(-1)\times(-3)+0\times3=16+3+0=19\). The constant 1 does not change the variance.

Step 5: \(y_3=\mathbf{e}_3^T\mathbf{y}\), with \(\mathbf{e}_3=(0,0,1)^T\). Then \(cov(u,y_3)=\mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{e}_3\) (p.26).

Step 6: \(\mathbf{V}\) is symmetric, so \(\mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{e}_3\) is component 3 of \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{b}\). Thus \(cov(u,y_3)=3\).

This unit showed that normal components do not make an MVN vector. The MLR model assumes \(\mathbf{y}\sim MVN(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})\). For a linear transformation, the mean is \(\mathbf{A}E[\mathbf{y}]\), the variance is \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}^T\), and the cross-covariance is \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{B}^T\). Lecture 6 and Lecture 7 use these results for the MLR estimators.
