STAT 331 · Lecture 6 · Multiple Linear Regression: Intro and Estimation

# Lecture 6: Multiple Linear Regression: Intro and Estimation

This lecture writes multiple linear regression in matrix form, estimates \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\), and finds the properties of the estimators (Lecture 6 · p.1–41).

Contents
01 · Recap: matrix calculus, random vectors, and the multivariate normal 02 · Data example and interpreting regression coefficients 03 · Estimating β: least squares and maximum likelihood 04 · Properties of the LS estimator, fitted values, and residuals 05 · Estimating σ², calculating the estimates, and practice

## 01 · Recap: matrix calculus, random vectors, and the multivariate normal

This unit restates three matrix tools that Lecture 6 uses, and writes multiple linear regression in matrix form.

Plan · Slides p.1–7

Step 1: Take the derivative of a scalar with respect to a vector (Slides p.3).

Step 2: Find the expectation and variance of a random vector after a linear change (Slides p.4).

Step 3: Define the multivariate normal distribution (Slides p.5).

Step 4: Use four properties of the multivariate normal (Slides p.6).

Step 5: Write the regression model as \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\) (Slides p.7).

The slides give no data in this part. Thus, all examples use small 2×2 or 3×3 matrices, and you calculate them by hand.

The later units use these tools to estimate \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and to find the variance of the estimate.

### 01.1 Notation Slides p.1–2

This section sets the notation for the full unit. Slide p.1 is the title page: "Lecture 6: Multiple Linear Regression: Intro & Estimation". Slide p.2 is the section page "Recap". This unit uses the notation of the slides. Added

Vector: a list of numbers. A vector has a bold lower-case name, for example \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\dots,y_k)^T\). Each vector is a column vector, which is one vertical column of numbers.

Matrix: a rectangular table of numbers. A matrix has a bold upper-case name, for example \(\boldsymbol{A}\) or \(\boldsymbol{X}\). "\(k\times k\)" means \(k\) rows and \(k\) columns.

Transpose \(^T\): the operation that changes rows into columns. \((y_1,\dots,y_k)^T\) is a column. \(\boldsymbol{a}^T\) is a row.

Scalar: one single number. A scalar has a plain name, for example \(z\) or \(\sigma^2\).

Identity matrix \(\boldsymbol{I}\): a square matrix with 1 on the diagonal and 0 in all other positions. Zero vector \(\boldsymbol{0}\): a vector with 0 in all positions.

With this notation, you can read each formula below one entry at a time.

### 01.2 Matrix calculus Slides p.3

This section shows how to take the derivative of a scalar with respect to a vector. Unit 03 uses these two rules on the sum of squares \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)\).

**What** Slides p.3

A partial derivative \(\partial z/\partial y_j\) is the rate of change of \(z\) when only \(y_j\) changes. All other variables stay constant. The derivative with respect to a vector puts all the partial derivatives in one column. A symmetric matrix is a square matrix with \(\boldsymbol{A}^T=\boldsymbol{A}\). In a symmetric matrix, the entry in row \(i\), column \(j\) is equal to the entry in row \(j\), column \(i\).

Matrix Calculus · Lecture 6 · p.3 Let \(z=f(y_1,\dots,y_k)\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1\\ \vdots\\ y_k\end{array}\right]\), then \[\frac{\partial z}{\partial \boldsymbol{y}}=\left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial z}{\partial y_1}\\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_2}\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_k}\end{array}\right]\]

- If \(z=\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y}\), where \(\boldsymbol{a}=(a_1,\dots,a_k)^T\) is a vector, then \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \boldsymbol{y}}=\boldsymbol{a}\)
- If \(z=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\) where \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a \(k\times k\) matrix, then \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \boldsymbol{y}}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{y}\)
and if \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is symmetric, then: \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial \boldsymbol{y}}=2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\)

Here \(z\) is a scalar, and \(\boldsymbol{y}\) holds \(k\) variables. Thus, \(\partial z/\partial\boldsymbol{y}\) is a \(k\times1\) column vector. Its entry \(j\) is \(\partial z/\partial y_j\). The scalar \(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y}=a_1y_1+\dots+a_ky_k\) is a linear form: each \(y_j\) is multiplied by one constant. The scalar \(\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\) is a quadratic form: each term is a constant times two entries of \(\boldsymbol{y}\).

**How** Added

Use these steps to find \(\partial z/\partial\boldsymbol{y}\) for a given \(z\).

How · Take the derivative with respect to a vector

- Find the type of \(z\). If \(z=\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y}\), it is a linear form. If \(z=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\), it is a quadratic form.
- For a linear form, write \(\partial z/\partial\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{a}\).
- For a quadratic form, compare each \(a_{ij}\) with \(a_{ji}\). If all pairs are equal, write \(2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\). If not, write \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{y}\).
- Write the result as a \(k\times1\) column vector.

**Self-check:** The length of the result must be equal to the length \(k\) of \(\boldsymbol{y}\).

**Self-check:** Expand \(z\) as a usual polynomial. Find each \(\partial z/\partial y_j\). The result must agree with step 2 or step 3.

**Example** Added

Let \(k=2\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,y_2)^T\). The three small examples below check the three rules of p.3 entry by entry. Then each example uses the point \(\boldsymbol{y}=(1,2)^T\).

Example (i): a linear form. Let \(\boldsymbol{a}=(3,5)^T\).

1

Expand \(z\) How step 1

\[z=\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y}=3y_1+5y_2\]

2

Find each partial derivative Self-check 2

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial y_1}=3,\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_2}=5\]

3

Put them in a column How step 2

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}=\left[\begin{array}{c}3\\5\end{array}\right]=\boldsymbol{a}\]

Example (ii): a symmetric quadratic form. Let \(\boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&1\\1&3\end{array}\right]\). Here \(a_{12}=a_{21}=1\). Thus, \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is symmetric.

1

Expand \(z\) How step 1

\[z=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}y_1&y_2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}2y_1+y_2\\y_1+3y_2\end{array}\right]\]

\[=y_1(2y_1+y_2)+y_2(y_1+3y_2)\]

\[=2y_1^2+2y_1y_2+3y_2^2\]

2

Find each partial derivative Self-check 2

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial y_1}=4y_1+2y_2,\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_2}=2y_1+6y_2\]

3

Use the rule \(2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\) How step 3

\[2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}=2\left[\begin{array}{c}2y_1+y_2\\y_1+3y_2\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}4y_1+2y_2\\2y_1+6y_2\end{array}\right]\]

Each row agrees with step 2.

4

Put in \(\boldsymbol{y}=(1,2)^T\)

\[z=2(1)^2+2(1)(2)+3(2)^2=2+4+12=18\]

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}=\left[\begin{array}{c}4(1)+2(2)\\2(1)+6(2)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}8\\14\end{array}\right]\]

Example (iii): a quadratic form that is not symmetric. Let \(\boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&2\\0&3\end{array}\right]\). Here \(a_{12}=2\) and \(a_{21}=0\). Thus, use the general rule \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{y}\).

1

Expand \(z\) How step 1

\[z=\left[\begin{array}{cc}y_1&y_2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1+2y_2\\3y_2\end{array}\right]\]

\[=y_1^2+2y_1y_2+3y_2^2\]

2

Find each partial derivative Self-check 2

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial y_1}=2y_1+2y_2,\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_2}=2y_1+6y_2\]

3

Use the rule \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{y}\) How step 3

\[\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{y}=\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1+2y_2\\3y_2\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1\\2y_1+3y_2\end{array}\right]\]

\[=\left[\begin{array}{c}2y_1+2y_2\\2y_1+6y_2\end{array}\right]\]

Here \(\boldsymbol{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&0\\2&3\end{array}\right]\). Each row agrees with step 2.

4

Put in \(\boldsymbol{y}=(1,2)^T\)

\[z=1^2+2(1)(2)+3(2)^2=1+4+12=17\]

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}=\left[\begin{array}{c}2(1)+2(2)\\2(1)+6(2)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}6\\14\end{array}\right]\]

In all three examples, the rule and the entry-by-entry derivatives give the same vector.

**Why** Added

The two chains below prove the two rules for a general \(k\). Each chain finds one partial derivative, then puts all of them in a column.

The linear form:

1

\[z=\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y}=\sum_{i=1}^k a_iy_i\]

2

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial y_j}=a_j\]

Only the term with \(i=j\) contains \(y_j\).

3

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}=(a_1,\dots,a_k)^T=\boldsymbol{a}\]

Definition on p.3. ∎

The quadratic form. Here \(a_{ij}\) is the entry of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) in row \(i\), column \(j\).

1

\[z=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}=\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{l=1}^k y_i\,a_{il}\,y_l\]

2

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial y_j}=\sum_{l=1}^k a_{jl}y_l+\sum_{i=1}^k y_i a_{ij}\]

Product rule: \(y_j\) is in the terms with \(i=j\) and in the terms with \(l=j\).

3

\[=(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})_j+\sum_{i=1}^k a_{ij}y_i\]

The first sum is row \(j\) of \(\boldsymbol{A}\) times \(\boldsymbol{y}\).

4

\[=(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})_j+(\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{y})_j\]

\(a_{ij}\) is the entry of \(\boldsymbol{A}^T\) in row \(j\), column \(i\).

5

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{y}\]

6

\[=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}=2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\]

For a symmetric matrix, put in \(\boldsymbol{A}^T=\boldsymbol{A}\). ∎

This section gives two rules: \(\partial(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y})/\partial\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{a}\), and \(\partial(\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})/\partial\boldsymbol{y}=2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\) for a symmetric \(\boldsymbol{A}\). Unit 03 uses them to take the derivative of \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)\).

### 01.3 Properties of random vectors Slides p.4

This section restates the rules for the expectation and variance of a random vector. Unit 04 uses the last rule, \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{A}\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\boldsymbol{A}^T\), to find \(\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]\).

**What** Slides p.4

A random variable is a number whose value comes from a random result. A random vector is a vector whose entries are random variables. The expectation \(E[\cdot]\) is the long-run average.

For a vector, take the expectation of each entry. The variance of a random variable is the expected squared distance from its expectation. The covariance \(\mathrm{cov}(y_i,y_j)=E[(y_i-E[y_i])(y_j-E[y_j])]\) shows how much two variables change together.

\(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\) is the covariance matrix (the name from Lecture 5). Its entry in row \(i\), column \(j\) is \(\mathrm{cov}(y_i,y_j)\). Its diagonal holds the variance of each \(y_i\). Below, \(\boldsymbol{a}\), \(\boldsymbol{b}\), and \(\boldsymbol{A}\) are constants. They are not random.

Properties of Random Vectors · Lecture 6 · p.4

- \(E[\boldsymbol{a}]=\boldsymbol{a}\)
- \(E[\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{b}]=\boldsymbol{a}^TE[\boldsymbol{y}]+\boldsymbol{b}\)
- \(E[\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}]=\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{y}]\)
- \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})=E[(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}])(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}])^T]\)
- \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{a}^T\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\boldsymbol{a}\)
- \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{A}\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\boldsymbol{A}^T\)

The expectation of a constant is the constant. The expectation moves through a constant matrix and through an added constant. For the variance, a constant matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) goes on the left, and \(\boldsymbol{A}^T\) goes on the right. \(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y}\) is a scalar, so \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y})\) is a scalar. \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\) is a vector, so \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})\) is a matrix.

**How** Added

Use these steps when you know \(E[\boldsymbol{y}]\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\), and you must find the expectation and variance of \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\).

How · Expectation and variance after a linear change

- Write the constant matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) (\(m\times k\)), \(E[\boldsymbol{y}]\) (\(k\times1\)), and \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\) (\(k\times k\)).
- For the expectation, calculate \(\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{y}]\). The result is \(m\times1\).
- For the variance, calculate \(\boldsymbol{A}\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\). Then multiply it on the right by \(\boldsymbol{A}^T\). The result is \(m\times m\).

**Self-check:** The variance matrix must be symmetric. Entry \((i,j)\) must be equal to entry \((j,i)\).

**Self-check:** The diagonal entries are variances. They must be \(\ge 0\).

**Example** Added

Let \(E[\boldsymbol{y}]=(10,20)^T\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{I}\) (2×2), \(\boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&2\\3&4\end{array}\right]\), and \(\boldsymbol{a}=(1,1)^T\).

1

Expectation How step 2

\[E[\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}]=\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{y}]=\left[\begin{array}{c}1(10)+2(20)\\3(10)+4(20)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}50\\110\end{array}\right]\]

2

Variance How step 3

\[\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{A}\,\boldsymbol{I}\,\boldsymbol{A}^T=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T\]

\[=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&2\\3&4\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&3\\2&4\end{array}\right]\]

\[=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1+4&3+8\\3+8&9+16\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}5&11\\11&25\end{array}\right]\]

The matrix is symmetric, and its diagonal is positive. Both self-checks pass.

3

The scalar case

\[\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol{a}=1^2+1^2=2\]

\(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y}=y_1+y_2\). This is the sum of two variables with variance 1 and covariance 0.

The order of the product is important. \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}5&11\\11&25\end{array}\right]\) is the correct result here. The product \(\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{A}\) is \(\left[\begin{array}{cc}10&14\\14&20\end{array}\right]\), which is a different matrix.

**Why** Added

The chain below starts from the definition of \(\mathrm{Var}\) and finds \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})\). It uses only the expectation rules of p.4.

1

\[\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})=E[(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}])(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}])^T]\]

Definition of Var on p.4, with \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\) in place of \(\boldsymbol{y}\).

2

\[=E[(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{y}])(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{y}])^T]\]

\(E[\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}]=\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{y}]\).

3

\[=E[\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}])(\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}]))^T]\]

4

\[=E[\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}])(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}])^T\boldsymbol{A}^T]\]

\((\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{C})^T=\boldsymbol{C}^T\boldsymbol{B}^T\).

5

\[=\boldsymbol{A}\,E[(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}])(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}])^T]\,\boldsymbol{A}^T\]

A constant matrix moves out of the expectation (\(E[\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}]=\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{y}]\), used on each column).

6

\[=\boldsymbol{A}\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\,\boldsymbol{A}^T\]

If \(\boldsymbol{A}\) has one row \(\boldsymbol{a}^T\), the result is \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{a}^T\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\boldsymbol{a}\). ∎

This section gives the result: after a constant matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), the expectation is \(\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{y}]\) and the variance is \(\boldsymbol{A}\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\boldsymbol{A}^T\). The next section uses these two rules to find the mean and variance of a multivariate normal vector.

### 01.4 Multivariate normal distribution Slides p.5

This section defines the multivariate normal distribution. The regression model on p.7 assumes that \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) has this distribution, so \(\boldsymbol{y}\) also has it.

**What** Slides p.5

The standard normal \(N(0,1)\) is the normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1. The abbreviation "i.i.d." means independent and identically distributed. Such variables are independent, and they have the same distribution. Two variables are independent if the value of one does not change the distribution of the other. The multivariate normal (MVN) is a distribution of a random vector. Its mean vector \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and its covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) fully set the distribution.

The density \(f(\boldsymbol{y})\) is a function whose integral over a region gives the probability that \(\boldsymbol{y}\) is in that region. The determinant \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|\) is one number that comes from a square matrix. For a 2×2 matrix, \(\left|\begin{array}{cc}p&q\\r&s\end{array}\right|=ps-qr\). The inverse \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\) is the matrix with \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}=\boldsymbol{I}\).

Multivariate Normal Distribution · Lecture 6 · p.5 Let \(\boldsymbol{z}=(z_1,\dots,z_n)^T\) be a random vector of i.i.d standard normal random variables, i.e. \(z_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1)\).
Then \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\) has multivariate normal distribution, i.e.: \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) where \(E[\boldsymbol{y}]=\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T\).
\(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\), if: \[f(\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{\frac n2}|\boldsymbol\Sigma|^{\frac12}}\exp\left\{-\frac12(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)\right\}\]

Slide p.5 gives two equivalent descriptions. The first description is a construction. It takes \(n\) independent standard normals, multiplies them by a constant matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\), and adds a constant vector \(\boldsymbol\mu\). The result \(\boldsymbol{y}\) is multivariate normal. The second description is the density formula above. Both descriptions use only two parameters: the mean \(\boldsymbol\mu\) (\(n\times1\)) and the covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) (\(n\times n\)).

**How** Added

Use these steps to get the distribution from the construction \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\), and to find the density at one point.

How · Get the MVN parameters and the density

- Read \(\boldsymbol\mu\). It is the constant vector that the construction adds.
- Calculate \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T\).
- Write \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\).
- For \(f(\boldsymbol{y})\), calculate \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|\), then \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\), then \((\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)\).
- Put these three values into the density formula.

**Self-check:** \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) must be symmetric, and \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|\) must be \(>0\). If not, \(|\boldsymbol\Sigma|^{1/2}\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\) do not exist.

**Self-check:** At \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol\mu\), the quadratic form is 0, so the exponential term is \(e^0=1\).

**Example** Added

Use the same \(\boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&2\\3&4\end{array}\right]\) as in Section 01.3. Let \(n=2\), \(\boldsymbol\mu=(10,20)^T\), and \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\).

1

Mean How step 1

\[\boldsymbol\mu=\left[\begin{array}{c}10\\20\end{array}\right]\]

2

Covariance matrix How step 2

\[\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}5&11\\11&25\end{array}\right]\]

This is the same product as in the example of Section 01.3.

3

Distribution How step 3

\[\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN\left(\left[\begin{array}{c}10\\20\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{cc}5&11\\11&25\end{array}\right]\right)\]

4

Determinant How step 4

\[|\boldsymbol\Sigma|=5(25)-11(11)=125-121=4\]

5

Density at \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol\mu\) Self-check 2

\[f(\boldsymbol\mu)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{\frac22}\,4^{\frac12}}\exp\{0\}\]

\[=\frac{1}{2\pi\times2}=\frac{1}{4\pi}=0.07957747\]

The second example finds the density at a point that is not the mean. Let \(\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol{0}\), \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol{I}\) (2×2), and \(\boldsymbol{y}=(1,-1)^T\). Added

1

Determinant and inverse How step 4

\[|\boldsymbol{I}|=1(1)-0(0)=1,\qquad \boldsymbol{I}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{I}\]

2

Quadratic form How step 4

\[(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{0})^T\boldsymbol{I}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{0})=1^2+(-1)^2=2\]

3

Density How step 5

\[f(\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{1}\,1^{\frac12}}\exp\left\{-\frac12(2)\right\}\]

\[=\frac{e^{-1}}{2\pi}=\frac{0.36787944}{6.28318531}=0.05854983\]

4

Check with two one-dimensional densities

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12(1)^2}\times\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12(-1)^2}=\frac{e^{-1}}{2\pi}=0.05854983\]

The one-dimensional \(N(0,1)\) density is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y^2/2}\). Section 01.5 uses this result for independence.

The figure below shows 300 simulated points \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\) from the first example. The center of the points is near \(\boldsymbol\mu=(10,20)\). The points spread along the up-right direction, because the off-diagonal entry \(\mathrm{cov}(y_1,y_2)=11\) is positive. The vertical spread is larger than the horizontal spread, because \(\mathrm{Var}(y_2)=25\) is larger than \(\mathrm{Var}(y_1)=5\).

[figure]
Figure 1-1. 300 points \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\) with \(\boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&2\\3&4\end{array}\right]\). The blue points are simulated values. The orange cross is the mean \(\boldsymbol\mu\). The matrix \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T\) sets the direction and the width of the cloud.

**Why** Added

The chain below uses the rules of Section 01.3 to prove \(E[\boldsymbol{y}]=\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T\). First, find the two parameters of \(\boldsymbol{z}\). Each \(z_i\) has mean 0, so \(E[\boldsymbol{z}]=\boldsymbol{0}\). Each \(z_i\) has variance 1, and different \(z_i\) are independent with covariance 0. Thus, \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{z})=\boldsymbol{I}\).

1

\[E[\boldsymbol{y}]=E[\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu]=\boldsymbol{A}E[\boldsymbol{z}]+\boldsymbol\mu\]

p.4: the expectation moves through a constant matrix and an added constant.

2

\[=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{0}+\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol\mu\]

3

\[\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})=\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu)=\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z})\]

An added constant vector does not change \(\boldsymbol{y}-E[\boldsymbol{y}]\). Thus, it does not change the variance.

4

\[=\boldsymbol{A}\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{z})\,\boldsymbol{A}^T\]

p.4: \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{A}\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\boldsymbol{A}^T\).

5

\[=\boldsymbol{A}\,\boldsymbol{I}\,\boldsymbol{A}^T=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T=\boldsymbol\Sigma\]

∎

This section gives the result: \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\) has the distribution \(MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T)\), and \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) set its density. The next section shows what stays multivariate normal after a linear change, a subset, or a condition.

### 01.5 Properties of \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) Slides p.6

This section gives four properties of the multivariate normal. Unit 04 uses the linearity property to get the distribution of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\).

**What** Slides p.6

A marginal distribution is the distribution of only some entries of a vector. A conditional distribution \(\boldsymbol{y}_1\mid\boldsymbol{y}_2\) is the distribution of \(\boldsymbol{y}_1\) when you know the value of \(\boldsymbol{y}_2\). \(\Sigma_{ij}\) is the entry of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) in row \(i\), column \(j\). It is equal to \(\mathrm{cov}(y_i,y_j)\).

Properties of \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) · Lecture 6 · p.6 Linearity: If \(\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{d}\), then: \[\boldsymbol{u}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol{d},\,\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol{C}^T)\] Marginal Distribution: If \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}=(y_1,\dots,y_m)^T\subset\boldsymbol{y}\) is a vector subset of \(\boldsymbol{y}\), then \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}\) is MVN-distributed.
Conditional Distribution: If \(\boldsymbol{y}=(\boldsymbol{y}_1^T,\boldsymbol{y}_2^T)^T\), then \(\boldsymbol{y}_1^T\mid\boldsymbol{y}_2^T\) is MVN-distributed.
Independence: If \(\Sigma_{ij}=0\), then \(\boldsymbol{y}_i\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}_j\) are independent.

Each property in one sentence:

Linearity: a multivariate normal vector, multiplied by a constant matrix \(\boldsymbol{C}\) and added to a constant vector \(\boldsymbol{d}\), stays multivariate normal. Its mean and variance change by the rules of p.4.

Marginal: any set of entries from a multivariate normal vector is multivariate normal. One single entry has a one-dimensional normal distribution.

Conditional: divide \(\boldsymbol{y}\) into an upper block \(\boldsymbol{y}_1\) and a lower block \(\boldsymbol{y}_2\). When \(\boldsymbol{y}_2\) is known, \(\boldsymbol{y}_1\) is multivariate normal. The slide writes \(\boldsymbol{y}_1^T\mid\boldsymbol{y}_2^T\), with transposes, and this has the same meaning as \(\boldsymbol{y}_1\mid\boldsymbol{y}_2\). This lecture does not give the parameters of the conditional distribution.

Independence: for a multivariate normal vector, covariance 0 gives independence.

**How** Added

Use these steps when \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) is known, and you must find the distribution of a linear combination or a subset. A linear combination is a sum of the entries, each multiplied by a constant.

How · Use linearity to find the distribution of a new variable

- Write the new variable as \(\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{d}\). Write \(\boldsymbol{C}\) and \(\boldsymbol{d}\). For a subset, each row of \(\boldsymbol{C}\) has one 1, and all other entries are 0.
- For the mean, calculate \(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol{d}\).
- For the variance, calculate \(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol{C}^T\).
- Write \(\boldsymbol{u}\sim MVN(\text{step 2},\text{step 3})\). If \(\boldsymbol{u}\) has one entry, write \(N(\cdot,\cdot)\).

**Self-check:** The number of columns of \(\boldsymbol{C}\) must be equal to the length of \(\boldsymbol{y}\). The length of \(\boldsymbol{d}\) must be equal to the number of rows of \(\boldsymbol{C}\).

**Example** Added

Use \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN\left(\left[\begin{array}{c}10\\20\end{array}\right],\left[\begin{array}{cc}5&11\\11&25\end{array}\right]\right)\) from Section 01.4.

(i) Linearity: find the distribution of \(u=y_1+y_2\).

1

Write \(u=\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{d}\) How step 1

\[\boldsymbol{C}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&1\end{array}\right],\qquad \boldsymbol{d}=0\]

2

Mean How step 2

\[\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol{d}=1(10)+1(20)+0=30\]

3

Variance How step 3

\[\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol{C}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}5&11\\11&25\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\1\end{array}\right]\]

\[=\left[\begin{array}{cc}5+11&11+25\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\1\end{array}\right]\]

\[=\left[\begin{array}{cc}16&36\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\1\end{array}\right]=16+36=52\]

4

Distribution How step 4

\[u=y_1+y_2\sim N(30,\,52)\]

(ii) Marginal: let \(\boldsymbol{C}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&0\end{array}\right]\) and \(\boldsymbol{d}=0\). The mean is \(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu=1(10)+0(20)=10\). The variance is \(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol{C}^T=\Sigma_{11}=5\). Thus, \(y_1\sim N(10,5)\).

(iii) Independence: let \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol{I}\) and \(\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol{0}\). Here \(\Sigma_{12}=0\), so \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are independent. Thus, the joint density is the product of two one-dimensional densities. The second example of Section 01.4 shows this at \((1,-1)\). The p.5 formula gives 0.05854983, and the product of two \(N(0,1)\) densities also gives 0.05854983.

**Why** Added

The construction on p.5 gives a direct proof of linearity. Let \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu\), with \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T\).

1

\[\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol\mu)+\boldsymbol{d}\]

Put in the construction of p.5.

2

\[=(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{A})\boldsymbol{z}+(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol{d})\]

3

\[\Rightarrow\ \boldsymbol{u}\sim MVN\big(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol{d},\ (\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{A})(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{A})^T\big)\]

The form is "constant matrix × \(\boldsymbol{z}\) + constant vector", so p.5 applies.

4

\[(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{A})(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{A})^T=\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{C}^T\]

\((\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{A})^T=\boldsymbol{A}^T\boldsymbol{C}^T\).

5

\[=\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol{C}^T\]

∎ The marginal property is the special case where \(\boldsymbol{C}\) selects entries. This lecture states the conditional and independence properties without proof.

This section gives the result: a multivariate normal vector stays multivariate normal after a linear change or a subset. Its parameters are \(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol{d}\) and \(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol{C}^T\). The next section uses this property to write the regression model as one matrix statement.

### 01.6 Recap: multiple linear regression Slides p.7

This section writes the multiple linear regression model first as one matrix equation, then as one multivariate normal distribution. Units 02 to 05 all start from this form.

**What** Slides p.7

Multiple linear regression (MLR) is a model for an outcome \(y_i\). The outcome is an intercept plus a linear combination of \(p\) covariates \(x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip}\), plus a random error \(\epsilon_i\). The regression coefficients \(\beta_0,\dots,\beta_p\) are unknown constants. The error variance \(\sigma^2\) is also an unknown constant. \(n\) is the number of observations.

Recap: Multiple Linear Regression · Lecture 6 · p.7 \[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_Px_{ip}+\epsilon_i,\qquad \epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\] We can write this: \[\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1\\y_2\\ \vdots\\y_n\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cccccc}1&x_{11}&x_{12}&\dots&x_{1p}\\1&x_{21}&x_{22}&\dots&x_{2p}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\1&x_{n1}&x_{n2}&\dots&x_{np}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0\\ \beta_1\\ \vdots\\ \beta_p\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c}\epsilon_1\\ \epsilon_2\\ \vdots\\ \epsilon_n\end{array}\right]\] Or more simply: \[\begin{array}{rl}&\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon,\qquad \boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\\ \iff&\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\end{array}\]

Notation note The first line of the slide writes \(\beta_P\) with an upper-case P. The subscript in \(x_{ip}\) and the last entry \(\beta_p\) of the vector use a lower-case p. This page copies the slide. Both letters mean the same number: the index \(p\) of the last covariate.

Each row \(i\) is one observation. The first column of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) contains only 1s. This column multiplies \(\beta_0\) and gives the intercept. Column \(j+1\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is covariate \(j\). Thus, \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is \(n\times(p+1)\), and \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is \((p+1)\times1\).

The statement "\(\epsilon_i\) i.i.d. \(N(0,\sigma^2)\)" is equal to \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\): all means are 0, all variances are \(\sigma^2\), and all covariances between different observations are 0.

[figure]
Figure 1-2. The size of each block in \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\). The first column of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) (left of the dashed line) contains only 1s, for the intercept \(\beta_0\). The number of columns of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is equal to the length \(p+1\) of \(\boldsymbol\beta\). Thus, the product exists, and its size is \(n\times1\).

**How** Added

Use these steps to write the matrix form from the \(n\) equations.

How · Write \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\)

- For \(\boldsymbol{y}\), put \(y_1,\dots,y_n\) in one column.
- For \(\boldsymbol{X}\), write \((1,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip})\) as row \(i\).
- For \(\boldsymbol\beta\), put \(\beta_0,\dots,\beta_p\) in one column.
- Multiply row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) by \(\boldsymbol\beta\). The result must be \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\dots+\beta_px_{ip}\) from equation \(i\).

**Self-check:** \(\boldsymbol{X}\) has \(n\) rows and \(p+1\) columns. Its first column contains only 1s.

**Example** Added

Let \(n=3\) and \(p=2\). The covariates are \((x_{11},x_{12})=(1,4)\), \((x_{21},x_{22})=(2,5)\), and \((x_{31},x_{32})=(3,6)\). To show the product, let \(\boldsymbol\beta=(1,2,3)^T\). The true \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is unknown, so this value is only for the algebra.

1

Write \(\boldsymbol{X}\) How step 2

\[\boldsymbol{X}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1&1&4\\1&2&5\\1&3&6\end{array}\right]\quad(3\times3=n\times(p+1))\]

2

Calculate \(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) How step 4

\[\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta=\left[\begin{array}{c}1+2(1)+3(4)\\1+2(2)+3(5)\\1+2(3)+3(6)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}1+2+12\\1+4+15\\1+6+18\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}15\\20\\25\end{array}\right]\]

Row 1 is \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{11}+\beta_2x_{12}\). Thus, \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN\big((15,20,25)^T,\ \sigma^2\boldsymbol{I}\big)\).

**Why** Added

The chain below starts from \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\) and gets \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\). It uses the linearity property of Section 01.5 with \(\boldsymbol{C}=\boldsymbol{I}\) and \(\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\). Both \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta\) are constants, so \(\boldsymbol{d}\) is a constant vector.

1

\[\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol\epsilon+\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\]

2

\[\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol{0}+\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\ \boldsymbol{I}(\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\boldsymbol{I}^T)\]

p.6 linearity: \(MVN(\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol{d},\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol{C}^T)\).

3

\[\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\ \sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\]

For the other direction, use \(\boldsymbol\epsilon=\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) with \(\boldsymbol{d}=-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\). Thus, the statement is \(\iff\). ∎

This section gives the result: the MLR model is \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\). Unit 02 shows a data example and the meaning of \(\boldsymbol\beta\), and Unit 03 uses the rules of Section 01.2 to estimate \(\boldsymbol\beta\).

### 01.7 Practice Added

The three questions below practise the vector derivative, the linearity of the multivariate normal, and the matrix sizes of the regression model.

**Q1.** Let \(z=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\) with \(\boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}4&1\\1&2\end{array}\right]\). Find \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}\) and evaluate it at \(\boldsymbol{y}=(1,-1)^T\). Check the result entry by entry.

Answer

1

\[\boldsymbol{A}^T=\boldsymbol{A}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}=2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}=2\left[\begin{array}{c}4y_1+y_2\\y_1+2y_2\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}8y_1+2y_2\\2y_1+4y_2\end{array}\right]\]

2

\[z=4y_1^2+2y_1y_2+2y_2^2,\quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_1}=8y_1+2y_2,\quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_2}=2y_1+4y_2\]

The entry-by-entry result agrees with step 1.

3

\[\left.\frac{\partial z}{\partial\boldsymbol{y}}\right|_{(1,-1)}=\left[\begin{array}{c}8(1)+2(-1)\\2(1)+4(-1)\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}6\\-2\end{array}\right]\]

**Q2.** Suppose \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)\) with \(\boldsymbol\mu=(1,2)^T\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&1\\1&3\end{array}\right]\). Find the distribution of \(u=y_1-y_2\).

Answer

1

\[u=\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{d},\quad \boldsymbol{C}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&-1\end{array}\right],\ \boldsymbol{d}=0\]

2

\[\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\mu=1(1)+(-1)(2)=-1\]

3

\[\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2-1&1-3\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&-2\end{array}\right]\]

4

\[\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol{C}^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&-2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}1\\-1\end{array}\right]=1+2=3\]

5

\[u\sim N(-1,\,3)\]

p.6 linearity property.

**Q3.** A multiple linear regression has \(n=50\) observations and \(p=3\) covariates, written as \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\), \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\). (a) Give the dimensions of \(\boldsymbol{X}\), \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})\). (b) Show that \(E[\boldsymbol{y}]=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) using the properties of random vectors.

Answer

(a) \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is \(n\times(p+1)=50\times4\). \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is \(4\times1\). \(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{y})=\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I}\) is \(50\times50\).

(b)

1

\[E[\boldsymbol{y}]=E[\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon]\]

2

\[=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+E[\boldsymbol\epsilon]\]

p.4: \(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) is a constant vector, and \(E[\boldsymbol{a}]=\boldsymbol{a}\).

3

\[=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\]

This unit completes the recap of Lecture 6. It gives two derivative rules for vectors and the expectation and variance of \(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\). It also gives the multivariate normal and the MLR model \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\). The later units use these tools to estimate \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and to find its distribution.

## 02 · Data example and interpreting regression coefficients

This unit uses a data set of hospital patients to start the multiple linear regression model. It then shows what each coefficient \(\beta_j\) of the model tells us.

Plan · Slides p.8–16

Step 1 (Slides p.8–9): meet the data set satisfaction.csv.

Step 2 (Slides p.10–11): look at the summary numbers and the scatter plots of the data.

Step 3 (Slides p.12): list the questions that the lecture wants to answer.

Step 4 (Slides p.13): write the multiple linear regression model in scalar form and in matrix form.

Step 5 (Slides p.14–16): interpret the intercept \(\beta_0\) and each slope \(\beta_j\).

This unit uses the coefficient estimates as known numbers. Unit 03 shows how to calculate them.

Basic words used in this unit · Added

This block defines the words that the whole unit uses.

Variable: one column of a data table. Each observation has one value of each variable.

Observation: one row of a data table. Here, one observation is one patient. The number of observations is \(n\).

Outcome (also called response) \(y_i\): the variable that we want to explain or predict. In this unit, the outcome is Satisfaction.

Covariate \(x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip}\): a variable that we use to explain the outcome. In this unit, the covariates are Age, Severity, and Stress.

The number of covariates is \(p\). The subscript \(i\) gives the observation. The subscript \(j\) gives the covariate.

With these words, the unit can start from the data.

### 02.1 Title page Slides p.8

This section tells where the new topic starts.

Slides p.8 Slide p.8 repeats the title "Lecture 6: Multiple Linear Regression: Intro & Estimation".

Multiple linear regression (MLR) is a linear model in which more than one covariate explains the outcome. Slides p.1–7 are a recap. The new material starts on Slides p.9.

The next section gives the data that the lecture uses for all of its examples.

### 02.2 Data example: satisfaction.csv Slides p.9

This section gives the data set. The model, the coefficients, and their interpretation in this unit all use these data.

**What** Slides p.9

Data Example · Lecture 6 · p.9
satisfaction.csv contains data on \(n = 46\) hospital patients. The variables are:

- Satisfaction: degree of satisfaction with quality of care (higher values = more)
- Age: age of patient in years
- Severity: severity score for patient condition
- Stress: patient self reported degree of stress

The data have 46 rows. Each row is one hospital patient. Thus \(n=46\). The data have 4 columns.

Satisfaction: the satisfaction of the patient with the quality of care. A higher value shows more satisfaction. It is the outcome \(y_i\).

Age: the age of the patient, in years. It is covariate 1, \(x_{i1}\).

Severity: a score for how serious the condition of the patient is. It is covariate 2, \(x_{i2}\).

Stress: the degree of stress that the patient reports. It is covariate 3, \(x_{i3}\).

The data have \(n=46\) observations and \(p=3\) covariates. The next section looks at the values in the data.

### 02.3 Exploratory data analysis: first rows and summary numbers Slides p.10

This section reads the first rows and the summary numbers that Slides p.10 prints. Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is a check of the range, center, and shape of the data before you make a model.

**What** Slides p.10

Slides p.10 prints the first 6 rows of the data:

| Row | Satisfaction | Age | Severity | Stress

| 1 | 48 | 50 | 51 | 2.3

| 2 | 57 | 36 | 46 | 2.3

| 3 | 66 | 40 | 48 | 2.2

| 4 | 70 | 41 | 44 | 1.8

| 5 | 89 | 28 | 43 | 1.8

| 6 | 36 | 49 | 54 | 2.9

Slides p.10 also prints six summary numbers for each variable:

|  | Satisfaction | Age | Severity | Stress

| Minimum | 26.00 | 22.00 | 41.00 | 1.800

| 1st quartile | 48.25 | 31.25 | 48.00 | 2.100

| Median | 60.00 | 37.50 | 50.50 | 2.300

| Mean | 61.57 | 38.39 | 50.43 | 2.287

| 3rd quartile | 76.75 | 44.75 | 53.00 | 2.475

| Maximum | 92.00 | 55.00 | 62.00 | 2.900

Minimum and maximum: the smallest value and the largest value of the variable.

Quartile: a value that divides the sorted data into four equal parts. About 25% of the data are below the 1st quartile. About 75% of the data are below the 3rd quartile.

Median: the middle value of the sorted data. About 50% of the data are below the median.

Sample mean \(\bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\): the sum of all the values, divided by \(n\).

**How** Added

Read the summary numbers of one variable

- Find the column of the variable.
- Read the minimum and the maximum. They give the range of the variable.
- Read the median and the mean. They give the center of the data.
- Read the 1st and 3rd quartiles. The middle 50% of the data are between them.

**Self-check:** In each column, minimum ≤ 1st quartile ≤ median ≤ 3rd quartile ≤ maximum. The mean is between the minimum and the maximum.

**Example · Read the two tables** Added

This example applies the four How steps to each variable in the two tables of Slides p.10.

Patient 1 has Satisfaction 48, Age 50, Severity 51, and Stress 2.3. Thus \(y_1=48\), \(x_{11}=50\), \(x_{12}=51\), and \(x_{13}=2.3\).

Satisfaction: the range is 26 to 92. The mean is 61.57 and the median is 60.

Age: the range is 22 to 55 years. The mean is 38.39. All patients are adults.

Severity: the range is 41 to 62. The mean is 50.43.

Stress: the range is 1.8 to 2.9. The mean is 2.287.

**Self-check:** For Age, 22 ≤ 31.25 ≤ 37.50 ≤ 44.75 ≤ 55, and the mean 38.39 is between 22 and 55.

Section 02.7 uses one fact from this example. No covariate has the value 0: the minimum Age is 22, the minimum Severity is 41, and the minimum Stress is 1.8. ▲

The summary numbers give the range and center of each variable. The next section looks at pairs of variables.

### 02.4 Scatter plot matrix Slides p.11

The summary numbers show one variable at a time. This section shows the relation between two variables.

**What** Slides p.11

Slides p.11 shows a scatter plot matrix of the four variables.

Scatter plot: a plot with one point for each observation. The horizontal position is the value of one variable. The vertical position is the value of another variable.

Scatter plot matrix (pairs plot): a square grid that shows the scatter plot of each pair of variables. Here there are 4 variables, so the grid is 4×4.

The diagonal cells of the grid show only the variable names.

**How** Added

Find the scatter plot of one pair of variables

- Find the name of variable A on the diagonal. Note its row.
- Find the name of variable B on the diagonal. Note its column.
- Go to the cell in row A and column B. Its vertical axis is A. Its horizontal axis is B.
- Look at the direction of the points. Lower left to upper right shows a positive association.
- Upper left to lower right shows a negative association.

**Self-check:** The vertical axis of the cell covers the minimum to the maximum of A in the summary table. The horizontal axis does the same for B.

**Example · Satisfaction against Age** Added

This example takes the cell in row 1 and column 2 of the grid. Its vertical axis is Satisfaction and its horizontal axis is Age. The figure below draws this cell again with the 46 data points.

[figure]
Figure 2-1. Satisfaction against Age. Each blue point is one of the 46 patients. The orange point is patient 1, with Age 50 and Satisfaction 48. The points go from upper left to lower right.

By How step 5, the points go from upper left to lower right. Thus Satisfaction and Age have a negative association. Older patients have lower satisfaction in general.

By the self-check, the vertical axis covers 26 to 92 and the horizontal axis covers 22 to 55. These ranges agree with the summary table.

This plot shows only two variables. It does not hold Severity and Stress fixed. Section 02.7 adds a line that holds them fixed. ▲

A scatter plot shows the association between two variables only. The next section asks questions that need all the covariates together.

### 02.5 Motivating questions Slides p.12

This section lists the questions of Slides p.12. A plot of two variables cannot answer them, so we need multiple linear regression.

**What** Slides p.12

Motivating Questions · Lecture 6 · p.12

- Is mean satisfaction associated with stress, conditional on age and severity?
- How does mean satisfaction differ for older patients vs younger patients with the same severity and stress scores?
- Given a patient's stress, age, and severity, can we predict their satisfaction?
- Later: is the (conditional) association between stress and satisfaction different for older patients than for younger patients?
- Many others...

Association: when one variable changes, the mean of another variable also changes.

Conditional on: with the other variables held at fixed values.

Question 1: Patients have the same age and severity. Does their mean satisfaction change with stress?

Question 2: Patients have the same severity and stress. How much does the mean satisfaction of older and younger patients differ?

Question 3: We know the stress, age, and severity of a patient. Can we predict the satisfaction of that patient?

Question 4 (later): Is the conditional association between stress and satisfaction different for older and younger patients?

Questions 1 and 2 hold the other variables fixed. Figure 2-1 cannot do this, because it mixes patients with different Severity and Stress.

The questions need a model with all three covariates at the same time. The next section gives this model.

### 02.6 The multiple linear regression model Slides p.13

This section gives the model of this lecture. The slides write it in two equivalent forms: a scalar form for each observation and a matrix form for all observations.

**What** Slides p.13

Multiple Linear Regression · Lecture 6 · p.13 \[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_Px_{ip}+\epsilon_i,\qquad \epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2),\quad i=1,\dots,n\]
Or
\[\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\quad \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\] \[\iff\] \[\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\]
Note: we assume \(p+1<n\)

The list below defines each symbol of the model.

\(\beta_0\): the intercept. It is an unknown fixed number.

\(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p\): the regression coefficients, one for each covariate. They are unknown fixed numbers. The slide writes the last term as \(\beta_Px_{ip}\). The capital \(P\) means the coefficient number \(p\).

\(\epsilon_i\): the error. It is the random part of \(y_i\) that is not in \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}\).

\(\epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\): the errors are independent and identically distributed. Each error has a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\).

\(\boldsymbol{y}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\): \(n\times1\) column vectors of the outcomes and the errors.

\(\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p)^T\): the \((p+1)\times1\) vector of coefficients.

Design matrix \(\boldsymbol{X}\): an \(n\times(p+1)\) matrix. Row \(i\) is \((1,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip})\). The first column is all 1s, for the intercept.

\(MVN(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\): a multivariate normal distribution with mean vector \(\boldsymbol{0}\) and covariance matrix \(\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I}\). Each error has variance \(\sigma^2\), and different errors are uncorrelated.

\(p+1<n\): the number of unknown coefficients, \(p+1\), is less than the number of observations, \(n\). Unit 05 divides by \(n-(p+1)\), and this assumption makes that number positive.

**How** Added

Write the model and \(\boldsymbol{X}\) for a data set

- Find the outcome \(y_i\) and the \(p\) covariates. Write \(n\) and \(p\).
- Write the scalar form. Put the variable names in place of \(x_{ij}\).
- Make \(\boldsymbol{X}\). Put \(n\) 1s in the first column.
- Put the values of covariate \(j\) in column \(j+1\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\).
- Check that \(p+1<n\).

**Self-check:** \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is \(n\times(p+1)\). \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) has \(p+1\) entries. Row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) agrees with row \(i\) of the data table.

**Example · The model for satisfaction.csv** Added

This example applies the five How steps to the data of Slides p.9–10.

**Step 1.** The outcome is Satisfaction. The covariates are Age, Severity, and Stress. Thus \(n=46\) and \(p=3\).

**Step 2.** The scalar form of the model is:
\[\text{Satisfaction}_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{Age}_i+\beta_2\,\text{Severity}_i+\beta_3\,\text{Stress}_i+\epsilon_i,\qquad \epsilon_i\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2),\quad i=1,\dots,46\]
**Steps 3–4.** \(\boldsymbol{X}\) has \(p+1=4\) columns. The first three rows come from the data table of Slides p.10:
\[\boldsymbol{X}=\left[\begin{array}{cccc}1&50&51&2.3\\1&36&46&2.3\\1&40&48&2.2\\\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\end{array}\right]_{46\times4},\qquad \boldsymbol{\beta}=\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\beta_2\\\beta_3\end{array}\right]\]
**Step 5.** \(p+1=4\) and \(n=46\). Thus \(4<46\), and the assumption is true.

**Self-check:** \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is \(46\times4=n\times(p+1)\). \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) has 4 entries. Row 1 of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is patient 1: Age 50, Severity 51, Stress 2.3.

**Coefficient estimates used in this unit.** An estimate is a number that we calculate from the data in place of an unknown true value. A hat shows an estimate, for example \(\hat\beta_1\).

Lecture 6 does not print the estimates for these data. Lecture 7 · p.51 prints a 95% confidence interval for each coefficient. A confidence interval is a range of values for an unknown coefficient, calculated from the data.

Each of these intervals has the estimate at its center. Thus the midpoint of the interval gives the estimate:

1

\[\hat\beta_0=\frac{121.911727+195.0707761}{2}=\frac{316.9825031}{2}=158.4912516\approx158.491\]

2

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{-1.575093+(-0.7081303)}{2}=\frac{-2.2832233}{2}=-1.1416117\approx-1.142\]

3

\[\hat\beta_2=\frac{-1.434831+0.5508228}{2}=\frac{-0.8840082}{2}=-0.4420041\approx-0.442\]

4

\[\hat\beta_3=\frac{-27.797859+0.8575324}{2}=\frac{-26.9403266}{2}=-13.4701633\approx-13.470\]

This unit uses the rounded values \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(158.491,\,-1.142,\,-0.442,\,-13.470)^T\). It has \(4=p+1\) entries. Unit 03 shows how to calculate these estimates. ▲

**Why** Added

This part shows that the scalar form and the matrix form give the same model. Row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) is row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) times \(\boldsymbol\beta\):

1

\[[\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta]_i=\left[\begin{array}{cccc}1&x_{i1}&\cdots&x_{ip}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\vdots\\\beta_p\end{array}\right]\]

2

\[=1\cdot\beta_0+x_{i1}\beta_1+\cdots+x_{ip}\beta_p\]

3

\[=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}\]

Thus row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\) is \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}+\epsilon_i\). This is the scalar form.

The second form, \(\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\), comes from the linearity property on Slides p.6. Section 01.6 shows this step.

Numerical check with patient 1 and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\): row 1 of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is \((1,50,51,2.3)\).

1

\[1(158.491)+50(-1.142)+51(-0.442)+2.3(-13.470)\]

2

\[=158.491-57.1-22.542-30.981\]

3

\[=47.868\]

This is \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1(50)+\hat\beta_2(51)+\hat\beta_3(2.3)\), the scalar form for patient 1. ∎

The model has a scalar form and an equivalent matrix form. The next section tells what each coefficient in it means.

### 02.7 Interpreting regression coefficients Slides p.14–16

This section tells what each coefficient means. The slides give one method: "To interpret a parameter, isolate it!"

Slides p.14–16 Slides p.14 and p.15 are the first parts of Slides p.16. This section follows the full text of p.16.

**What** Slides p.14–16

Interpreting Regression Coefficients · Lecture 6 · p.14–16
To interpret a parameter, isolate it!
\[E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip}]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}\cdots+\beta_Px_{ip}\]
What does \(\beta_0\) represent?
\[E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1}=\cdots=x_{ip}=0]=\beta_0+\beta_1(0)+\cdots+\beta_P(0)=\beta_0\]

- \(\implies\beta_0\) is the mean outcome when all covariates are set to 0
- May not be interpretable: e.g. what does it mean for age to be 0 in a sample of adults?

What does \(\beta_1\) represent?
\[E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1}=x_1,x_{i2}=x_2,\dots,x_{ip}=x_P]=\beta_0+\beta_1(x_1)+\beta_2(x_2)+\cdots+\beta_P(x_P)\] \[E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1}=(x_1+1),x_{i2}=x_2,\dots,x_{ip}=x_P]=\beta_0+\beta_1(x_1+1)+\cdots+\beta_P(x_P)\]

- \(E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1}=(x_1+1),x_{i2}=x_2,\dots,x_{ip}=x_P]-E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1}=x_1,x_{i2}=x_2,\dots,x_{ip}=x_P]=\beta_1\)
- More generally \(\beta_j\) represents the difference in mean outcome for a one-unit change in the \(j^{th}\) covariate, holding other covariates fixed.

Conditional expectation \(E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip}]\): the mean of \(y_i\) when the covariates have the given values. Read the bar \(|\) as "given".

\(\beta_0\): the mean outcome when all covariates are 0. If 0 is not in the range of the data, \(\beta_0\) has no practical meaning.

\(\beta_1\): the difference in mean outcome when covariate 1 increases by one unit and the other covariates do not change.

\(\beta_j\): the difference in mean outcome when covariate \(j\) increases by one unit and the other covariates do not change.

The words "holding other covariates fixed" are a necessary part of the interpretation. They agree with "conditional on" and "with the same" in Questions 1 and 2 of Section 02.5.

**How** Added

Interpret one coefficient \(\beta_j\)

- Write the full conditional expectation \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}\).
- For the intercept: put 0 for all covariates. The result is \(\beta_0\).
- Check in the summary table if 0 is in the range of each covariate.
- For a slope: write the conditional expectation two times, with covariate \(j\) equal to \(x_j\) and \(x_j+1\).
- Give the other covariates the same values in both expressions.
- Subtract the first expression from the second. Only \(\beta_j\) remains.
- Write the interpretation: a one-unit increase in covariate \(j\) changes the mean outcome by \(\beta_j\), with other covariates held fixed.

**Self-check:** The interpretation names the covariate and its unit. It gives the direction and size of \(\beta_j\). It says that the other covariates are held fixed. With an estimate, it says "estimated mean outcome".

**Example · Interpret \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\)** Added

This example uses \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(158.491,\,-1.142,\,-0.442,\,-13.470)^T\) from the example in Section 02.6. It follows the seven How steps.

**Step 1.** The estimated mean satisfaction is:
\[\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\,\text{Age}+\hat\beta_2\,\text{Severity}+\hat\beta_3\,\text{Stress}=158.491-1.142\,\text{Age}-0.442\,\text{Severity}-13.470\,\text{Stress}\]
**Step 2 (intercept).** Put Age = Severity = Stress = 0:

1

\[158.491-1.142(0)-0.442(0)-13.470(0)\]

2

\[=158.491=\hat\beta_0\]

Thus \(\hat\beta_0=158.491\) is the estimated mean satisfaction when Age, Severity, and Stress are all 0.

**Step 3.** The example in Section 02.3 shows that the minimum Age is 22, the minimum Severity is 41, and the minimum Stress is 1.8. No patient in these data has Age 0. Thus \(\hat\beta_0\) has no practical meaning here. This is the case of the second bullet on Slides p.15.

**Steps 4–5 (slope of Age).** Hold Severity = 50 and Stress = 2.3. Use Age = 40 and then Age = 41.

1

\[\text{Age }40:\ 158.491-1.142(40)-0.442(50)-13.470(2.3)\]

2

\[=158.491-45.68-22.1-30.981\]

3

\[=59.73\]

1

\[\text{Age }41:\ 158.491-1.142(41)-0.442(50)-13.470(2.3)\]

2

\[=158.491-46.822-22.1-30.981\]

3

\[=58.588\]

**Step 6.** Subtract:

1

\[58.588-59.73=-1.142=\hat\beta_1\]

The terms \(-22.1\) and \(-30.981\) are the same in both lines.

**Step 7.** For each one-year increase in Age, the estimated mean satisfaction decreases by 1.142, with Severity and Stress held fixed.

**Self-check:** The covariate is Age. The unit is one year. The direction is a decrease and the size is 1.142. The sentence says "held fixed".

The same steps give the other two slopes:

\(\hat\beta_2=-0.442\): for each one-point increase in Severity, the estimated mean satisfaction decreases by 0.442, with Age and Stress held fixed.

\(\hat\beta_3=-13.470\): for each one-unit increase in Stress, the estimated mean satisfaction decreases by 13.470, with Age and Severity held fixed.

The figure below shows "held fixed". It uses the same axes as Figure 2-1. The orange line holds Severity and Stress at their sample means, 50.43 and 2.287, and changes only Age.

At these values, the line is \(158.491-0.442(50.43)-13.470(2.287)-1.142\,\text{Age}=105.395-1.142\,\text{Age}\) (values rounded to 3 decimals).

[figure]
Figure 2-2. The 46 points of Figure 2-1 (blue) and the estimated mean satisfaction with Severity and Stress at their sample means (orange). The slope of the orange line is \(\hat\beta_1=-1.142\). The green points are on the line at Age 30 and Age 50. The line decreases by \(20\times1.142=22.84\) over these 20 years.

Other fixed values, for example Severity = 60, move the orange line up or down. The slope stays at \(-1.142\). Thus \(\hat\beta_1\) describes only the change in Age when the other covariates are held fixed. ▲

**Why** Slides p.14–16

This part shows why the subtraction leaves only \(\beta_j\). It starts from the model of Slides p.13.

1

\[E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip}]=E[\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}+\epsilon_i\,|\,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip}]\]

Model, Slides p.13

2

\[=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}+E[\epsilon_i]\]

Given the covariates, the first part is a fixed number

3

\[=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}\]

\(E[\epsilon_i]=0\)

4

\[E[y_i\,|\,x_{i1}=\cdots=x_{ip}=0]=\beta_0+\beta_1(0)+\cdots+\beta_p(0)\]

Intercept: put 0 for all covariates

5

\[=\beta_0\]

6

\[E[y_i\,|\,x_{ij}=x_j+1,\ \text{others fixed}]=\beta_0+\cdots+\beta_j(x_j+1)+\cdots+\beta_px_p\]

Slope: covariate \(j\) is \(x_j+1\)

7

\[E[y_i\,|\,x_{ij}=x_j,\ \text{others fixed}]=\beta_0+\cdots+\beta_jx_j+\cdots+\beta_px_p\]

8

\[\text{line 6}-\text{line 7}=\beta_j(x_j+1)-\beta_jx_j\]

All other terms are the same in lines 6 and 7

9

\[=\beta_jx_j+\beta_j-\beta_jx_j\]

10

\[=\beta_j\]

Line 8 needs the other covariates to have the same values in both lines. Thus the interpretation of \(\beta_j\) must say "holding other covariates fixed".

The result does not depend on the start value \(x_j\). Thus Age 40 to 41 and Age 30 to 31 both give the difference \(\beta_1\). ∎

This section gives the interpretation of the coefficients. \(\beta_0\) is the mean outcome when all covariates are 0. \(\beta_j\) is the difference in mean outcome for a one-unit increase in covariate \(j\), with the other covariates held fixed. The practice questions below use these interpretations.

### 02.8 Practice Added

All questions use the model of the example in Section 02.6 and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(158.491,\,-1.142,\,-0.442,\,-13.470)^T\).

**Q1.** Interpret \(\hat\beta_3=-13.470\), the coefficient of Stress. Two patients have the same Age and Severity, and their Stress values differ by 0.5. Find the difference in their estimated mean satisfaction.

Answer

Interpretation: for each one-unit increase in Stress, the estimated mean satisfaction decreases by 13.470, with Age and Severity held fixed.

By the derivation in Section 02.7, a change of 0.5 in Stress gives the difference \(0.5\times\hat\beta_3\):

\(0.5\times(-13.470)=-6.735\)

The patient with Stress 0.5 higher has an estimated mean satisfaction 6.735 lower.

**Q2.** Two patients both have Severity = 50 and Stress = 2.3. One patient is 30 years old and the other is 50 years old. Find the estimated mean satisfaction of each patient and the difference. Write the difference with \(\hat\beta_1\).

Answer

1

\[\text{Age }30:\ 158.491-1.142(30)-0.442(50)-13.470(2.3)\]

2

\[=158.491-34.26-22.1-30.981\]

3

\[=71.15\]

1

\[\text{Age }50:\ 158.491-1.142(50)-0.442(50)-13.470(2.3)\]

2

\[=158.491-57.1-22.1-30.981\]

3

\[=48.31\]

Difference: \(48.31-71.15=-22.84\).

With \(\hat\beta_1\): \(20\times\hat\beta_1=20\times(-1.142)=-22.84\).

The Severity and Stress terms are the same for both patients, so they cancel. Only \(\hat\beta_1(50-30)\) remains. The older patient has an estimated mean satisfaction 22.84 lower.

This unit went from the data to the model, and from the model to the meaning of each coefficient. The next unit uses least squares and maximum likelihood to calculate \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\).

## 03 · Estimating β: least squares and maximum likelihood

This unit uses two methods to estimate the coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol\beta\) of a multiple regression: least squares and maximum likelihood. Under the model assumptions of the slides, the two methods give the same formula \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\).

Plan · Slides p.17–22

Step 1: State the model and the symbols again, and say what we estimate (Slides p.17).

Step 2: Least squares. Write \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)\), take the derivative, set it to 0, and solve for \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) (Slides p.18–20).

Step 3: Calculate \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\) by hand for a small data set, and solve the equations (Added).

Step 4: Maximum likelihood. Write the likelihood and the log-likelihood, and find the link to \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)\) (Slides p.21–22).

### 03.1 Title page: Estimating \(\boldsymbol\beta\) Slides p.17

Slide p.17 shows only the title "Estimating \(\boldsymbol\beta\)". This unit uses the model \(\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon\) with \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\). The next lines give each symbol again.

\(\boldsymbol{y}\) is the \(n\times1\) outcome vector. It holds the outcome \(y_i\) of each of the \(n\) observations.

\(\boldsymbol{X}\) is the \(n\times(p+1)\) design matrix. Its first column is all 1s. The other \(p\) columns hold the covariates.

\(\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\dots,\beta_p)^T\) is the unknown coefficient vector. \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) is the \(n\times1\) vector of random errors.

\(MVN(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\) is the multivariate normal distribution with mean vector \(\boldsymbol{0}\) and covariance matrix \(\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I}\). Thus, the errors are independent normal, each with variance \(\sigma^2\).

Estimator \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\): a formula that uses the data \(\boldsymbol{y}\) and \(\boldsymbol{X}\) to give a value for the unknown \(\boldsymbol\beta\). The hat \(\hat{\ }\) means "calculated from the data".

The slides use the satisfaction data: \(n=46\) patients and three covariates (Age, Severity, Stress), so \(p=3\) (Slides p.9). The example in this unit uses a smaller data set so that you can do each step by hand. Section 03.2 now uses least squares to find \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\).

### 03.2 Least squares estimation Slides p.18–20

This section finds the \(\boldsymbol\beta\) that makes the total squared difference between the data \(\boldsymbol{y}\) and the model values \(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) as small as possible. Slides p.18–19 build up p.20 line by line, so p.20 holds all of the content.

**What** Slides p.20

Least Squares Estimation · Lecture 6 · p.20 Want to minimize the sum of squares, i.e.: \[\begin{aligned} S(\boldsymbol\beta)&=(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)^T(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\\ &=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\\ &=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{y}-2\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta \end{aligned}\] \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial S(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=-2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}+2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta&=0\\ (\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol\beta&=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\\ \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y} \end{aligned}\] assuming the columns of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are linearly independent

The next lines define each new term in the statement.

Sum of squares \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)\): for one candidate \(\boldsymbol\beta\), square each difference \(y_i-(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)_i\) and add the squares. Thus, \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)_i\big)^2\). It is one number.

Least squares estimation: use the \(\boldsymbol\beta\) that gives the smallest \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)\) as the estimate \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). This estimate is also named OLS (ordinary least squares).

Derivative with respect to a vector \(\partial S(\boldsymbol\beta)/\partial\boldsymbol\beta\): the partial derivatives of \(S\) with respect to \(\beta_0,\dots,\beta_p\), in one \((p+1)\times1\) column. At the minimum of \(S\), this column is 0.

Inverse matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\): the square matrix with \(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{I}\). The identity matrix \(\boldsymbol{I}\) has 1s on the diagonal and 0s at all other positions.

Linearly independent columns: no column of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is a linear combination of the other columns. Then \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\) has an inverse, and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) is unique.

In words: set the derivative of \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)\) to 0. This gives the system of equations \((\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol\beta=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\). These equations are the normal equations. When the columns of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are linearly independent, the system has one solution, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\).

**How** Added

Calculate \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) from data

- Write \(\boldsymbol{y}\) (\(n\times1\)) and \(\boldsymbol{X}\) (\(n\times(p+1)\), first column all 1s).
- Calculate the \((p+1)\times(p+1)\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\). Entry \((j,k)\) is \(\sum_i x_{ij}x_{ik}\) for columns \(j\) and \(k\).
- Calculate the \((p+1)\times1\) vector \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\). Entry \(j\) is \(\sum_i x_{ij}y_i\) for column \(j\).
- Make sure that \(\det(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})\neq0\). This shows that the columns of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are linearly independent.
- Solve \((\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol\beta=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\). The solution is \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\).

**Self-check:** (1) \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\) is symmetric, and its entry \((1,1)\) is \(n\). (2) Entry 1 of \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\) is \(\sum_iy_i\). (3) Put \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) back: \((\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) must equal \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\).

**Example** Added

This example does the five steps by hand on a small data set. It has \(n=4\) observations and one covariate, so \(p=1\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^T\). With \(p=1\), \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\) is \(2\times2\), so you can find its inverse by hand.

Data: \(x=1,2,3,4\) and \(y=2,3,5,6\).

1

Write \(\boldsymbol{y}\) and \(\boldsymbol{X}\) How step 1

\[\boldsymbol{y}=\left[\begin{array}{c}2\\3\\5\\6\end{array}\right],\qquad \boldsymbol{X}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4\end{array}\right]\]

Column 1 of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is all 1s. Column 2 holds \(x\).

2

Calculate \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\) How step 2

\[(1,1):\ 1+1+1+1=4\]

\[(1,2)=(2,1):\ 1+2+3+4=10\]

\[(2,2):\ 1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2=1+4+9+16=30\]

\[\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}4&10\\10&30\end{array}\right]\]

**Self-check:** the matrix is symmetric. Entry \((1,1)\) is 4, which is \(n\).

3

Calculate \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\) How step 3

\[\text{entry }1:\ 2+3+5+6=16\]

\[\text{entry }2:\ 1(2)+2(3)+3(5)+4(6)=2+6+15+24=47\]

\[\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}=\left[\begin{array}{c}16\\47\end{array}\right]\]

**Self-check:** entry 1 is \(\sum_iy_i=16\).

4

Make sure that the inverse exists How step 4

\[\det(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})=4(30)-10(10)=120-100=20\neq0\]

Thus, the two columns of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are linearly independent.

5

Find \((\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\) How step 5

For a \(2\times2\) matrix with rows \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\), the inverse is \(\frac{1}{ad-bc}\) times the matrix with rows \((d,-b)\) and \((-c,a)\).

\[(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}=\frac{1}{20}\left[\begin{array}{cc}30&-10\\-10&4\end{array}\right]\]

6

Calculate \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\) How step 5 · Slides p.20

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\frac{1}{20}\left[\begin{array}{c}30(16)-10(47)\\-10(16)+4(47)\end{array}\right]\]

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\frac{1}{20}\left[\begin{array}{c}480-470\\-160+188\end{array}\right]\]

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\frac{1}{20}\left[\begin{array}{c}10\\28\end{array}\right]\]

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\left[\begin{array}{c}\hat\beta_0\\\hat\beta_1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}0.5\\1.4\end{array}\right]\]

**Basis:** Slides p.20 gives \((\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol\beta=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\). Step 4 shows that \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\) has an inverse, so the solution is unique.

7

Put \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) back into the equations Self-check 3

\[\text{row }1:\ 4(0.5)+10(1.4)=2+14=16\]

\[\text{row }2:\ 10(0.5)+30(1.4)=5+42=47\]

**Self-check:** the results 16 and 47 are equal to \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\).

Now calculate the smallest sum of squares \(S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\). The model values are \(0.5+1.4x\). These are 1.9, 3.3, 4.7, 6.1. The differences \(y_i-(\boldsymbol{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})_i\) are 0.1, −0.3, 0.3, −0.1.

\[S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=0.1^2+(-0.3)^2+0.3^2+(-0.1)^2=0.01+0.09+0.09+0.01=0.2\]

Thus, for this data set, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(0.5,\,1.4)^T\) and the smallest sum of squares is \(S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=0.2\). ▲

The figure shows that \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) gives the minimum of \(S\). Only \(\beta_1\) changes. \(\beta_0\) stays at \(\hat\beta_0=0.5\). For this data set, the result is \(S=0.2+30(\beta_1-1.4)^2\), where 30 is \(\sum_ix_i^2\).

[figure]
Figure 3-1. Small data set \(x=1,2,3,4\), \(y=2,3,5,6\). Top: \(S\) has its minimum at \(\beta_1=\hat\beta_1=1.4\). Bottom: the log-likelihood (Section 03.3) has its maximum at the same point.

When \(\beta_1\) moves 0.1 away from \(\hat\beta_1\) on either side, \(S\) increases from 0.2 to \(0.2+30(0.1)^2=0.5\). This shows that \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) gives the minimum of \(S\).

**Why** Slides p.20

The derivation uses two matrix calculus rules from Unit 01. The next two lines state them again.

Rule A: if \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is a constant vector that does not contain \(\boldsymbol{y}\), then \(\dfrac{\partial(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol{y})}{\partial \boldsymbol{y}}=\boldsymbol{a}\).

Rule B: if \(\boldsymbol{A}\) is a symmetric matrix (\(\boldsymbol{A}^T=\boldsymbol{A}\)) that does not contain \(\boldsymbol{y}\), then \(\dfrac{\partial(\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y})}{\partial \boldsymbol{y}}=2\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\).

Here the variable is \(\boldsymbol\beta\), so put \(\boldsymbol\beta\) in place of \(\boldsymbol{y}\) in the rules. The chain first expands \(S(\boldsymbol\beta)\), then takes the derivative.

1

\[S(\boldsymbol\beta)=(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)^T(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\]

2

\[S(\boldsymbol\beta)=(\boldsymbol{y}^T-\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T)(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\]

\((\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)^T=\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\).

3

\[S(\boldsymbol\beta)=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\]

4

\[\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}=(\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y})^T=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\]

\(\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\) is \(1\times1\). The transpose of one number is the same number.

5

\[S(\boldsymbol\beta)=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{y}-2\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\]

This is line 3 of Slides p.20.

6

\[\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta=(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y})^T\boldsymbol\beta\]

Form \(\boldsymbol{a}^T\boldsymbol\beta\) with \(\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\), which does not contain \(\boldsymbol\beta\).

7

\[\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\]

Rule A.

8

\[(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^T=\boldsymbol{X}^T(\boldsymbol{X}^T)^T=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\]

Thus, \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\) is symmetric, and Rule B applies.

9

\[\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\]

Rule B with \(\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\).

10

\[\frac{\partial S(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}=0-2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}+2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\]

\(\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{y}\) does not contain \(\boldsymbol\beta\). Steps 7 and 9 give the other two terms.

11

\[-2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}+2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta=0\]

At the minimum, the derivative is 0.

12

\[2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta=2\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\]

13

\[(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol\beta=\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\]

14

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\]

Multiply on the left by \((\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\). It exists when the columns of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are linearly independent. ∎

You can check step 11 on the example. Use \(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}=(16,47)^T\) and \((\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(16,47)^T\) from step 7 of the example. Then \(-2(16,47)^T+2(16,47)^T=(0,0)^T\).

This section gives the OLS estimate \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\). Section 03.3 starts from the probability model and gets the same formula.

### 03.3 Maximum likelihood Slides p.21–22

This section uses the probability distribution of the model to find the \(\boldsymbol\beta\) that makes the observed data most probable. Slide p.21 builds up p.22 line by line, so p.22 holds all of the content.

**What** Slides p.22

Maximum Likelihood · Lecture 6 · p.22 Under our assumptions, we have: \[\boldsymbol{y}\sim MVN(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})\] \[\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2|\mathbf{Y})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{\frac n2}|\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I}|^{\frac12}}\exp\left\{-\frac12(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)^T(\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I})^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\right\}\] \[\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2|\mathbf{Y})=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log\sigma^2-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)^T(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\] Look familiar?
So \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{MLE}=\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{X})^{-1}\boldsymbol{X}^T\boldsymbol{y}\)
• I.e. MLE=OLS (when all our assumptions hold)

The next lines define each new term in the statement.

\(\mathcal{L}\) is the MVN density with mean \(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol\beta\) and covariance matrix \(\sigma^2\boldsymbol{I}\).

Likelihood \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2|\mathbf{Y})\): put the observed data into the density, and read the result as a function of the parameters \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(\sigma^2\). The bar before \(\mathbf{Y}\) means "the data are given".
